Thank you all for being here. I'm so glad we could all have dinner together today. The lentil stew is almost ready. I was thinking we could start with a little appetizer. What do you all think about bread and cheese to begin? That sounds lovely! You've always been great at bringing us all together, Kerrie. You've really made this house feel like home. I've been thinking about my next project at work and I'm considering applying for a certifiable qualification. I know it'll take up a lot of my free time but I think it could really boost my career prospects. That's a good idea. I had to upskill last year for my role and it was definitely worth it. But don't forget to balance work and life, like you have. How's the move going, by the way? Oh, the move! [laughs] It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. We're still unpacking boxes and looking for the right places for everything. But we got the new fridge last week and it's been a game-changer. It's so much more efficient than our old one. I hope you don't mind if I ask, Vik, have you seen the new episode of 'The Riots'? I thought it was quite good. Yeah, it's been on my to-watch list. Speaking of TV, I think the new series on BBC Sounds is really good. Well done to the team who made it, nice to see local talent shine. Yes, absolutely. And in other news, I heard there's a new health center opening in Peterborough soon. Hopefully that'll improve access to medical care for everyone. That’s fantastic! Medical care can be such a struggle to access sometimes. And on a lighter note, have any of you done any crafts recently? I've been into knitting again, it's so therapeutic. I've been experimenting with baking bread. It's surprisingly challenging to get it right, but so satisfying when it works. And Vik and I have been planning a party for our friends. You guys will be invited, of course. That sounds fun! What’s the theme? I was thinking we could do a DIY decorating party. Bring some old furniture, we'll paint it and give it new life. That’s a great idea! I could bring my new sewing machine and we could recover some older cushions or something.

Hey Mum, did you hear about that new type of car's engine? I read today that it's more efficient and eco-friendly than others. Oh, really? That sounds interesting. Are you still into cars quite a bit? Yeah, it's a hobby of mine. Especially when it comes to new technology in the field. I find it fascinating how far they've come in recent years. It's great to see you're still interested in those things. I used to love listening to your grandfather talk about cars and technology. He was quite something when he was younger. Hahaha, yes! He had quite an old school approach, but I used to love it. He had this old Ford just like the one in his youth. And the places he took us to! I remember we used to drive everywhere. He enjoyed taking us on journeys around the countryside when he had time. Yeah, those were some good times. But, you know, it's interesting to see the shift from print versions of things to digital. I'm still torn about it sometimes though. For me, there's something about holding a book in my hands or reading literary magazines that I can't quite replace with a digital version. Even though I love the convenience of course. Absolutely, I totally agree, there's something special about the feel and smell of a physical book or print piece. But at the same time, I love how easy it is to access information and different formats in digital. It's funny, the other day a colleague was talking about 'The London Review of Books' . She mentioned that despite it now being available online, people still complain about the price of the print version. Right, I've seen that the digital version is actually quite affordable, but they charge a lot for the print, which always seems a bit ridiculous to me. I guess it's about covering costs and value perception. Exactly, it's an interesting business model. While I agree on changing the business model in some ways, there's also value in the actual production of print that sometimes gets overlooked. Plus for us older folk, it's sometimes just easier to just physically hold something, isn't it? Definitely. It reminds me of France though. When we visited for the family vacation last summer, you know, everything almost felt less crowded or less digitally overrun.

Right, so who's got the best holiday story first? We've all had our fair share of shenanigans. I've got a good one from our trip to Mallorca last year. Got so sunburned, I had to peel off like a banana. Still have the picture as a reminder. Oh, haha! You always overdo it when it comes to the sun. I've got a story too, but I think it might be of a slightly different variety... I had an absolutely hilarious time in York with some mates during the Christmas market. I still get a laugh when I think about my silly reindeer antlers. Reindeer antlers, dear? I can already see it - did you dance around the market like you were part of the festive spirit? Ah, yes - oh yes! [chuckles] I might have even boogied a bit with the live music there. [chuckles] York's always got something special, doesn't it? But you guys are nothing compared to the time I got lost in the village near my mum's place during a family holiday. For a moment, I thought I was the only one who knew how to read a map. Everyone else's sense of direction just... vanished! Lost in a village? That sounds more like a comedic sketch to me. [smirks] Well, at least you weren't sunburned for it like me, or dressed up as a reindeer. Oh, can we talk about the really good times? Like when we all went camping and had that epic night with the barbeque and burgers? That was a real holiday success. Oh, that was brilliant! The food and the company - perfect combo. Did anyone challenge one another to do things like a relay race or who could eat the most marshmallows? [laughs] Speaking of eating, did you all remember when we tried to make pasta from scratch on that one holiday and it ended up more like spaghetti sludge? [all chuckle] Haha, yes! That was a disaster. But it was also hilarious. Imagine, all of us sitting there, each trying to take a bite of our creation, only to realize we needed a real chef! And let's not forget those impromptu dance sessions during the coldest nights in the tent. We had music playing on speakers we somehow managed to bring along and just let loose. [laughs] I remember when we decided to have a night of impromptu karaoke.

Ah, I've been reading about this fascinating topic of wild winter camping. I discovered that many people these days consider it an ideal activity for disconnecting from the digital world and reconnecting with nature. What do you all think of this idea? Oh, yes, I’ve heard of it. Both clinical and anecdotal evidence suggest that being in nature can greatly improve our mental health. As a psychotherapist, I have recommended some of my patients to try things like hiking or camping to help reduce anxiety. Winter camping especially offers a calm and peaceful environment, less crowded due to the weather. Absolutely, and from a Scottish perspective, there's nothing quite like waking up in the middle of nowhere with nothing but the sounds of nature around you. I recall one winter camp I went on near Glen Coe - the stillness of the snow-covered landscape was almost surreal. That sounds wonderful. Glen Coe is a breathtakingly beautiful place! But as appealing as it sounds, how does one prepare for such an endeavour? Is it as difficult as it seems or are there some major considerations we should be aware of? It is certainly a challenging activity, especially in winter. You need to plan well in advance - choosing the right gear for the cold is critical. The basics like a sturdy tent, warm sleeping bag, and good clothing are a must. I found that breathable layers are the key. Also, making sure someone knows your itinerary and expected return date can be lifesaving in emergency situations. Good point about safety, Alex [Speaker_3]. It is essential. Besides the gear, you also need to be aware of your physical health. Winter doesn’t come with the same risks as other seasons - the risk of hypothermia or frostbite is much higher. I’ve had patients who have had issues due to poor preparation. Fascinating! And, as a research assistant, I noticed in studies that stress levels tend to decrease when one is immersed in natural environments for extended periods. However, I also understand that some people might find winter camping too extreme. What about that? Isn't there an alternative? An alternative? Well, there’s always ‘camping lite’ - short trips near urban areas, or even just spending a day or two hiking in the nearest hills if you're new to it. I think that could be a great starting point for many of us.

Hey, I'm on my way home from work and I've been thinking about our plans for the weekend. Have you decided what film we want to watch yet? Not really, to be honest. I've been working quite late this week. Still trying to get through this book though, it's fantastic. Why don't we choose one of the new classics? Or even a rare indie film you've been wanting to see? I'm up for that. I've never had a chance to dive into indie films much. But even if it is classics, it has to be something with a strong storyline. I thought you might say that. What about 'Trainspotting' or 'American Beauty'? They're both just fantastic films with strong stories. Oh, 'American Beauty' is a brilliant film! What's new about 'Trainspotting'? I've heard so much about it. Well, Ron Moore, the author of the book, recently released a new book similar to 'Trainspotting'. It's called 'Skagboys'. He talked about what led to the events in 'Trainspotting'. It's quite unusual, but very interesting. I've heard about it. It seems kind of dark, but the 'Trainspotting' book was quite the read. Did you enjoy it? It was a bit intense, but it was gripping. His writing style is so unique, it keeps you engaged. Speaking of intense books, have you ever read 'A Clockwork Orange' by Anthony Burgess? Haven't gotten to that yet. I've seen the film, though. It's quite the movie. Kind of clashes with my kind of upbringing, but it's an interesting take on society and behavior. Exactly! Burgess had this whole concept of violence and choice, and blurred the lines between moral good and bad. It's quite thought provoking. It's one of those films that you can't really sit back and just watch - it forces you to think. Right. Another film that does that is 'Fight Club'. Have you seen that? Yeah! That's a film that stays with you long after you've watched it. The themes of identity and consumerism are still very relevant. Absolutely. Even though it was made back in the '90s, we still grapple with those themes. Definitely. And now our thinking about films has me wonder what we'll cook for dinner this weekend? Want to pick up something new this time instead of just...

Alright, children. Our story theme today is "Fantasy Worlds". You all are going to create your own fantasy worlds using this comprehensive LEGO box. Remember, the more detailed, the better. Oh wow, LEGO! Can I make a castle and a dragon? Yes, Emily, you can make whatever you want as long as there are enough pieces for everyone and it fits within this box. Yes, and I want to make a magical forest. Can you help me, Mum? Of course, I can help. Let's sit down together. Remember to use the different shapes and colours. Unidentified_child: What about magic places from stories or films? Great question. Fantasy worlds can be based on anything - you can even use the setting from your favorite book or movie as inspiration. Ooh, like the Hogwarts Express or the castle from Harry Potter? Exactly. Remember, the most important thing is to have fun while creating. We can draw it on paper first to sketch out our ideas, if that helps. Can we use paint or markers while building? Stickers and markers can be used for decoration, but we can't use paint directly on the LEGO pieces as it might damage them. We can make sure to keep the space clean, however. Can you tell us a story about when you were little and used to play with LEGO? Well, I used to spend hours building different spaceships and finding new ways to make them aerodynamic, even if I just had basic bricks. That sounds like fun! It was. But I also used it as a way to learn about design and engineering. You can use building blocks like LEGO to visualize and understand complex concepts in math or physics. Unidentified_child: You mean like how structures need to be balanced? Exactly. It's a great way to teach balance, stability, and creativity. Can we show our creations later at the Brownie Promise evening? We can show them to the family. You could even talk about what inspired each piece of your fantasy world. Oh! And we can tell why we chose certain colours. And don’t forget, sometimes our thinking changes as we build. That's okay. You can adapt your world as you go along. Unidentified_child: I know! And then maybe you can show us how to make a computer program to move the LEGO pieces? Well, that’s a bit complex for today, but we can talk about coding and how to make simple games in PowerPoint or Excel for moving objects.

Ah, good morning! I hope you're enjoying the brunch. I made your favorite pancakes and freshly squeezed orange juice. Morning! Everything looks lovely. I particularly love the freshness of the orange juice here. It really does make all the difference. Yes, absolutely! Speaking of freshness, I've had an interesting morning already. I got a bunch of junk mail and noticed how much of it is now digital. It's almost strange actually, as I always remember getting envelopes through the letterbox for my mother when I was younger. That's true. You get everything from e-bills, adverts for exercise equipment I have no interest in, to just plain old nonsense. It's changed so much in our lifetime. And just like that, gone are the days of the lovely friendly postman delivering a little village news to your door! And to think, even the deliveries now seem to bypass human touch, except for packages from online shopping, of course! But even those often arrive in a plain brown box. Off topic a bit but yes, it's amazing isn't it? Sometimes I think the world moves too fast. Definitely. It's certainly changed how we engage with each other and interact in daily life. Speaking of engagement, I passed through the city center yesterday. They've got roadworks on the main street again, so it's chaos there. Well, at least it's not a job to tackle. I had enough of roadworks, especially after being an engineer for all these years. But really, chaos is never much of a problem when compared to some of the jobs you face as a teacher! Yes, that's true. The students keep the day interesting. Although, this morning I did get to indulge in one of my favorite pastimes during my commute – reading about medieval sites around Yorkshire. Oh, I always loved those when I was younger! I used to love exploring those deserted medieval villages. There's something hauntingly beautiful about places long abandoned and left to nature. Exactly! It's fascinating to sit on a crumbling wall and just imagine all the history there. I was thinking of taking a trip to one of them soon. Either that or maybe working on my herb garden. I finally found the perfect spot in the back yard to plant some herbs. Herbs are a great hobby. So many uses and it's just rewarding to see something you grew getting used in your own cooking.

Right, I'm going to make sure to grab that paracetamol from the cabinet. The chill from outside is getting to me and I can feel a headache brewing. You should. Better to tackle it early before it worsens. By the way, have you seen the size of those questions on this medication course I'm doing? It's insane! Oh absolutely. I'm still struggling with some of those fractals I had to learn for my graphic design course. Right, let me not get started on those. Tell me about it – After a few hours, my eyes were going batty. Might just need to have a bit of what we had at Carol's on Sunday – her roast dinner was the best we've had all year. Exactly! My portion of that roast beef was just... manna from heaven. Next Christmas, I'm on roast duty. You'd better not mess that up! We're talking about perfect Yorkshire puddings here. Absolutely. And I'm sure we could all do with perfecting the art of making them. Speaking of which, I saw a roasting pan in the catalogue. Do we spend or keep it simple like we always have? Hmm, maybe we should just pull out the old book of recipes for Christmas and stick to what we know, don't you think? I like the idea of keeping it simple, it's the warmth and the company that matters more anyway. Right, and it's not the first time we've done just that, and it always works a treat. Okay, that's settled. Now, another thing – does anyone remember storing those herbal teas I got for us last year? I really need to get into a routine of drinking them. Let me check. I remember I store them in the kitchen cupboard next to the spices. That’s so typical of you, always keeping things organized like that. You could use a lesson from Speak 2 in the organization department. Ah, but you're the one with the skilled hands for turning those fine lines into pictures and graphics, so we balance each other out. True. And that reminds... I was thinking of making a little trip to visit family in Ashford over the New Year. Oh really? Sounds like a great idea! Maybe we can convince her to join us on a little adventure? Sure, why not?

Hey, long time no see. How have you been since we last caught up? Yeah, it's been ages! I've been studying pretty much non-stop, but I've also managed to pick up some part-time work as a survey programmer now, which is actually quite fun. Oh, that's really interesting! I've been totally buried in this new project at my job, but it's been manageable. I've actually been quite proud of myself for meeting all the deadlines. You know, I've actually been watching this series called 'Killing Eve' that you should totally check out. It's about a MI6 agent who gets into this cat-and-mouse game with a female assassin. Oh, I've heard of that. It does sound intriguing though. I've been trying to make time for TV shows since moving to London. It's crazy how much time it takes to get settled into a new city. Completely agree. It's crazy how similar our situations are - it seems like we've both been between worlds in our own right. I still find myself counting the days until I'm finished this grad course. Same here. I often find myself wishing I could just stay in one place, but the work opportunities here in London are too good to pass up. Speaking of which, I saw there's this event by the Thames next weekend, and they're showing some amazing ukulele players from all over the world. That does sound lovely! If I'm free that weekend, we should definitely go. We might see some interesting and talented people there. Absolutely, it'll be great to catch up that way. By the way, did you hear about that policy change in the city’s planning committee? More or less. As a student, I've seen a lot of discussions on it. It seems like it's going to affect a couple of new projects near my flat. From what I gathered, they're changing the zoning laws to accommodate more student housing. I can see why that could be a bit of a hot topic for us. Yep, that's what I've been hearing. I thought it might make the housing market a bit more affordable for students, but then again, it might lead to even more crowded areas and less community green space. Definitely valid points from both sides, isn’t it?

Hey, I've been reading about how regular exercise can help prevent heart disease. Did you know that's one of the main causes of premature death in this country? Yes, I've read that too. It's frightening, really. I think we all just assume we're invincible until we're face to face with it. But even small changes, like getting out for a walk each day, can make a big difference, right? Absolutely. I set a reminder on my phone to remind me to get out and about. Sometimes it's just a 10-minute walk, but it counts. I just need to find the motivation. It's easy in London with all the parks and things to do, but when I was living in Edinburgh, it was harder. What's wrong with Edinburgh? It's beautiful and there's the Meadows, the Botanic Gardens... Yes, but it's quite hilly, so even just walking across the city can be quite strenuous. And it's often cold and windy, or raining. Oh, I see. Well, no excuses here then! The rain might discourage me, but the rest of the time, the parks in Wimbledon are lovely. Speaking of Wimbledon, I saw there were some new houses going up near the Common. They must be very expensive, right? I wouldn't want to buy one there myself, but in terms of investment, maybe. One never knows with the market, but it’s definitely desirable. Yes, doesn’t come cheap. But it’s not just about the location now, it’s the eco-friendly credentials of the build, and all the design... Exactly. The young people looking to buy nowadays are just as interested in greenery and energy efficiency as price tag. And then there's the schools. It's a no-brainer if it's within a good catchment area. You'd think so, but sometimes I wonder. We all make trade-offs. I mean, in this new build I saw, it’s almost like a gated community. And that does bring up a social aspect too. I was in Islington recently and the diversity of the residents there... it was just so different from Wimbledon or maybe even Edinburgh. I think part of that is just the nature of the area. Islington has always been more cosmopolitan. Indeed. But there's another thing that strikes me - the changing social fabric with all these new developments.

Hey there, Sarah! How was your week? Hey, Amelie! It was alright. Just the usual corporate stuff. You? Pretty much the same. You know how it is. I really need to find the time though, the new budget is supposed to come out soon and there's been a lot of uncertainty around it. Yeah, I've heard about that. I mean, I guess as a civil engineer I have different priorities, but it does feel like everything is set for a bit of change, keeps changing backwards and forwards, doesn't it? Definitely, and it's a bit nerve-wracking for sure. Especially with the sector going through some restructuring. You've been thinking about your post grad and career stuff, right? Definitely, but from what I've observed - and maybe it's just hearing from friends - it seems like a lot of the younger people in the field are being left out with all the changes. It's hard to plan ahead, you know? That sounds quite frustrating. It's never easy, especially when the ground keeps shifting under your feet. I'm not really sure what I can do to impact it, but certainly I've been trying to stay updated and see where the changes will most likely affect our team and our activities. That makes sense. For my part, I'm trying to stay positive and flexible. It's a bit of a cliché, but it really does feel like the jobs we're training for are significantly different from what we'll be doing a few years down the line. But that also means we’re probably well-prepared for change, right? I'd like to think so! It's a unique skill set we're developing now. Speaking of change, have you heard much about that Broadway revival of "The Phantom of the Opera"? We were just discussing it the other day - it’s supposed to be fantastic, they’ve matched it really well according to the reviews. Yeah, I’ve heard about that! I actually listened to the soundtrack and it really got me excited. I’ve always loved the music in that show. You aren't one of those people who only listens to musicals when they are  actually  in a musical, are you? Oh, definitely not! It's just the music has got a certain pull, doesn't it? I could listen to "Music of the Night" forever.

Ah, I'm losing my touch with painting. You know, it's been ages. [The sun is setting and he looks around at the half-painted backyard fence.] [Walking over carrying a can of beer] Cheers, mate. Still improving though, innit? That’s one hell of a paint job! Thanks, Phil. But seriously, I'm going about this all wrong. [Lets the brush hang and gazes up at the sky.] [Smirks] Oh, I always say, keeps you active. You get to see the town from a different angle too, seeing all those new developments around. [Glances around the neighborhood] [Chuckles] True that. London’s changing a lot, but so is Liverpool. I noticed when I read that the Northern docks are now part of the Mersey Maritime Museum, that’s going to be huge. [Pauses to scan the environment] [Sips his beer] Yeah, we need that. Gives the city some history and character. [Looks at him] You know, between you and me, next week I’m running a short film course for a group of kids. I'm hoping it might reignite my old passion for acting. Not sure the wife would agree but who knows? [Smirking] Ah, the eternal actor. Never lets go of the dream, do you? Though I must say, it’s better than buying a new taxi every five years. Honestly though, I think it’s good for you to do something outside work, keeps you young at heart. [Laughs] Agreed, mate. Keeps the mind sharp and who knows, maybe it proves useful for tax clients who want to make videos or something. [His eyes gleam with the thought of new possibilities.] [Walks towards him, curious] Tell me more about the film course. What do you plan on teaching? [Proudly] Basically, acting for beginners. We’ll do some scenes, some technical stuff like camera angles and lighting. You know, the fun stuff. It’s a two-week course. [Intrigued] That sounds like fun and very informative. Could be useful for me too, maybe I can get some students interested in drama. [Offers] Hey, if you could spare some time, why not pop over and see how it’s going? We could use an extra pair of hands or, you know, just some moral support. [Smirks] [Smiling] You know I'll be there. You seem to enjoy it and that’s the most important part. Though, I do need to ask, are the practicals already sorted out?

Ah, I love this view. You can really see the beauty of Poland from up here. The sun is setting and painting the sky with such vibrant colors. Oh, yes! I've never seen anything like this. It's like time almost stands still sometimes, isn't it? It kind of is. You think about your daily worries and they all just seem... small, in a way. It makes you appreciate the simpler things, like the way the light filters through trees, or the smell of pine needles. Absolutely. It's like our perspective shifts just by being here, isn't it? Even the little village we're about to drive through, I bet it has its own story. Oh, I suppose we could make up stories about everyone we see. What, like who that couple could be? Are they on a honeymoon? Perhaps parents on a family trip? Or maybe they're just local folks out for a bit of fresh air. And those next couple coming towards us on the path, what about them? Maybe they're hikers planning to camp out for the night? I often meet tourists who are on these amazing journey. Speaking of journeys, we've planned the expenses for this trip pretty well, haven't we? Despite using the campervan, it's been less expensive than I thought. Definitely. The campervan really helps with food and accommodation, which are usually the biggest expenses. And we've been able to get by with part-time work and some savings. I'm so glad we decided to go for it. There's something about clearing all the clutter and just hitting the road that really feels liberating. I know what you mean. The idea of a simpler life appeals to me. Less stuff, more experience, more time with each other... Exactly. And changing the scenery keeps life interesting. I was getting really stuck in a rut before this trip. I'm sure you're not stuck now. You look just as vibrant as this landscape. Besides, it's great to have company. We should almost be at Tarnow by now. Maybe we can look up some social arrangements we want to make, or places we definitely want to eat. Totally. We've heard great things about the local specialties. Someone mentioned there's a fantastic bakery right in the town center. Bread and donuts already sound like the perfect end to the day.

Hey everyone, did you hear about the Hay Festival last year's lineup? I discovered some really amazing authors that I never knew before. Ah yes, I think there was a rumour that JK Rowling might make an appearance. Still, now, the only festival I care about is the Blackpool Illuminations. Going over the years and stays the same, and I love it. It's so much fun with the family. Now that you mention Blackpool, isn't it set for this weekend? We should plan to go. It’s something fun for the kids, right? And we could try those new shops you spoke about in the town centre. What do you say, everyone? Yeah, that would be fun! Maybe we could also catch some theatre before we hit the shops. There’s a play by Anthony Horowitz we could look at. And since you have such great taste in books, Dad, pick the best bookstore in Blackpool, as if you didn’t know already. Right! And while we’re on the subject of literary events, did you hear that their next landmark book or author announcement might be at the next festival? I keep missing on the updates, but it sounds like it could be promising. You’re always on top of the literary news, Speaker_2. It’s quite impressive. Speaking of updates, let’s also not forget the upcoming train strikes. Have we got a backup plan for travel if they confirm dates for when we’re planning to go to Blackpool? I've been trying to stay on top of it too, but I couldn’t find anything confirmed yet. But maybe we should plan to leave a bit earlier or check ahead if it’s happening over the weekend. Perhaps we could use public transport until the last leg if it’s feasible. But the problem is that usually side roads get jammed up as well when people try to avoid the railways. Good points. Speaking of inconveniences, did any of you hear about the Queen's health? Last I checked it was stable but... Yeah, that sure threw things off for the Platinum Jubilee plans, didn’t it? It did. Imagine having to celebrate such a monumental anniversary when the whole world is so uncertain. Reminds me of how we celebrated my last exam week. [laughs] Exams, eh? I remember those well. It’s like planning a whole moving process - so many things to pack, unpack, and then deal with the unexpected.

Ah, I'm so glad you could all come without notice. It's wonderful to see you. Now, isn't that just like my surprise visit? Always catching everyone off guard. You really know how to turn up without warning, Mother, but that's exactly why we love you! Yeah, and it's always a fun day! But why have I dragged you out today, eh? Besides coming to see my old self... We've been discussing sorting out this place a bit. Yes, Mum. Your home. It's been a subject of conversation for a while now. And with technology as it is, I suppose we could make use of some of those new-fangled gadgets to make the process easier, perhaps. Exactly, we were thinking there might be some apps or tools that could help us sort and organize. Make it feel less daunting, you know? Apps for decluttering? That sounds like something I could get on board with! Now, now, I'm not calling anything "clutter." Just a bit of... tidying up. But yes, technology can be a great help. We were also talking about the importance of not making it too stressful for you, Mother. We know you've had some mental health concerns, especially after your mother passed away. Yes, and all the changes since then have been a bit of a challenge. But doesn't mean I'm not up for a bit of the old "spring clean." You're incredibly brave, Grandma. I know it's hard, but you're doing the right thing by sorting things out. Plus, I bet we'll find all sorts of little gems and funny things to remember when we do! That's the spirit! I suppose you're right. This is about letting go, but also holding on to memories. Exactly. And we're here to help you every step of the way. Either physically or just for support. Can we start with my room? It's a bit of a disaster zone and I’ve been meaning to sort it out... but this way, you won't have to tell me to do it! Alright then, your room it is. But remember, this needs to be your decision too. I don't want to overstep. That’s a thoughtful consideration, Mother. We can all decide together which areas to tackle first and share the workload. Great!

Right, so here's what I've been up to since I've been back from university. I've started working more with clients, and it feels good to be applying what I learned in the real world. Mostly, I've been working with social media for brands. That's great! Social media work can be quite demanding. Do you find it challenging to keep up with the latest trends and algorithms? Yeah, it's a right juggling act, innit? But I find it fascinating how it all works behind the scenes. You know, like understanding how content performs differently on each platform. I'm a bit lazy with social media. I mostly just scroll through my feeds and occasionally like something. But I do enjoy your stories when I see them. How's the work-life balance been? Ah, that's another story! [laughs] Sometimes it's like I never switch off, but it's rewarding when you see a campaign take off. It also keeps me very current with the digital world, which is useful. Speaking of current, how do you handle the maintenance of your tech? I find it tiresome. Oh, I've become pretty handy with it. I even got a new laptop for work, which has been a game-changer. But of course, there are always the niggles – updates, drivers, things like that. [looks at the new laptop] [interested] Oi, that's a right whiz-bang machine you've got in your hands, mate! What makes it tick? What's the processor like? What's the spec? It's a 13-inch MacBook Pro with an 8th-gen Intel Core i5, 16GB RAM, and 512GB SSD. It's really responsive. But I just had to try it out, so I tried to install a few retro games. Do you lot remember those days when we used to play all-night LAN sessions? [chuckles] Oh, definitely. While you were dealing with the modern byte, I was on my own LANs, struggling to connect to my mate's Wi-Fi because his router would always phantom drop for no reason. That takes me back. I thought I was clever when I managed to set up my own router at home. [laughs] Yeah, but this new laptop just makes all the tasks so much quicker and smoother. Yeah, but with all this talk of computers and retro tech, are we missing out on the world outside?

Ah, I love this bistro. It has such an inviting ambiance. Makes me feel like I’ve been transported back to London but with the added quaint charm of this little town. What are your thoughts? I really like it too. Especially now, after this pandemic. It's nice to see questions back open and feeling like society isn’t crumbling. But speaking of crumbles, have you noticed the situation with our elderly relatives? It’s been tough for them with everything closed. Oh, absolutely! My grandmother keeps coming up with new reasons to stay home due to her mobility issues. She feels so isolated. It really makes me sad. Exactly. It's like we've been fed this narrative about staying away to save lives, but then we're forgetting the mental health part of the equation. I feel like we've lost a year of our lives. Exactly! My dad, he's always been into his garden. But now, even that therapy seems distant. He says it's hard to focus or even want to get dressed in the morning. Sometimes I'm worried that those next couple of years, especially now that he's semi-retired, will just slip away from him. I understand the sentiment. I've noticed it too, in the communities I work with. People are genuinely struggling with the shift. Especially those who were already battling with their own demons, let alone societal ones. Right. Honestly, as someone who’s been laid off for a while, it’s been really hard to keep myself motivated. Some days, I feel like I’m losing my identity. Like when I don’t have a job or a purpose, it’s like I’m the elephant that’s always hidden but never discussed. Except, in my case, it’s been rather in-your-face. It’s strange, isn’t it? We put so much of our identity into our employment. Especially since our societal structure sort of expects that from us. But personally, teaching English to foreign students really saved me during the lockdowns. Because, no matter the location, learning a language is essential, and so is the human interaction it brings. I suppose that's true for me with teaching too. Teaching gives me a structure, something so much needed. It’s one of the few things that helps me not to sink completely. Did you have to adjust your teaching methods during this period?

Hey everyone, did you hear about the Dorset Steam Fair's upcoming event? They're announcing their 2023 schedule soon and I'm thinking of going. It sounds like a fun escape from daily routine. Hi Emma, isn't the fair just lovely? I haven’t been in years but heard rumors there might be some new attractions this year. It would make a nice day out for you, sweetie! Oh yes, and I bet there'll be plenty of traditional fair food. But have you managed to get tickets yet, or would you like us to help with that? I could check online to see if they're available. Thanks, Sue. I have looked online but it wasn’t very clear when and how to buy tickets. Do you think we should just buy in advance from their website or can we do it on the day? Perhaps it's better to buy them in advance, just to avoid any potential disappointment. But maybe it depends on your plans? What are your thoughts on the possible dates, Emma? I’m a bit flexible. But I suppose I’m more interested in going on a weekend. I saw they’re planning to have a busy weekend with multiple activities. How about you all, are you up for going together? It would be lovely to go as a group, wouldn't it? It can make it much more fun for all of us, especially for you, Ron, to see the trains and things. And for the rest of us, it can be nice to take a break and enjoy some good company. That sounds like a good idea. But it's also important we consider how we can make it accessible for everyone. Do you know about the facilities for visitors with disabilities over there? I did find some information on their website a few months ago, but it’s always good to double-check since things can change. From what I remember, there were ramps and accessible toilets, but maybe it’s best to call ahead and make sure. Yes, making sure they’re accessible is key. I’ll give them a quick ring before we make any plans final. It’s always important to check, especially for us. Wise, indeed. And have you all noticed the property prices around here? It's quite astounding how the market has changed. Over in Bournemouth, it's all the more noticeable.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up today. It's been ages. How have you all been? You're all doing such well, it's wonderful to see. Speaker_2 and Speaker_4, I need to compliment you both–I read your most recent articles and they were fantastic! Really thought-provoking. Oh, thank you! But truly, I think the credit lies with my student, Speaker_3. He has such a passion for theological debates, and I couldn't help but share some of his insights. It was nice to see him get excited about something outside of school too. Yeah, actually. I've been thinking a lot about Twitter lately. Technology and these platforms can be really powerful for spreading ideas. But then again, I saw this really rude tweet about the UK weather and just wondered if we can't mix both passion and respect even in how we share our complaints. Exactly, Speaker_3! It's all about balance, as much as anything creative. I wrote a piece the other day on the rise of artisan businesses in Yorkshire and it did well because it was positive and showed respect for the people behind the craft. But it's hard, isn't it, when we see such negativity online. I couldn't agree more. You know, I attended a concert the other night at the church here in Thirsk. It was a real mixture of performances, really varied, but all the speakers were so respectful and uplifting. But then, of course, as soon as I got onto social media to share it, I saw someone suggesting that the venues for such events should be more modern. It’s all about empathy and understanding, I think. Speaking of things that are important to the local community, the recent events have really brought us together. It's been touching to see all the support for those in need. As a teacher, it's wonderful to see my students being so involved and compassionate. Do you think schools are doing enough to teach about this sort of thing, though? It's one thing to learn about empathy in class but quite another to see it changing the world. Speaking of schools, my exams are coming up soon… I'm a bit stressed about that. You know, I often think that we need to look at past events and how they've shaped us to understand the future better.

So Grace, today we're talking about all those dentist appointments and hearing tests you're having to deal with. Yeah, it’s so annoying! Why do I have to have hearing tests every year? So doesn’t that mean that you weren’t the center of the universe that day?! Oh, indeed. You think one day was me enough, but nope, it had to be us both. That sounds quite big for me. It’s okay. We’ll make sure it’s fine for you. And you can always talk to me about anything that feels too much. Plus, I’ve heard the Easter chocolate part of the trip also includes a DIY chocolate-making workshop. Chocolate?! That’s a win. See, all part of the fun, Grover. But Ashaad loves science and tech, so something related to those could be a hit. Ooh, I like that. Can I help with the clues or something? Definitely. You can help brainstorm ideas and even help make some of the clues if they’re simple enough for you. We can all work on it together.

Hey, I'm so glad we could finally hang out after all these weeks. How's everything going with work and what's new with you? It's great to see you too! Work's been pretty busy, you know how it goes. Still trying to get into the groove after a pretty intense month. I'm actually kind of tired today, but a lovely chat with my best friend makes everything better. I know, I'm right there with you. Work never really gets easier, does it? But it's always better when you can share it with a friend. Definitely, and actually, you know what I've been thinking about? Since we had to postpone that pub trip from last Easter, we should just plan it this year. Oh, actually, I was just thinking the same thing. And let’s make it a bit special this time. Maybe we can book a whole table, get some food in advance if they allow it, and just... relax. After the past year, we really need it. Exactly. And maybe invite a few more friends, keep it small and manageable. But yeah, I’m really up for that. Definitely. I’ve been meaning to look into prices again too. And while we're at it, have you seen mum and dad at all recently? They're fine, still carrying on their usual. Mum's been insisting on getting us to drop by for dinner more often, especially after your mother decided to start her own little baking business. She's making all sorts of delicious treats and they are really good. I saw that on Facebook! I wish I could get my hands on those scones now. Speaking of food, have you heard from Emily? She was thinking of starting a cooking class online. She definitely was. She’s been a bit busy, but I'm sure she’s still experimenting with that idea. Yeah, I think she's really passionate about it and it would be great to support her. We could even use her class as a party theme, or a meetup somewhere. Brilliant idea! Let’s keep that in mind. Speaking of ideas, I’ve actually been considering a small pet for the flat. Maybe something like a cat. Oh, I'd love to have a pet. But do you think we're ready, though? They're a big responsibility.

Ah, I had a lovely glass of wine while listening to's anecdote about those lectures all at sea. Really, teaching oral surgery and sailing at the same time sounds like quite an adventure! Yes, it seems to have been quite the experience! Speaking of adventures, did you hear about the Prague trip they're now offering for the bargain price of £200? I've heard about it, actually. Now, Prague isn't just about the price, it's also about how even when it's fully booked, they still managed to get us in. Old NHS connections, I reckon! Though today's perks don't quite compare. Though, let me tell you, even then, there were times when we managed some really nice little advantages. Like that time I got to sail with the crew to a dental convention. That does sound incredible. We used to be so envious of your NHS perks, the sailing trips, and those ‘lectures at sea’. Well, now those kinds of perks are much harder to come by, I’m afraid. In fact, it reminded me, I’ve been considering buying a property in the countryside. There's this quaint way of doing it in France. You don't even need to meet at the notary to close the deal; you can simply sign at home and send it through the post! That's quite unique! How does one even start in France regarding property? Oh, it’s much simpler than you'd think and they've got a system down pat. Essentially, you would first choose a property and then your French real estate agent would handle much of the administrative part including inspections, negotiations, and such. The final signing usually occurs at the property itself or the agent's office in France, but there are options for notarised remote signings as well if you can't be there in person. Yes, that's right. And it's not just technical; it's a very changing landscape. Speaking of changing landscapes, have we talked enough about how our local town has changed? I mean, some of us remember when this used to be full of character but it's been losing its soul so much in recent years. You know, I completely agree. I could go on about how much I miss the old café just over the street. We used to meet there every Saturday.

Hey, I've been thinking. What if we create an educational online platform that uses case studies of moving images to teach communication strategies and social relationships? That’s a fascinating idea! Case studies are great for teaching complex social interactions and communication skills. It’s like, the viewers can learn through seeing real life examples, right? Exactly! I mean, people learn through stories. Fiction, real life, whatever it may be, we often learn more about ourselves and our relationships through storytelling. And moving images are more digestible than texts, at least for many. You can tell a complex story in a shorter amount of time. Plus, with engaging visuals, it keeps viewers interested. Absolutely. But let’s think about execution. How would we source the material? Would we need to create original content or can we curate existing case studies? Curating existing content could be a good starting point. There are plenty of documentaries and case studies already out there. Plus, there are educational institutions and archives that could provide material if we reached out to them. Great point! And on the creation side, we could start by targeting common scenarios and common issues people face when communicating, like conflict resolution or empathy-building. And while the 'case studies' label makes it sound more formal and substantial, even simple things like, you know, a chef teaching a young cook or a team leader teaching a new team member can be helpful scenarios. That’s exactly the sort of thing! We could include really relatable situations that people from all walks of life can understand and learn from. So, we’d develop real-life examples, break them down into digestible modules that can be studied, and include interactive elements like quizzes, discussions, or even virtual ‘workshops’ or group analysis? Yeah, that’s the direction I was heading with it. The learning materials could range from short videos to more in-depth analysis or even game-like activities that help practice the skills taught. Because a key benefit of interactive elements like games or virtual workshops would be that people can practice and apply what they learn more effectively. Plus, it encourages feedback and peer-to-peer learning, which is powerful. And let's not forget about the educational uses of it! Teachers would love a versatile tool like this for their classroom. We could potentially offer tailored content for different age groups or for people working in specific fields where communication is crucial.

I keep thinking of Rachel and her trip to Cornwall. I'd almost forgotten how much she loves the sea. Yeah, the stories she used to tell us about long beach walks with her family back in the day are still the best, aren't they? It's infectious how much she loves being by the sea and connects it to those happy childhood memories. Absolutely! I remember she once said, "To me, the sea isn't just about the water and the waves; it's about how it makes me feel. It's a reminder of freedom, of possibilities, of seeing the world from a different perspective." Exactly. She's always been like that - deeply thinking about her experiences and trying to understand why certain places or things affect her in certain ways. It's part of why she's such a good psychologist, isn't it? Indeed, it's one of the reasons she was so passionate about studying behavioral therapy. But, you know, it's interesting how the sea holds such deep personal meaning for many people, isn't it? Yes, it's universal. I think it's because it represents both change and constancy at the same time. It's always moving, always changing, yet it's always there. That's a good way of putting it. I remember when we met - we were both in the same graduate program, and we'd often take breaks at the local beach near the campus. I think those moments, idly watching the sea while we gossiped about our lectures, helped us bond. I recall that! And now, whenever we're facing a tough day, it's the sea we think of. Going for a walk along the coast, just clearing our heads, reconnecting with something bigger than the stress or worries of daily life. I just wish we could do that right now. Instead, we're just window shopping for another city or town to visit by the sea. Because a walk around the block just won't cut it, would it? Haha! But seriously, maybe soon, we should plan a weekend trip. There's a lovely coastal village a few hours away... Oh, yes, please! And maybe we could take a small boat trip? Rachel was telling us how liberated she felt after kayaking in the sea once. As if I needed any more convincing! Do you remember how she got stuck on a rock once and had to swim further?

Who knew I'd spend my Sunday educating my friends on fashion while we watch this. [The group is watching a London Fashion Week live stream on TV] Oh, definitely unreal! [Looking at Speaker_1] Is that a new coat you've got? Yeah, isn't it grand? I just got it last month and it's become my go-to. [Eagerly] And, it's absolutely bang on trend this season right? Erm, yeah, it’s “coat-dress keeps coming back into fashion, isn’t it? [Confused] I swear I saw those on the runways. [Chuckles] I’ve been following this from London trends. [Gets up to get a glass of water] Actually, when I was studying my teaching postgrad, we had this whole module on fashion for the youth. That's really cool! [Looking interestedly at the TV] They should’ve a segment on the show where they walk us through making those outfits at home… Like, style hacks and that. [Smiling] That’s it. But yes, maybe a YouTube series or something we could follow together. [Eyebrows up] Oh, that’s a plan! Meeting idea just formed. [All three exchange a look and nod] Definitely! Maybe over Zoom or any of the apps for fashion meetups? [Slightly hesitating] Yeah, maybe. How about we discuss next week over a coffee or dinner?

Hey Mum, did you finish reading that book you've been talking about? I'd really like to hear more about it. Oh, talked about it enough already, I thought. You know I love that one! But yes, I finished it and thoroughly enjoyed it, though I did have a bit of a fear of finishing it. You know how it is when books become part of your life for a while! I know that feeling. I had the same fear with 'The Hunger Games' when I finished it. Are you still interested in photography? We could try taking some pictures together some time, if you're not lazy like last time... Actually, it's been... interesting. We got a new manager last week and she's been pushing for a lot of changes. Some of them make sense, but others I'm still trying to wrap my head around. I’m more of a creature of habit, so it's taking some time adjusting. But enough about me, tell me more about college. I heard the assignments have been quite challenging? Oh, totally! It's not like last year at all. But honestly, it's teaching me so much, even though I sometimes feel overwhelmed. We've been discussing things like the importance of different lenses and how they really change the photo, you know? That’s great! I remember when I first started in photography myself, it was a hell of a learning curve. But you're doing really well. And who's your favorite photographer now? Right now, I really like Ansel Adams. The way he captures light and the blurred backgrounds, it's just so appealing to me. But also, his story about perseverance even when things weren’t easy, it's really inspiring. I knew I could count on you to pick someone interesting. Reminds me of a bit of that comedian we saw last month. You know, she talked about fears in her stand-up, how they're often just exaggerated thoughts we give power to. Maybe we should consider that when it comes to our photography fears and even the new changes at work. Yeah, maybe. But sometimes it's hard to see things from outside when you're really close to it.

Ah, good day to you both. Lovely to see you. I was just getting into the garden when you arrived. The sunlight was lovely today, don't you think? Indeed, it was a lovely day today. I almost forgot it was sunny until I stepped outside! But speaking of gardens, have you seen those baby birds in the nest across the road? Ah, yes! I have. I think there are five chicks in there. I've been keeping an eye on it for a few days now. They seem to be growing fast. That's fascinating, isn't it? Even with my years of teaching, I still find the process of birth and growth so intriguing. Reminds me of the time I spent making 3D prints for the kids at school. They were amazed by how something can go from a flat piece of plastic to a fully-formed object. 3D printing, eh? That was a bit out of your expertise, wasn't it? But it was great seeing the kids' faces light up. Now, onto something entirely different - have you heard any news or gossip on the gang at Fortham Football this season? Not much to be honest. But the last report I read said they're planning on strengthening the defense. Their shabby workmanship in that area has cost them points before, you know? Indeed, good defense is key in football. Though I'd take a good offense over anything, to be fair. Like Arsenal in their heydey - they had both! That's right, they did! But speaking of workmanship, I've had a few issues with some renovations in my house. The new roof installed last month has already started leaking, and if I'm honest, the quality of work is terrible. I just had the same problem recently with a builder. The job was supposed to be finished months ago, but it's still not right. It's frustrating, really. There must be laws against such shoddy work. It might be worth complaining to the local council's building regulations office. They can help ensure the standard of work meets certain criteria. Either way, it's good you're taking action. I plan to. It might be worth checking if you need any documentation or evidence. Just to cover all the bases. I remember when I was complaining about a faulty washing machine and they asked for the receipt and everything.

Ah, I'm so glad we could find some time to catch up. I've been meaning to reach out to you about something that's causing quite a bit of upheaval at home. Of course, dear sister. You know you're always welcome to share any burdens with me – or joys, for that matter. What seems to be weighing on your mind? Well, my situation with our daughter has become quite complicated. She's been living abroad with her husband for years, but he's found a job here in Brighton, and she's decided they should relocate. Oh, that's actually quite a change. I can imagine it must be a mix of emotions for both of you – excitement from getting your child closer, but also the upheaval of adjusting to a new life together in retirement. Exactly. I do want to see her more regularly and have her here where I can watch her children grow, but at the same time, it's also a bit overwhelming thinking about the changes this will bring to our quiet life here. And it's not just about us, it's what's best for her and her family. I can see why it would be quite challenging. But it's also heartening to think of the opportunity to strengthen family ties again. Yes, it is good in many ways. However, we've never lived with family under one roof since she was a teenager, so this will take some adjustment for both us and them. It sounds like an opportunity for new shared experiences, but I also understand that it can be quite an adjustment. We might have to think about some practical arrangements to make sure everyone feels comfortable and has enough space. That's exactly what we're discussing. She's offered to contribute to household expenses, which is very kind of her, but we still have to figure out logistics. Like, will they need to rent their own place separately or are they comfortable with our living situation? It could be useful to have an open discussion with her about what she thinks would work best. Perhaps she's also thinking about shared spaces versus independence. It might be a good idea to consider all these options together. That's a great point. It’s something we need to discuss as a family. I suppose one of the biggest concerns for me is not to overstep and have them feel like they're intruding.

Ah, good day, John. I hope you've been keeping well. I brought today's newspaper, quite a piece on the upcoming Scottish referendum. Thought it might be talked about at our seminar next month. Hi there, Mike. A nod and a hello! Yes, I’ve been keeping an eye on that situation. It’s quite the controversy, isn’t it? I suppose this is one of those moments history is being made. Absolutely. I had a lecture on politics and diplomacy yesterday, and we even touched on it briefly. The complexity is quite overwhelming, especially for my students who are seeing this first hand. I can imagine. I was going through some old notes last week in preparation for my politics class and it’s astonishing to see how things have changed. But back in my day, it wasn’t as politicized as it seems to be now. Exactly, and it makes it a bit more challenging to teach as sometimes you need to remain neutral. But, I must say, these kinds of events make for great discussions in class. I agree. I’ve even drawn some parallels with the Brexit situation this year. One side view it as a positive move towards independence, while the other sees it as a grave mistake. Makes you think. Exactly. It’s all about perspective and the lens through which you view these events. Speaking of lenses, have you had a chance to interview your potential replacement for the history department yet? I heard about the vacancy. Ah, yes, I have. One candidate stood out quite strongly, a young fellow from Edinburgh. Seems very passionate about Scottish history and political science doesn’t come secondary to that. That’s promising. How was the interview process? Quite smooth, surprisingly. He’s done his research well, and his enthusiasm is a breath of fresh air. The only tricky part was discussing job terms and salary, but he was quite open to negotiations. Of course, that's always the part nobody enjoys. Naturally. It's always a bit of a balancing act, isn’t it? I was on a job interview for a seminar position in London not too long ago and it felt like a real test of my patience as much as my knowledge! Haha, quite the experience, isn’t it? Patience and knowledge go hand in hand in those situations. Absolutely. Did you bring anything else along?

Everybody gather around and listen to this story I recently read from an online forum. It's about a British family who moved to the States and encountered some bizarre customs. Go on, tell us more. I love hearing about the oddities of other cultures. Yeah, do tell. I've always been curious about how the British manage in the USA, especially the food habits and idioms! I can already imagine the look on someone's face when they try to order “a cup of tea” and get a big fizzy drink instead. Oh, that's actually quite funny. I remember a story from when I worked abroad, in New York, where I had to explain what “full English breakfast” is to a group of bewildered American colleagues. Oh, oh! My personal favorite tale is about a British couple who took their kids to an American diner for the first time. The kids were so excited to get breakfast and ordered pancakes, but when they were served with maple syrup, they thought it was jam. They ate the pancakes with jam and both parents wanted to hide under the table! That sounds like something right out of a sitcom! The Americans assumed jam while the kids misunderstood. That’s so classic! I wonder if American children really eat that early in the morning. Here, we usually keep it to cereal and toast. Yeah, and then there’s the whole concept of “football”… I mean, they call it “soccer.” We have to be careful not to get our sports mixed up. True, and the pronunciation! I always struggle with “tomato” and “aunt” and “water.” The ‘t’ in tomato and water sounds just so strange to an American ear. The accent really throws them off! I once tried to order a “bacon butty” and they were confused about what I meant by “butty”. Speaking of confusing things, we also use different vocabulary for things like “lift” instead of “elevator”. And American measurements! All these cups and ounces instead of metric units. It must be so confusing for an outsider. Did anyone else encounter issues with household appliances? Like, most American kitchens use gas ovens and range tops, and we're used to electric. Yes, and don’t even get me started on the central heating systems! In the States, it’s more about individual units in each room, while here in Britain, we expect a radiator in every room.

Oh, did I find bargains or what? I've brought home so many cool new things from that street market today. Ah, you've really indulged. I've just picked up this collection on modern Chinese literature for our upcoming lecture series. Yeah, but look at these . This blouse was only 100 yuan and it's gorgeous! And these sandals, they fit perfectly and they were a steal at 150. Well, I guess there's no arguing with that. You've got an eye for a good deal. It's a bit more expensive, but the quality is amazing and they even have these traditional Chinese styles that are perfect for when we invite guests. So, you were shopping specifically for work then? Both for work and for our social life here. These are kind of formal, while the rest is more relaxed. I figure if we're at university events, we should look the part, right? And at home, we can be comfortable. I agree, looking appropriate does show respect for our hosts. And isn't it fascinating how the traditional styles are influencing contemporary designs too? I read an article about that earlier today and found it quite interesting. Yes, the fusion is beautiful. There's something about the detailed work and the choice of materials that speaks to both traditional craftsmanship and modern sensibilities. I hope to integrate some of that into a lecture or two. That would be fantastic. I can see students really enjoying that. Speaking of which, have you noticed how much cultural ins and outs you've picked up here in just a short while? You're even getting into the language a little. I'm sure in comparison to local speakers I still sound rough, but yes, it's so much fun. Every time I go shopping or even just to a café, it's like a little lesson in culture and language. The vendors are always so patient and helpful, teaching me little things. Just like how they patiently deal with my attempts at ordering food. It's amazing how our thinking changes, though. I mean, when we first came here, I must admit I was a bit skeptical about the marketplaces... overcrowded, maybe a little chaotic.

Ah, I'm going to bed soon, so first things first. To recap today's rugby match, was it good? I was a bit late to the party due to IT chaos at work but I did manage to catch some of it. Yeah, it was brilliant, Dad! Ireland played fantastic. Especially when Brian O’Driscoll gave that one heck of a hit. But wait, what chaos did you get into at work? You never tell me about the tech troubles. Speaker_1 : Oh, just the usual. keeps coming up with new ways to test our patience. You'll learn all about it when you're older and in my shoes. [Interrupting with a pint of beer in hand] Well, let’s not go there too much. Speaking of brilliant, did anyone actually sign Oisin’s birthday card yet? He’s going to bed soon and we haven’t even written a single word yet. Oh dear, I've got it right here. Let me just finish this sentence... [pauses, takes a swig of beer]. "May you always soar high and never ever watch any more rugby till you're 12? Maybe?" Speaker_1 and #2: [Both chuckling simultaneously] Grandma! The kid is still coming up with excuses about sports at school. Today he said he was going to try out for the rugby team, but apparently, they still have some "diagonal running" to learn first. [Giggling] Ah, the silly things kids say. Oisin really is sporty at heart, even if he’s a bit dramatic about his 'diagonal running'! Yeah, but seriously, the team plays great rugby in that school. I went to one of their matches last year. The kids were so enthusiastic it was infectious. Yeah, I’ve been seeing that a lot in school. More kids are joining sports teams. Maybe since the new sports facilities were rebuilt. Yes, that's a great development. There was a time when sports were a bit of a luxury. Nowadays, there are more opportunities. I must say, it's heartwarming to see such enthusiasm from the young ones. Absolutely. Now, about tonight... we promised to do some stargazing later if the weather permits. We can show Oisin the stars. Did anyone check if the sky will cooperate? [Glancing at her phone] Not yet, but I’ll check it out. Hopefully, the clouds will part by then. That would be so cool! I've never really seen many stars where I live in Bristol.

Hey Lucy, did you hear about James and Emily?? They's had their first baby today. Congratulations to them! Oh wow, I talked to her last week, and she did mention they're expecting anytime soon! That's so exciting. Yes, absolutely! So questions for you then: have you thought about starting a family soon? Honestly, I have thought about it, but right now, I'm really focused on my career. Besides, it feels like a big step! How about you? You're at a different stage of your life and your career, right? Well, I'm lucky in that my parents were very supportive, despite me being the only child. But let me tell you, even then, I had the feeling that there was something missing from my childhood. Ah, I see your point. I imagine having a sibling or a child would be quite different from what you experienced. Definitely. But it's interesting to hear different people's points of view. Some people love being the only child, and some love the camaraderie. Now that I'm a language research co-ordinator, I find it fascinating how these familial dynamics differ across cultures and even languages. That's really interesting. Speaking of languages, how’s that new Italian course going? It's going well. But honestly, it's been a real challenge balancing studies and work. I'm always trying to learn more about phonetics and different dialects in Britain, as part of my job, you know. That sounds interesting and useful. I also have to work on my foreign languages skills for work. I deal with international clients sometimes, so knowing a few languages could be helpful. Right! I often think about the different career paths we could have taken, based on the languages we know. I feel a bit lucky to be able to use my bilingual skills in my role. It's quite handy, really. There was a time when I thought about studying languages further, but then my job here at Cambridge opened up, and I grabbed it. Nowadays, I often wish I could dedicate more time to learning languages. Us linguists are always trying to learn more! There's something satisfying about figuring out a new grammar rule or understanding a new dialect. Totally. Even just the day-to-day use of language is fascinating. I realised recently I started using words that came from certain dialects more frequently since I've been working with people from different regions.

Right, so everyone's seen the photos of my first guitar's passport. I brought it back from a trip to Spain. It's a beautiful thing, don't you think? Right, really indispensable for a language instructor now, is it, a Spanish guitar? Exactly! I'm thinking of taking some lessons now, learn some proper chords and stuff. I've never had much to do with guitars myself. But I've got a keepsake from my grandfather, a medieval board game. You'd think it's useless, but actually really fun. Oh, board games! I used to play Risk with my mates all the time when I was a bit younger. Do any of you read online about strategies or stuff? Actually, that might be a good idea. I've heard you can watch videos about improving your game on YouTube. I'm more of a player than a strategy typer. As long as it’s fun, that’s all I need. Speaking of fun, I just saw this documentary on mixed martial arts last week. Absolutely fascinating the training and dedication involved. Yeah, it's impressive. I tried learning Taekwondo once, wasn’t my thing really, but it’s interesting to see how it’s evolved. I'd take gardening over martial arts any day. There’s a different kind of satisfaction, really therapeutic. I'm all about that. Smelling that fresh soil, fixing broken plants doesn’t come close to beating it. Well, that kind of makes you all horticulturists in your own right. I won't say no to that. I've actually started growing tobacco. It’s surprisingly easy to care for. Tobacco? That's quite a venture. You know, there’s a linguistic aspect to all these hobbies. Think about how gardening can be seen as a language in itself, right? All the technical terms, the timing, the care for plants like they're children of sorts That's an interesting point. Yeah, I suppose there’s a real technique to getting the best out of things. Just like learning languages, it’s got its own system. Exactly! I remember when I was just learning to paint, it felt like I had to learn a whole new language. Different brush strokes, techniques, etc. And also, there are specific terms in gardening that might not even be in English. You'll come across words from Latin, how it reflects our understanding and classification across languages Speaking of languages, I've been teaching at this summer camp where the curriculum includes functional English for living and working in the UK.

Hey, I'm going to make pasta for dinner, can I ask you something while I cook? Of course, go ahead. So, I noticed you've been working from home more often since the pandemic and I also work from home, but I haven’t seen many savings in fuel and car costs despite driving less. Do you have any tips? Hmmm, actually, that's a brilliant topic considering our conversation earlier about why I never drive to work. Really? What was that about? Well, you know how I started this new job, and I realized the train fare is cheaper compared to parking fees and fuel, so I decided to stick with that. That's smart, but what about when you need to drive, say for errands or trips? Well, that's true. I actually realized that most of the time, I only drive when necessary. Otherwise, I just order online or use public transport for longer trips. That makes sense. I guess for us, who don’t work within driving distance, it's more about general car costs and occasional long trips. Exactly. I’ve also started looking into car sharing or carpooling with friends for those rare occasions. It’s good for the environment and our wallets. I hadn't thought of car sharing. That's a great idea. Yeah, it’s something we should consider. It could be more efficient for us both, considering we’re probably in a similar situation. Absolutely. Plus, it’s a good opportunity to save and maybe even enjoy some company. Definitely. I’ve also been using apps to compare fuel prices around my area. You’d be surprised at the difference it makes just choosing the right station. Oh, wow, another money saver. Apps can really be helpful in these situations. Exactly. And changing the car’s maintenance schedule can save too. Regular servicing helps maintain fuel efficiency. I hadn’t thought about that. I will make sure to schedule my next service soon. And have you ever thought of an electric or hybrid car? They can be expensive upfront, but you save a lot in the long run. I’ve looked into those, and I agree, they are quite pricey. Totally. But thinking ahead, it might be a good investment. There are also government incentives for electric vehicles. That’s true. I've seen those ads. But honestly, I just want to get a better deal on the type of car I have now.

Ah, good morning everyone! Lovely to see you all's here. Grace, today's the big GCSE results day isn’t it? Hopefully they've done well, wouldn’t want the tea trolley to be out but be needin' a stiff drink to steady the nerves now, would we, Linda? Aye, just ginger ale for me and Fred then! Grandma, I'm pretty sure they actually want champagne, not ginger ale! Well, keeps yer spirits up alongside a nice cup o' tea, I always say! True, Fred! Idle minds, and all that. So, shall we get settled then? I've made up a bit of a spread - sandwiches, scones, that sort of thing. Great, thanks! I could do with a snack after all that revision. Well, if I’m honest, I was more involved in the local lads' cricket club than in studies. Times were different; the war had its own rules for us, you see. That's very true, Fred. The war really tore up the rule book, especially for your generation. But it's remarkable how things really have changed since then. 'E's right. I don't think anyone understands properly unless they lived it. It was hard for us all, different ways. Yes, I can imagine. Could we perhaps speak to the plumber today and sort it out? You aren't stuck for a day of it, are you? I'll ring him today, if it's alright. Gives us something to do while waiting for the results. Speaking of results, does anyone know when the schools actually let go? Last I heard, it's being emailed or something? I think it's 4 PM across the board. But yeah, email and then maybe calls if everything's gone well. Good... because we don't want to be fumbling around like we're not sure what's what. I can just see us, watching the clock and then the door across the hallway! Oh, I can totally see that! Maybe we can have everyone come over for a little celebration once we know the news, eh?

Who knew pirates and Shakespeare had so much in common, besides being things we enjoyed learning about in school? I talked about pirates in the playground and made everyone say "Arrr!" all the time! Did you know, though, that Shakespeare himself wrote about pirates in "The Tempest"? That's right! And that makes us even more excited to go to Stratford next week. Oh, can we actually meet real pirates? Well, seeing the circus workshop in a real circus will be quite an adventure. Maybe we’ll see some very fancy pirate costumes in action. Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up tonight. It's been ages. You know, I was thinking about when I was teaching in Saudi Arabia... Yes, that sounds interesting! I was part of a small expat group and we found these hidden pubs where we'd meet and enjoy a pint. It was quite the adventure in itself, trying not to get caught.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up here. It's been ages. How have your respective schools and work situations been going, Speakers 2 and 3? Did you hear that truffle talk from Jevica last night? I don't know much about these culinary rarities, but she sounded excited. Oh yes! Truffles are quite the luxury item, aren't they? A bit of a passion hobby of hers. I wish I could dabble in those things, but my hands are tied with births and babies all day. What, like the mushroom thing? They're highly prized in high-end cuisine for the unique, earthy flavor they add. But it's not just the mushrooms themselves, the hunt, the art of finding them—it's a whole culture. Almost like wine tasting, but for truffles. For me, it's the stories that fascinate me most, how people from all over come together to hunt truffles. Reminds me of when I travelled to America. They don't have the same truffle culture over there, do they? No, not really. But the food culture in general is so different, especially in certain parts of the country. Their passion for really good burgers is unmatched, though, I'll give them that. Burgers! I've always wondered what real American burgers taste like. Well, when we get into the true British food discussions... Let’s just say, burgers are not a traditional part of our culinary skills. We've had our fair share of culinary knocks, but the world keeps learning from each other. It’s one of the beautiful things about our world today, that we can share so much across cultures. Absolutely. Speaking of sharing, I heard there's this new show on about chefs competing for the best truffle dishes. Have any of you caught it? Not me, I've had enough drama with pregnancies and labour to seek out cooking shows for entertainment. Yeah, but I heard about it. Someone at school was talking about it. I might ask her to borrow it or... Remember to be careful with those borrowings, they can lead to late nights and early mornings if not managed well. Speaking of watching things, are we going to catch the youth football game at the next service stop? I hadn’t considered that. Bolton Wanderers could use some family support. Though, it would be tough to stream live from here.

Ah, I'm so glad we could find a spot to grab lunch. I'm Sarah by the way, language research co-ordinator at the press. Right, so we should be at James' place in about thirty minutes. I hope today's road conditions are better than yesterday's. We encountered quite a bit of fog on the way to the campsite.
