There's a mix of both, but for 'like new' and 'new with tags' items, you might want to look on there, too. Though, sometimes people just don't describe things well, so you have to use your judgement. Oh, right. I remember you found those mugs with all the maths jokes from the 90s there. And they were only like five pounds each! Yes! But it proves the point - the item might say 'like new', but sometimes it has a bit of wear. Always check the photos and questions the seller if you're unsure. Got it! And, what about the community aspect? Do people on eBay chat to each other or leave feedback? Absolutely! The feedback system and the ability to browse through a seller's past transactions is brilliant. It builds trust and helps you make informed decisions. I see. Plus, I can see people's reviews on Amazon and see if it's what they promised. But I guess it's not always easy if you're buying rare or used stuff. It's about balance. Both platforms have their strengths and weaknesses. For 'known brand', new stuff, Amazon is often great and you know what you're getting. For more unique or second-hand items, eBay can be a treasure trove, but you've just got to be a bit more careful.

Ah, good morning! How was your week? Busy. It’s always busy when you’re in control of production lines. But it’s rewarding. You’re right. There’s a lot to be said for feeling like you’ve accomplished something. I miss that part of life. You do a lot for the family and the community. That’s very fulfilling too. Thank you, of course, I do what I can. But it’s very different from my old life... Right. I remember when... I mean before we had all this technology. Like when we started ordering groceries online, that was a big change! Yes! And let’s not forget about those phone calls when we had to read out the numbers! And the internet! It’s amazing how fast it’s all changed. The world has moved so quickly, hasn’t it? Sometimes I wish it would slow down a bit. I know what you mean. But it’s progress, isn't it? I mean, as much as it is a change from what we used to know and love, it brings plenty of benefits. I’m sure it does. I just worry sometimes for the younger generation. You know, with all the social media and so on. It’s not always the best influence. That’s true. But at the same time, it’s also bringing people together, connecting people across the globe... Communication is never a bad thing. Although I do wish they would concentrate more on actual conversation. All these texts and doesn’t anyone actually talk anymore? Fair point. But it’s also expanded our vocabulary, introduced new ways of thinking and expression... I suppose so. It’s just... it’s different. I miss the simplicity of a good old phone call or a letter. Letters will always be special, but times are changing. We just need to adapt, but also keep some traditions alive too. Indeed. It’s a balance, isn’t it? Change versus maintaining the past. I suppose that’s what life is about: finding that balance. Exactly. And speaking of balance, we should probably get some lunch ordered or started. Good idea. What’s everyone in the mood for? We could try something new or we could do a classic family meal. What do you think? Either would be good. But maybe something that everyone likes. Like that pasta recipe you like?

Hey everyone, so what are we all thinking of doing for Christmas this year? Got any solid plans? Oh, I've been meaning to tell you all. I'm actually going to try flying out to see my relatives in Australia. It's just, the thought of spending Christmas day traveling isn't very appealing but they'd kill me if I didn't make an effort. That sounds quite adventurous! I've never spent Christmas day actually flying before. I'd be absolutely terrified of missing it for my family though... So how are you sorting out all the food for the trip? Yeah, actually. Food is probably my biggest concern for the flight. You know, they don’t have pub grub in Australia. Just kidding, just trying to make light of it. You can always pack your own snacks! Or maybe even bring some British treats to share with your Aussie relatives. It's all about balance, right? Yeah, and also, how are you planning on dealing with the time difference? Flying across the globe can be quite stressful. I've been looking into that. I was thinking maybe a quick nap on the flight would help me adjust. Also, planning to arrive early so I can get some rest before the fun begins. Actually, while we're on the subject of traveling over Christmas, have you all heard about the chap who apparently hit a deer with his car on the motorway? He decided to cook it as 'Christmas dinner'. Quite, uh, unconventional! [laughs] Now that is quite the story. Shows there are no rules for Christmas celebrations! Though I don't think I'd ever suggest that. I've heard of roadkill being eaten before, but to make it Christmas dinner? That's just... different. More like "first-world problems"! I mean, hitting a deer is a serious business and probably not something to celebrate, but still, it's quite a quirky anecdote. True, but you have to admit, the idea of having unexpected roadkill for dinner would be a party starter of a story – if that were some kind of skill or tradition for you. [laughs] As long as it's not me who has to prepare it! I’ll stick to good old Aussie barista stuff... but this is quite the conversation. Maybe I should stick to less extreme Christmas dinner plans. Yeah. Speaking of which, any of you wanting to change your plans and get something more traditional?

Hey lads, I've been thinking - who else besides me can't help but slip into their local twang when around others from their hometown? That’s actually quite common, isn’t it? I still can’t quite shake off my occasional London intonation, especially when talking about specific places or events back there. Yeah, it’s kind of embarrassing sometimes. But I get it completely. It happens to me too, and I'm right here, surrounded by you two. It’s always funny how it emerges, especially when we’re in our local context, right? Like we’re all auto-pilot when it comes to accents with our mates or family. Totally. And then there’s the car talk, right? Oh, good one! Speaking of which, Anthony - do you think we should take your old Nissan on this trip or look at renting something? It’s a bit of a journey, after all. Make it the Nissan, it’s reliable and we’ve done long trips in it before. Plus, it's mine, so no renting or sharing issues. Unless any of you have a better argument, that is? Well, if we're keeping the Nissan, has anyone noticed the paint job still holding up? Last time I checked, the weather had gotten at it a bit. Yeah, but the car itself is solid. And honestly, if we're all fine with it, it’s probably the most cost-efficient option. Plus, it’s got character, really - which is something you don’t always get with a rental. Plus, it’s like my baby. Or would that make it my... Nissanjou the giant? Only you would try and make that connection, Anthony. But seriously, let’s consider the less fun side of things: fuel efficiency, insurance, and the fact that we're carrying a good amount of luggage for a few days. Valid points, but we can deal with all that. There’s always fuel efficiency to factor in but changing cars now would just add unnecessary stress and time. True. I’ll just make sure to give it a good clean and prep before we set off. We’re good on insurance as long as all drivers on the policy have the necessary driving credentials, right? I think so. We can double-check if you want. Let’s just do that. And in the meantime, anyone have a preference for the route?

Hey guys, did you hear about that new Avril Lavigne album? I discovered today that she's actually been involved in the process and it sounds really different. Yeah, I've heard that but I need to check out her Instagram to see the actual sneak-previews. You know, sometimes they do some questions and answers kind of thing. I'd totally hit that if she was offering them out, but honestly I'm more excited about the new Arctic Monkeys album. I read somewhere that it's very political and it sounds like it's keeps coming backwards and forwards with how it makes you feel. Yeah, I fucking love Arctic Monkeys. But isn't Idles the best thing right now for political music? They're so powerful, just like the sound is. Idles? Nah, mate. I'm more into the old-school stuff, like Radiohead or even Muse. But I get you, they're pretty into politics as well aren't they? True, but Idles is something different, you know? They're raw and intense. It's like listening to a really intense therapy session at times. For me, it's all about the moment you're in and how the music makes you feel. Like the physics of sound waves and how they make your heart race. Yeah, that’s a cool way to think about it, man. Like music can alter your brain chemistry or something. Exactly! It's pretty spiritual in a way. There's this theory that in ancient Greece, Pythagoras proposed that certain melodies could even heal the body. And that’s pretty legit in a way. That's wild! I never knew about the Pythagorean theory of healing music. Is that like psychoacoustics or something? Yeah, that’s one of the early forms of that concept. I tried to learn more about it for a project last year and found it really interesting. It's all about how sound waves interact with our brain and body. Totally! I read somewhere online that sound waves can even change the shape of water molecules or something. That's crazy! But what about film scores, have you guys heard about the new score for that new sci-fi movie? It's supposed to be real intense and has got all these layers. No, what movie? It’s like...oh what’s it called? "The Quantum Odyssey"—it’s supposed to be like a mix between "Interstellar" and “Inception”.

Hey everyone, did you hear about Luke's latest achievement in his Balanceability class? He's nearly mastered all those balancing tricks! That sounds amazing! I must say, Luke has shown great commitment. Is this something you really like, kiddo? Yeah! I love it! Especially when we pretend we're on roller coasters or jumping off those big blocks. I can just imagine! But actually, it's impressive how Balanceability helps with so many other life skills. It teaches you how to overcome challenges and focus. Remember when you both were struggling with those tightrope exercises, but with a bit of determination, you both nailed them? Yes, it was a bit scary at first, like trying to succeed at something you're not sure you can do. But when you finally get it - oh, the sense of accomplishment is amazing! Totally! It's like being on top of the man-made waterfall next to the swimming pool in the park. Knowing you can do something you thought was impossible. Exactly! And those kinds of feelings or learning experiences translate to other areas, like facing assessments at school. It's all about setting goals and believing you can achieve them. Speaking of assessments, I know it can feel scary, but if you learn to approach them the way you approach the Balanceability challenges, like focusing on one step at a time... Aha! Or, like building a really tricky LEGO set! If you focus on one part at a time, you get it done! That's a terrific comparison, Isaac! It really is about breaking down big things into manageable parts. And the sense of pride when you complete them - whether it's balancing or building or tackling a tricky subject at school. You know, it also makes me think about our homeschooling situation. It's a bit like balancing - we find what works for us, what challenges us, but we also need to make sure we're moving forward steadily. Absolutely, though I appreciate the structured environment of formal schooling, homeschooling allows for flexibility and a tailored approach. But, as you said, it's all about balance and making sure we're covering the right ground. Speaking of balancing, have either of you mentioned anything interesting about school to me lately? Yeah! Our school friend's house is being renovated and it now has a swimming pool with a man-made waterfall!

Right, so I'm trying out this new exercise routine from's online. I've been meaning to shake up my workout for ages, and it sounds pretty good. It talked about this 'Tabata' method. You do 20 seconds of really intense training, then 10 seconds of rest. Rinse and repeat for four minutes. Sounds intense but intriguing isn't it? What kind of workouts do you do, by the way? Oh right, the Tabata. I've heard of it too. They recommend it for both cardio and strength training. I’m actually a bit lazy when it comes to exercise but I try to stay active with walking. I’ve been walking to work for the past year and I’ve really noticed a difference in my energy levels. That's excellent. It's good you're staying active in a way that works for you. I tried jogging a few times but I just can’t seem to stick with it. It’s okay, we all have our preferences. I’m big on consistency over intensity. And it seems like it’s working for you, what with those consistent energy levels. For me, it's finding a routine and sticking to it no matter how small it is. I’ve been diligently doing this Tabata twice a week for a month now. It's tough but I feel a lot better after. It’s like the saying goes, 'Small changes can lead to big differences'. Plus, you said 'consistently', which is key. It’s easy to overdo it and then burn out. Definitely. And with work, family stuff, it’s hard to balance everything… I can imagine that. As a production controller, my work has also been on the go since...the pandemic began. More reason for those tiny exercises. Plus, I feel more focused and less stressed afterward. If it helps, that's all that matters. So, what about your relationships? There’s a lot of talk about boundaries and changing expectations after everything that happened last year. Oh, that’s a big conversation. I’ve been in a new relationship since November and it’s been…interesting. We both want different things at the moment, if that makes sense. Different things like what? Stability versus adventure, you know? I want to take things slow but he’s more into, 'let’s just enjoy now and see what happens'.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together for's pizza. I never tire of these weekly Domino drives. It's become such a highlight of our week, wouldn't you say, Chris? Yeah! It's always so nice chatting and just eating pizza together, Auntie Sue. It feels like we're kind of like a real family sometimes. That means a lot to hear. I've always thought you remind me very much of... I'd almost say... your dad. Which reminds me! Did you finish that Easter book for him? You promised me. You'll need it to send, you know. Oh yeah! I've just had a bit of a busy week. But yes, I've nearly finished painting it up. I'll get it to you by the weekend, promise. That's my boy! And how's school been? Anything exciting planned? I remember when I was your age, I thought school was the most boring thing, but you seem to have managed to keep it interesting. Well, between the lessons, I've been getting into a bit of a cricket club with some of the other kids. It's been pretty fun. That's good fun, that is. I used to play cricket when I was in school. Though at our age, we were hauling crates, not bats! Honestly, I feel like we all have our silly things we get into at different ages. But you never stop, do you, Uncle John? And what about those log hauls? I've been meaning to come see that. Oh, that? Well, it's part of the job, you know. But I must say, I've been thinking of getting into something a bit different. Perhaps start my own business, do a bit more with livestock locally. That sounds exciting, Uncle John! Like what, animal sanctuaries or something? Not sanctuaries, no. More along the lines of local cattle sales – make that worthwhile for the farmers around here. Been doing some market research, just exploring. That's ambitious! You know, we could help you with that. You know, network, and all that. Yeah, I'd value the advice. We could all do with looking to the future, no matter what our age. Though sometimes, thinking about the future, I just wish I could go back to your age and live it all over again, Chris. Don't worry, Uncle John!

Make sure to grab that tea. I need a proper cuppa while we chat. Absolutely. I've got Earl Grey. Do you prefer that or something less strong? I love Earl Grey! Thanks for thinking of me. By the way, have you seen that new pub on questions road? They've got the best homemade ale I've ever tasted. Ah, that sounds great! I haven't made it there yet, but I've heard great things. Speaking of inns and pubs, have you ever been to The Black Horse in Sunderland? Oh, yes! That was one of my favorite pubs growing up. The best fish and chips you'd find anywhere. Perfect! I love proper pub food. And the best of all, the portions are huge. My brother and I would often go there after football matches. It's amazing how much you can eat when you're 18 and football-thirsty. Sounds good. I couldn't compete with you at that age, though. Maybe not. But it was great fun. Also, when you’re out at different pubs, have you noticed how prices vary for vegetarian dishes? Yeah, that’s a pet peeve of mine. It really shouldn’t cost more to leave out the meat, should it? Honestly, I feel the same. There’s one pub near here that does a really good veggie burger for around the same price as a meat option. That’s fairer. I wish more places were like that. Makes the choice to go vegetarian more appealing. Absolutely, and if more people are choosing veggie, maybe less meat would be produced, which in the long run could also lower prices. Right! It's also better for the environment. Plus, there are so many delicious vegetarian dishes out there. True, and changing the menu to include more vegetable-based options would also mean fresher choices. Exactly! It's like for celebrity chefs, they make veggies look so fancy and delicious. And it's surprising how many celebrities have actually gone vegan or vegetarian. Did you know that Leo Dicaprio and Beyonce are vegan? And Ellen DeGeneres became vegan and even released a vegan cookbook. Yeah, and even more funny thinking about, Paul McCartney's driving force for veganism is due to his love for animals. It’s true! And don’t forget that purely from a culinary perspective, vegan and vegetarian dishes can bring such variety into the menu.

Whoever thought that a weekend in Hereford would turn into a battle of wits. Articulate is proving more challenging than I thought. You lot thought you could just pick this up off the shelf and play? Especially when some of us have had way too many glasses of cider and the pronunciation of words starts getting tricky! But isn't that the fun of it? Teaching us all to articulate better? And here we are, coming from different parts of Wales and still finding our common ground over words! True, but I've just had to redefine what 'articulate' actually means. It’s like speaking a different language sometimes. Cheers to that! I’m not going to lie, it's been a while since we’ve all sat down and played a game like this. It’s brought back some nice memories, though. You know, I think the hardest part is coming up with a category that has multiple options so we can keep it interesting and not get stuck on one word all game. I’ve got an idea. Why don’t we each think of a category and roll to see who gets to be the first judge? It can add some extra excitement to the game. I love it! And maybe we could also add a rule for each round? Like, the first round is all about Welsh words, and the next can be about words from different parts of England or something. Oh, that could be a game changer. I don’t think I know many words in the different Welsh dialects. Well, that’s exactly why we’re playing! To learn. And to remember we’re all here to have fun, not just to win. I think changing the categories and having a fun rule each round might keep things interesting and prevent it from becoming too competitive. What do you all think? Sounds like a plan. Plus, it allows everyone to participate more equally, especially if we have a word we’re not 100% sure about and still want to use. You know, this reminds me of game nights growing up. The rules were always a bit flexible, and it was all about laughter and thinking creatively. That’s the spirit! Okay, so we’re doing Welsh words for the first round, and for the first rule, no dictionaries or phones. We have to go from memory.

Who'd like to start with the educating? I'd be happy. As an historian, I've always loved how the mechanics of a card game mirror old systems of governance and hierarchy. You've got your kingdom , your court , even a bartering system . That's fascinating! Speaking of trading, have you guys noticed how often card games reveal character traits? Like how some of us are quite the... I'd say, 'strategist for peace', always trying to keeps things fair and agreeable. [chuckles] Yes, exactly! Even lazy contestants can come up with some clever verbal tactics to avoid having to pick up the cards in certain games. It’s like they have negotiation degrees wrapped up as mere strategy. [laughs] Well, let’s hope negotiation doesn’t become our primary strategy tonight. It's been so long since we've all gathered like this, for a game, just for the fun of it. What game should we play? And who’s going to explain the rules to Speaker_3's friend, their first time here? For a new player, something simple would be best. Perhaps 'Old Maid' or 'Snap'. They're pretty self-explanatory and great for getting the 'feel' of playing cards. Perfect, let's go with Old Maid. It's light-hearted and allows plenty of banter while still being challenging enough to keep everyone engaged. And before we start, can someone explain why we're playing at a holiday cottage in Hereford instead of, say, in Cardiff? Just a small query from the tourism department… [smiling] We decided to switch it up this year, give everyone a bit of countryside fresh air. And let the boys or less boys who just got back try their hand at a few real games. Speaking of fresh air, did everyone notice the lovely view from the window by the fireplace? It's supposed to be perfect for a card game. While you’re dealing, the natural environment adds a certain... tranquility to the whole experience. I couldn’t agree more. [pauses for a moment, smiles broadly] Actually, this reminds me of a funny story. Last time we played cards like this, my daughter, 5 at the time, decided she was the 'bank'. She took all the chips and just held them in her tiny hands asking 'Do you have 5 pounds for a biscuit?'. Classic holiday cottage moment. [laughs] That's priceless.

Hey everyone, did you hear about that new sci-fi series on Netflix? I started watching it yesterday and it's super cool! The characters' journey through different dimensions is really interesting. Oh right! I've been really lazy with my TV time lately, but I saw a preview of that. Is it worth watching? It's pretty good, but I'm still getting into "Powers" - that's the best show I've seen in ages! Actually, I've set a new goal for this month to watch as much as possible. Been meaning to watch Game of Thrones but I've been so busy with work. [laughs] I’m sure you've got your work cut out with that one, even if you're not as busy as Speaker_4! Yeah, [Speaker_4], your job sounds pretty cool actually. Does it involve going into action scenes or is it mostly office work? It's a mix, actually. Right now, I'm mostly working in engineering and design. Sometimes it's desk work, but sometimes we have simulations or tests that are pretty action-packed. Wow, that must be exciting. I’ve always thought being an engineer would be super neat, but the path to get there can seem intimidating. I also really liked the idea of being an engineer, but when I did vocational work at school, it just didn’t feel right for me. Now, I’m thinking more about doing an apprenticeship as an accountant. It seems practical and the benefits are great. Me too! I’m considering different university courses related to that, but the thought of deciding the next 3-4 years of my life is kind of terrifying. Did any of you apply to universities yet? Yeah, I’ve been going through a list of potential courses. The idea of moving so far from home is also getting to me. It’s exciting but quite daunting. I’ve been thinking about moving to London for uni. It's closer to my preferred course options, but accommodation and lifestyle changes are a bit concerning. Have you looked at student loans or bursaries? That might help with worries about money. Definitely worth considering. Besides, the experience of being away from home could be really valuable. It’s like Speaker_5 said – consider all your options carefully, including apprenticeships or part-time work. They can be very rewarding. You guys are all so organized.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together tonight. It's been ages. You know, I was thinking about going for a stroll out after dinner. It's supposed to be a beautiful evening. You two want to join me? Oh, yes, that sounds lovely! We could use some fresh air. Going for a walk and maybe pick something up from the market if we get the chance. Can I come too? Walking is so nice... keeps me active, you know. Of course, sweetheart, you're coming with us. We'll keep it at a slow pace, and I can even lend you a walking stick if you need one. You really shouldn't need a stick, though. You're still as spry as a squirrel. Oh, I appreciate the sentiment! But sometimes... you know, the creaks and groans of an old body. Well, let's stick together, then. We'll take it easy and this way, we can all see how lovely your estate is. I'm sure it's beautiful. Though, I must say, I prefer seeing the countryside on two wheels. Ah, you're quite the cyclist, aren't you? Yeah, there's something about the wind in your hair and the world passing by that I adore. And there’s always that slight fear of losing control... doesn’t come with walking. Well, I’m more of a walker myself. But cycling can be thrilling. Especially the way you get into nature without worrying about any potholes or uneven roads, as one does when walking. If you think about it, both walks and cycles have their own unique charm. Cycling and driving offer you a bit more control and changing scenery quickly. While walking, especially in places like this, helps you connect with nature a bit more deeply. I suppose it's all about perspective. And timing. I've heard tell that Cambridge has some of the best cycling routes. Oh, indeed. There’s this path right along the river that's just beautiful. We could all do that another time. If you girls are up for it. I’d love that. I’d love to join you for that walk. That sounds like a plan already made. We’ll just have to pick a better weather day for that. Don’t worry, we are quite flexible. I've got all day to suit your plans.

Ah, I'm so glad we could find a corner to chat. I'm just getting into the swing of things at Alumni Day and it feels great to meet new people. Absolutely. It's lovely to catch up with graduates and other academics, isn't it? I'm actually part of the language research team back home. Really? That sounds fascinating. I'm a Language Research Co-ordinator from Aylesbury, actually. We've been doing some fascinating work on local dialects in rural England. Have you come across any unusual ones in your work? Oh, we've had our fair share of unusual dialects in our research as well. I recall a project on Cockney rhyming slang. But honestly, I think the most interesting dialects for me are the ones that are in danger of being lost. Like the ones from old mining communities, for instance. Lovely to meet both of you. I couldn't help but overhear your discussion on dialects. As a University Lecturer in Linguistics, this sort of thing is right up my alley. I've had the pleasure of researching the development of dialects in the UK, particularly focusing on the differences between north and south, as well as regional variations in Wales and Scotland. Ah, yes. Wales is quite remarkable in that respect. Especially the linguistic influence of the Welsh language on English in the north. Ah, the Welsh language is fascinating. A unique Celtic language, unlike anything else in the UK. I've been trying to learn a bit myself, but it's quite complex! Absolutely! But worth the effort. Have you ever thought of visiting the Basque country in Spain for its language? It's quite isolated and maintains a unique linguistic lineage. Fascinating suggestion. Indeed, the Basque language - Euskara - is one of the most fascinating examples of a language isolate in Europe. Its origins and structure are largely still a mystery to linguists today. Really? That's quite intriguing. I've also been interested in languages from other parts of the world. I've studied a bit of Mandarin Chinese. It’s so different from the way we structure language in the West. Oh, China is definitely an area of interest for me too. The history of Chinese characters is such a rich topic and so different from our alphabet. And yet, so eloquent in its own way. Yes. I recently read an article about how certain dialects in China are shedding some of their unique linguistic features due to the central government’s emphasis on Standard Mandarin.

Hey everyone, great to see you all again! It's been ages. I brought some photos from our trip to Scotland last year. Ah, lovely! I love seeing pictures. You two been doing much traveling? Yeah, we haven’t really gone anywhere new since the grandkids moved to America. We’ve been pretty busy with them and settling them in out there. I know, I heard of that. Now, have any of you seen the Facebook updates about the “ice bucket challenge” keeps coming up? Oh yes! I think I saw one from Sarah Williams. It’s hilarious, isn’t it? It is in a way. It’s also raising a lot of awareness for ALS. That’s the point - and making people donate as well. Exactly! My mom did it and even donated some too. My work got involved with a charity last year. We ran a marathon and raised thousands. It was so fulfilling. That’s brilliant. What was the charity? It was for local children’s hospitals. The different departments in the practice got together and funneled all our fundraising. That’s good to hear. Speaking of charities, I saw there’s an event in the town center soon for the animal shelter. Oh, I'd love to take part in something like that. Yeah, it’s fantastic for the community and all those lovely animals. Let’s make a plan to attend that together. It’ll be good for everyone. Everyone: Yeah, that sounds like a plan! That reminds me. Did I tell you, I’ve been thinking a lot about the project for the local history club? What is it this time? We’re looking at the local dialect of Bedford over the past 100 years. It’s fascinating, really. Definitely. I’ve noticed how much the way people speak has changed here over just my lifetime. That’s true. And now with so much of the younger generation picking up more Americanisms and all... Yes, but it’s also interesting to see the older words and phrases being used by those who’ve stayed local. And don’t forget those silly jokes we used to tell, always ending with “for company.” Everyone laughs. Anyway, I’m glad we’re keeping the local dialect alive however we can. Why don’t we start recording some of those old sayings? It could be a fun project for the club.

Ah, I'm losing patience. This coffee machine was supposed to make life easier but today it's just adding stress. You would think at my age I've had enough years of coffee-making experience but this modern contraption has me stumped. Just push the button, love! That's all this kind of machine requires. Come on, Mother, it's not socialism yet where machines make the coffee for you! Oh, Phil! You're keeps coming backwards and forwards with your jokes. I guess, technology isn't always our friend, is it? No, it's just that we like things to be straightforward. I had the same problem trying to set up my PC last week. I suppose organization and moving have always been a challenge. On that note, did either of you happen to check out the removal and storage costs yet? Oh, bless you for bringing it up. I was just thinking about it and wondering how much it's going to cost. The estimates are coming back higher than expected. I've been looking into it. It's not the actual move that's the issue but all the packing and storage that's driving up the cost. Storing everything over the winter is going to break the bank if we're not careful. Perhaps we should consider a bit more sorting out first? I know it's hard to part with old things but in our case, really old things that probably won’t be used again. We might achieve better storage and moving costs through a bit of decluttering. Well, there's the rub. I do feel a bit sentimental about a lot of our possessions, and if I'm honest, the decision of what to keep or let go is quite difficult. I hear you. It's hard to let go, especially when there are so many memories attached. We've been doing it in phases. While moving, I've also been going through my old transcripts and notes. Some of the technology I used to work on in the oil industry is now outdated. It’s actually quite therapeutic and cost-effective to let go of some of that stuff. Reminds me of zero-obligation waste, a policy that could apply to more areas of life. That makes sense. There's something to the idea of being free from burdens beyond just things we physically own.

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without the kids this time. It's so chaotic during the school holidays. How are you holding up with all the work you have? [laughs] You know, it's been a whirlwind, but I am enjoying the company – at least when I can get it without interruption! [laughs] That's my situation right now. I've been teaching language right up to Christmas, and I'm just looking forward to a break. The kids always make things more interesting, but sometimes a calm coffee is just what I need. You know, I've started reflecting on our Christmas plans. [pauses for a sip of coffee] We did Easter with your family just last year, didn't we? Yes, that was lovely! We had a lovely time, and the kids enjoyed seeing their cousins and everything. I was thinking maybe we could replicate that. Since it worked so well last time, might be a good idea to do Christmas in Totnes again. How about it? I love that idea! Totnes has such a nice, cozy atmosphere during Christmas. It would be so lovely to have everyone together again. Plus, the kids would love the fun activities and all the festivities. Exactly! And I was thinking, we could even make it a bit more special this time. Maybe hire out the little hall down at the Totnes Museum for Santa's arrival? We could set it up ourselves – olden days in Britain, all that. Your expertise could come in handy here, couldn't it? And we could make it a family project. [laughs] True, I could use that TEFL background to come up with some fun language games and activities for the kids. Maybe even have the older ones join in to help with the festivities. Perfect idea. I was thinking along those lines. Your family skills are still so impressive. Organizing Santa's arrival would be no problem with you around. And we should also make sure we'll have time for adults to relax and chat. Definitely, that’s what I would want. Maybe we could also set up a few family game nights in the lead-up to Christmas. That always brings everyone together and is so much fun. [smiling] Sounds like a plan to me. And speaking of family, how's everyone else doing? Any news from your brother or sister?

Alright, everyone, what did I miss while I was'sitting on these gods today?;) Oh, you know, just the usual talked about whether Bobby's snoring has indeed improved since he started that yoga thing. That’s one for the books, isn’t it? Going from "night time freight train" to "whisper of the forest"? But actually, has anyone tried out those new Richmond sausages they’ve got at Waterfields? I keeps coming across them on social media, they look delicious. Yeah, actually. I tried one at the pub the other day, just had a pint. It was alright, but then again, all sausages are good with a pint. But I was thinking we should actually go sample them properly next week. I’m in. Pick your date. But while we talk about food, did I ever tell you about this one time my grandma caught me trying to use a handkerchief? Oh for the love… I’m sorry, it just seems quite formal to carry a handkerchief around… True. Where did you get that from? Was it one of those posh sets your mum got you? It was a bit of a disaster actually. Grandma was mortified. Said I looked like I'd walked right out of Downton Abbey. Oh, bless. I never had one of those, but all those stories of stuff from "back in my day" always sound like they come from a different world. Yeah, like using handkerchiefs… or not snoring. More like "wasn’t a handbag, was a satchel". Grandma used to say whenever we ended up arguing over what’s "proper" and what's just old-fashioned. I think the key to not being old-fashioned is realizing when traditions can be… updated. Like, sure. Updating traditions or just adding a bit of irony to them. Still, I mean, have you all heard about that sausage business in town? Yes, the Richmond ones. That's what we're talking about. Clearly, I need to catch up. Do they sell sausages to take home too? Absolutely. I’ve seen that they have their own little butcher’s shop where you can pick up fresh sausages. Definitely worth a try. I can’t believe we haven’t all just gone there yet. I mean, if it sounds good online and everyone’s talking about it, it must be worth a look, right? Might do, but honestly, after sitting here for so long at the pub, all I can think about is getting back to my bed before I end up snoring back here!

Hey Dad, how was your weekend? Did you get a chance to watch that match today? I missed it but heard it was intense. Ah, yes! The match was unreal! Made my weekend. We won by quite a bit too. Still, though, the other team wasn't bad – gave us a run for our money. I knew it! I'm going to have to catch up on it later. What did you end up doing other than watching the match? Well, for most of it, I was out in the garden, putting in those new bushes you helped me pick out last week. You know how I like my garden to look tip-top! I remember. You've been looking forward to that for ages. How is it looking now? Well, it's coming along nicely. They're already starting to take shape. I have to say though, the weeds were quite a challenge this time of year. Gardens can be a lot of work, but the results are rewarding, I suppose. Speaking of which, how's the business side of things? Been any deals or issues recently? Ah, it's always something, isn't it? One of the farmers I work with is having some trouble with the harvest this year due to the weather. But we're managing ok; just a lot of extra planning and communication, really. Well, at least you're always prepared for emergencies. I'd take that over the usual, you know? Speaking of which, I've been thinking about maybe coming out to help around the farm sometime. We haven't done that in ages and I think it'd be fun. Oh, that would be brilliant! There's always work that needs doing. Except, we've been meaning to set up a new system for the farm, and getting that just right is quite a challenge. Perhaps we could make a weekend of it? I'd love that. A whole weekend? That's a bit ambitious, isn't it? But yeah, I love spending time out there. Maybe we'll plan something for May or June when things are a bit calmer. Sounds like a plan! Maybe we could also set up a BBQ. We always have a good time with that. A BBQ would be awesome! And we can catch up with the whole family. That would almost make this lockdown feel worth it.

Hey, good to see you. I heard you've started teaching online during lockdown? Is that working well for you? Yeah, it's been a bit of a learning curve but overall quite positive. I love that I can do it from home and it's given me the freedom to plan my day as I want. That sounds great! I've been doing the same with my language classes. And, funnily enough, a lot of my students have been interested in learning different dialects. Any interest in that for you? Not really, to be honest. I've always stuck with standard English, but it's interesting you mention dialects. Did you know your parents used to speak in a distinct dialect when they grew up in Hertfordshire? Oh, absolutely! Everyone in Hitchin used to have that distinctive “Hertfordshire accent.” Although, it's pretty much died out over time. It's amazing how quickly language can change, isn’t it? Definitely. It's the same here in the Midlands. But you know, it's funny. Since having my daughter, I've noticed how she picks up words and pronunciation. Now that she's learning to talk, it's quite fascinating to see. Oh, the early stages of language development are so fascinating, aren’t they? I teach kids as well and it’s always amazing to see how quickly they pick things up. They can learn a lot from exposure, right? Absolutely. I’ve also taken an interest in teaching her phonics before she starts in school next year. You know, I didn’t even know about phonics until I started looking into early years education. How about you - did you learn phonics when you were younger? Not really, or at least, not in that way. It was more just reading and writing the way we all did back then, without any particular structure. I’m also interested in bilingualism and how children pick up languages so naturally. That's really interesting. I've also been thinking of starting my daughter on learning a second language. Maybe something like Spanish or French. What do you think? Is it a good idea to start so young? Oh, for sure. Research shows that the younger you are, the easier it is to learn a new language. And it doesn't necessarily need to be intense, just consistent exposure. Maybe even start with those kids’ language-learning apps or videos.

Ah, I see you've got a bird feeder up there. We have birds coming to ours nearly every day. Yes, haven't talked about that recently. Got some of various sizes but I need to make sure we refill them regularly. That's a lovely bird feeder. I made one myself last year and it was a bit of a struggle but quite rewarding when the birds started using it. Really? I might have to try that myself. Any tips on how to make it? It's all about getting the right kind of hole size and diameter for the kind of birds you want. I used a rough size guide from the internet. And I used wood that was weather-resistant. Right, makes sense. Must keep checking that the holes don't get blocked either. I suppose. Though sometimes it's interesting to just watch them trying to get the seeds out of there. Yeah, it's entertaining! We've got various species coming in. It's nice to see them all thriving, especially in the winter. Speaking of this, it would be quite good to have some cake now. Anyone tried gardening the patch over there? I think we need to clear some of the weeds first. It was a bit overgrown, but we can tackle that after tea. Ah, excellent idea! I made this lovely sponge cake this morning, still warm from the oven. That sounds perfect. Alright, I'm all for post-tea gardening then. First, let's focus on getting this cake eaten! Yes, good idea. You know, I just measured my blood sugar this morning. It's been a bit up and down. Do any of you know much about managing diabetes? Of course, I've had experience with that. With my own parents, you see. Regular monitoring, diet control, exercise... You've got to be quite structured about it. I hadn't thought about it much but it's just as important for us as it is for anyone younger. We might take it a bit more lightly given our age but it's just as serious. Absolutely. Mobility exercises and just being active in the garden can make a big difference. Not just that. Even with things like feeding birds or just going out into our own garden, it gets us moving and keeps us engaged. Right, this whole activity with bird feeders and gardening helps to keep us active, which is also good for the mind.

Ah, I'm so glad we could meet up here in Cyprus. It's been ages since we last saw each other. How are you enjoying the holidays so far? Can't complain. The sun and sea here are quite lovely. But I miss the hustle and bustle of the city – London or Sedgeley, it’s always something going on back home. True, but there's a certain charm to a slower pace of life, isn't there? I found myself enjoying the quiet morning walks along the coastal path near my villa here. You're staying in the villa, then? I was considering renting a house for the month, just need to finalise some details. Yes, it's nice to have some family members visiting too, actually. Makes for some lovely dinners - though making sure the invitation list is immaculate is always a challenge! I can imagine. We've decided on a nice spread of mezze for lunch, then maybe a little dessert later? And wine. You're ordering or should I? I'll take care of it, thank you. For me, a halloumi salad and maybe some grilled seafood. And yes, wine is a must. Shall we have a white, while the sun is still shining? Sounds perfect. I'll let the waiter know. What about pets at home? How are the kids handling them? Oh, my niece is absolutely loving being around our little dog here. She's been playing caregiver really well. But back home, we're also dealing with some health issues with the family – my mother’s been struggling with her hearing aids lately. I'm sorry to hear about your mother. Hearing aids can be quite tricky, can’t they? I've dealt with a few less fortunate side of things, where those same aids weren’t properly supported. She finds it quite frustrating. Limited support services here in Cyprus for older adults, but we're trying to navigate it all and find some alternatives. While I was dealing with all that, I also lost my father last year. It's… still quite raw. I'm so sorry, dear. Funerals can be quite something. But do you find that spirituality or perhaps some form of spiritual practice helps navigate the grieving process? It depends on the person. Personally, I've found that being around nature and the community helps. There’s something peaceful and grounding about it.

Hey Mum, Dad! It’s great to be here and catch up. I brought some lunch; hope that’s okay. How are you both doing? Speaker_2 : Oh, we're doing great. It's lovely to have you home. A bit of help with lunch won’t hurt, though! So, how’s the project coordination going? It’s been busy but rewarding. The new team members are really coming into their own, and we actually have a meeting with potential new clients this week. Speaker_3 : Sounds like great news. You know, when I was in my early days, I had to coordinate with a team for agricultural supply chains. It's a different dynamic, but I can imagine similar pressures. Yeah, definitely. It’s more about people management than planning logistics in agriculture but the pressure to perform is the same. Anyway, I’m sure you know your stuff. Definitely. You’re going to have to tell Ron about the team achievements when we meet up. And what about rugby? How did the team perform recently? Actually, the Leicester Tigers were pretty impressive last weekend. We’re hoping it’ll be a good season for them but it’s always different when watching from home. I used to follow the sports headlines, but now I find I prefer the local matches more. There’s something about seeing the game up close. True, but the national leagues have their own energy. Speaking of things local, have you both thought any more about the house renovation plans? We have. We were discussing maybe doing a small extension to the kitchen and getting a new layout. But the redesign is the real headache. You could always get one of those virtual planning tools. They’re really helpful. Or maybe just measured drawings and a mock up. I’ve worked with a few designers who are really good at that kind of thing. That’s a helpful tip. We’ll definitely consider it. And what about you, Emily? How’s everything with work and on a personal level? Oh, personally, things are good but work-wise, like I mentioned, I’m currently just trying to keep everything manageable so I can focus on the new project. It’s going to be a lot of work. You could use a break, couldn’t you? Even just a day or two away somewhere. Yeah, I was thinking about that.

Have you seen that new episode of Catfish? Yeah, today. I thought it was super intriguing. The woman was claiming to be a model but actually works at the local bookstore. You can just see how vulnerable the guy is to believe anything because he’s lonely. It's questions like this that make me wonder about the psychology behind it. Why people believe these lies about themselves? I think it has a lot to do with social validation and I'd be lying if I said it didn't intrigue me too. You know, the whole idea of not being good enough unless someone else 'sees' you as a certain way. Idk, I feel like some of them just get a kick out of the thrill of it. Like, what's the excitement in just being honest? True. And the fact that it usually involves a pretty stellar ego too. It's not just about the thrill of lying—it's about how you think you deserve a better story, better life, better someone. Exactly. It’s like those old Jeremy Kyle episodes where people just lie or cheat because they feel justified? I mean this is a lesser version, but conceptually similar. Absolutely. I used to watch Jeremy Kyle all the time. It was so cringe but in a way, it was interesting to see people's reactions when their lives were laid bare. Yeah, but at the same time, I wonder if TV shows like that, especially things like Catfish, can sometimes perpetuate the problem by making it seem 'normal' or 'exciting' to engage in these forms of dishonesty. True that. It's like they frame the deception as a kind of twisted 'love story' or 'epic quest for truth' rather than what it actually is—people getting caught in their own web of lies. And the public likes it. The world is just fascinated by drama, reality or not. But at the end of the day, it really isn't romantic or exciting to be lied to or cheated on. It's just hurtful. I guess what's intriguing about these shows is the 'exposure.' The feeling of: "I just found out what this person truly is, and it's not what they presented." It feels like a reveal or a discovery. True. It’s like peering into a different world—a 'real' world maybe compared to what we see on social media or formally.

Ah, I'm so glad we could take a break from all this studying. Got any recommendations for a good book about Paris? I've always been fascinated by the city, but I don't know where to start. Oh, Paris isn't just a city, it's a way of life – n'est-ce pas? But books, yes! Have you tried Hemingway's "A Moveable Feast"? It's a great insight into the expat life there and of course, his love for food and drink. Alternatively, if you're interested in history, Victor Hugo's "Les Misérables" gives you a deeper knowledge of the city's history, especially the 19th-century period. Cool, I've heard of "Les Misérables". Might just cosplay as Jean Valjean. That could be quite the party trick! What about languages? Are you still trying to master that French you were so enthusiastic about a few months ago? Still trying... struggling is more like it. But it's fun! And you're always a great help. You speak so many languages - English, German, French... even a bit of Italian. How did you learn them all? Oh, it's been a journey. I started young. My mother insisted on us learning the languages of the places we lived. Then, of course, university and personal interest added to the mix. What about yourself? Planning on traveling once this crazy semester is over? Honestly? Possibly, but it's tough with the university schedule. But definitely planning for a break soon. Maybe even a family trip to Italy. Haven't seen some of our family members since forever. Italy! Well, there's the bees that I've been looking after. They need to be checked on, and if one of your relatives is the keeper or just into nature, that's a great connection point. Plus, the food of course! You were telling me about those bees. Is it working out? Quite well, and it's been a great learning curve. But also, it's reminded me of my time in Vienna. Did you know that my parents – both from Vienna – had beekeeping in their family? No, I didn’t. But that’s fascinating. I've zero knowledge about honey production, except that it's quite the process. It's quite precise and almost artistic in its own right. And the care for the bees – it teaches you so much about nurturing and patiently watching over something you care about.

Can you believe that driver just cut us off? He was clearly not paying attention to the traffic. Yeah, people are getting more careless with their driving these days. It's just so unsafe isn't it? I remember when people used to have respect for fellow motorists. You know, I had a friend who always got into trouble due to speeding. She would claim she was late because she couldn't afford to be on time due to lazy traffic – always had a scathing remark about it. It just seems like there is an increasing number of bad drivers on the road. And when you mix that with the traffic we're experiencing today due to holiday travel… It's madness out there, especially if you also factor in how some towns have managed to barely cope with the influx of people. You couldn't pay me to live in some of these towns around here. I mean, have you seen how some of them are this time of year? Oh, I know what you mean. I passed through the outskirts of Guildford on my way in this morning, and the queue to get into the town was scandalous. It made me think – do people actually check for traffic before they leave or? Possibly, but it's not just the town in itself, it's also the lack of planning around the holiday traffic. We have all these nice roads that are needed for building but leading nowhere doesn't help much. Building? Just last week, I saw a new high-rise being constructed just outside town. That's all great and good until people realize they don't have anywhere to park, and the roads are clogged. Exactly! And then there's paying all those solicitors for disputes over planning permission… it's a headache. Reminds me of a time I spent weeks trying to sort out a claim for improper parking boundaries near my old flat. Ended up paying so much in legal fees, it was worth it just to move to a better area. Ah, solicitors... and then there's the MOTs. We just got ours done last week. I was dreading it because I knew the car needed new tires and probably some maintenance work. But at least it’s not like the old days where you’d hear about people never taking their cars in for any sort of check until it was purely out of necessity.

Ah, I'm losing my train of thought again, Alan's passport. I know today's the 23rd. It's not until the 27th, so we've got plenty of time. You're right though, we should make sure to get the other forms ready as well, just in case. Yes, and don’t forget the photographs. You'd think they'd have some at the post office, but they never do. Or maybe they just can't be bothered with old people, eh? All very well for us to be early risers and all, but they expect you to get there at 8 am sharp, or you're fucked. Bloody hel [laughs], you have a point there. 8 o'clock just says it all, doesn’t it? Everyone’s waiting for the retirement places to open, and the whole place’s just a rush. And to think we used to do that most of our lives. We sure did. But now, even applying for a passport feels like a job. [chuckles] It does, it does. I can't believe it's coming up to my 80th year soon. All these years working and nothing to show for it but these damned applications and whatnot. The system's still the same, isn't it? Always in favour of the hustle and bustle. Can't imagine why anyone listens to that lot in government, they keep making life worse for the likes of us who just want to go about our quiet days. Quiet days indeed. But you never know, we might just get a pleasant surprise. Maybe the forms will be straightforward this time. [laughs] You and the paperwork. I'm more holding my breath for that to happen than I am for Alan's passport to come through. Well, I reckon that passport’s just the start. Next up will be the travel plans. You were right to book early. It will be nice to have some proper holiday next summer, after all these years. I’m looking forward to that. We could sit on deck somewhere, watching the sea, not a care in the world. Can’t wait. But for now, let's just plod on with these forms. Gosh, I thought applying for a pension was a real battle, but this passport business gives it a run for its money. Yeah, well, at least the pension sorted itself out in the end.

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. I've been meaning to reach out to you about that band I told you about from Sunderland. You wouldn't believe the beat and the energy they bring. It's got this really raw, almost industrial feel to it. Wow, Sunderland, right? I'd love to hear more about that. But first, I have to ask: how was the plant you gave me last week? I'm trying to keep it alive with no expertise whatsoever! Oh, it's doing surprisingly well given my black thumb. You just need to make sure it gets plenty of light, okay? But yeah, the band’s name is Factory Idle, they’ve been around for a few years now. They’re a bit like the Arctic Monkeys but with a much grittier sound. That sounds interesting. I should look them up. You know, while we talk about local music, I attended a really thought-provoking lecture on music and cultural identity in Wales. It got me thinking about how similar themes play out here in England as well. That’s really fascinating! So, music has this universal language, yet it’s shaped by local and regional cultures. It's like, even if different parts of the country use the same words, the accent, the inflection, the rhythm can completely change the way the message is received. Absolutely. And the same can be said for gardening, ha! But seriously, the lecturer pointed out that music can be both a reflection of local identity and a shared cultural experience, really weaving people together across different regions. That's a great point. Like when I moved from Sunderland to Cambridge for uni, I had no idea how much the lilt of my accent would become a topic of conversation. Some people thought it was exotic or funny, which was really strange. But it made me realize how much our local music and dialects, they shape who we are. And yet, despite all the regional differences, we find common ground in certain cultural touchstones. From football to certain music genres, right? You can be from completely different parts of the country and still bond over a shared love of Oasis or something. Exactly! It’s about finding those shared identities that cut across different cultural backgrounds. And if you think about it, that's what's happening with your research and music right now.

Hey, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. I've been meaning to reach out to you about something that's been on my mind a lot lately. You're right, this is quite ideal–I don't have any exams this semester, so I'm actually quite free. What's been on your mind? It's the topic of unemployment and how it's affecting our demographic. I've been working with some statistics recently as part of my job, and it's very concerning. The numbers of early 20-somethings out of jobs is staggering, even with most having some form of postgraduate education. It feels unfair that many of us are just riding on benefits. Yeah, I've seen something like that too. As a PhD student, we're in a bit of a bubble though—University life can make the outside world seem very distant sometimes. Exactly! It's easy to forget until you step out of the academic bubble. But, you know, it's not just about the stats. It's about the individuals. Someone I know from Sunderland went back to live with parents after he graduated with a decent degree and couldn't find work. That’s tough. My cousin faced something similar. He had to move back to the Midlands after graduating. It's tough for morale, and puts a strain on family too, right? Absolutely. And then there's the mental health aspect to consider. Feeling 'unemployed' can lead to feelings of worthlessness. It's a serious issue for policymakers to consider. That's a very valid point. But I don't think enough is being done about it. I mean, we talked about university fees which seem only to be increasing, while the quality of education doesn’t seem to improve at the same rate or less. Spot on! And, as someone who comes from a Higher Professional Occupation background, it's even more jarring. The thing is, we were sold this dream that if we worked hard, got good grades, a degree, a postgrad degree even, we'd be set. But the actual jobs market isn’t as receptive as it used to be. Our generation feels like it’s been sold a lie. I couldn't agree more. It does feel like a broken promise. However, have you considered how this might be a broader economic issue rather than just an education or unemployment issue?

Hey Mum, look what I found in Grandma's stuff. It looks like she's been working on a picture book. There are pictures of the whole family, and talked about her life. Can you tell me what this is all about? Oh, bless her heart. It's her project. She was thinking of creating a book for the grandkids, to share our family's stories and history. Oh, yes! I wanted to make a book showing our family tree, stories from before we all moved around. It was supposed to be a fun way to share all the experiences, and I used to share it with my students too. It just never got finished. Was it for your own kids or the whole family? What happened that you gave up? It was for all of them. But sometimes, creative projects take time, and life gets busy. And now with the grandkids, it feels more possible. Though between us, I've really enjoyed what you’ve drawn recently. Shows a lot of talent! Yes, Grandma, you’ve always been good at art and stories too. And while the kids' own book idea is in good hands, I thought maybe we could continue what you started, bringing it together now. That would be so cool! We could help finish it, maybe even add our own stories and pictures. Like, really get everyone involved. Yes! That’s a great idea. And I think it could be therapeutic for me too, working on something so positive. We can do it during the holidays when we all have more time together, right? Do we need to stick to just family stories or can we include other things too? Like, what if we add in different family styles? Or include some step relatives too? Definitely include them. I was thinking about that too. Like, including your dad’s partner’s children and all of it. We’re all connected so we might as well celebrate all the different forms our family takes now. Yes! And maybe some pictures from when we had that big family trip to Ireland. We could put those in too. Ireland is a big part of our family history now, especially with your father. But yes, including different family structures is a great way to show this isn’t just about... ...traditional nuclear families. Exactly. It’s important for the kids to see that families are complex and beautiful across many different backgrounds and arrangements.

Hey, I'm going to have to shave first thing in the morning. Got a bit of stubble growing and I hate it when it feels rough when I'm talked to someone. You're right though, stubble can be super annoying. Especially now, the days are getting a bit longer and I find myself shaving just to feel presentable and manageable. Exactly! It feels like I’ve hardly had time to ruin my skin before I need to shave again. All this light and stuff makes it even worse keeps coming through. Totally get it, I find shaving to be such a hassle. But it's just part of being a grown up, right? Plus, I've just started to like the bit of stubble sometimes. Makes you look a bit more masculine, I feel. [laughs] Hence your stellar crushes every other day, I bet. I’m more on the side of smooth and clear, though. [laughs] Maybe. But it's funny because it's so subjective isn't it? Sometimes I look or feel really proud of myself if I've managed to keep it on side, you know? Absolutely. It’s just perspective. Where I come from, the rough 'tache can be quite the statement. That’s really cool, though. I come from a place where shaving's just like a basic necessity for most guys, especially university students. True, but sometimes it really is more than that. For instance, when I was at uni, there were some guys who really embraced their hair - doesn’t matter if it's on the face or the head - and they kind of influence others to do the same. Yeah, totally the case here. Seems like the guys who grew those amazing beards just won the crowd over. But for a girl, shaving body hair is a whole different conversation, isn’t it? Oh, absolutely. While you're worrying about stubble on your face, I'm sure I'm making sure not a single strand on my legs or underarms make an appearance. Funny how different we are when it comes down to it. And yet, we're both students trying to navigate the same social pressures. True. Though, I've started almost enjoying this ritual of just being all about care for yourself. Clearly, I’m out here, ready to conquer my day. I can see that. It’s weird though, I just realized when discussing this that there's still this expectation for women to be this ‘hairless’...

Right, so here's what I've been thinking… if we're gonna have our beer recommendations for the night, let's do it alphabetically. I've got my 'A' already picked out—a Newcastle Brown ale, just to keep it local. Brilliant idea! You know, I've always found questions like this kind of annoying at trivia nights or whatever, but actually talking about it over a pint sounds quite fun. I'm gonna go with an 'E'—would that be too simple, eh? Allsopp’s “E”, even though it is mass-produced, it’s a classic. Not at all, mate. Simple and good is sometimes the best. What made you choose 'E', you have any connection to it or just because of the name? Not really any connection, actually—I just like how “Pale Ale” sounds. What's wrong with going for the straightforward? Absolutely nothing! It's a golden rule sometimes, isn't it? Keep things simple. What about 'D', Danny? Did you pick it out already? I was thinking Dog & Fox or maybe something like Drafts For Wolves. We could keep it on theme with symbols or animals. I prefer the animals, anything to avoid heavy branding. Speaking of symbols, it's actually fascinating to think about how the different types of alcohol have associations to the societies we're part of. It stems from quite interesting cultural histories, if you think about it. Totally, like how certain types of drinks can almost determine the kind of social events you go to, or the type of music you might listen to while you're there. I've noticed it doesn't just stop at drinks, either—we also have associations with certain music genres or even certain types of fitness activities, like boxing, if you're into that. Exactly! I’ve been boxing for a few months, and honestly, it’s a whole different world. The community is really supportive, and it's a very physical but also very mentally demanding activity. It's kind of like a whole other language—you'll hear guys in the gym talking about strategy and technique, and if you don’t speak “boxing,” it sounds like they're speaking gibberish. But it’s actually really methodical. That’s interesting, sports have a real language of their own. Like the terms used in football. Did you hear about the racism stuff going on in football again?

Ah, I'm so glad we could find some time to discuss this. I've been meaning to reach out to you about the council's funding initiative for our historic building project. You're right to bring it up at this time. It’s now or never considering this quarter’s deadlines. Exactly! The potential for funding is definitely an opportunity we shouldn’t miss. But, to be honest, I'm a bit of a novice when it comes to bidding for these kinds of projects. Could you walk me through how you've approached similar projects in the past? Of course, sweetheart, I'd be more than happy to advise you. First off, the key thing I’ve found is to really understand your client’s interests and highlight how your project aligns with them. That makes sense. So, making sure the proposal isn’t just about your own vision, but also communicating how it serves the greater good of the community? Absolutely! Funders, whether local councils or national trusts, are always on the lookout for projects that not only preserve heritage but also contribute to community engagement or even economic development. Now, I'm not saying you need to make it all sound overly commercial but balance is key. That’s very helpful, thanks. Another concern I have is the practical aspects of the renovation. Especially if we’re to make it sustainable without compromising the historical integrity. That’s a common challenge, indeed. I always advocate for a hybrid approach. Use traditional craftsmanship as much as possible but also incorporate modern materials and techniques where they are compatible and add value. How do you suggest we balance it? It’s easy to get carried away with the ‘green’ or ‘sustainable’ aspects and lose sight of the primary goal. The secret is in doing your homework. Research what’s worked for similar projects. For example, if you were doing a project in my neck of the woods, you’d find that they love using traditional materials and local builders but also now use a lot of reclaimed materials and energy-efficient appliances where they can. That does make sense. Plus, I think we can use local suppliers and craftsmen to help support the local economy too. Absolutely! And don’t forget to involve the community as much as possible. You could even host open days or workshops during the renovation process to engage them and maybe even get some volunteers involved.

Make yourself a cup of tea. I'm making it from that new Earl Grey you got. Oh, yes! I've been meaning to try that. Thanks, love. No problem at all. So, now that the weekend’s here, got any plans? Just catching up on some PhD work. But I've been thinking about my next research topic. I might dabble into dialectology, perhaps focusing on regional differences in accent across England. That could be really interesting, especially given our own mixed backgrounds. Sunderland and Birmingham, that's quite a linguistic contrast. Exactly! It's fascinating how even within England, our dialects can be worlds apart. You know, as a semanticist, I've always been intrigued by how language can shape our perception and how dialects can reflect societal structures and history. It does make you think. I've met so many people from different parts of England, and each time it's like they're speaking a slightly different language. It never gets old for me, that's for sure. I'm with you. I mean, it's astonishing how much our dialects reveal about different socio-economic conditions, exposure to global languages, and even migration patterns. Yeah, the North and its harsh industrial past, the Midlands with its more mixed influences, and the South with its accents often tied to economic and academic centers. Fascinating stuff. Absolutely! For instance, I've noticed that certain phrases from the North, like "canny lad" and "proper job," don't quite carry the same weight in the Midlands. It’s not the meaning that changes, but the connotation behind it, which is so tied to place and identity. Right, and then you’ve got your rhoticity, non-rhoticity. The North keeps that 'r', while parts of the South drop it. It’s just so revealing of where people come from. Exactly. Accents are like our cultural DNA. They can tell you so much about a person’s background, social class, education. It’s incredible. And it’s so much more than just how one sounds. It’s also about identity and community. When I was in university and meeting people from all over England, we almost shared this secret language just through our accents. Absolutely, and then you encounter the variations within those broad geographical areas. Sunderland, where I'm from, has particular idiosyncrasies that even other Northern cities might not share.

Hey everyone, did you hear about the strict new dining rules at Matilda's school? Seems like no more packed lunches unless they are healthy. Oh wow, that's quite a change! Emma, isn't your lunch now all the fruit, veg and protein? Wow! I love my packed lunches. Mine are always so yummy! What if I want a chocolate bar, can I still have one? Well, even if you want it, school rules. You can still have a small treat once in a while, but mostly you've got to have balanced lunches. It's like having your own mini Granny picnic at school! So, does that mean we can't have a little money for the tuck shop even? Yes, but you can save it up for special occasions or give it to someone else if you don't need it. Ugh, but what if I share and still want to buy something? Well, that would depend on the amount available and the rules provided by your teachers, but generally, you can't spend it on just fun snacks anymore. However, the school will still have some healthier options if you forget a packed lunch. So, can we still spend money on buying stuff at school? A bit, but not all the time. And actually, in our case, because we're preparing for the school tennis tournament, maybe all of you could concentrate on saving that money for team events or treats after matches. Tennis tournament?! That sounds fun! Is it like a big circus with clowns and stuff? No, it’s just a school sporting event, but it will be a lot of fun! And maybe if we do really well, we could even have some special treats from Mrs. Smith, our PE teacher who loves rewarding effort. Can we still have a party after it though? Like, after the tournament but also after the final day of school? Well, if we save up nicely for the treats and parties, maybe. Can I go to the circus if I save up all my school money? That would be a treat! If you save up generously for treats or events, and if we budget properly, we can all plan something fun together for the holidays. But right now, concentrate on those sports and hobbies for any extra treats or activities you might like. So if I really do well and save, I can go see a real circus and maybe even meet some clowns?

Everybody, I hope you enjoyed the film as much as I did. It was so thought-provoking, isn’t it? The director clearly had a lot to say about social inequality. Yes, quite a film isn't it? Reminds me of when I was younger – always something questions you in films back then. But I did find it a bit difficult to follow sometimes, right? Actually, I thought it was really well done. So keeps you engaged. But it got me thinking – have any of us ever wondered about the kind of films we show our students today compared to when we were at school? Does anyone here have any experience with teaching? Oh, actually, as a teacher, I read quite a lot about that. There’s a lot of debate going on right now about how to modernize the curriculum while still retaining some of the old favourites. It’s a delicate balance sometimes, isn’t it? Yes, I remember discussions about this at school. Someone should make a film about that! But jokes aside, I think it’s important. One side says it’s about keeping our foundations strong, and the other says we need to be more modern and applicable. I think both have their place. Speaking of which, I saw there was a debate in Cambridge recently about how we teach history. It’s amazing how political it gets, even at that level. What were people saying? Well, as I understand it, some argued we’re not teaching enough of the complexities and nuances and that we needed to broaden the scope beyond just dates and events. Yes, and then you have some on the other side saying we’re already falling behind in basics. Seems to me like there’s a missed opportunity here to tie more of the curriculum to industry. I mean, I’ve seen students struggle to connect what they learn to real-world applications. I’m no expert, but when I was younger, my Dad used to take me to museums, and that was more interesting than some of the lessons. Maybe we need more of that today – hands on experience, interactive learning. Absolutely, Speaker_3 has an interesting point there too. This ties into the national curriculum. It’s all very well to talk about 'real-world applications', but what does that look like when you’ve got to meet all these different standards and still make everything fun and engaging.

Ah, I was just reading about World War II last night. Dad was involved in that. Fought in Italy, he did. You wouldn’t believe the stories he used to tell, Harold. There was the one about finding a German soldier just trying to surrender, but the American troops didn’t have a translator. I remember my grandfather talking about those times too, but he was more about the pre-war and early years of his life. Tells of growing up in Middlesex and how life was so different even before the war. Harrow was a different place before the war, yes. Full of rich families, but after the war it seemed like the whole character of the area changed. Smaller London, but a village like atmosphere. Yeah, Dad was in the navy from '39 to '45. Lots of action in the Mediterranean and parts of North Africa. He hated it, but he had to go. Our dad was in the land army, barely out of school. But these days we couldn’t imagine anyone our age doing that, could we? Absolutely not. For me, it’s hard to comprehend the hardship they went through. Not just the fighting but the rationing, the lack of comforts we now take for granted. It’s the little things people don’t think about, really. Like the weather. Nowadays we’re used to complaining about a bit of rain or cold, but back then people rejoiced at a sunny day after years of cloud and uncertainty. Indeed. Weather used to have a different meaning. And food, of course. Rationing...sounds terrible now, but back then you were just grateful for what you got. Speaking of food, do you remember when ration coupons were things you really needed? Seems like just commerce now. And the furniture of the time. I noticed in some old photos, the living rooms looked so sparse. No clutter, but also no comforts. Just what you needed, but nothing more. Right. And even things like the police. Reading about the Home Guard and how ordinary civilians pitched in. Can’t imagine today people volunteering like that. The police too. I mean, today they're zero-tolerance with so much, but back then they cleared up most situations without even involving the police. Community took care of community. Maybe that's what we're missing these days. A little bit of that community spirit.

Hey Dad, so I've been thinking a bit about our arrangements for the move. When we leave your place tomorrow, how do you want me to sort out the rest of the stuff? Good question, son! First off, I'd like you to make sure you've got all of Mum's questions answered regarding the mortgage and the movers. It's her last day in the old house, so she'll want to know everything's taken care of. But actually, before that... I had a bit of a chest infection for a few days which left me feeling quite sick.
