Think I'm better now, but I just want to make sure you don't catch it. Oh, dear! I wasn't aware you've been under the weather, Dad. Sorry to hear that. I’ll keep an eye on it, but from what I can tell, you’re fine now, aren’t you? Yeah, I'm much better now, thanks for checking. But as for the arrangements, your mum seems to have most things under control, but it's good to double-check. Let me know if you need any help with those questions. I’ve got a bit of expertise in that area. Sure, I’ll give her a call tonight. I’ve been helping her with some logistics too, like sorting the finances and everything. It’s been quite a task, but we're managing so far. Good job, son. Well done. Thanks, Dad. A bit of an odd conversation to have in the car while we're driving, isn't it? Between life, mortgages and all that, but that’s pretty much where we’re at right now doesn’t it? Yeah, kind of a 'life moves on, but some things don't really change,' eh? But the fact we can have this conversation, man to man, it’s just what’s needed. Exactly. Speaking of mortgages, I’ve had a few heated discussions with Mum about it recently. She’s been quite worried about the rates changing. You’ve always been good with that sort of thing, Dad… do you think we’ll make it? Well, I know it’s always a worry, but we've done our best to plan for everything we can. The market is unpredictable, but we’ve got a good deal. You could even say it’s better than we had hoped for.

Right, so we need to finalize the birthday meal plans for Mum. I was thinking we could have a nice Sunday roast, but clearly, we don't want anything too heavy for the birthday girl. What do you think? A roast sounds lovely! But maybe a lighter version? We could have some kind of fish dish instead? Or maybe lamb shanks, they're still quite tender? Good idea! Something light and easy to eat would be perfect. Fish is a great choice. Plus, it'll give us a wide range of menu options if people have dietary restrictions. Yes, exactly! Even Mum will have to keep to certain dietary requirements since she's been having some problems with her digestion. Right, so what about the menu planning? We need to make sure it’s easy for everyone to make their choices. And we might have to ensure we’ve got enough seating arrangements for the day. True, and we should also check if there are any guests with dementia or similar conditions. Perhaps it would be helpful to have a simple menu with few choices, and maybe even a photo menu? That’s a brilliant idea, having photos for the menu is such a thoughtful touch. It would certainly make things easier for everyone. And while we're on the subject, what about the table layout? We can’t have people feeling too cramped, but at the same time, we want to keep them all close enough to have a good conversation. I was thinking we could pull out one of the larger tables and set it up in a U-shape. We have enough space in the living room and it would allow everyone to see and talk to each other easily. That would work really well. And while we're on the subject of rearranging things, have you noticed how cluttered the cupboards are? We could use a few lovely, scented candles to light the space and make it feel cozy. And perhaps some nice fresh flowers on the table as well? Oh, definitely! While you’re dealing with the cupboards, can I take care of the candles and flowers? I was thinking we could make the dining area feel like a little sanctuary for Mum’s birthday. That would be so lovely of you. I might also want to pull out some of those family photos we cleared out recently.

Right, so I'm due for another visit at the dentist's. Tooth gods spare me; these wisdom teeth are getting too much. They're ruining my life, honestly. Had the first one taken out last year. It was horrendous–I almost passed out and then the hole, oh the hole – massive! Why does this kind of dental work always involved a hole in my cheek and a chunk of pain out of proportion? Oh, the horrors of dental work! I know, innit? The memories of my own keeps coming back. You get used to it in a way, but it's still, like, 'Really? Again?' After the first one, I had to learn how to swallow properly again because of the numbness, just like you said. But holes, holes are the worst part. You can't taste or enjoy your food for ages. What's wrong with evolution, right? Exactly! It's all archaic, man. One of these days we’ll invent a better way, like, just zap them out or something. Anyway, the worst part will be the recovery. I heard my mum or dad say something about how they had to cope with us kids going through this as well, when we were younger. Yeah, they often mention that while the kids seem to suffer more, the adults think the worst is the anxiety beforehand. Once the extraction's done, apparently the pain isn’t as bad as the anticipation – at least, that's what my parents say. But I think it’s comforting to have a family in it together, really. Makes you feel less alone. That's true, they always highlight how painful it was for them, but in a funny way. It’s like the survival story they always tell us. Actually, that kind of makes me feel better if I’m honest. But the fact we’re going through the same, kinda together, gives a weird level of comfort. On that note, did your family say anything about moving back to uni before we dive deep into this wisdom teeth saga and the potential for more holes? Since we're also thinking about that next semester. Ah, moving back to uni – it’s a bit up in the air at the moment. I know I need to get it sorted, because if I don’t, I might miss the deadlines for the halls. Same.

Hey everyone, did you know that today is actually the Spring Festival or Chinese New Year today? The Lunar New Year is celebrated all over the world by people of Chinese descent. It's the most important festival on the Chinese calendar. Aww, yeah! The year of the Rat started! That's so cool! What's the Spring Festival? Well, it marks the beginning of a new year according to the Chinese lunar calendar. It's usually in January or February, depending on when the new moon occurs. There's always a zodiac animal associated with the year. This year’s the Rat, but next year is going to be the Ox. So, what we could do for Chinese New Year, is maybe try to make some traditional dishes? Or, perhaps, we could have a little celebration here at home, watch a movie about its significance or make a fun craft? Ooh, that sounds like fun! And it would be kind because it's celebrating someone else's special day. Yeah! For a random act of kindness, we could make some homemade Chinese lanterns to put up around the house. Or maybe we could even paint some lucky red envelopes for the kids? Those are great ideas! Do either of you know anything about coins or monetary units in China? Because using them as part of the celebration would be really fun. Hey, wait! We can use our chess and draughts pieces for money, just like in the game Monopoly. That would be fun and it's like we're bringing real parts of China to our celebration. Yeah! Except, we could do all the transactions in Mandarin or Cantonese for extra fun. I love that idea! It’s so creative and thoughtful. Speaking of creative acts of kindness, have either of you heard about milk monitors for animal sanctuaries? No, what’s that? It’s where people who are lactose intolerant – like me – donate lactose-free milk to animal sanctuaries where animals might need it. A little act of kindness like that doesn’t cost much but means a lot to the animals. That’s so good. We could look up if there’s an animal sanctuary around here and see if they could use anything like that. Definitely. That could be a fun activity for us. And another fun idea – since we're talking about random acts of kindness and fun activities for Chinese New Year – I know we've talked about dyeing hair before.

Hey Mum, did you hear about that car accident last night? Yeah, it sounds pretty awful. I was talking to someone about it at work this morning. Are you okay? You've been quiet for a while now and I thought maybe you might have heard something. Oh, don’t worry about me darling, I’m fine. It just made me think about that Alice in Wonderland book you got me recently. Do you remember those falling gardens? They reminded me a bit of how time moves fast and backwards sometimes, especially after something shocking like an accident. Hahaha, yes! True! But it seemed so real in the story, despite being so absurd in our world. It just shows how strange life can be. Exactly! Speaking of strange things, have you been noticing how many seagulls there have been lately? They seem to have taken over the town. Yeah, it’s crazy! I read online that there might have been something that attracted them last year, like a food source or something, and now they’ve turned Hastings into their home! Really? That’s interesting. Maybe it’s a new urban legend. I think most people just kind of assumed we’d always have seagulls. But in a way, it’s like they're trying to make Hastings their own Wonderland now. Well, as long as they’re not causing injury, I suppose it’s silly to mind! They add a certain character to the place. Definitely. And speaking of adding character, I saw a fantastic costume shop near town last week. Did you?! Tell me about it. Are you planning to do anything for Halloween or just in case you need a fun day out? No specific plans yet, but they had the most amazing costumes. I saw one that looked like Wonderland characters, but also lots of classic horror movies. That’s so great! I remember changing the theme of our reading weeks in school to books like Alice in Wonderland or Doctor Jekyll and Mr. Hyde for Halloween. Those were always so fun. That’s so cool, Mum. Did you make all the costumes yourself? Well, most were store bought, but a few times, we had to improvise or just go all out with makeup. There was one year we did a little theatre thing and came up with our own rendition of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.

Ah, I was pondering over the meeting we had last night. It felt like we really made some headway for those folk fighting the solar panels. I've been deep into this kind of activism for years, although never as vigorously until now. It really seems to be escalating now, the fight between renewables and – well, questions about the kind of renewables we really need and where they'd be best placed. Absolutely, I couldn't agree more, Margaret. It was fractious at times, wasn't it? But it was also quite heartening to see people get alongside with something they believe in. You know, it's funny, those folk with the solar panels plan – they seem to think just because it's renewable, it's automatically accepted. Indeed. I think the biggest problem there was the attitude of 'renewable' as though it's an invitation to develop anything anywhere. It's almost as if the presence of a solar panel or wind turbine automatically purges the area of any conflict of interest. But, of course, it doesn't. And these people are entirely right to question it. Precisely! And it's not that we're anti-renewable. It's about sensible planning and being aware of the impact on our local environment and communities. Where those solar panels were planned for – it's a rural landscape in a sensitive area. We can't just let these energy firms or the council bulldoze through sentiments and careful land management without considering broader implications. I think one of our main points is that the council and these companies often really need to be shown the evidence of the benefits and the drawbacks. And that takes some research and a clear analysis. I was thinking… would it be a good idea if we pooled some resources, kind of a 'one-stop shop' for understanding policy, procedure, and impact analysis? Now that's a clever idea. As someone who used to run a business, I can tell you that if you're going to argue against or for something, you need solid data. It's also about presenting it clearly. From technical feasibility to socio-economic impact, the better informed we are, the stronger we are. Plus, if we could find out – I know it’s a pipe dream in some ways – but what research exists or is being funded, it could be quite telling.

Ah, I'm losing patience. I need to sort out driving lessons. Grace has been talking about it non-stop and I thought it would be a good idea to learn myself. After all, she needs a chaperone, right? Just don’t expect me to do your questions for you, Dad! Between us, though, I think it’s an excellent idea. It’s not just about being a chaperone—it’s about learning something new as well. I could help you find a good driving school. You could indeed. You know a thing or two about knowledge and stuff like that, don't you? Even if I have to learn to park! You two are just as persistent as the other. But seriously, learning to drive at your age can be good for mental agility, and we could even go on drives together. Speaking of which, I have some brochures here about holidays. Since we’ll be driving, maybe we could consider a road trip? We could start with somewhere local and work our way up to bigger expeditions. A holiday sounds nice, especially if it’s a driving holiday. What’s on your list, dear? Well, there are some lovely spots in the Peak District that are easily accessible. And if you feel adventurous, we could even try Scotland or Wales. Though, for an initial trip, perhaps somewhere closer? Like Bristol perhaps? I love visiting there—Bristol City Centre has changed so much, really modern with that funky atmosphere. Bristol sounds alright. And maybe we could plan a stop by Stonehenge on the way. I’ve always wanted to visit that. You could even do all of them one by one. But the first question is getting the car sorted, right? Have you thought about insurance, Dad? Ah yes, insurance. Terrible thing. Just proves we’ve all got to pay for being out there on the roads. I’ll look into it, but changing the car to a more learner-friendly one would also be a good idea. Don’t worry too much about that. Just start with a sensible, reliable car, take your time with the lessons, and the insurance should be manageable. And if anything, having the experience of being a learner with the grandchildren can be quite bonding... once we get over the anxiety, of course! I’ll look into that insurance with you. And maybe we can make it a family outing.

Dad, I'm going to park down at the corner, I've got a bet today and don't want to risk getting clamped. Ah, horse racing again, are we? You're hooked on that app, aren't you. Still, just be careful out there. Yeah, just one today, I'm not sure if my horse's got the stamina for the long run. Have you ever backed a horse, Dad? Heh, when I was your age, even if I could afford it, it was a different world. You kids and your mobile phones, pinging all the time. I can barely keep up with all the notifications. Yeah, it's a bit like the betting line, isn't it? Constant updates. But sometimes it can be a lifesaver. Like the other day, I got a notification about the weather and knew to grab an umbrella before I headed out. True, technology can be both a blessing and a curse. I admit it's saved me from a few soggy walks. Though between you and me, I quite like the old ways. Like proper tea and biscuits. I'm curious, what's this newfangled "instant gardening" I keep hearing about? The kids all talk about the 'food banks'. Oh, that's about community gardens and stuff, where people can come and grow their own vegetables. It's amazing really, nice for people who perhaps can't afford fresh produce all the time. But isn't it bizarre that we need these food banks? Shouldn't the politicians be dealing with that sort of thing? Politics... doesn't change much, does it? Still just a bunch of talking heads. Though, food banks do help, but it's all about survival when you're at the bottom of the heap. I remember times when we had to stretch a few pounds, literally. Exactly. Which reminds me, Dad, we were discussing before lunch about moving to Brighton. I've heard it's supposed to be quite a lively place. You've never lived there, have you? Brighton? I spent a few years there in the 50’s. It was rough around the edges, but full of character. Reminds me of a time when we didn't need apps to tell us the weather or where to park. It's funny, isn't it? We've got freedom and choice, but sometimes feels like just more stress.

Hey mate, did you hear about James' latest golf move? He hit a hole-in-one; grabbed the ball and immediately started teaching others how to do it, right in front of his opponents. Oh, yeah. That must have been a sight! But speaking of skills, have you started working on that advanced Python class yet? You'd totally hit another hole-in-one with that! Nah, I've been too busy trying to perfect my sarcasm. It's quite the skill, you know. You get people questioning their whole existence with just a few well-placed words. You need to learn from me then. I've been perfecting that since we were kids. Thanks, but I think my sarcasm is quite sharp. You know how they say "the quickest way to a man's heart is through his stomach"? Well, I discovered a quicker way - through his sense of sarcasm. True that. It's like Shakespeare for the modern age - playing on expectations or words for comedic effect. Exactly! Shakespearean sarcasm is like the gold standard. "Fair is foul and foul is fair" - the whole play is one big "are you kidding me?" at Scotland's weather. You're quite the Bard fan, aren't you? But speaking of less highbrow stuff, how's your current job going? Alright, I guess. It's a bit "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" - But it pays the bills and the lattes. Jack has been working in a coffee shop, eh? Seems fitting. More dull than dull, but a steady income, I guess. Yeah. Although, I think I'll "play" more after my studies are done. Maybe move and try my hand at something else. Where’s that? Don’t know yet. London’s always an option. But for now, I’m just enjoying my student life, trying to soak up as much knowledge as possible. It’s like the pursuit of knowledge - the win isn't the destination; it's the journey. Wise words. But let's not forget the pursuit of complete freedom post studies. No more early morning lectures . But that won't be for a while. I know! And don’t forget the skill of “winning”, which, let’s be honest, is basically just not losing at anything. Right, like not losing your afternoon at the golf course, or winning at procrastination. Exactly! You know what else is a fun “win”?

Right, so everyone's weekend plans? Thoughts on brunch or hitting up those new brewery bars? To be honest, don't know much about these Cambridge bars, but down in Surrey, we've got some top-notch places. Still up for suggestions though! Yeah, I kind of feel the same. Cambridge stays pretty busy even on weekends, but Lewisham can get pretty lively too. I've heard this bar right near the river, Flask I think, is quite good. Flask! Yeah, that’s a great spot. I've been a few times before but I could go again. Right, Flask is on my list then. Did any of you go to that yoga event by the botanic gardens last week? Oh, I did actually! It was a bit of a morning kick to be honest but it was alright. I wanted to go, but my diet didn’t really allow for brunch then yoga, haha! Next time though. You couldn’t believe the queue though, could you? No, I wasn't really surprised, considering it was a sunny weekend and free yoga. I’ve been trying to cut down on heavy carbs, while still working out. It’s harder than I thought, but the weight is coming off. It can be quite tough, but it’s amazing how different you feel when you take care of yourself. Speaking of which, how’s the new flat going, [ANON]? ANON: It’s all good, but getting it decorated and settled in is taking forever. Well, redesigning the lounge alone might take a while. Don’t worry, it’ll all come together eventually. Maybe we can help out or grab dinner there the next time you’re back up north? ANON: That would be so lovely! You know me, once everything is done, it’ll feel like home. While you’re sorting out the flat, changing the layout can also help with Feng Shui. True – I’ve read some stuff about minimalist arrangements for better energy flow and relaxation in the home. ANON: Oh, I didn’t consider Feng Shui when figuring out the furniture layout, but that’s definitely something. So, this weekend then – Flask? Maybe meet there at around 12 and we grab some food around? Sounds good to me. And maybe we can get something light, considering diets and all. Perfect. Light brunch and then some time hailing around the market afterwards?

Ah, I'm going over the garden to see if the bamboos have started growing. The sun is lovely today. Reminds me of the eclipse we saw years ago. You mean the one in 1999, the total solar eclipse that passed over London? I remember we went outside and had our homemade glasses. But even with them, the light was so strong! And didn't the two of you almost move houses because of it? Or was it during another eclipse? You get very enthusiastic about these celestial events. Yes, exactly! Even thought there have been many others since then. But, today's eclipse coverage on TV is getting more and more technical, I find. It's good that we can study these things now - though making sure the TV licence is paid properly still keeps me on my toes sometimes. Oh, completely! Especially when sometimes you watch programmes online and forget about the actual TV licence. Offline it seems like black holes are the current thing - or at least the latest orgy of interest. But that was before the plant shows. You ever seen that painting programme with Monty Don? Yes, I love it when he talks while he paints. He has so much knowledge about the plants and the techniques used. It's really educational, but in such a gentle way. Ah, gentle. He is, isn't he? Quite the opposite to some of today's discussions in political correctness, really. Can't agree or disagree without being 'right' or 'wrong' these days. Indeed, and I'm not sure it's always about "right" or "wrong". Just being respectful, you know? I don't understand why people get so upset about it. It’s about being sensitive to the fact that the language we use can be hurtful or problematic to certain groups. It’s about evolving with time and respecting one another's dignity. While I agree with changing outdated terms and ideas, I find that sometimes they go a bit far. Anyway, I want to show you the new boundaries we made in the garden. The fence is so much better now. And the plans to set up the owl box? I hope the neighbors don’t mind. As long as the owl box doesn’t become another arguing point with them. Do you remember when they got so upset about the fence before? I just hope they don’t complain about the bamboo this time.

Right, I'm going to Sunderland tomorrow to see the family. Dad's birthday is today actually; he's 60. Ooo, big day for him. What are you going to do? Is there anything special happening? Just the usual, I think. We'll probably have a family dinner at one of the local pubs. But my sister's got this thing planned at the Hoppings that I don't fully understand yet, but she says it'll be fun. Oh, I've got no idea what that is. Sounds like something from the deep north. Hahaha, yes – it's a big old funfair, but I think this time they've got some of that new tech like zip lines and stuff. My nephew’s really hyped about it but my dad might find it a bit too much. Zip lines? That sounds exciting. Does it have the big wheel and all those standard funfair rides? Yeah, there's a big big wheel similar to the ones we get in London. And it's usually set up near the seaside, or as much as Sunderland has that, so it's nice weather permitting. That sounds different from anything we have down here. Where did you get the idea for 'Hoppings'? It sounds more like a dance or something. It's actually the nickname people have for the annual funfair held at Seaburn, near Sunderland. A bit confusing for outsiders, but it's a big event there. Ah, I see. Shows how little I know about some places in my own country. Anyway, since you're heading that way, have you considered the train? Actually, I like driving because I can stop off and see some countryside. The A1 is usually okay, but I worry about the traffic a bit. Plus, having the car gives me the chance to visit bits of the northeast without having to rush. There's this lovely old cathedral in Durham that I always like to visit but never get a chance to when I'm short on time. Durham Cathedral's amazing, isn't it? I had a field trip there in school for history. I remember being blown away by the structure. It’s one of the most stunning cathedrals in England. You know, most people think of the biggest ones in London, but Durham's Norman architecture is just as impressive and maybe even more atmospheric.

Ah, good morning! I was up at four am, listening to the birds. On the tin, it was supposed to be dawn chorus, but I couldn't identify much of it! Still, it was quite lovely, wasn't it? Good morning! I couldn't sleep past seven, so I heard it all! I'd have had to do a bit of bird identification, but I didn't get into that much. I did wish I could sleep as well as the birds seem to... I had an alarm clock going off in my mind before my real one did! Haha, well, I've always wondered about that, actually. Like how lazy humans have to be to invent such gadgets. Feeding the birds gets me going in the morning, keeps me on schedule, even if I'm not as keen on getting up early as our feathered friends. I suppose keeping busy with birds and wildlife is a nice way to wake up, but I do feel a bit guilty for sometimes not being creative with their food. Do you mix it up often, or is there a trusted mix that works? I do try and keep it varying, especially now that the seasons are changing. Mixing it up is quite good for them, but sometimes I just grab what's in the cupboard. Where did you get your love for birds and feeding them from? Was it part of a childhood experience or something more recent? It's an acquired taste, really. I've always been interested in nature, but my real interest in birds started when I lived in one of those terraced houses, really small garden but lots of sparrows. It was a real lesson in small-scale ecosystems and the diversity even in such a small space. True, and the sounds! I always feel like they're telling us something, you know, if only we understood it. But the different calls can be quite the puzzle, can't they? I just tried to learn a few basics, like the robin's song. Simple, yet effective for a bit of early morning cheer! Exactly! That’s what gets me, trying to decipher the calls. Sometimes I think my nerves might be as frayed as a bird's – I went to the dentist last week and had to get a filling done. It was a real test of my patience!

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up, Sarah. It feels like ages. How have you been? I've been okay, Helen. Just enjoying my life as a single parent. It can be a bit overwhelming at times, but the kids are my world. You know, I've been thinking about some changes too. Going through IVF and deciding to become a solo parent forced me to rethink my priorities and consider a career shift. Oh, I'm so sorry to hear about your IVF journey. And how did that turn out? Well, it was a tough process, but it taught me a lot about resilience. Although it didn't result in a pregnancy, I came out of it with a deeper understanding of myself and my needs. So, I decided to leave social work after many years of service. It was a huge change, but I felt suffocated in that role. Now, I'm trying to write a children's book. It's been an interesting experience, creative yet very challenging. That sounds like a big change, but also very fulfilling. You know, I've been thinking about making changes too, especially after my postgrad course. We talked about it briefly last time, but I'm seriously considering yoga therapy. I find the practice so grounding and it seems to help with the stress of being a teacher. Kids in this generation are different, you know? Always glued to their devices and lacking attention sometimes. Ah, the world of teaching is indeed changing rapidly. I've had to adapt too with the new focus on integrating technology into learning. But sometimes it feels like the benefits and the drawbacks are blurred. On that note, how do you feel about how people use social media, especially parents and their relationship with their children? As a social worker and now a single parent, I've seen both sides. Oh, absolutely. It's a worry. As a teacher, I've seen kids as young as eight acting more mature online than they do in person. It's concerning. But personally, as a parent, I've had to set some boundaries. While I see the benefit of staying connected with my neice and nephew on social media, I'm also aware that sometimes it takes away from the time they should be spending face-to-face and in the real world. Exactly! And it seems like people are increasingly using social media to show only the best parts of their lives.

Thank you so much for inviting me over for a cup of tea. It's been ages since we chatted. How's life treating you, especially after retirement? It's been a mixed bag, to be honest. I miss the structure of work but now I have the freedom to do things I always wanted to try. But days can sometimes feel a bit dull without something to focus on. How about you, how's life as a language teacher? It must be rewarding but also quite challenging with all those different accents! It is indeed very rewarding. I get to see people improve over time and learn about their cultures, seeing the passion they have for languages. It can be tough too, especially with the varying levels of students' background knowledge and sometimes dealing with limited resources. So what's the biggest struggle for you in teaching? Is it the lack of resources or the students themselves? Both can be challenges sometimes, but I think it's more about finding a balance for each individual student. You know, some students might already have a strong grasp on the basics while others might struggle with the simplest concepts. And sometimes, dealing with students from diverse or even disadvantaged backgrounds adds an extra layer of complexity. I can imagine. When I was teaching in the Midlands, most of my students came from working-class backgrounds. Lack of resources and educational support at home was a substantial barrier for many. It's really hard on the teachers too. Absolutely. But it's also the most rewarding when you see those students, despite all the odds against them, really flourish and enjoy learning. One of my students actually used to be a part-time cleaner and now they're aiming to become a translator. It's things like that that make the tough days worth the while. That's fantastic to hear. I've had similar experiences. Some of my most memorable students were those who were truly dedicated despite their hardships. It changes your perspective on the impact we can have as teachers. It really does. Speaking of impact, have you noticed any changes in educational standards or methods since you retired? Oh, sure. There's been a lot of emphasis on digital literacy and using technology more effectively in teaching. I'm not sure how I feel about it all just yet.

Right lads and lasses, I'm pretty sure we've all been thinking about today's feast, eh? Should we nudge about which grub we've got sorted? Ye'a, I've brought some pasties from Sunderland. Still have the taste of the coast in 'em – do hope you all like it! Delicious! Pasties are the best. I’ve brought a few links of Cumberland sausage and this big tub of confit potatoes. I had them in Alsace and it’s my new favourite way to eat spuds. You'll need those to go with those pasties! I’ve retrieved a tub of decent scallops from the seafood market this morning. Smoked haddock if we want fish too. Brilliant, we'll have a proper English feast. And to drink, should we stick to your local booze? I brought up a couple of bottles of cask ale from Leeds. Ron, you know how it is, the local spot? Nah, this German beer I got for you all. Heirich Daniels or Bitburger. They’re both decent so pick your poison. I’ll go with the Heinrich. It’s pretty quaffable. And what about music? Any playlist ideas? I was thinking we could do a bit of Friday night retro. Should we stick to the classics – Beatles, maybe? Good idea. I could add some Oasis to that? Or maybe something a bit harder? Like a bit of Arctic Monkeys? Or would that be a no from some of the lads? Nah, I think all of you here like a bit of the Monkeys. Seems fitting for our age group together. Perfect idea. I can add some newer bits. How about we also include some German or French classic? It's about culture, after all and it's always good to learn a bit about the others. Good call, Ron. I’ll pull some Kraftwerk and some soundtrack from Quentin Tarantino for good measure. That’s so brilliant, mixing all up! Can we have a playlist name? Like 2000+ Borders. 2000+ Borders sounds class! You all clearly have great tastes. Now, on to movies. Anything stand out that we need to watch before the year out? For me, it has to be "Montage of Heck". The new Kurt Cobain bio-doc... I can’t agree more. Though if we pick a simpler one, "The Grand Budapest Hotel"? It’s always so joyful and witty.

Hey everyone, did you hear about that new gym that's opening up in Cambridge? I think it's going to be pretty sweet. They're even offering a discount for students. That's right! I got the email about it. It says they have all the latest equipment and even have personal training sessions if you're interested. Speaking of exercises, have you guys noticed how the weather has been lately? I'm actually struggling to get motivated as the mornings are so grey. Yeah, keeps changing right? But it actually affects our mood too, right? I swear, when it's sunny, I'm in a much better mood at the gym. Definitely! I find when it's sunny, I have more energy to get up and go. But in winter, it's a lot harder. Agreed. One thing that always cheers me up, no matter the weather, is music. Have you guys heard that new Ed Sheeran album? It's amazing! I haven’t had a chance yet, but I heard it’s good. I recently listened to that new song by this up-and-coming band from Liverpool called The Riots. I think I missed that one. You know, the kids' camp I volunteer for in the summer is a lot about music too. It’s really nice bringing music and exercise together. Ah, the kids' camp! How was it this year, Alex? It was really good. One of the kids actually asked if I could teach them how to play "Wonderwall" on the guitar. It was pretty fun. That's cool! I always wondered what it would be like to volunteer for something like that. Yeah, I’ve done computer game development for kids in the past. It’s similar, but focused on digital. The kids were way more interested in making their own games rather than following a traditional sports regime. There must be something about creating something that motivates them. Definitely. It's amazing to see them so engaged. They learn so much - not just about the activities, but also teamwork and expressing themselves. That’s true. And it must be rewarding to see that. Speaking of creating, I’ve been thinking about starting a blog. Got any tips on that? For sure. As an editor, I’ve got a bit of experience. First off, you need to decide on your niche or topic. And don’t forget to keep your content concise and engaging.

Ah, I'm losing my voice from screaming at the TV. We have to win today. The Northern lads never lose to the team from the Midlands when it comes to this competition. You're right though, you've really got to give the Black and Whites credit this season. They've played some fantastic football. You've got no argument from me there. But this is a special day, and I have a feeling it's going to go our way. Do you remember when we used to go to the stadium for these matches during Easter? Of course! We'd have a great time, seeing all those families with their Easter eggs in the stands. It always seemed like the best accompaniment to the match. And we'd often watch the same film afterwards. Do you remember that one about a little village in the English countryside? It's on again this Easter. Want to watch it when the match ends? Yes, definitely! That was a hilarious film. Reminds me, there's a new one that similar type coming out soon. I saw the trailer. Someone should make a sports comedy next. I think it could be a hit. I'm sure it could. Now come on, focus on the game. We need to stay positive if they're going to pull through this comeback. They've got the entire St. James' Park behind them. They do at that. But it's not just about encouragement, it's about skill and strategy as well. I feel like we're missing an opportunity to exploit their left flank weakness. Ah, always the strategic thinker. And yet, they've still taken two goals from us doesn't they? But it's not over yet. Look at the clock - only 10 minutes to go. Anything can happen. That's very true. I just hope our lads hold up under the pressure, they've matched the opposition’s energy so far. They have, and we can't let them down now. We've been through so much together as a family, and changing the channel to that Easter film on YouTube might just be the distraction we need to keep the spirits up. You're right again. But before we do that, let's truly soak in this moment. It's not every day our teams face off like this. Agreed. And let’s hope it ends in tears of joy for them and maybe a few tears of relief for us.

Ah, isn't this great now, the old photo album is out? We can have a proper look through and reminisce a bit. You'd have grown up with the twins by now! Yeah, sure. Might just show me up, though. I bet they were cute as buttons in every single pic. Alright, alright. Let's have a proper look. These were the early days. You both were such tiny rascals. Ah, darling, why don't you start at the beginning? They were both bubblier than the fizz in a bottle of Guinness from day one! Alright, let's go. You were measured in months in this one weren't you, lads? Speaking of Glasgow, your gran here was a couple of years after us but just as full of life. You know, I can sort of see it. But does everyone have to be so serious in every picture? It was indeed a different time, lad. They were tiny and overwhelmed by so much new and foreign. You know, it's funny. I was reading about the London marathon. It's amazing how many people take up running or start training thinking about something so big. Oh, I can imagine. Remember when your father was planning to run it? I’d bring the class out to St. George’s Field for a “London Marathon Viewing Party” if it passed by the school. That's right! I had almost forgotten that. You were always proactive with bringing the community and events together, as if the whole city was part of your classroom. I never realized, running the marathon is a big deal. It really can be. It's about perseverance, training, and often raising money for charity too. Indeed! And when we went to Iceland years later, equipped with our newfound appreciation for distances and terrains. That trip was a marathon in itself. Iceland? What was that like? Oh, it was incredible! We saw so many places, took photos at every stop. Some were just plain silly, like the ones at the craft fairs where we indulged in too much sweet and sticky things. You know, I used to bring my classes on outings sometimes. It wasn't just about geography or history; often it was about showing them the world was full of wonders and sometimes even little wonders at your

Thank you so much for inviting me over for dinner, it's been ages since we've caught up like this. Well, it's about time! I'm so glad we could finally make this work. Right after we moved to this new house and I settled into this role, things have been manic. It's been lovely to have you, dear. I've been meaning to ask, have you tried any new recipes of late? Now that you're settled, maybe? Ah, keeps changing as I experiment with different cookbooks. But for tonight, it's a classic, comfort food theme. Scones with clotted cream, just like dear old England used to be. Scones - lovely. But actually, while we're on the English theme, we could do with hearing more about your childhood and how things used to be back then. Oh absolutely. You know, we used to play quite a lot of traditional English games like hopscotch and skipping. It wasn't so common with the newer games that came in or even the toys. Nowadays, I see this 'it's a small world' toy or whatever is trendy and I find myself saying, "gosh, when we were kids, we were so inventive. We made entire worlds with just a few sticks and some imagination." Well, technology has certainly changed the way children spend their time, hasn't it? I remember sitting for hours knitting or crocheting, making hats for the cold winters or soft toys for the children. That's quite right. I was terrible at it but marveled at the patience and the skills that came with it. I've actually taken up knitting during lockdowns. It's been surprisingly therapeutic, you know? But it's just me, I'm the odd one out compared to most young people today who would rather scroll through their phones or play video games. While I agree technology offers a world of learning opportunities, there is something unique about these traditional skills. Absolutely. And in these busy times, I find myself turning back to real books over eBooks. There's something about holding a physical book that feels comforting and almost nostalgic. I could never give up my eBooks entirely though. There's just something convenient about having access to thousands of titles right at your fingertips. I've heard of these eBooks but I think I'd just end up being confused if someone handed me an e-reader.

Ah, I'm starving. I swear, it's almost as though I'd been working all these years for those sandwiches. You're right though, you've really earned it. A bit of rest after all this time is fair, isn't it? It certainly is. You know, I wish I could have settled into retirement a bit younger, but I had to wait till now. Costessey was always... ...a bit limited in opportunities, to be honest, especially for a lad like me who didn't quite have the head for sticking with school. I understand that, we both come from areas that were sometimes... limited. Harrow was a bit of a mix though—wealthy areas and then, just beyond the station, you'd see the signs of neglect and poverty. I didn't always understand it, as a child, but... And now we spend our days in a world very different from the ones we grew up in. No judgment, but... it's a different pace this side of life, isn't it? Absolutely. I found the childminding actually very fulfilling in its way. It was its own kind of work, really, bringing up those young ones. But it didn't exactly prepare me for a job market that was less... patient with older workers, especially without 'proper' qualifications in fields that were really booming at the time. 'Proper' qualifications... I had my share of things that didn't quite translate from Costessey to the wider world. But you know, we both did our bit, didn't we? Whether it was the school or the clubs or just looking after our own families, weren't we both... useful? We were. We were useful, valuable in our own small ways, but... it's strange, after all these years, to sit here thinking about what could've been. You working, I perhaps taking on more of a career in early childhood... It’s like sitting in a room full of what-ifs. But, I think, one of the things we've learned is that being useful doesn't have to mean being employed by someone else. Being here for each other, looking after our own little patch of England... that's been work we didn't formally qualify for, but it’s the most rewarding kind. Absolutely. And now, in our retirement, I think we're finding that usefulness in each other too.

Hey everyone, great to see you all! How was your week? Mine was pretty hectic; these GCSEs are nipping at my heels. Cheers, well, my week wasn't too different! The kids are nice but it's all the paperwork, you know? Oh, don’t get me started! But on a happier note, have you all seen the new ads that have been out? There’s one for the new cat food I’m really impressed with; very well-written. Ah right, yeah, actually, let me pull it up on my phone here, see if I can show you. Oh, by the way, have you two heard about Sally’s new dog? It’s gone and chewed up her car seat. Oh god, poor Sally! I should probably get her some of that chew toy you were going on about. Yeah, and speaking of creative solutions, have you heard the story about little Jack at school? He brought in a model of the Eiffel Tower made out of spaghetti and rubber bands. The whole class was talking about it this morning. Ha! That is genius! Kids have the best sense of perspective. Reminds me of when I tried to give my niece some educational gifts and she just wanted the box and to make a castle out of it. Well, technology-wise, have you guys considered getting into some new educational apps? I found one for primary phonics that really does seem to help the kids stay engaged. Yeah, all those educational apps can be pretty useful. But I’m still waiting for the real breakthrough in tech where the homework just does itself. Wouldn’t that be nice? I’m thinking of taking a holiday soon though; really need a break from the routine. Oh, where were you thinking of going? I’m dreaming of a Spanish retreat for a week or so. There’s something about the warmth and culture that really draws me in. That sounds amazing. I’ve always wanted to go on a language course abroad but never found the time. I spent a week in Brighton last summer though for work and I really enjoyed just exploring. Brighton is lovely! And if anyone is going to a beach holiday soon, watch out for the sand. One of my kids got it everywhere and it was a nightmare to clean. I’ve heard sand can cause more trouble than it’s worth with the cleaning.

Ah, good day everyone. I've been meaning to move houses for a while now. You know how it is, the old council estate is slowly falling apart, and the landlord doesn't seem all that concerned. Is that right? I've noticed the same thing. Our estate is one of the oldest in the area, and while it's got a certain charm, it definitely shows its age. I've been thinking of moving too. The maintenance has gone downhill ever since they privatized it. Speaking of keeps changing, I've just finished reading "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" again. It never gets old! Did you all read it as kids? Oh, absolutely! I think "Philosopher's Stone" is still my favorite in the series. I've never read it all the way through, but my sons love it. It's a shame that sometimes these estates can't aspire to the magic of a Hogwarts. Yeah, and what's with the council never doing anything about the gang activities that happen sometimes around this area? It's quite worrying. That is concerning. The local crime rate can certainly affect the quality of life here. It’s the main reason I’ve been trying to find a safer place for my family to live. It’s always something isn’t it? There’s crime, and in school, we’ve started to learn about things like ISIS, and all the conflicts in the world. It can get quite overwhelming. Indeed. These topics are difficult to discuss, especially for our younger attendees. But it’s important to stay informed and aware. More reason for us to support a safer community, perhaps through local community initiatives. I used to regularly volunteer for a local skills workshop for young people. Organizing sports activities or skill-building workshops can help keep kids engaged and away from negative influences. Yeah, that sounds like a great idea. Plus, I think we should have more activities like that in school, instead of always focusing on so much homework. It does seem like a good approach. However, as a receptionist, I sometimes have to deal with people almost my age who are just looking for work. There just aren’t enough jobs for everyone. That’s a challenging aspect too. Job creation and better training programs are crucial. For example, I've seen some great progress in vocational education where apprenticeships can often lead to well-paying jobs...

Ah, I'm so excited about our trip to Nepal! We've been planning this for months. It's been ages since I've been on such an adventure, and I have to admit the thought of the various high-altitude treks does give me a bit of nervousness now and then. But I'm really looking forward to it. Oh, Jane, I remember when we used to have those kind of adventures when we were younger. I've been thinking about suggesting a guided tour, don't you think? It would be nice for us to have that extra support, given our ages, and would let us focus more on enjoying ourselves. Yes, good idea! After all, at our stage, we need all the support we can get. Speaking of support, what about ensuring our food needs in Nepal? Do you need to pre-order any special dietary items, perhaps gluten-free meals? Yes, we are taking that into account. In fact, Ron, my husband, is quite used to cooking gluten-free these days. But we'll need to check with the tour provider on what's available. That reminds me, I've started this new routine for our free school meals system which includes all sorts of different dietary needs including gluten-free. It's been quite an adjustment but the kids seem to be liking the variety. That's interesting to hear. Over here, in the village, we're lucky to have a wonderful Farm Shop and Village Shop which cater to many dietary needs. Speaking of which, have you tried the new sausage rolls from the Village Shop? They are quite the talking point! Yes, I have! I must say, they're much appreciated, especially now that I'm the school display co-ordinator. It's good that local shops are on board with such initiatives. Right. And side note, I’ve been seeing those Tour of Britain cyclists training through local roads. Do any of our kids take part in sports like that? Actually, my daughter Annabelle is an Iron Woman and has been training a lot for the past few months. We're very proud of her accomplishments. Fantastic! What’s her routine like in terms of food and snacks when she’s training? Well, it's quite regimented. A lot of protein and complex carbohydrates. However, she's found it quite challenging sometimes, especially when she's away from home.

Right, so I'm over at Annie's house in Cambridge. We have Grace and Sarah here as well. Nice! It's been ages since we all got together. How've you all been? It's been good, considering, but I kind of regret going back into admin after finishing my postgrad. It feels like a step back sometimes. Yeah, I know what you mean, Sarah. Conference co-ordinating can be quite straining too. Lots of pressure and weird hours. Speaking of jobs, did you hear about the production company downtown? They're looking for production controllers. I've been considering sending off my CV. Might just do that then. How's the work-life balance been treating you, Grace? It's alright. Some days are better than others. Like most admin jobs, it's either really quiet or completely manic. But I also get to work from home quite a bit, so that's a bonus. That's true, the flexible hours really help. So, have you guys decided what we do tonight yet? I'm free to plan something if you want. We could go for drinks somewhere. I saw the 'Rusty Nail' pub had a pretty cool beer selection. Do either of you have anything planned? Not yet. Sounds good to me, though. I'd love to try some of those craft beers. Yeah, let's go for drinks then. It’s a Sunday evening, we can make it simple. How about 8pm at the Rusty Nail? 8pm works for me. Is that okay for everyone else, too? That's great. Seems like the best plan for now. Perfect. So, we are on? Grab our coats and let's head out. Absolutely. We should also catch up on life outside work. Sarah, tell us about your hiatus from theatre. You were really passionate about it. It was tough. I still miss it, but work and life have a way of getting in the way. But I'm looking at trying to get back into it soon, maybe with an amateur group. That could be really fun. We almost didn't make this catch-up. Annie was asking what we planned to do and we settled on this randomly. It shows we've got our priorities right — our friendship. Even when we get bogged down at work. Exactly. It’s really important to keep these social ties.

Ah, I'm so glad we could find a time to catch up. I've been meaning to reach out to you about something that's causing quite a stir in our local community. Fire away. You look quite animated about it. What’s brewing? Well, as you know, the local library in Plumstead is due for demolition and rebuilding. But the proposal doesn’t seem to consider our elderly residents or students who rely heavily on the library. That is a worry. Libraries provide so much more than just a quiet place to read. Exactly. So a few of us have started a petition to try and persuade the council to reconsider. It’s a bit of a long shot, I know, but every signature counts. Good on you for taking the initiative. Is the council hearing any complaints or have they already made up their minds? They've held a few meetings and made it clear they’re thinking in terms of modernizing. They believe a new building with digital facilities will serve the community better. But I can't help thinking they’re missing a lot. Like the value of physical books and quiet spaces for study or meetings. I understand the sentiment. There's a certain charm to browsing the shelves of a library. Digital is important, but it can’t replace the experience of physically holding a book, smelling the paper... Ah, the smell of old books... A memory trigger right there. For sure, speaking of which, I've been trying out some mnemonics and memory techniques from that new brain training app I downloaded. It’s helping a bit, but I still struggle with the name that rhymes with Helen... Let me guess, you mean Clementine? Precisely! Clementine. Every time I try to remember her name, I end up thinking of that fruit. Oh, that classic one. I recall from my days of studying for my graduate degree, I used to use the “Memory Palace” technique. You create an imaginary place in your mind, then place items you need to remember in specific locations in this “palace.” Sounds a bit whimsical, but it worked for me. Sounds interesting. I might try that. Speaking of studying, how’s your week been at work? I heard you're on a new shift pattern. Yeah, it’s been a bit of an adjustment. The new schedule means longer days but with more breaks.

Ah, good day, old mates. Lovely to catch up over some lunch. On the road these days, what's been happening with you both? Cheerio, well, not much. Still here in the village, isn't it? Just trying to enjoy this fine weather before winter sets in. You've been out and about? Indeed, I have. Went out with the grandkids a bit last week, got some of that lovely autumn sunshine. I had them collecting conkers and it was so much fun. We even made some string and all. You two been keeping busy? Busy? Well, not exactly. I've been trying to sort out some of this clutter in the house. Sentences of just trying to make it habitable. You're telling me. Dust everywhere, papers piled up... [chuckles] Even started reading some old newspapers again out of boredom. Clutter, pollution of the mind, they say. But, you know, it's hard to let go. I couldn't believe the amount of stuff I had when I went through my mother's house. A treasure trove, really. Sure, but it's a balance between keeping treasures and the dilly. [laughs] Speaking of treasures, how about we order in? Stunned at the café, they do a mean fish and chips. Though, sometimes I wonder if it's worth it – prices are through the roof! Indeed, it's shocking how much things can cost these days, isn't it? The way we’re always being taxed... never ends. Food, parking at the coast, even the dentists… it's all a raid on our wallets. True enough. Except, I've been meaning to visit my dentist. Last visit was ages ago. Seems like the government's got their hands in everything just like the Jehovah's Witnesses are everywhere. Ah, yes, those Jehovah's Witnesses. I've seen them around here and there, but never really stopped to talk. You'd think after all these years of knocking on doors – I mean, some are quite friendly in their own way. I recall a few years back, they were quite vocal about election times. Discussion on who we should vote for, of course. Again and again with the election. It’s like almost as much effort as attending church. Though, I don’t think they'd appreciate being compared to churchgoers, eh? Well, I can't say I've ever joined the club, but I do wish people could vote for change instead of just the usual suspects.

Ah, I'm so glad you could both make it from Edinburgh. It was quite a surprise; we hadn't spoken about your visit beforehand. How was the journey? It was quite manageable, actually. There were quite a few delays at the train station, but considering, we made fair time. We had some lovely views outside once we got past London though. But, I must say, the weather took a turn for the worse as we arrived. Oh no, hope you didn't get too soaked! And how was Tokyo? You must be still buzzing from all the excitement. Yes, Tokyo was absolutely fascinating. The city’s energy is unlike anywhere else, and the food, of course, is incredible. Though, let’s admit it, even after two weeks, the jet lag was still catching up with me. But the whole experience was truly enriching. And to be honest, it's made me appreciate some of the log burners we've seen here, as sometimes London didn't always feel as warm. Right! Speaking of warmth, have you both tried the new Italian place down the village? They say their pasta is exceptional. Oh, we have, actually. It's a pleasant addition to the community. Their carbonara is surprisingly traditional, and the staff are very welcoming. Quite a change from the usual local eateries. Exactly. It's good to see some new blood in the village. Though to be frank, my real excitement came from visiting the antique shop on the high street. They had this really unusual log burner, designed from the 17th century. And the fudge they sell there is to die for, if you're into that sort of thing. Antique shops are always a treasure trove, aren’t they? I do love seeing things from different eras. And yes, definitely, try the fudge. It’s homemade and absolutely delicious. I noticed a lot of restoration work in the village too. Is it all by local craftsmen? There’s a mix of local and outsourced work. Some of the large-scale projects, they’re bringing in professionals from further afield – I heard there’s even work being done by people from India. Which leads me to something else, have you both heard about the changes in the school system? They're considering a policy to outsource some administrative tasks, and it’s causing a bit of stir. Yes, the outsourcing debate.

Ah, I'm losing my patience with this Sat Nav business. It's supposed to make things easier, but all it's doing is taking me on these long, convoluted routes. Why can't they just give me a straight road to where I need to go? [laughs] You know, questions like this remind me of conversations we used to have at the pub, eh, John? Sat Navs weren’t even a thing back then, and we managed just fine! [chuckles] Well, it’s not that bad, is it? I mean, it keeps me from getting stuck somewhere I don’t want to be. Like when I used to drive the children around for their childcare jobs. [grumbles] Not like it ever actually shows you what's going to happen ahead. Was stuck on that A47 the other day for an hour. And to think, we used to just use a map and common sense. [nods] That's true, John. Back then, when we were working on the civil engineering projects, we often relied on maps and old experience. And you know what? It usually worked out alright. Oh, come on, it’s no use being grumpy about technology. We're retired, most of us, and this world is moving faster and faster. We just need to keep up. [sighs] I know. But it’s technology that's driving prices up, isn’t it? Like buying a house now, it’s ridiculous. I remember when we could get a really good place for under £100,000. And tax and pension – can't even catch up with how much things are costing these days. [shakes head] Terrible, isn’t it? And the politicians seem more interested in their own pockets or fighting each other rather than fixing any of these problems. [sighs deeply] Speaking of money, have either of you got your pension sorted out? I’m still trying to figure mine out and it’s been a bit of a nightmare changing the plans from what my husband set up before he passed. Mine was more straightforward because I had a workplace pension, but still, I have to pay my fair share of taxes. It feels like I’m being taxed from everywhere: income, property, even that infamous council tax! [nods] Yeah, and it’s not just income. I noticed how much we pay on water and services now, compared to when we first moved to Costessey.

Ah, I'm losing patience. I need this computer running by tomorrow. I called today and the techie person said that since it's six months out of warranty, they wouldn't fix it under warranty. Is that right? That's not fair, the thing’s only a year old! I know, and it was a pretty expensive model. But the woman at Dell insisted that it’s now out of warranty. Oh dear. Maybe we can find a local repairman? That's a thought. Or maybe there's something wrong with the warranty, like they didn't register it properly. Or maybe we can file a complaint. You've got your paperwork right, have you? I have all the receipts and records from when I bought it. They even sent an invitation to register the warranty online which I did. It's just they said the warranty expires six months after purchase, not a year. That doesn’t sound right. I've dealt with Dell warranty issues before. It's usually twelve or twenty-four months. That's what I thought too. We should call them again and push back. I can try helping. I've got some basics in computer repair. That might be useful, but this is a bit more complex, I think. It seems the motherboard is fried or something. I'd rather look into the warranty, see if we can argue the point in writing or something. Okay, good idea. Maybe we can also check online forums. Sometimes people have similar issues and come up with workarounds or find loopholes in the warranty. You could also do some research if it’s worth repairing versus buying a new one. Maybe the repair cost wouldn’t be too far off what a new one would be. True. If we can't get it fixed or can't get them to honor the warranty, maybe it’s best to look into a new computer. You know, I can do some of that. I was on the phone for hours with Amazon last week for a different issue and I just decided to send it back and wait for a new one. Good point! It's probably quicker and safer in the long run. What about the Fajita sauce we made last night? Did you put it out for dinner? Ah yes, good thinking! Sticky out ears, funny thinking you’d

Who wants to start on those pizzas? I do! Yay for pizza night! Me too! Do they have handstands on the menu? Only if you're ordering from the circus menu! But let's get questions back to food real quick. Do you guys want plain cheese, or would you like some toppings? I want a plain cheese, but can I have a side of chips? Sure, we can get you that. Can I get pizza with ham and pineapple? That's my favorite! Of course, dear. I'll make sure you get a lovely slice. So, can we make a fairy garden while we eat pizza? What's that? It's a small garden we can make with flowers and little fairy figurines. It's creative and we can set it up in the little corner over there by the window. Yeah, and we can talk about the Loch Ness monster while we eat! Did you know it's this big sea creature that lives in Scotland? That sounds cool! I think fairy gardens should have tiny boats for the fairies to explore. Maybe even a tiny Loch Ness monster? That's a good idea! And remember, it's not really a monster, it's just a legend. Oh, okay. But can we still think it's a monster? For the garden, I mean. Sure, you can make the Nessie a friendly guardian of the garden. Now, is the pizza ready? Everyone: Yes! Alright, let's eat and then we can start on the garden. So while we eat, can we play a little math game? How many slices will you each get if I cut the pizza into four equal slices? Four! Each of us gets one! That's right! If there are three of you, how many slices do we need to make? Three! Because 3 x 1 = 3. Brilliant! And if we have 4 slices in total... I get one! And the two adults. So, 1, 1, 1, and 1. That’s 4 slices taken care of. Can we try more math later? Like... if you have 5 fairy figurines and 3 of them go missing, how many do you have left? That's a little advanced for now, but I'd say we could try some basic subtraction later. So, 5 - 3 = 2. You would have 2 fairy figurines left. I want to try!

Have you all had a chance to try Istrian pasta or any other local specialties today? I grabbed some for lunch and thought it was delicious. Oh, yes! I've had two lunches here already and really enjoyed the fish soup. It's the kind of hearty meal that instantly makes you feel like you're truly visiting Istria. Is that a part of the traditional cuisine here? I've been wondering, does Istria have its own unique culinary identity? Absolutely, it does. Istria is a unique blend of Italian and Croatian cultures, and that shines through in the food. Along with the fish dishes, the pasta is also quite distinctive. They make use of locally sourced ingredients, just like the pasta you tried. That makes sense. I also tried some truffles on my pasta. They're apparently quite famous here. Yes, black truffles are a big deal. They even have truffle hunting tours here. Really? How does it work? Do you go out into the woods and search for them like treasure hunting? I'm not quite sure. But I bet it would be fascinating. Speaking of foraging, has anyone noticed the local wildlife around the hotel? Oh, definitely. Especially the birds. I saw a group of starlings by the pool today. Their singing is quite beautiful. Yes, I love listening to birdsong. It always seems to bring a bit of calm. But have you all noticed the weather? I'm glad we didn't have to bring our winter coats. But it's still quite breezy in the evenings, isn't it? Yes, it is. And the swimming pool is great, but the outdoor pool may be a bit chilly in the early mornings and evenings. If you think this is breezy, you should have seen the weather in London recently. It's been quite unpredictable. That's interesting. My teacher mentioned something about climate change in our science class and that London’s weather might be affected more because of its urban environment. As a Midwife, I've also noticed changes in the environment that affect health. But let's not get too serious about this. What about something fun? Where is everyone thinking of visiting here in Istria? I was reading about Pula and its Roman heritage. They have some fantastic ruins and museums. Oh, Pula is definitely worth a visit. I might actually drive there tomorrow or this weekend.

Right, I had a bit of an issue with that debt collector this morning. They really won't let up, will they? Oh, yes. They seem to just be on repeat, right? Still, now, the show’s on pause, let’s get back to lunch. I saw a great TV show this week, "PPI and You" was the title, I think it’s very informative. That sounds boring, I prefer something with more drama, like a party. I suppose seeing people, new faces, makes for a good change. I used to love attending parties in London when we lived there, but now, I prefer smaller gatherings. Perhaps a dinner party soon? We could even plant some seeds to use in cooking. Seeds? You mean like actual garden seeds? Or maybe in the context of… sewing? We could start a little project. I’ve always wanted to try driving again, ever since I last drove before Vikki was born. Well, if you're busy planting or driving, how about I set up our system for this magazine article about PPI? It’s quite relevant at the moment and might help us understand better. Well, technology baffles me, but if it helps, I’m all for it. And in return, maybe I’ll get you guys to come over for dinner and we can discuss it. That sounds like a plan! But it’s not just about the PPI article, how about this; we could use the computer to start singing practice for when we go to the Church next? That’s a great idea! I’ve always loved singing in the Abbey. We could even look at old recordings or use online tutorials. I haven’t sung since my choir days, but I’m sure the old pipes still work. Or maybe it’ll be a new hobby? And Vikki and Tyler might join in! A little singing practice never hurt anyone. And speaking of Tyler, did he say anything about his driving lesson the other day? He was all excited about how he parallel parked. Parking’s just the start, but it’s good he’s keen. So, let’s all come together next week for dinner and a little singing practice. We can even make it a little event, like the old parties, just with a simpler menu. And I'll make sure to come up with a few old party tricks.

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up, Margaret. It's been ages. How's your day been at the court today? Oh, it's been quite eventful, but I suppose that's the usual here isn't it? Really? Anything particularly noteworthy? Well, we had a few interesting cases this morning, but honestly, most days it's just the same routine, right? Definitely. I used to think that teaching was predictable, but now I see it varies greatly depending on the lesson. That's true. I have to keep myself occupied with little tasks, but I suppose that's just part of being a court usher. I mean, even though most cases are scheduled, sometimes there’s delay or an unexpected need to step in. That must keep you on your toes sometimes, doesn’t it? Oh, it does. But it’s quite interesting in a different way. I learn so much about people and the kind of situations they find themselves in. That's fascinating. I'm often this side of the bench, teaching language, but listening to their stories could broaden my perspective. I think so too. You don't always get to hear about people's real lives in everyday conversation. Speaking of lives, how's your family? Do you still see much of Aiden and Emily, especially with your part-time job? They're doing fantastic actually. Aiden's at uni and Emily’s working and living in London. We catch up whenever I'm in town. That must be quite proud and bittersweet, having them all grown up and living their own lives. Yes, it’s both a joy and a little sad at times. But it means I get to travel to see them more now, even if it's just for the weekend. That's great, I always find travel to be so enriching. It really broadens your horizons. Absolutely. Though now, for me, I have to say it's more about seeing my family than trying new places, but I still enjoy a good journey when I can. I could use a break from the usual routine of teaching and the London traffic. I've been thinking of taking a short break to Scotland, perhaps visit my brother. He still lives near Hitchin. How is Scotland treating you? Oh, it's still my home, although I often miss the pace of city life.

Everybody, I'm so glad we could all come together like this. It feels so good to be surrounded by all my loved ones. It does! I'm so happy! Mummy, can we play some rhymes? Yeah! Mummy, please! We love rhymes! Alright, alright. Let’s get into the spirit, shall we? What rhymes do you want to sing? Mary Had a Little Lamb! Or maybe The Wheels on the Bus! Yes! Both! Alright, let's try Mary Had a Little Lamb first. "Mary had a little lamb, little lamb, little lamb. Mary had a little lamb, its fleece was white as snow." That was fun! Can you remember any more, Mummy? Oh, I can think of plenty. How about Hop, Little Squirrel? Or maybe Hickory Dickory Dock? Hickory Dickory Dock! Yes, please! "Hickory, dickory, dock, The mouse ran up the clock. The clock struck one, The mouse ran down. Hickory, dickory, dock." What a silly rhyme. Mice shouldn't be on clocks! Indeed. But isn't it fun imagining all these little stories through our rhymes? What's that you're holding, Mummy? Is it a book of rhymes? Oh, that? That's a book of children's poetry. Let me see if I can find something else you might enjoy. "In the meadows warm and wide, Twinkling dewdrops left their bride As the sun arose and kissed the ground The flowers woke up, dancing all around." Oh, that was nice! What’s it about? It's a rhyme about nature, about how the sun wakes up the flowers in the morning. Isn't it lovely to think about the little things in nature that make the world so beautiful? Yes! It’s like... having lots of money but also being happy with little things. Oh, funny thinking you’ve brought that up. What do you mean? Well, some people... I’ve heard... they have lots of money, like the Queen, maybe? But they might still not be happy. Maybe if they had enough money to have happy things, like books and rhymes, that would make them happy, right? Yes! Like the Queen could give us lots of money to buy books and have parties! Well, money can indeed buy us many things, but happiness... That’s a different story. Happiness can come from those little things, like our rhymes and being together. But sometimes, it can also come from having enough to live comfortably and doing things that bring us joy, like visiting new places or helping others.

Hey, I was thinking over the weekend - who first decided that inventing things should be monetizable? Haha, good one. It’s kind of funny because I was reading about how Thomas Edison tried to monetize his inventions. Still, now, the system’s so complex, right? So true. It’s insane how even kids can patent their gadget ideas now. Yeah, right? I was browsing a few articles about that. There’s this kid from China who got a patent for his hoverbike. Crazy stuff. Whoa, China's really dominating in innovation, isn't it? What with their advancements in tech, space exploration... Absolutely, it's like they're among the world leaders in science and tech now. And it’s not just about making money, but also about being a hub for innovation and creativity. I get that. But with all these inventions and tech, how do you think the future of work will be like? Oh, that’s for sure a mind-boggling question. I mean, there are rumours about jobs becoming redundant due to AI and automation. Exactly! I just read how a certain tech giant is investing heavily in AI. They’re even saying that they might make substantial profits from AI in the next decade or so. That’s super interesting. But, to invest in something as revolutionary as AI, you'd need serious capital, right? True, corporations are the ones that can afford to invest in that and they benefit the most from it. Yet doesn’t it feel unfair that it’s the big players who are leading the charge? Definitely, and if one day AI can invent the next big thing, who gets the patent? The engineer who coded it or the company that paid for it? If it was me, I’d argue that invention should be about solving problems or making lives better, but nowadays it’s often about changing the world to profit more. Right. It feels like sometimes, the real inventors - the ones who start with a simple idea - just aren’t equipped, financially or so on, to make it big internationally. So true. And yet, without their start-up stage, without their initial curiosity-driven inventions, we wouldn't have the foundation for what we have now. Perhaps what we need is a system where inventors are better supported, not just financially, but through resources and education. That makes sense.

Ah, I'm so glad we could both make it here. The skiing conditions are supposed to be fantastic this week, aren't they? Absolutely! I've been checking various forecasts, and it looks like the resorts around here are all reporting top-class snow, even late in the season. Well, that's perfect! We definitely need to capitalize on that, don't we? Have you thought about our itinerary yet? Actually, I came up with a rough plan during breakfast. Considering we get a late start today, why don't we just relax for a bit, then head out to the nearby village to check out some shops and perhaps have a quick pint at that traditional bar in the square? It’s cosy and has great service. Brilliant! Yeah, a pint never hurts. And the village, it has such a lovely atmosphere. I’ve heard they have some amazing Bulgarian wine, do you know if that’s true? Oh, spot on! The wine is excellent. And it pairs well with whatever meal we pick up there. I heard the bakery near the square does a wicked meze platter. Perhaps we could grab some of that and have it as our lunch? That sounds like a great idea! I’ve been craving some authentic local food. And a meze platter is perfect, you can pick and choose what you want. Exactly. And then we take it back here to the hotel to enjoy it before hitting the slopes later. How about if we aim to start around 2, get a good lunch in, and then maybe do a couple of runs before the apres-ski festivities start in the evening? Sounds like a perfect day! You’ve really thought all of this through. I can’t wait to try that grape brandy, I’ve heard it’s a specialty here, isn’t it? Yes, definitely. It’s called Rakia and is often enjoyed while snacking on something savory. I’ll make sure to pick some up for us to try. We could sit outside if the weather holds up, it’ll be lovely. Wonderful! I’m feeling really well organized today just because of this planning session. It’s such a relief not to have to worry about what we’ll do or where we’ll eat. Me too. And this way, we can just relax and enjoy the holiday.

Ah, I'm losing patience with these badminton rackets breaking. Every string I try to re-string ends up snapping after a few hits. I've been trying using cable ties but the ball just doesn't fly right. Is there something I'm missing? Cable ties, eh? That's quite an innovative way to try and fix it isn't it? I remember once, I had this student who used them to keep his wooden bow intact while sailing – worked remarkably well, as long as there was no significant strain involved. However for a badminton racket, it might be a bit tricky given its weight and the constant impact it receives. Exactly! The strain is too much for just cable ties. I've been questioning if the dimensions of the racket have anything to do with it. Maybe the strings I'm using aren't right for its specific dimensions? Dimensions and materials definitely play a huge role. The racket's size, the balance point, string thickness and tension are all factors. What if we experiment with thinner strings but tighter? That might provide more strength. And it would save costs because thin strings are generally less expensive. That makes sense. For a start, this racket is maybe 28 inches long and has about 25 grams in weight. If we’re going for thinner, stronger strings, maybe we need to look into graphite or titanium – but those cost a pretty penny, right? Certainly, high-quality materials will increase the cost significantly, but for ensuring less breakage, it might be worth it. However, before we dive into that, why don't we trail another idea: positioning and weight distribution? What if we attach some small weights to the frame to distribute the impact better? Good point!
