Ah, I'm so glad we could find a spot here. The Bell Pub has always been my go-to when I'm in town. It feels homey, you know? Exactly. It's got the ideal blend of cosiness and just enough character to make it stand out – which is rare in this kind of setting. You've been staying in Norwich a lot lately, haven't you? Mostly for work, yeah. I've been doing a bit of research on the local history. Norwich is so rich in that, it's really fascinating. Have you ever noticed how much knowledge just disappears if nobody writes it down? True. It's such a dynamic process. I've been following some threads online about local history too, and it's astonishing how dedicated some people are to keeping that history alive – from village wars to pre-industrial agriculture. What's been keeping you up to date on all that? Well, it's mostly for my lectures. I've been thinking of broadening the curriculum a little, including some of these local historical points. It'd make it so much more relatable for students from here or even just interested locals. That sounds perfect. We should connect some dots here, maybe even collaborate on some content. I've been exploring some digital archeology while on this job. There's so much good stuff lurking in the deep web – think about all the old websites, now-defunct platforms, and forgotten social media – it's like a digital Pompeii. Oh, absolutely. I've found in my research that really old forums and user-generated content platforms are treasure troves. What's been popping up that you find particularly interesting? Oh, it's the mundane stuff that's so revealing. Just last week, I stumbled upon an old, unused design for Facebook – imagine if the news feed looked like that! More focus on pictures, groups weren't the central feature. The early adopters really took it in a different direction. And think about all the early blog platforms like LiveJournal or Xanga. Reading those posts is like listening to a first-person audiobook from the early 2000s. That's so cool. I've had students express nostalgic feelings about these old platforms but it's hard for them truly grasp what they meant at the time. This kind of firsthand history is invaluable for understanding the evolution of the internet.

Hey, I'm starving. I need some beans on toast or something. Sure, I can put that together for you. But first, let's talk about that film. You love 'Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs' though, right? Yep, it's one of my favorites. It's just got such an unusual theme. I mean, a town with a food machine where food falls from the sky? It's such a simple concept, but so smartly executed. Exactly. And it has a great message too, right? Like, about the dangers of greed and exploiting Earth's natural resources for your own gain. Precisely. And thinking about that, have you noticed how even kid's films can have really mature themes? Like, from racism in 'The Princess and the Frog', to gender stereotypes in 'Frozen'. Yeah, I've seen that too. But sometimes it's also creative and very appropriate for the film's context. True. But it also raises an interesting point - how much should kid's or even family films tackle serious issues? I mean, is it too much or should they be used as tools for educating as well as entertaining? I think it depends. Some kids are old enough to understand and process complex topics, but others, not so much. It's a bit of a tightrope to walk, I think. Aye, definitely, especially if it's not handled carefully in the film itself. They need to ensure it's not too heavy-handed or insensitive. Like when I saw 'Coco', I thought it handled the theme of death and the afterlife really well for a kid's film. Yes, 'Coco' is a great example. It was surprisingly mature, but in a way that made me, as an adult, appreciate it even more. It's also a reminder of how much value we’ve had from movies as conversation starters, really. Definitely. I think the film industry has really advanced in making diverse and thought-provoking content, though there's still room for improvement for sure. Yep, absolutely. And it also makes me think about how we've discussed all these things so openly and frankly today. Like religion, race, and even feminism. Yeah, and it's all the more important because these topics have become taboo in some public conversations. But with close friends and family, you feel like you can really discuss anything and get different viewpoints.

Ah, good day! How have you been? Same old. You know how it is, just driving around and chatting with folks from all walks of life. Had the usual mix of passengers today, including a couple from out of town who seemed puzzled by our Liverpool accent. You know, people often think it's all just "Scouse" but there's actually quite a bit of differentiation, especially between north and south! True enough, I've always found it fascinating how influential local dialects are. It can even change how you perceive certain ideas or concepts. Speaking of influences, have you been following the EU referendum outcome? It was quite the news last year. Oh, I've been following it from a distance. Honestly, it's been a bit disheartening. Seems like the divide between the political classes and the regular folk has just grown wider. And to be frank, it's made certain conversations with passengers a bit tense. It certainly has. I wrote a few articles on the topic, focusing on how these political events influence language and perception. You know, the shift in discourse, the rise or fall of certain terms... For instance, the use of "New Labour" symbols has almost disappeared since Blair. I remember when Blair was in power. I wasn't exactly engaged in politics back then, but I knew a lot of people who were. It seemed like there was hope at that point. Now, though, it feels like a different world. Like nobody's really taken the reins, you know? Yeah, the era of New Labour did bring a lot of change and a certain idealism. However, over time, it became clear that some socio-economic disparities persisted despite the rhetoric. It's the nature of politics, really – promising the world and, unfortunately, delivering only slices of it. Right. Seems like the government's more concerned with staying in power than actually solving the issues that really matter to people like me and my passengers. Jobs, housing, healthcare... these are the things that hit home, not parliamentary squabbles over EU regulations. Accurate observation. As a lecturer, I can tell you that these issues often come up in class discussions. Students want to understand not only the political and economic theories, but also how they truly impact daily life. It’s one thing to see statistics; it’s another to experience the lived reality. Well, let me tell you, living in Liverpool, we've seen our fair share of those political promises and broken hopes.

Hey everyone, did you hear about that new BNC recording's online workshop I attended today? The analysis of dialectal variations in South Eastern England was so fascinating! I talked to someone who's studying similar stuff on Welsh dialects. Want to hear more about it? That sounds interesting! I kind of do something similar in my editing days, though mostly with texts and transcripts rather than recordings. Like how words get "borrowed" from one region to another, you know?  laughs  It's like how even though I've heard loads of English people say "cyber space" instead of "cyber, space," you'd still see it written as "cyber-space" in Wales. Exactly! And that just shows how language is shaped by social interactions as much as by the place we're from. It's almost like we're each writing little versions of ourselves into language. It's also funny how some words are so deeply ingrained, yet we don't even realize they're regional. For example, in Wales we'd say "lovely" a lot more than English folks, at least from what I've noticed. Oh, totally. We say "lovely" all the time. I find "nice" is used more in England though, while "lush" is more of a North Wales thing. And you can't forget the influence of social media and technology. It's amazing how quickly slang and even grammar rules change across platforms, especially with younger people. Oh, for sure. LinkedIn is the worst, I swear. Everyone's so formal "proper English" but on Twitter, they're casual as can be. It's like the same people, different masks.  chuckles  Yes, or like how people "flip" between languages or dialects depending on who they're talking to or where they are. That brings me to living abroad. If you think hearing all these small differences is fascinating, try being in a place where everything around you is new! I was actually shocked by how much Brits abroad clung to certain phrases or customs. Definitely. I lived for a while in Spain and saw it often. People just want something familiar, something truly "blighty" to cling to. It's like comfort food for the ears. But sometimes it's the opposite, right? People try too hard to fit in and lose their own language or accent. That’s true. It's a delicate balance. I've seen colleagues who came back from abroad and sounded more "BBC" than ever.

Hey, I'm going to make pasta for dinner, can I bother you to help me prep the veggies? You're still at university, I don't know if you even know the proper way to dice an onion. Ha, it's all about the practice. Go ahead and do your questions if you're unsure. Between us three and your partner Sarah, we should have this house fully renovated by March, right? Speaker_3 : Hey guys! Just got home. Oh, Sarah mentioned you were cooking tonight. Can I help get dinner started or would you rather I just get started with the bottle of wine? Sarah’s actually supposed to be here soon, but I can have you do the wine. Is that a new tattoo? You didn’t mention. Yeah, got it done over Thanksgiving break - "Two roads diverged" from the Robert Frost poem. It's a bit of a classic, I know, but it's meaningful for me. That's a beautiful spot. And you know, it holds quite a lot of meaning. Past, present, what's to come. I hope you don't regret any decisions you make. Sure, but it's a balance between regret and learning from the journey, isn’t it? Anyway, we can talk about that later. How's the internship going at the literary magazine? Do you have any papers lined up for the Christmas issue? It's going well. The team is great, I love the type of work we do. The Christmas issue is still being discussed but there's a strong push for a round-up of some fantastic indie authors and some holiday-themed pieces. But it's tough, isn't it? There’s always this last-minute rush, and then you're all exhausted by Christmas. I can only imagine. Exactly. But I just found out they want me to write a piece about tattoos and identity, so I think this will fit right in. That's perfect and it really makes your tattoo relevant to work - a win-win. We could sit together and discuss it, if you want. Or does it feel too personal for work? I think it’s appropriate. Personal, but also so much about identity and how public art like tattoos influences personal identity. It will be very insightful. And if you're feeling stuck, just remember the power of metaphor. Your tattoo is already doing half the work for you.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up tonight. It's been ages. How have you both been since last we met at Aunt Helen's wedding? I've been well, thanks for asking. Quite busy with work, as usual. But now, let's focus on tonight's feast! That lasagna you made looks incredible. You always manage to make something so nourishing, Sarah. Ah, thanks! I'm glad you like it. I've been experimenting with new recipes. All very traditional Italian. You know, I've actually been meaning to try out my own Italian cooking class, but I never seem to have the time. Well, you should try it sometime. London has plenty of good ones. Maybe even here in Birmingham. Sorry we're late, by the way. Traffic was terrible coming from the centre. No worries at all, we were just chatting about food and cooking. So, have either of you been on any interesting travels recently? Actually, I took a short break to visit my sister in Brighton. The sea air was lovely. I’ve been meaning to visit Brighton myself. I’ve heard great things about the food scene there. Have you tried the seafood? Oh, the seafood is wonderful. But honestly, my sister's homemade fish and chips were the highlight of my visit. Speaking of food, I've been trying really hard to cut back on my sugar intake, but it’s not easy. I always end up craving something sweet after a long day of work. I know that struggle. I recommend trying dark chocolate or fruit. They're healthier options if you're in need of something sweet. Yeah, and a good workout can also help to curb those cravings. Speaking of which, I've started doing some Pilates online. It’s really improved my core strength. That's great to hear! I’ve been meaning to take up some sort of exercise class too. I tried yoga a few years ago but it didn’t stick. Maybe Pilates or even a dance class would be more my speed. I couldn’t agree more with trying Pilates. It's quite versatile and doesn't require a lot of fancy equipment. And if you're feeling adventurous, there's always Zumba. My friend in London loves it, swears it's a great workout and a lot of fun. That does sound fun.

I keep reading that Chinese people think our idea of stopping to take care of our toe nails is super quirky and clearly a sign of our deep-seated need for self-care and vanity. It’s just, the concept of a spa day – which is basically a status symbol back home – isn’t really a thing here, and the idea of getting a "toe nail treatment" makes some of our colleagues and students actually laugh! Exactly! But it’s also fascinating how even in teaching, those tiny little cultural differences sneak in and affect how knowledge is received or even, how we deliver it. It’s not about the subject matter, but the way we frame it that gets accepted or rejected. Totally. Like, when we discussed Plato in our class earlier today, I could see the students here making connections between his ideas and traditional philosophies like Confucianism or Daoism much more readily than students back in England. While in the English context, it often aligns more closely with Christianity and Western thought. It’s so interesting how the ground you’re standing on shapes your interpretation. Definitely. It makes you realize how culture isn’t just something different; it's a completely different lens through which you view everything. Speaking of lenses, how’s everything with our friends back home? Ah, they’re all doing well. Mike's just had a job change and is really enjoying his new position. Sarah had her little one last year and is doing great as a mom. John is still messing about trying to get a novel published but is hoping to hear back from agents soon. It’s great to hear that. We really miss them and our social groups but, on the other hand, this experience has been invaluable. Absolutely. Our students here are so... different, and yet, so eager to learn. It's really humbling to see the importance education is given here, regardless of the cultural framework. True, and changing the world takes place one lesson at a time. Well, if I teach enough people not to laugh at menial spa treatments, maybe I’ll truly be considered a cultural ambassador! You're already leading the charge by embracing the toe nail treatment. That's almost as revolutionary as any cultural shift. As long as my students are learning and adapting, I don't really mind being a funny-looking foreigner with pristine toe nails.

Ah, good to see you. I was just checking out the film section here. Have you seen any of the Oscar contenders this year? Ah yes, I did watch some of them. Are you still into films quite a bit? Always! But I’ve kind of switched to questions because some of these new films are so bizarrely narrated and produced. Like this year, "Sound of Metal" - brilliant film but also minimal language right? Exactly! That was a really immersive film. As a language teacher, it’s always fascinating to see how stories can be told without much vocals. It challenges our lazy reliance on dialogue as the primary storytelling tool. Absolutely! It actually made me think about how valuable sound is to film, not just dialogue. But back to language, do you find that the South-East UK accent still has a strong bias in media and film? Oh, completely! Birmingham as a city also has its very distinct accent, but if you go further up north or even into London it's like a whole different tongue. I find that those regional differences often get glossed over in media. It's certainly problematic, both in reflecting society accurately and in terms of representation. I've noticed it too, especially while teaching – it's hard to find materials that reflect the diversity of British dialects. Exactly. As a company director, though, accents shouldn't really matter, but in jobs like yours, especially as an educator, it's crucial for making all students feel represented, isn't it? Definitely. And that’s why I try to incorporate material from different parts of England in my lessons. Well, from what the curriculum allows, which isn’t always enough. Right, and it can be quite a career. Seems like the education sector hasn’t changed much since I was in school. The workloads are still ridiculous and funding is always tight. How do you manage it all? Lol, it's a balancing act. While teaching, I’ve also been trying to publish some research on language acquisition methods. It's quite fulfilling though because you can see real impact if your research translates into new teaching tools. That’s so cool! I’ve always admired academics who see the real world application of their work. Speaking of seeing the impact, have you had any new ventures in the company or job changes? I recently moved into a new position.

Dad, I'm so excited for our holiday! Jamaica Inn's supposed to have such a great atmosphere, right? Yes, it's one of the most atmospheric places in Cornwall. And did you know that it was also the setting for Daphne du Maurier's novel? No, I didn't! Can you tell me about the book? I love books and I'm sure the actual place must be even more exciting. Well actually, I've always been more of a Sherlock Holmes and Lewis Carroll kind of man... So, coming here, alongside all the medieval history and architecture, I think it's a bit like going to a fairy tale – with a twist of old England. That sounds amazing! I've read a bit about the buildings too, but what about the scenery we're seeing now? These colours on the road... this deep green and that blue sky? It's so vivid, I feel like I'm inside a painting sometimes. You know, we're in the northwest, so it's like a precursor to the wilds of Cornwall. Almost like we're journeying through those stories I love. For me, it's like a journey through the Wizard of Oz or Alice in Wonderland. These roads seem to just lead us into new worlds. Speaking of which, have we passed any of the wind turbines yet? We did on the way out of Manchester. Well, they keep popping up here and there. The shape is so industrial mixed with natural, it feels like an old storybook in itself: the smoke-filled chimneys and windmills of old transformed into green energy. I like how they break up the view, it's like seeing tall, giant flowers waving in the breeze. Actually, that reminds me, do you remember when I was little and we used to talk about different languages and how some use pictures like symbols or dots? Ah, you mean Morse code, Braille or even signs? Yes, those were always fascinating to me. I always loved how you could convey whole concepts through very limited symbols. Yeah, and how some of it feels like a riddle? Like if I saw a series of dots or flashes and had to figure out what they meant. It's like being a detective! It's all about codes and deciphering – very Sherlock. Yeah, or just being Wonderland's Alice trying to figure out what those symbols mean, or translating languages like a wizard using a translation spell.

Right, so everyone's seen the prices at petrol stations these days? It's crazy. I nearly choked when I filled up last week. It feels like it's been years since petrol was affordable again. Cheap petrol is but a distant memory for me now! But speaking of fuel, did you folks hear about that attempt to cross the Channel by swimming? Sounds bonkers, if you ask me. Oh, that’s quite a feat! But yeah, it’s not just fuel that’s keeps changing backwards. Remember when cinema prices were less than a few quid? Now, you’re lucky if you can see a film for less than a tenner. Totally, and it’s even happening with rent. Everyone’s always saying property prices are through the roof. I almost choked when I saw the new rent prices for my old flatspace. It's like they doubled overnight. While we’re on the subject of big changes, have you ever thought about how different things were during the war? I lived through it, though I was just a young lad. Things were a lot simpler, but maybe worse in some ways. That perspective is invaluable, dad. I can only imagine it. But it makes me realise how much things have evolved, not just in terms of cost, but in technology, politics, everything. Like, take A-levels for example, or even primary school curriculums. My nieces are doing things now that we'd never even heard of back in our day. Oh, it's the same with the games we played. We had to make our own fun, you know, no fancy smartphones or tablets. But the memories we made... I know, right? The simplicity of a board game or a few dice. Now, my friends will spend hours discussing game strategies on the phone. You can’t even cheat at games anymore without everyone noticing on their screens. I suppose that’s progress. Though, I still think we had it better in terms of exercise. Walking to the sweet shop or playing football after school was our gym. Mobility and healthcare have definitely come a long way though. I’ve seen relatives struggle with things we now take for granted, like just being able to move around freely or accessing healthcare more easily. And cars! Sure, they’re much more efficient and safe now, but I do miss the simplicity of older models.

Hey Mum, welcome back to Bedford. How was the move? It was a bit of a hassle, but everything is settling in slowly. It’s just chaos at the moment. I don’t remember where I put the weaver fish recipe you wanted though, and I need to defrosting something for dinner. You'd think you'd have that one memorized after all these years. I’ll check the kitchen, actually, I still have that recipe somewhere. Thanks, love. You know me too well. By the way, have you been keeping an eye on anything while I was away? Like the list of items I wanted to move over from my London flat? Yeah, I was about to sort through that actually. There’s a mix of your usual stuff and some odds and ends. I started compiling a list and made a rough scan of what you already brought over. That’s a massive help. Tonight, could you maybe go through that with me? I need to finalize the move. Also, I’d like to get a bit more organized before we start any bigger projects like looking at new houses on the market. Definitely. I’ve been dilly-dallying on that all week while I’ve been here. We can tackle that this evening. Speaking of which, how’s the jet lag been? It’s always an adjustment coming back here after London. It’s been tougher than usual, I think. The time difference does seem to hit me really hard. One night it was 2 am and all I could do was gaze out over Bedford. I don’t think I’ve ever connected with the local rhythm like this before the move. Yeah, that kind of makes sense, doesn’t it? Maybe it’s the fact you’re actually here now, not just visiting. Have you settled on any specific areas to look for a house? We talked a bit about different parts of town last time we spoke. Not really narrowed it down yet but I’m thinking a mix of something modern yet not too far from the center might be ideal. Though I have to admit, I’m also really thinking about the health aspect for me and Peter . We need something with easy access to public transport, maybe parks nearby. That sounds great. Bedford still has some lovely areas. And concerning health, how’s your memory being?

Have you seen the new reforms for A-Levels?? It's making me nervous. Yeah, I've seen the news about it. It seems like they're proposing some significant changes to the way A-Levels are assessed and run. Still trying to get my head around all the details myself. Exactly! It's a bit daunting, especially as research manager, I feel like my whole education system now seems to be in a constant state of flux. That it is. And it's not just changing for students, it affects everyone involved in education from teachers to parents to industry, really. It's such a foundational part of our society, so changes can have big ripple effects. Totally, and it's even happening as I'm looking to send my younger sibling through the system in a couple of years. That must be a worry. On the one hand, I suppose it's always good to be progressive and adapt, but how do we ensure changes are actually improvements and not just random shifts for the sake of it? Exactly! Sometimes I think the problem is that the people making these decisions are years removed from actually going through this system themselves. I understand the sentiment. When I was doing my undergrad, the system was already quite different from what I'd imagine at A-Level. Do you think there's anything we can do to get involved or have more influence over these changes? In theory, as higher professional occupations, we should have a voice in these matters, right? But often, it feels like the voices of those most affected — students and working teachers — get drowned out. Which is a shame. I've talked to some professors about this, and there seems to be a bit of pushback from within the academic community as well. That's good to hear! Maybe, as a group of researchers and educated professionals, we can advocate better for students. It feels like we should be raising concerns that are less confrontational but still pointed, you know? You're right. We could perhaps start by reaching out to local education policy groups or even contributing to some of these debates online. Absolutely. We need to show that we care about this stuff deeply and not just because of personal interests. It might be worth even engaging with local MPs or policy advisors. Many of them are quite open to feedback and engagement, especially from folks who work in relevant fields.

Right, so I'm reading this history stuff at uni and I've hit this chapter about the black plague. Have you lot ever learned about it? Oh yeah, the black plague! I studied that. It was horrendous, wasn't it? People thought the end of the world was coming. Yeah, it was really bad. I remember my history teacher telling us about how it spread across Europe. It makes you think about how lucky we are to live in a time with antibiotics and stuff. But even with all our medical advancements, people still get sick and die. It's like, we've moved on a bit, but not that much really. I know what you mean. It's just weird to think that things like that happened. I mean, we read about it in a textbook and it sounds like something from another world. Exactly. But what's interesting is how it changed society. It led to a lot of changes in labor laws and how cities were organized. And it also marks the beginning of the end of feudalism in some areas. I never thought about it like that before. So it wasn't just a health disaster, it was a socio-economic disaster as well. And it led to a lot of scapegoating too. People blamed the Jews and the poor and the sick. It's interesting how history can show us the same patterns repeating themselves. Yeah, it's like we're still dealing with those same issues today. Like with the COVID-19, people were blaming certain groups too. That's a good point. It's like we haven't learned much from history. Makes you wonder what we're doing wrong or what we need to do differently. But the plague also led to some of the first advancements in medicine. They tried to understand the causes and developed quarantine rules. Ah, okay, so even in all that horror, there's something positive. That's kind of hopeful. Yeah, and it's interesting to see how they tried to deal with it, though a bit late. They quarantined ships and tried these new treatments. It's just sad because so many people died. I mean, if we knew then what we know now, it could have been mitigated so much better. Definitely. It's just... the scale of it all is just so... Yeah. It's just crazy to wrap your head around.

You know, sometimes I've found it really hard to move on from friendships that no longer serve me. Really? Like, what happened? Well, I had this one friend from uni who I was really close to, but after we graduated, our interests and priorities just kind of drifted apart. Yeah, that can be really tough. You feel like you have to hang onto the friendship just because it was once important. Exactly. But even though it felt right at the time, it just became too much. So you phased out of the friendship? I tried that. But she's someone who just keeps reaching out, so even though I was not as keen, she kept the communication alive. That's really hard to handle. Yes, because I didn’t want to be mean or hurt her feelings, but at the same time, I barely see her now and our last conversations are just so shallow. I've been in similar situations. What was the hardest part about letting this friendship go? Honestly, I think the hardest part is the guilt. Even though I knew the friendship wasn't providing much for me anymore, the fear of being seen as a bad friend really held me back. That's very relatable. But do you think perhaps she's holding onto the friendship more than you are? Probably. Now that I think about it, all the effort was mostly from her side. So would you say it's sometimes okay to allow a friendship to kind of phase out naturally? Yes, I think so. As long as you're not just ghosting someone or being completely unresponsive, I think natural drift is okay. If you think about it, we all have finite time and emotional space. It's healthy to evaluate who we should prioritize and who we can let naturally drift away. I guess I needed to make that realization for myself. It wasn't until I focused on nurturing friendships that actually made me happy that I felt freer to allow some connections to naturally dwindle. It sounds like you've grown a lot from this experience. Definitely. But what I realised too is, it's okay not to force connections that just aren’t there any more. Some connections are seasonal, and that’s okay. I think that's a great perspective. So, what advice would you give to someone who’s in a similar situation?

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up, Aunt Susan. I've been meaning to call and update you on my university life but things have been so hectic with exams and all. It's lovely to hear from you, dear. I must say, you sound a bit stressed! Is everything alright with uni? Yeah, totally fine. Just the usual academic pressure and some extracurricular stuff I'm juggling right now. But honestly, I'm really enjoying it. I just found my passion for Art History keeps coming up in all my courses - it's fascinating how it ties in to so much, you know? Even my Philosophy module was engaging because it seemed to overlap so much with some of the artistic movements in 19th and 20th century Europe. Art History! Wonderful choice. There's so much depth to each period and style. I still love exploring those topics myself, even though my main medium has always been painting. Really? That's so cool, Aunt Susan! When did you first get into painting? Was it something you started as a hobby or did you study or learn from someone? Oh, it was both, really. I come from a family that encouraged creativity from the early days. But specifically with paint, I started properly in my late twenties. It was more of a hobby at first, but then, over time, it became such a central part of my life. I've had a couple of exhibitions here in London, which have been really rewarding. That's wonderful, really. Did you go through any formal training, or was it mainly self-taught? Mostly self-taught, but I've attended a few workshops throughout the years. There's this one particular mentor who helped me discover my style and technique. She was so insightful, and her methods really made painting more approachable for me. Who’s she? Maybe I’ve seen her work? Perhaps! She’s called Renee Dupont. She’s got a studio in Notting Hill. Her work is amazing — mostly abstract pieces, really emotive. Definitely rings a bell. I think we popped into a small art gallery near there once. The art pieces truly captured the essence of the city, if you know what I mean. That's definitely her. She could capture London's vibe almost as well as a photographer. Speaking of capturing things, Aunt Susan, have you got travel plans coming up?

You know, I'm really starting to think we've got too many sedentary days in this campervan trip. Should we try to squeeze in some gym time? Definitely, we've had enough of long driving days! But perhaps we should eat something now, before we go. If we do a bit of a workout, we can digest while we drive back. Smart thinking, as usual. Although, I wish I could get this stomach of mine to be more... accommodating. All this worry about eating before working out. It's weird how it makes me feel. Well, it depends on what you're going to do at the gym – if you're going for a heavy strength training session, it's definitely better to eat before. But just like cardio or yoga, you're probably okay waiting until after. Yeah, cardio sounds nice, perhaps. Though I have to say, being out of work for so long, its funny how things like looking after my diet or going to the gym seem trivial compared to the struggle of just finding something fulfilling. You know, it's interesting how those kinds of priorities or even attitudes towards health and body image can differ depending on where you come from, or even your socio-economic status. Exactly. I sometimes feel while I'm job hunting, it's the most awkward time – people can be so condescending or judgmental. It's like people connect being unemployed with being somehow lazy or less capable. Or, it's assumed that you're not in a race against time for your health, or your general well-being. Which is really unfair. Plus, doesn't helping others with English as you do also keep the mind sharp? Isn't that a form of mental fitness? Definitely. And let's not forget about all the cultural insights you get in that job. Plus, the fact that you keep learning. That should be valued more. It's really disheartening to see how quickly people and institutions forget about what's valuable in people - the skills, experiences, potential... It's like it all comes down to that piece of paper - the degree, experience. But what about all the other things? The adaptability, patience, empathy, creative problem-solving? So true. And yet, it still feels like those things often go unnoticed or underappreciated. Maybe particularly for women as well. Ah, yes, definitely. The gender bias issue - it's everywhere, isn't it?

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. Look how today's weather's turned out, isn't it wonderful for the garden after all the rain? You're right, Lily. It's as if Mother Nature decided to favor us this weekend. Though, speaking of gardens, have you seen those spiders in the garden room? Quite large and vibrant, aren't they? Oh, I've seen them of course, quite the impressive ones. Reminds me of when I was decorating this room, keeps coming back to how it suits a coffee session like this. Yes, it does. This room has become quite the little haven, hasn't it? Makes me forget sometimes I've got a full house down there. How's the garden looking after all that rain? Oh, it's bursting with life. And funnily enough, I made a small bout of milk the other day - hand-poured, as if we didn't have enough trouble with the creamer. Quite the traditional experience, if I do say so myself. Almost like those old mugs you'd watch thrown in the local festival. Oh, that brings back memories. Used to love those days. Nowadays, the festivals seem more about logistics than about throwing pots while the kids play. Though, they are good for the community. Speaking of which, did you hear about the power cuts at Margaret's house? Ah yes, I did. A bit of an alarm, but good that it isn't in our neighborhood, really. She's lucky it didn't happen when she was making those hand-thrown mugs of hers. I'd be in a real state if that were the case. Very true. It's like remembering times before all these modern...conveniences. Though, I must say, the lack of distractions during those power cuts can be...quite a conversation starter. Absolutely. Though, we had one last week that was less confronting but still led to some good laughs. We were changing the light bulb in the garden room and Dad almost fell while trying to check it. Fortunately, I was there to catch him. Makes you think of all these little risks we take when we're overconfident with our ageing bodies. Ha! The things we do when we're set on improving something right then and there. I remember almost upsetting a bird's nest once while pruning.

Hey everyone, did you hear about that incredible beach we can visit while we're on holiday? I've read it's one of the cleanest beaches in the UK! Yes, I've seen that. It's got quite a reputation isn't it? We should definitely check it out! But have we decided on a concrete plan yet? We need to consider everyone's ideas and preferences. Ah, holiday planning! I remember when we used to just pack up and drive wherever we fancied. All very spontaneous. Nowadays it feels like an art form sorting out accommodation and visits! Well, I've been thinking. Since there's a new exhibition at the museum in [attraction name], maybe we can do that in the morning then head to the beach in the afternoon? That actually sounds like a good mix. [Attraction name] is well worth a visit. And we could include a picnic on the beach? It'll be more relaxing and cost-effective too. A picnic, yes, that's a great idea! Can we grab some local food and beer? Someone should make sure to bring my accordion or a guitar. A bit of music would really set the mood on the beach! Definitely, I can ask [friend's name] if they’d like to join us. They’ve always wanted to learn more about that area. Any other ideas? Someone mentioned trying out the local surf school. If any of us are up for trying something new, that could be fun. Surf school, hmm. I’m not sure I'd be much good at that, but certainly worth a try! And speaking of new experiences, how about a walk along the coastal path? We can take in the sea views and enjoy the fresh air. We can do all of those things really. But we should check availability, try to plan around a few days, and of course keep it flexible so we can make adjustments based on the weather or other factors. Absolutely, planning flexibility is key. I’ll look into arrangements first thing tomorrow. What about accommodation? We could try booking a nearby self-catering place. Ah, I was on Facebook yesterday and saw this funny post about Obsessive Compulsive Disorder . You know, about how people think OCD is just about being really neat and tidy. But it's actually a serious mental health condition isn't it? That’s right, Alan. I think some folks just don’t fully understand what it’s like to live with it. It's about those intrusive thoughts and behaviors, isn't it? Exactly, Idle, dear. I used to teach a module in psychology about OCD and I think a lot of students, as well as the general public, have misconceptions about it. They think it’s just about organization or cleanliness, but it’s actually a type of anxiety disorder. That was my experience too, Sophie. While OCD might manifest in behaviors like excessive cleaning or checking things, it's often a coping mechanism for deeper anxieties. Yeah, and the poor bloke this post featured on Facebook, his OCD was about having to count different objects in the house. If he noticed he’d passed under the same light bulb too many times, he’d think he’d brought bad luck to the family, or something like that. It must have been quite distressing for them all. Honestly, I feel for people dealing with that sort of thing in silence. If I’m being completely honest, we’re quite lucky not to have those sorts of issues. Speaking of things that might affect families, have you heard the latest about chicken pox outbreaks? There seems to be one in our area, if I recall correctly from the news. Yes, that’s a concern. I saw a notification about it on the local council’s website. Hopefully, it won’t hit our family. It’s always worrying about our youngest, isn’t it? Indeed, the thought of any of our young ones going through that is distressing. I had it when I was young. Funny how it just seemed like a normal childhood illness back then, but now they treat it quite seriously with vaccinations and such. Exactly. Advances in medicine and awareness about such diseases have been quite helpful in preventing the spread and the severity of symptoms.

Speaker_1   : Oh, I was thinking of booking that trip to Germany. I've always wanted to visit Berlin. Did you learn German at school, Lucy?   Speaker_2   : Yeah, I tried. It was tough for me. I've always loved the way Kentish dialect can make everyday words sound so unique. Like using 'zip' for a can or 'lurgy' for a cold.   Speaker_3  : Funny how those words stick. I always take guests from the north or abroad on a little tour of local Kentshire-isms. Like the Bridge pub, and explaining how 'that's a bit tatty' actually just means 'it's worn out'.   Speaker_2  : Yeah, and describing where you're from with things like the 'Nine Locks' makes our county sound like it has its own special language.   Speaker_1  : I know! Hey, I'm so glad we could catch up without the kids this time. Yeah, it's about time! I've been meaning to ask you, how have you been handling everything with your job and Alison's diagnosis? To be honest, it's been a massive struggle. Every day feels like a reminder of the uncertainty and the worries. She's been going through chemo, and it's just so tough to see her go through it. I can imagine. My sister went through something similar a few years ago. She was diagnosed with breast cancer too, and it was like her whole world turned upside down. It was tough to see her in such pain, both physically and mentally. Yes, that must have been so tough for you and your family. It's the emotional toll of cancer that really hits us hard, isn't it? And the waiting, always waiting for the next test result or appointment, it's exhausting. Exactly. And then there's the mental health aspect, which can easily be overlooked. Alison has been seeing a therapist, and I've been trying to support her as much as I can, but it's a really hard balance to strike, making sure she has her space but also feeling like we're with her every step of the way. We make sure to do things together, or just have quiet nights at home where we don't talk about the cancer. She sounds like she's doing better than she lets on, then. She really is. But you know what's been a game changing moment for us? Getting onto that new Facebook support group for families dealing with cancer. It's been such a lifeline, hearing other people's stories and just knowing we're not alone in this. That's such a great idea. I'll look into that.

I was thinking of investing in a couple of books for your school summer reading list. Have you decided what you're going to read yet? Hmm, not really. That sounds amazing!

Hey Lucy, great to see you again! How was your year? I've been hearing so much about your job and how busy it's been. Oh, it's been quite eventful. I might take a trip over to the southern end to see the coast. That sounds lovely. And while you're there, definitely try some local seafood!

Alright, so I've decided I'm gonna try and get into that gig tonight. You know, the one at The Distillery? It sounds like it could be a pretty fun night. What are you up to, you coming? Thank you all for being here. I'm thrilled to be coordinating this book club. On the menu tonight are some fabulous wines and my latest culinary experiment – a deep-fried brie and cranberry tart. But sometimes I do find it gets a bit nostalgic. For example, my mum used to say, “old so-and-so,” meaning an old acquaintance, but now people just say “old mate” or similar. Again, it’s about those regional variations. It’s like our job can also be about being ambassadors of our regions!

Hey everyone, gather round. Dad has been dying to share his travel stories from our trip to the Lake District. Well don't keep us in suspense! What was the most memorable part of your trip, Dad? Ah, good morning everyone. Bit of a lazy Saturday morning's grogging around. Nothing like a bit of social chit-chat and a well-earned brew to kick off the weekend, eh? I had planned to visit some local spots and maybe hit the cinema later today, but nothing's quite decided yet. I'm still struggling to actually decide where to go. Film-wise, though, I'm eyeing this new sci-fi epic coming out. Have either of you heard anything about it? Sarah, I've been meaning to check it out too. From what I've heard, the reviews are pretty mixed. But if you like sci-fi, then you might as well. It's good sometimes to just step out and immerse yourself even if the reviews aren't perfect. Speaking of stepping out, have you two thought about looking for a nice place to grab brunch? There's this spot around the corner that recently opened. I couldn't believe their breakfast menu, it's all English classics done right or as much as one can while still experimenting a bit. I'm thinking maybe we could plan something there this weekend if anyone's keen? I'm sure we could all use a bit of the 'eat out' experience in good company. Do say, I am always up for exploring new places to eat, especially if it's brunch and nice atmosphere. Anything English classic always sounds right, especially after this week of different international eats at the venues for my culinary workshop. That actually sounds perfect and timely. I need a break from my writing and screen staring. But it's not just about the food though, how about making it a bit of a highlight? I can find if there’s a good book club meet or any events around the city this Saturday that might align with our interest, if anyone's particularly looking for something more intellectually stimulating. That's a great idea, Sarah! Always something going on around here for book clubs or science talks. Even if we don't go on to an organised event, we could maybe just discuss a book together over brunch if that sounds cooler to you. I've been meaning to revisit 'Dune' so we could use this as an excuse to have a real talk about it.

Hey everyone, gather round for a moment will you? Today's Reg's farewell dinner. It'd be awesome to hear from each of you about the highlight of our time together. You're right. There have been so many hilarious moments. Like the time Reg’s Satnav got us stuck on a backroad in Saudi Arabia. Hilarious and terrifying at the same time. Yeah, that was wild. He kept saying, "Trust Google, trust Google," and then we saw a map for a place that looked like it was right next to a desert. Ha! And then there was the time we decorated his house for Christmas. It looked like a lamp shop exploded inside. Reg would be proud of our memory of his decorating skills. What about jobs? Anyone venturing out of what they're doing now? I did project coordination last year and loved it. But sometimes it can be very pressuring. And you’re always on call. It never ends, does it? Absolutely. But that’s what keeps this job interesting. I mean, I've been an administrator for a while now and the routine doesn’t change much, but it’s the variations in the projects that keep me in good spirits. Well, you can't beat the satisfaction of a solid days physical work for me. It’s nice to see something tangible at the end of the day. Though, I do miss the camaraderie of the army. It was fantastic growing up in a community like that. I know what you mean. Even in my current job, there's the sense that you're working towards a goal, a project completion. I don’t think I’d be able to do a career that doesn’t have measured progress. And, speaking of milestones, I noticed a lot of our chat ended up on family or couple goals. Any updates? There’s some talk of me moving to London for a better job in my field. You know how it is, better opportunities, though scary too. You should go for it. I know it’s daunting but, take it from me, it's always worth trying if you're passionate about it. I agreed with the move. It’s terrifying but so rewarding if it pays off. Maybe meetups could become less rare once we’re settled if you all move there too. I’d love that.

Hey, I hope you've all been staying healthy and well. We have such beautiful weather today; it's perfect for a walk around the gardens. Oh, absolutely! I've been meaning to get here for ages. Let’s talk health and life, shall we? I’ve been trying out some new yoga routines, finding them quite beneficial for managing stress. But my biggest concern lately has been getting into a solid sleep routine again. Do any of you have tips or techniques that work for you? Sleep for me is always a challenge, especially given my job with irregular working hours. But I’ve started using essential oils, like lavender, in my sleep space. It’s been surprisingly effective. That’s a great idea! Lavender has been proven to help with relaxation, as have certain teas like chamomile. I’ve also tried adopting a tech-free policy before bedtime to help my mind wind down. It takes some discipline, but it’s worth it. That makes sense! Distractions before bed can certainly interfere with good sleep. I’ve tried meditation as well, though it’s taken me a while to stick with it. Do you have any favorite apps or resources for guided meditations that you could recommend? Absolutely! "Insight Timer" has a wealth of resources, including meditations designed specifically for sleep. I think the diversity in its content helps keep it interesting long enough for me to fall asleep. Ah, thanks for the suggestion! I’ll definitely look that up. Also, have you considered a sleep study or something like that if you’re still consistently struggling? It’s a bit of an investment, but sometimes there are underlying issues that we can’t tackle on our own. That’s a good point, but I think I’ll try some of the more natural approaches first. I have the luxury of being able to just take a day off when needed, and recharge, which isn’t the case for everyone. If you think about it, even just taking small doses of self-care, like what we're doing here today, can make a big difference. Definitely. And on that note, these gardens are fantastic. The management here seems to do an incredible job maintaining such a variety of plants. Have you noticed the new section they’ve added over by the pond? Yes, I have! Is it still the one with the focus on native Swedish species?

Hey everyone, gather round. I've been thinking about our speech patterns. I mean, we all have quite distinctive accents. Don’t forget how people always assumed I was from Milton Keynes rather than Gillingham. You two from Kent here probably have really regional accents. Still, now, the way technology recognizes voices, it’s quite fascinating how easily they can pinpoint our localities and even emotional state sometimes. That’s true, Sarah. I’ve noticed how often my voice appears to be Southeast London to people, even though I’m from Harlow. But even with technology, it can still get it wrong sometimes. Yeah, I remember when I was working – well, when I was working, before I retired – we had this new computer system that struggled to understand anyone’s accent. People would get stuck in loops of saying the magic words for it to recognize them. They even had an option to switch to a more neutral accent if you wanted to bypass the recognition problem. That was frustrating, wasn’t it? But technology’s come a long way, right? And now people barely ever call or converse on phones anymore. Everyone’s messaging or relying on voice assistants, like Alexa. But that still doesn’t account for accents. It’s as if some voices are considered more “standard” than others by these systems. Exactly! And speaking of technology, I was thinking the other day about parental control settings on gaming consoles or streaming devices. It’s an interesting dynamic, technology allowing for restrictions while also serving as a window to all sorts of experiences for kids. True, and sometimes as caregivers, we have to grapple with that duality – allowing them to explore while keeping them safe. I work with kids and… it’s quite a balancing act. Makes me think about my own childhood, how technology has changed the way we learn, play… or just live. My side of the family grew up in completely different circumstances. I grew up in a rougher part of London, but we never really had much access to this type of technology back then. All we’d really do was play in the streets or watch a bit of TV. Yeah, reminds me… do you all remember “Thunderbirds”? I used to love that. Funny how those shows from when we were young stuck so much with us. I reckon if we were talking about a censorship or recommendations on show types for children now, the conversation would be pretty different.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together tonight. It feels like ages. How was your day, Ian? You've been such a quiet young one lately, so much has been going on with various projects at work. It was just okay, Mum, thanks for asking. We had questions on this topic of baking today in food class and I couldn't help but think of you making that amazing baked Alaska at our Halloween party last year. Ah, I'd almost forgotten about that! Well, it was quite the event, wasn't it? You and Thomas were dressed as... I think it was a duo, but I've forgotten. [laughs] It was us as a ghost duo. [laughs] You even provided the music for the party, Mum. Was it from your own playlist? Yes, it was! I love curating music playlists, and it turned into a contest at the party, trying to guess the next song. It was quite the hit, let me tell you! Did your class discuss anything else about baking or cooking? Actually, yes, we were tasked with researching a dish and this boy, let's call him Alex, brought up this whole debate about grating cheese for pasta. There was this suggestion that older kids might find it harder because of their age. It was weird but kind of stuck with me. Ah, that stems from some interesting prejudice about certain tasks being equated to certain ages or perhaps physical strength. But, you know, age isn't always in itself a barrier. I remember preparing for baking competitions when I was much younger than you and certainly not "old." These stereotypes don't apply universally, do they? I think so, Mum. Alex seemed really certain about it, but I could tell some of the others weren't convinced. Well, there may be physical differences that can affect, say, the ability to grate certain types of cheese with ease, but skills are acquired, and there's usually a way around these if you really want to. That’s what makes discriminating based on age so short-sighted. Makes sense. Plus, I recall in my experience of leading programmes and recruiting team members. The age of someone joining the workforce isn't always an indicator of performance or ability to absorb new knowledge. However, it's definitely something that still sometimes affects hiring decisions, sadly. Really?

Ah, good morning! I hope you're sleeping well after that jet lag. Good morning! Yes, thank you for having me. It's lovely to be back in Swansea. You know I love this city, and it’s nice to have some quiet time to visit. It's just so quiet isn't it? I find it a bit too quiet sometimes, but I suppose that's part of the charm. Absolutely, and there's still so much life despite that. Speaking of keepsakes, I still have the letter you wrote me from my time in Japan. I remember writing that. I've been meaning to write letters more often. There's something lovely about putting thoughts to paper. I read it back sometimes, when I need a bit of inspiration or just a comforting touch. It's amazing how much you can convey in a letter. Especially when it's from a friend you made in Japan. What a year that was! And now I'm jealous that you're getting flying lessons. So excited! It's been a dream of mine for ages. One day, I might even use it for work trips. Not to mention, it has been fun so far. I love the feeling of being in control of the air. That must be incredible. When I was in New York, I remember how much I enjoyed flying over to the island , even if it was just for an hour or two in the air. Oh, I couldn't agree more. There’s something about flying over landscapes that's quite exhilarating. But it's not just about the views; I find it quite meditative too, kind of like writing, actually. Definitely. I suppose that's why those two activities weren't too out of character for each other. Do you think you'll write about your experiences learning to fly? Maybe. I’ve been meaning to write more about my travels and changing perspectives. It's funny, my time in Japan really changed how I look at a lot of things. It’s often the places we live that shape us the most, isn’t it? I've found that England does give me a certain perspective that's very... situated, and distinct from the Welsh. There's definitely something about living in different parts of the UK that shapes who we are and how we think.

Who knew I'd make it here eventually? Took me nearly an hour to get to this coffee shop. You're always late, aren't you? Still, now that the show’s over, we can actually play this game. Yeah, let's focus. Any big plays brewing? Well I had a plan but now I'm scrambling. Stuck with an “A”. You know, it's funny, those early 'A' words in English come from Old Norse. Is that right? I learned a bit about Norse etymology in my history of language course. What's that got to do with scrabble? Just being tangentially related, as sometimes you need creative plays to win. You're not suggesting using Old Norse for high-scoring plays, are you? For me, it's all about the unusual words. Anyone studying English at uni has that advantage. The rest of us can just play Scrabble and pretend to be smart. Well, at least you have high SATs scores for that one. Speaking of studies, how is uni treating you all? I'm just about survived my last year of culinary arts. But it's tough, isn't it? I'm doing a graduate degree in business, but I do miss the time when academics weren't so intense. I just tried to relax a bit with some children's books from our childhood. Children's books? What's that about? I think we’ve all shared reading those on sleepovers. Like Where the Wild Things Are or Mr. Men. They're surprisingly complex when you grow up. I guess it's always fun to revisit childhood influences. Did anyone else read about Mr. Bump and Mr. Men in A-Level English classes? I did, and I came across some analysis that compares Mr. Tickle with Mr. Bump and the social implications of their happiness levels. That's deep. You're overthinking any of the children's books at this point. Anyway, back to Scrabble. I really wish I could make this a word: SYNS. Is that a word? Or did you just make that up? No, it's short for "synthetic". We can use it I guess. Oh, you’re right! There's also 'sync' and 'synergy'. Someone's really trying to win here. Just having fun. Though now that you mentioned it, synergy does sound like a good word from a scrabble perspective. We should keep that in mind next time.

Ah, I'm losing my train of thought again, Alan's passport. I know today's the 23rd. It's not until the 27th, so we've got plenty of time. You're right though, we should make sure to get the other forms ready as well, just in case. Yes, and don’t forget the photographs. You'd think they'd have some at the post office, but they never do. Or maybe they just can't be bothered with old people, eh? All very well for us to be early risers and all, but they expect you to get there at 8 am sharp, or you're fucked. Bloody hel [laughs], you have a point there. 8 o'clock just says it all, doesn’t it? Everyone’s waiting for the retirement places to open, and the whole place’s just a rush. And to think we used to do that most of our lives. We sure did. But now, even applying for a passport feels like a job. [chuckles] It does, it does. I can't believe it's coming up to my 80th year soon. All these years working and nothing to show for it but these damned applications and whatnot. The system's still the same, isn't it? Always in favour of the hustle and bustle. Can't imagine why anyone listens to that lot in government, they keep making life worse for the likes of us who just want to go about our quiet days. Quiet days indeed. But you never know, we might just get a pleasant surprise. Maybe the forms will be straightforward this time. [laughs] You and the paperwork. I'm more holding my breath for that to happen than I am for Alan's passport to come through. Well, I reckon that passport’s just the start. Next up will be the travel plans. You were right to book early. It will be nice to have some proper holiday next summer, after all these years. I’m looking forward to that. We could sit on deck somewhere, watching the sea, not a care in the world. Can’t wait. But for now, let's just plod on with these forms. Gosh, I thought applying for a driver’s license last year was a nightmare. This is just as bad. [laughs] Yeah, well, at least we've got each other to muddle through.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together like this. It feels like ages since we've done this together. That sounds familiar. It's the first time we've all been together in a while, and it’s nice to have everyone here without distractions. It's days like today that make me wish we could do this more often. Have you all tried the new app, ‘Foodiel’? I’ve been using it to find new recipes. Oh, I’ve heard about it. Do you like it? Yes. It’s good because it’s based on what ingredients you’ve already got at home. Reduces waste and is very quick to use. That does sound convenient. What’s the best recipe you’ve found through it? Let me think… Oh, I made a pasta dish with cherry tomatoes and pecorino cheese. It was so simple and delicious. That sounds lovely. And you’re always on about fitness. How’s that going? Yes, it's been a bit challenging with this holiday, but I’ve been trying to keep up with yoga sessions. Not enough swimming with the weather we’re having. Swimming! Good idea. The weather’s warmer at least. Any other fitness tips, or are you training for anything specific? No, not really specific. Mainly just wanting to keep active. Speaking of which, did you hear about the new train station opening? Finally. No, I didn’t. When’s that due? Apparently they’re planning to open it next month after those inconsistent delays. Oh, that’s great news. It’s been so long in the works. It definitely was frustrating those delays, weren’t they? But useful to hear it’s finally ready to go. It should make things much easier for us if we want to travel further afield. Definitely. It’s been a pain taking buses or driving everywhere. I know what you mean. Driving can be so tiring and unpredictable with the traffic around here. Hopefully, public transport will become a real option now. It will be. Just wish they could fix the delays on the existing lines too. I’m sure they’ll work on that as well. It seems things are gradually improving around here. For sure. I just hope they keep up the renovations and maintenance once it’s open. Agreed. Maintenance is the key. Well, it certainly is better news than we’ve had before.

Hey mate, been meaning to catch up for ages! How's things been since our last chat? Hey! Fine, thanks. Just been deep into this new novel I picked up. "The Lie" - have you read it? No, haven't had a chance yet. But I'm hooked on Shakespeare now. Just started a new TV series on BBC. Oh, that makes sense then. I'm right there with you on Shakespeare. Film adaptations can be hit and miss though, can't they? True. That's why I'm looking forward to the new version of Macbeth coming out. I heard it's quite dark and gritty. Really? I wasn't aware of that. I'd love to catch that. Do you read any good books related to politics or something like that? Yeah, actually. Just finished a book on Europe's history since 1945. It was eye-opening. Interesting. Right up my alley. I couldn't believe the amount of major shifts between countries after the war. I hope you don't mind, but I'm a bit of a politics and history nerd. Absolutely not, I'm the same! The modern political landscape is so complex and so interesting. Makes me wish more of my university seminars were about that, not just the usual grind of theory and lecture notes. Honestly, some of my course mates can go deep on theory in class, but really struggle with connecting it to real-world applications, don't you find? Totally. That's one reason I wish we could do more project-based learning or even internships. Then you can see the direct impact and relevance. Yeah, totally. But then again, seminars can be useful for a different kind of thinking. The debates we had on EU politics were particularly fun. Oh absolutely, debates can be so stimulating! Though I do wish sometimes my course mates would speak a bit more freely. Some are really good on paper, but in a group setting, it feels like they clam up. Same. But I suppose that's just something you learn over time. I mean, university can be a big transition too. True. And then there's the whole 'balancing social life and work' thing. Just thinking about all the stag weekends I've planned or been to. I'm pretty sure that's a whole new level of balancing! Oh, I just went to one in Wales over Easter.

Hey Lucy, great to see you again! How was your job interview? I hope it went well. Oh, it was actually cancelled at the last minute. Had the whole day off then, but I still managed to catch up on some work. That's frustrating! So, how are you finding life at Pearson? It's good. The team is really supportive and it's been great to learn about the publishing industry. But honestly, I'm really missing the structure and set working hours. Starts to feel like I need a plan or something for my future... You always had such clear plans Lucy. Remember your dreams to set up a food company? Did that work out in London? Yeah, actually. I had the idea but life in London was faster and more expensive than I anticipated. So, I decided to put it on hold indefinitely and look for a more stable job, hence Pearson. It's good money for now, but creative entrepreneurship seems further away than ever. That’s quite a change. It’s tough, isn’t it, when passion and reality clash? I recently had a similar dilemma about whether to keep doing project coordination or dive into studying further for something more research-based. Exactly! Sometimes you just can't have everything. Though, I genuinely enjoy project coordination – the people, the solving complex problems… But the creative side is still there, itching at me. I imagine it’s tough to balance. Speaking of balance, how is your family in Manchester? How was your last visit? Family's good, thanks for asking. Last visit was fun but also... doesn’t help that my cousins are getting married left and right. There’s always someone holding a stag or a hen party. Honestly, I just want to find the one and join them side of things, you know? I hear you! Ex-boyfriends, another story? You mentioned online last time but never in full. Let’s just say the past few months have been interesting. It’s one of those… complicated messes that you can’t avoid talking about with close friends like you. But I’m trying to keep it real, take care of myself, learn from it all. Well, that sounds like the right approach. It’s good to have you around, no pressure but keep talking when you feel ready. On a lighter note, have you tried out any new food here?

Make sure to grab that tea bag from the top shelf, babe. I want today's tea to be perfect, just like my mum used to make when I was a little girl back in Sunderland. Sure thing, love. Black or green? Let’s go for black today, just like at home. It stays strong and warm, you know? Though I do miss our tea breaks at university, where the brew was almost always Earl Grey and it didn’t matter how early in the morning it was. Oh, I remember those. Your tea habit started showing up pretty early in the day, didn’t it? Did you say something about your mum’s tea just now? Yeah, she used to make the best brew. There was something about making sure the water was just right—I still follow that rule now. She taught me so many things, from how to make a good cuppa to handling botany projects in the garden. Speaking of which, have you seen the new plant I got? It's supposed to bloom within the year, but it's already giving me a lot of joy just watching it grow. Oh, I’ve seen it. It looks fun. What is it again? Something exotic? It’s a species of orchid. I’ve been getting into indoor gardening more. It’s quite relaxing after a long day of working or studying. There’s something soothing in watching green things thrive, don’t you think? Alright, I think the water is ready now. Yeah, it’s therapeutic. I used to help out at my grandparents' garden in Birmingham when I was younger. My granddad was always telling me things about different plants. Seems like the Midlands was where his green thumb was strongest. You know, your family skills are rubbing off on me—seeing how you care for your plants and cook. I might just take you up on changing the topics from academic research to cookery one day. I’d teach you, for sure. I have a few family recipes that are invaluable. But back to plants, I've also started trying my luck with a small herb garden. Thyme, rosemary, some basil. It’s surprisingly easy once you get the hang of it. That sounds like a good project. Perhaps we could even work on a recipe together that uses some of your fresh herbs. For example, I heard about this one pasta recipe that calls for basil—you often like making this when we go back home.

Ah, good morning! How was your weekend? Oh, it was pretty quiet, to be honest. Spent most of it grading papers. You wouldn’t believe the number of well thought out arguments I need to read! I completely understand, though I kind of regret going into academic work after days like today! Ha! But we get into this job for a reason. I guess we’ve just got to find ways to enjoy it. True. But even so, it must get a bit stressful sometimes. Oh, yes. There was one lazy student who’s always on my list. But, you know, that’s just part of the job. So, did you manage to relax in the garden at all over the weekend? Actually, yes. One of my most lovable hobbies is gardening. It's very therapeutic. I also caught part of the Wales international match on the telly. We’re going through quite a rebuilding phase at the moment, but I still enjoy their style of play. For me, it was a mix. I watched some of the Arsenal match, but also tried gardening for the first time. It seemed quite relaxing, but I may need some advice from an expert like yourself. Sure, happy to help. I used to have quite a green thumb myself – until the weather in Wales caught up with me! There is one thing I found quite interesting… I read somewhere that some former football players are now pushing their children into joining the police force or the armed forces. Yes! I’ve seen that too. There’s kind of this proud tradition behind it, especially in Wales, where many people have family ties to the forces or the police. I just thought, isn’t that a bit of a surprise? You’d imagine them advocating sports or something related to football instead. Not really, and it’s not just about physical fitness or changing the world. It’s about discipline and community. Many of these players come from working-class backgrounds, and joining such services offers stability and a sense of public duty. That makes sense. I guess it also provides an alternative if professional sports doesn’t work out. Exactly. Plus, those kids often go through almost as rigorous training as the players themselves. Did you know, I also found out that some top snooker players have surprisingly young children! I heard about Mark Selby’s son for example.

Ah, good morning everyone. How was everyone's first day's groceries? On the road, are we set for the celebration at the weekend? Mummy, mummy! There's a really nice new park near Grange Park, we saw it when we came back from Auntie Sarah's. Can we go there and play for a bit tomorrow? Oh absolutely sweetheart, we can make that a lovely treat before we head home. And how about the keepsakes for the Christening? Have you sorted out the projector and the slideshow, mum? Yes, I've got most of that covered. But I wasn't sure if we want to have any activities for the children - any ideas? How about a little "Welcome to the Family" ceremony? Just have everyone say a little something to the baby? It'll make it more inclusive and fun for the kids too. Yeah, and we could have a piñata! Mummy, could we please have a piñata?! We could have a piñata, provided it's a small one and not too chaotic for the setting. And have you finalized the guest list? Sticking with 20 people or think we could fit more? We've had to stick to 20 people as space is a bit of an issue. But we can definitely have more fun with the venues for each activity, considering we’re hosting in the garden. Can we also have a treasure hunt? Perhaps we could have a treasure hunt on the last day or just a smaller one the day after. Seems like the kids are really looking forward to a few activities, aren't you? Yessss! And can we still go to that new cake shop we passed by yesterday? We can absolutely do a cake tasting before we decide on the Christening cake. Don’t forget to check some for kids’ allergies though. Absolutely, gluten-free, dairy-free, the whole works if needed. Can we show Daddy the new park tomorrow? He'll want to go too! Of course, let's get all the family in on the park visit. Do you two think it'd still be fun if we include all of us? Definitely. And while we're at it, has anyone taken care of getting Auntie Sarah's travel details... and Uncle James' confirmation...? Ah, good catch! I was meaning to call James this morning actually. Maybe we can also make sure all the contributions and gifts are organized nicely too, so Mrs. Robinson doesn’t get overwhelmed with little notes and ribbons.

Ah, good morning everyone! Lovely to see you all's here. I brought today's newspaper and freshly made coffee. How are we all doing this morning? Morning, all! I'm doing alright. Just got off from work and I'm excited about the weekend. You know, I've always wanted to try this new Italian place downtown. Mm, can I have some coffee now, please? And... um... can I have a cookie too? Of course, sweetie! Here you go. Now, how was work today? You okay with it being busy, darling? Yeah, it was alright, thank you for asking. The shop was slammed as usual. Might have been down to the new collection. Unidentified : Yay! More coffee! Thank you, Gramma! Ah, you're welcome! Did I hear you say you wanted to go downtown this weekend? Let's plan that, then. Perhaps we should visit the park too. It's been a while since we've all gone together. Sounds like a plan! For me, a nice Italian meal on Saturday would be perfect after work. And maybe if we're busy the next day, we could just rest and watch the game? What do you think? Perfect! Do we also want to plan a bit further ahead? We've been talking about a holiday to New York. The kids still want to go to Central Park and the Natural History Museum. Yeah! And see the giant teddy bear! Oh, that reminds me of Helen's wedding. Do you remember that giant teddy bear decoration? Of course! That was hilarious. How are we doing with the plans for that trip? Have we got a rough idea when we can go? Well, we were thinking next summer. It's still a bit far off, so we can start planning now. Speaking of holidays, was it really hot at your party last week? I was there briefly but it was boiling! Horribly hot, but it was a great party! And it's always fun for the dogs too. Yay! Dogs! Again and again! You love the dogs! Did you know, Sweetie, that we're thinking of taking them with us to New York if we can arrange a place for them to stay while we're out? Really? Pleeease? That would be... that would be um, paw-fect! That could be a bit of a challenge, but if we can manage it, why not?

Hey mate, got a sec? I need some advice on this passport requirement for our study abroad. Sure thing, what's the deal? Everything alright? Yeah, just got the email from our program coordinator. Apparently, the immigration team is a bit stringent about the questions on this kind of form. You handled yours smoothly, yeah? Ah, yeah. It was a bit of a faff actually, but I got there in the end. They asked loads about my academic history and how it ties in with the course. You've probably got similar stuff to fill out, right? True, true. Idk, I feel like I’m overcomplicating it. You know, like, "Have you ever been denied a visa?" What even does that mean? [chuckles] Well, have you? No, no - but like, what if my application didn’t get processed in time, or if there was some mistake? But according to the document, it's got to be for whatever reason. Yeah, that’s a bit of a trick question. It's about giving a straightforward answer, even if it’s "No." Regarding anything missed or delayed, if you can provide a bit of context - like in your case, maybe you didn’t apply for a visa because you were already in the UK on a current one - keep it concise and clear. They just want to know if there have been any previous issues. Oh, right. I never thought of it that way. Shows how much I've changed since that time when I was applying for my current study permit - that was hell! [laughs] Yeah, but you made it through, and that's what matters. Now, about this side of commerce, they’re asking about a "risk assessment" of the country we are going to. Do you know if we’ll actually be explicitly working within any high-risk sectors while we're there? Not that I know of. But wait, I think my course might involve a project on local market trends, does that count? Well, I suppose if we're talking business, it could be considered a form of economic analysis, which isn't typically high-risk. [thinks] Alright. That makes sense. So just sticking to the paperwork and maybe asking our department for more context if needed. Yeah, definitely. Get in touch with someone in your department and ask them to confirm or clarify if anything seems unclear to you.

Hey everyone, gather round for a bit of a conversation about dreams. I was just thinking the other day that if I didn’t have my current job, maybe I’d open up a little café. You know, just a quiet place where people could relax and enjoy good food and drinks? That sounds lovely, Tom. It kind of reminds me of the time I was seriously considering moving to France to open a bookstore. It was a bit out of our budget, of course, but the dream never really died.
