It’s when the Parliament keeps coming backwards and forwards with nothing getting done. Yeah, but why was everyone so angry? I heard it's just like the holidays but for Parliament? Well, let me explain it to you like this, lad. Prorogation can be useful sometimes, like when the government needs time to form new policies. But the problem is when they use it to delay uncomfortable votes or to avoid scrutiny. So, it’s like when my school would decide that summer is too hot so we won’t have school. But Parliament isn’t supposed to have a summer or winter holiday like that. That’s a great comparison! But no, Parliament is always supposed to be busy doing its job. Prorogation is like the school deciding it's too hot so they close down the whole school for a month or two, right in the middle of the term. Ah, I see. Like, my teacher could decide to take a month off from teaching and then we wouldn’t learn anything for a while? Exactly. It’s about the principle of it. Just like how us pensioners are supposed to get the support we need, but if they prorogue and end sessions, we might not get the time or attention to our issues. That makes sense. So, it’s just like, if the government doesn’t want to deal with something, they can prorogue and then it doesn’t have to be done for a while? That’s part of it, son. It's more nuanced than that, but in simple terms, it's a bit like that. The problem with the recent ones is that people felt it was just to avoid having to take accountability for their actions. Okay, so it’s not just taking a holiday, it’s like when you could use it for dodging work? Yes, exactly. You put it quite simply and correctly. In recent times, there’s been debate because some people believe it was being used in a less-than-honourable way.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together tonight. It's been ages. How's every one been doing? Yeah, thanks for having us over, Granny. It's been fun here. Is that the new neighbors you've been telling us about, who just moved in across the street? It's nice having some new people around. I've noticed them out in their garden a lot lately. Indeed. They seem friendly. Our garden is looking a bit bare this time of year, but still, there's something comforting about the bare branches before spring comes, isn't there? Absolutely. And speaking of spring, have any of you seen the blood moons we've had recently? They were quite something. Yes, I saw the last one! My science teacher was going on about it. It was pretty cool, even if the sky was a bit cloudy where we are. I wish Granny was around to see it. She'd have loved the science behind it. So, you were saying about the new neighbors... this reminds me. I've been thinking about how our family meals have evolved over time. When I was working, it was all about the timing of everything. Now, with the grandkids around, its more about teaching them the right way to eat. Yeah, Granny keeps telling me about table manners all the time. I think it's good though; it does make eating together more formal and nice. We have tried to keep it that way with you two when you come over. But it's hard when you're just used to eating with your parents and siblings. Absolutely right. I remember when you were a bit less into it when you were your age, but I just thought, they'll pick it up. And they do, eventually. Speaking of eating, Granny's cooking is really good. I love it when she makes a dinner for everyone. It’s a pleasure to do it. You kids make me feel useful for a change. You're always useful, Granny. And such a help with the kids. It must be nice to not have to worry about work for a change. It's different, definitely. But seeing the kids enjoy what we do makes it all worth it, even if it is a bit of a struggle at times. I remember when you were just as young.

Ah, I've been reading about that Scottish referendum in the news. It's quite a surprise; I didn't think they would come this close again. Do you think they might succeed this time round? It's certainly a possibility, isn't it? People have always been passionate about independence, but I think questions about the economy and what it means for the future might make some people hesitant this time. Yes, I've heard there are those who are quite fractious on the economic aspect. Our friend Alex for instance, always says that keeps coming up in their local pub conversations. That's fascinating, yes. Economics is such a deciding factor. But isn't there also the cultural and political aspect that gets people engaged in these discussions? Absolutely. I think that's what resonates most with many people. It's the desire for control over their own destiny. Hence the passion. It's a complex situation. I've met a lot of creative types in Hove, filmmakers, freelancers, artists, who are quite enthused by the independence movement. They seem to see it as a way to better control cultural and arts funding, perhaps. That certainly makes sense. As a teacher, I see this in the classroom. The younger generation often feels very strongly about 'taking back control' in all sorts of areas. Interesting perspective. Speaking of taking control, I had an interesting conversation with one of my recruits the other day. A young fellow applying for a job here. He actually mentioned in the interview that he's interested in moving to Scotland if the independence happens. He sees it as an opportunity to be part of a new system, perhaps. True, and the possibilities that come with it. It could be a game changer for many, depending on how it plays out. More broadly speaking, this referendum could just be the start of a lot of change across the UK, not just in Scotland. Yes, that's for sure. It's hard to predict but it's a very changing time. It’s a good thing we have people like you, passionate teachers who are also eager to engage in these discussions with the younger generation. Well, speaking of younger generations, have you heard about my niece's recent decision to go for a PhD? She's always been very academic and it's wonderful to see her pursue her interests further.

Okay so today we had lentil soup and that Whole Foods pizza for lunch. Wasn't talked about at all the whole way down. You two just finished your meal when we set off. Still feel guilty, though—should've definally stuck to questions or some kind of game. Ah, you're always right at the forefront, Aaron. Table manners and conversation etiquette. But it was nice, really. You know, a quiet lunch. Sometimes less is more. Right, Ann, just like in class. The more questioning you do in your life, the more growth you have. So Aaron, shall we keep that lesson in session while we’re in the car? What’s the plan for the afternoon? Pick your battles. Ooh, I barely have a plan. But last night we were talking about possibly getting a dog. I’d say that’s worth discussing or even arguing over. Or maybe we can turn this into a decision-making game. Anyone up for that? I think the most substantial decision we're making right now is whether to turn off at the next junction or keep going. Should we make a group decision for this or take a voice vote? Oh, for sure. We can make the most trivial daily motions into democratic processes. 'All in favor of turning left...' But it's actually quite interesting the way we make decisions as a group. It's like we've got all these different... I guess you'd say, career skills at play here—activity co-ordination, decision-making in customer services, teaching strategies for weighing arguments. Oh absolutely. It’s funny, though, Ann. Last year when you and I went to Italy together, the whole trip was more about getting to the next gelateria than actual sightseeing. Funny how priorities change, isn't it? Now, back to decisions. I propose we all have a say, but if we are deadlocked, Aaron, as the youngest could have the tie-breaker... but only if he agrees to walk the dog if we eventually do get one. Deal! And don't worry, if we discuss this enough, maybe by the end of the journey we'll have outlined a whole book of rules for group travel. By the way, anyone else catch that news about the potential increase in tuition fees next year? Supposedly from what I saw, it could make it very unattractive for some students, especially outside of big cities.

Hey, I'm going to drive today to my first client's place. I hope today's traffic won't be too bad. Ooh, traffic. Always a headache, isn't it? Are you heading into the city? Actually, the road’s quite clear today – no major questions or accidents reported yet. So you’re likely to make good time, Lily . Hopefully so, although you never can predict with British weather. But, talking about traffic and journeys, I was out on the country roads last week and saw a herd of cows blocking my path once! Oh, cows on the road! I remember when I used to commute from Timperley to Manchester, I often had to contend with those big black and white creatures in the middle of the road. That must have been a sight. Speaking of cows, I recall being on a farm visit for my agritech work once. The cows there were so well-behaved, but I know it's often not the case on public roads. So, do you think there's a way to train farm animals to be less confrontational on highways? Honestly, most of it comes down to farmers properly securing their land. Good fences are good neighbours, as they say. But sometimes, the animals are just curious and stray onto roads. I agree with Aiden . It’s mostly about preventative measures, really. But you never can completely stop the odd escapee or two. I suppose it doesn’t help that many rural roads in the country are the only means of transport for the animals and the farmers to bring them to market, if I’m not mistaken? Exactly, and it's a balance between preserving the rural character of the countryside and ensuring it's safe for drivers. I used to drive through those rural areas to get to places a lot when I worked at BT. We had to be careful, of course, but it was a simpler time. Nowadays, I don't drive any more, but it's just as well – the speed and so much else about driving seem to have changed beyond recognition. Speaking of changes, I've noticed how the use of technology has increased almost everywhere. Even in the countryside, there’s talk of using drones to monitor and manage farmland. Do you think that could help with things like livestock safety or coordinating farming practices more efficiently?

Ah, I'm so glad we could all make it tonight. It's been ages. How have you all been? You're all doing such well, it's wonderful to see. Speaker_2 and Speaker_3, I need to compliment you both–you're doing great with the transcription work, I hear. Oh, thank you! It's been a challenge, but rewarding. I've been working a lot with that elderly gentlemen from our parish, right? Yes, Thomas. He's so kind and has such an interesting history. I love how much he enjoys sharing those stories with me to transcribe, though sometimes it takes me a while to understand all his old dialect. I hear that! I used to have to explain things to my class in simpler terms when I was teaching. Was a good practice in clarity, though! And what about you, dear? How is retirement treating you? Well, it's a bit of an adjustment, to be honest. All these years immersed in numbers and equations and now it's... less so. But I've been enjoying my time joining a local choir. It's been wonderful for this old maths teacher to see music from a new angle. That's wonderful! Where did you get the idea for joining the choir? Honestly, it was the pastor's wife who convinced me. She said it would be good for community and a nice change for me. It has been, definitely, especially after teaching all those years. Community is key, isn't it? We all should help each other out more. I've been doing some community volunteer work in the evenings when I'm not too busy working on my own projects. That's terrific! We should actually coordinate more things together. Right now, I'm looking for more opportunities to help out and also, maybe, teach some digital skills to younger people in our community. Oh, that's a wonderful idea! Youths today could really benefit from understanding transcription work, video editing, all that. You sure you could sit down and explain all that to them? Well, I'm sure we can start with small steps and see where it takes us, but yes, I'm definitely interested in exploring that if anyone is willing to participate. I might be able to help. I've worked in this industry quite a while and there's a lot to share.

Alright, everyone, what did you find out last night's parent's evening? Yeah, what about you, Lucy? Well, um, my teacher said I’m doing quite well in reading. But she mentioned I’m finding Maths a bit tricky at the moment. I knew it! I’ve noticed you get a bit stuck on those sums sometimes. And you, Charlotte, what did your teachers say about you? They said I’m fine in most subjects. But I, like Lucy, struggle with Maths too. Really? Both of you? Might have to think up some fun ways to help you both at home after dinner then. Like what? Well, we could play some Maths games or make it more appealing with toys. Let’s talk about it during dinner, okay? Right now, let’s grab a bite. It’s Pastel de Carne - ground beef and vegetables in a tomato sauce. Hopefully, that won’t smell like cooked human flesh, or we might have a bigger problem. Cooked human flesh?! That sounds funny. What would it even smell like? I don’t know, let's hope we never find out! But in, like, books? What do they say cooked human flesh smells like? That's a bit of a disturbing question, but I think in books they would say it smells awful, awful and the description would probably make you squirm. So why would the book say that? Is the point to try and make it a bit nasty, or? Yes, sort of. It’s to make it unappealing, to amplify the horror of the situation in the book. But in reality, the smell would be really, really off - not like anything we'd be interested in. I suppose. But what about World Book Day characters? Did you see what they were wearing at school? Oh yes! I was a rabbit from "Alice in Wonderland". It was fun. And you, Charlotte, who were you? I was a character from "The Gruffalo". Very good choices! I bet you both looked brilliant. It’s really cool that we get to do that. It also helps reading skills, doesn't it? Seeing a character come to life is a great motivation to pick up a book. Yes, and tomorrow afternoon I’m going to the circus with school because my grandma is going to come pick me up after school. That's exciting! We’ve got some plans ourselves for a day out, but we’ll need to figure out after-school arrangements this week.

Ah, I was talking to Mary yesterday at the curtain shop. She was telling me that the kids have really been enjoying working there. They're even learning a bit about the business side of things, you know? That's wonderful. It's good for them to have a bit of responsibility and something to keep them occupied outside of school isn't it? What kind of work are they doing exactly? Oh they're just mucking in with the rest of the staff, really. But they seem to be enjoying it. Speaking of keepsakes, I was thinking about organising Oisin's birthday party soon, seeing as Thanksgiving is coming up. Have you heard him using any new words or phrases recently by the way? Mudder, I want to read my book about rugby when I'm big. Ah, bless him! He's getting more and more interested in rugby, isn't he? He barely speaks and already knows about rugby. You're his step-grandma though, aren't you? He really looks up to you. I’m more than happy to be involved in organising his party. Now that I’m retired, I have plenty of time on my hands. I think we should do a theme of his own; he seems quite the enthusiast for it, right? Yeah, we could definitely keep it a rugby theme, maybe even convince one of his dads to coach him in some basics before the party? That'd be brilliant. We might have to organise it pretty soon though. How about leading up to the real rugby match that’s happening the week after the party? Good thinking! We could make it all part of one big celebration. But the problem is that we need to sort out where it’s going to be. The garden might be a bit small for a full-blown rugby themed party. How about we use one of the community centres or maybe the local park if the weather is good? You can usually rent those things out for parties. That's a great idea. Plus if we go for a park, we could have a bit of a picnic, take advantage of the outdoor space. And maybe involve some of the other little kids from around the neighbourhood. Yeah, pickeT! I’ll look into that then. Also, with the party coming up, I should probably start thinking about Oisin’s wardrobe.

Hey everyone, did you hear about that new Scrabble's online tournament? They're offering a cool £500 prize for the winner. Thought it could be a fun little challenge for us all to play. Hi Emma, isn't the online version kind of different from playing face-to-face? I mean, some of those words don’t always cross my screen the same way they do on the actual board. I played a couple of rounds actually, Jack. Took some getting used to but it's still fun. The time constraints keeps it interesting. Plus, there are benefits like not having to carry bags of word tiles around. Haha. Right, right. I can see that. But I do miss the tactile feeling of the tiles and the sound of turning them over. Do you read online boards the same way though, Simon? I suppose not. Hence the need to rethink certain strategies, like quickly reading diagonal moves or finding words with high-point letters on the fringe. Exactly! It's good for strategy and vocabulary. It got me curious – between the three of us, what or who do you think is the favorite to win this online tournament? I’d say it’s between you and Simon. Emma has the funniest made-up words but may need the brute force of the Scrabble dictionary. Simon and I have probably the most extensive vocab list. Ah nice, I'd take that as a compliment, especially if 'brute force' in vocab refers to really obscure words that never see light of day in normal conversation. doesn’t come much more obscure than the colloquialisms we use when we're from the North and South of England! Let’s all play and see who can come out on top. Shall we set up a little in-house tournament? We could create some of our own rules for it. If we do, will we use all possible words or stick to something less... inscrutable? Some of Simon's previous word choices make even me pause. Good question. I think a mix would be best. Maybe we start with standard rules but also set up a special 'regional dialect’ round so we can use those North/South colloquialisms. That's a great idea! Plus, could use it as an opportunity to learn more about each other's local expressions. We could also impose punishments for using words that no one else understands.

Ah, I'm so glad we could finally meet up after all these weeks. I've missed you like crazy. Me too! It feels like forever since we last met up and had a proper chat. Yeah, it's crazy how fast this semester is flying by. I can barely keep up with assignments and seminars already. Honestly, I wish I could sleep as much as I want right now. I had a lecture till 5PM yesterday and I was out like a light as soon as I got home. Oh, I totally get it. Like, did you even try to stay awake today? Nah, nope. Might have dozed off even during the lecture. Was probably faster than the professor. That's wild. I mean, I've had my fair share of naps during lectures too. But sometimes, I wonder how we're going to manage when we actually have to juggle work and studying in real life. True, true. I hope we don't turn into those stereotypical sleep-deprived students. Definitely not. Speaking of which, did you catch The 1975's new album? I'm in love with the tracks. Especially "Playing on my Mind". Oh, yes! I saw the video drop and I've been listening to it non-stop. I love how they're evolving as an artist. I know right? And "Fallingforyou" is like my new anthem for this semester. We're such music geeks, aren't we? Indeed. It's one of those things that I just won't stop talking about with you. Like when we argue over who's the better band, Arctic Monkeys or Oasis? Yes! You always side with Oasis and I'm all about the Monkeys. Well, I just think their songs are more relatable. But I mean, doesn't matter who we like better; the fact that we can enjoy music together is what matters. Totally. Speaking of which, have you seen Olly's latest Instagram post? Yeah, the one with him playing his guitar. Totally makes me wish I could play something. Sure does. I mean, this year we should try... I don't know, maybe learn one new song together? That actually sounds like a fun project. Yeah, why not? Yes! And we could practice during breaks or maybe even jam together during summer. Now that's something to look forward to. Alright, what's all the noise about?

Hey, I've been reading through the agenda for the council's planning committee meeting next week. Our application is on it. I've never spoken at one of these before, have you? No, this is the first time for me too. But I think this is a great opportunity for us to highlight how this kind of activity can benefit the local community. Besides, our research offers unique insight into how public urban spaces can be refurbished to better serve everyone, especially the younger generation. That's a great point. But even so, it's a bit daunting. I've been practicing my speech, but I'm worried about the structure. Have you thought about how to structure the presentation? Maybe we should split it into sections - introduction, context, specifics of our proposal, and then conclude with the benefits and impact? Ah, that sounds like a good plan. Plus, we could add some visuals. I can scan through our research project and pick out some key images or diagrams that illustrate our points very well. Great idea! I can focus on writing the core content, and you can help with the visuals or even present some of the key points. We really need to stick to the time limit though. Absolutely. I think most committee meetings allow about 10-15 minutes for presentations. So if we structure it right, we can make the most of that time. And remember, it's important to show how our proposal aligns with the current policy objectives of the council as well, right? Definitely. If we highlight how our activity can help the council meet its goals, they're more likely to be receptive. I've been looking at their previous planning reports, and the focus is indeed on improving public spaces and supporting local community initiatives. Right, and it can't hurt to emphasize that too. Also, I think it would help a lot if we can relate the local aspects of it. We need to show them that we're not just talking about a generic idea but something that will have a tangible and positive impact here in our area. You're absolutely right. It might also be good to do a quick mock presentation beforehand. That way we're sure we're not deviating from the key points and can gauge how our ideas flow together. That sounds like a great plan.

Hey, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. I've been meaning to reach out to some old school friends and update my social media, but it's just so much fuss and drama. You know how it is. Aah, yeah, I totally get that. Let’s face it, some of those platforms encourage way too much complaining and gossip, and it ends up getting out of control. Anyway, how have you been? I heard your project at work is going well. Yeah, it’s going relatively smoothly, considering we're still working remotely. But you know, I just had to deal with this one colleague who creates extra work for everyone. It's such a pain, but I guess that's just part of being a project co-ordinator. I wish I could just pinpoint places of annoyance in my day - oh wait, how about that new menu at your local cafe? They seem to have forgotten basic human needs, like offering a standard, affordable sandwich! It's like they want to charge you for barely any food. Oh, for sure! And their tea selection has gotten even worse. They only seem to care about this trendy herbal stuff, no decent English Breakfast left! Oh, have you heard about the news about prices going up though? It's like everything's about to get even more unaffordable. Yes, it’s crazy. I mean, we’re mental health nurses, we already know the world is bonkers, but it seems to be getting more and more silly. And in my work, I’m seeing more and more people coming through because of all this stress and stuff. That doesn’t surprise me at all. I’ve been meaning to watch that new documentary about mental health and climate change, but I haven’t had time. I guess it’s the same stress that’s keeping me away from things that are good for my own mental health. You should watch it. It actually makes a solid point about how our environment is influencing our moods and everything. I might even suggest it to some of my clients. Speaking of moods, we really should plan a day out soon. Just a nice day in some park, or maybe a walk. Perfect, I've been dying to get outta the house. It'll give me a chance to catch up on some gossip, and maybe see the neighbour.

Hey, I'm going to make some tea while you watch that film. Would you like one as well? Yeah, sounds good. Thanks. You wouldn’t happen to have Matcha on hand, right? There was this really interesting bit on the BBC about how the matcha industry is booming in the UK because of the hype around health and wellness. Ah, did you just catch the commercial where they said “buy now and be the first to experience…”? That’s how most “health and wellness” keeps coming backwards due to consumerism, isn’t it? Exactly! Like the NLP training I just read about today. It’s marketed as a quick fix for just about everything, but half the time, what they’re really selling is the magic of advertising and language manipulation. I see. As a language teacher, I’ve actually studied some NLP, but its application in advertising is... interesting. It’s creative, but also misleading. Reminds me of these mobile phone adverts. You ever notice how they never show you the actual price or detail the data plan or even the recycling unit in the back so often this is a ecological and wasteful practice? Absolutely. It’s shallow. And funnily enough, while I was job hunting for my current role, I had a lot of friends who were into the ‘minimalism’ and ‘zero waste’ movements, so buying secondhand phones and avoiding current models was a big thing. Like car boot sales or charity shops for phones? I've seen people selling mobile phones all cleaned up and ready to go. Plus, it’s better for the environment… unless they chuck the old ones away the wrong way. You bring up a good point about environmental impact. And let’s not forget about illegal side of commerce, right? Every week I read about phone crime. Thefts are so common because of their value and portability. It’s crazy how widespread this is, even in Birkenhead. Definitely a problem. And it’s not just phones. You ever go to these car boot sales? I mean, I know there’s the odd genu-wine bargain but often it feels just like a glorified garage sale. Though, I did find an old sports meme T-shirt once that sent me right back to being 16. Haha, memories. But you know, the real job I’m proud of these days is working on my MA dissertation about how certain types of imagery used in dieting campaigns can be more harmful than helpful, especially to people with dyslexia who might struggle to fully understand what they’re getting themselves into.

Hey everyone, welcome back to ANON’s! It's been ages since we've all caught up like this. How's life been treating you all? It's been pretty good, thanks for asking. We’ve got quite a few new neighbors around now and I’ve been trying to get to know them. Speaking of which, have you guys tried out any new mobile phone apps recently? I heard about one that helps you keep up with the climate where you are and it actually influenced where I wanted to go on holiday. Actually, that sounds really interesting. I’ve been meaning to look into sustainable living more and stuff like that, but I never had time. I’ve been pretty busy at the BBC, preparing for the next season. We've got some fantastic new content lined up though, which is exciting. You're always on the go with your journalistic work, how do you manage to balance your life? I’ve heard you guys have a stressful schedule. Yeah, it’s a bit of both. The job can be hectic, but it’s also very fulfilling. I’m just careful to keep track of my time and make sure I have enough space for myself. Plus, with this new app on my phone, I've been trying to use my breaks more productively by taking a few minutes each day to read or write. That sounds like a good approach. I’ve been writing a bit more on the side too, though not quite for work. It’s been a nice way for me to take a mental break from being a radio producer. Speaking of writing, have any of you picked up a new book recently that you’d recommend? To be honest, I've been spending most of my free time lately reorganizing the house and the garden. I kind of went a bit overkill with the whole buying a house experience and I'm still trying to sort everything. But side of that, I’ve been listening a lot to the BBC 6 Music. I noticed a lot of their content is really well-made now, must’ve had something to do with your team, huh? Definitely a credit to the team. It’s been a lot of work but it’s paying off. I’ve been in a similar boat with trying to make my home feel more like my own.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up tonight. It feels like ages since we've all been in one place to talk about old times. Do you remember when we first moved into this area? The late 1960s? Oh, absolutely! It was a real culture shock for most of us coming from different parts of the country. I remember my wife and I moved here straight out of college, just a couple months after we got married. And you? Yeah, me too. I came here straight out of my teaching course. Manchester was fine, but opportunities were limited. This area was seeing a boom in educational institutions at the time – lots of new schools and colleges. I came from a London practice, looking to settle down a bit and take on a quieter life. And of course, I had to retrain as a dental surgeon, that was quite a challenge. Exactly! I remember during our interview process for dental school, the interviewer asked if we could deal with the 'unusual' habits of people from the local area. We all had a good laugh about that! That was a classic! I remember this one time on our first post-grad dental course, we traveled to Athens. It was just days before the Greek military assumed control. Oh, the good old days at university! I wasn’t there, but I can imagine. I used to have some Greek roommates who swore that if you didn’t tune into politics, you wouldn’t understand why things happened the way they did in Athens. It was quite the adventure, I assure you. And the jetlag combined with a sudden change in the political climate… it was like a hellish dream. Tell us about finding places to live! I recall all of you went through a lot of issues, whether it was sourcing affordable rentals or buying your first homes. I must say, I found a lovely little bungalow right at the edge of town, but it needed a bit of TLC. Oh, you’re absolutely right. I think all four of us rented initially. You know how it is – you don’t know if you’re going to stay for years or just a short while. I remember my wife and I spent our weekends doing DIY, fixing up the old place we rented. We did the same! And it was good fun, actually.

Ah, Marion, it's so lovely to finally have some time to chat. I've heard so much about you from mutual friends, but clearly, we've never had the chance to really talk before. Yes, it's wonderful. I've just moved into this area a couple of weeks ago, and I've been finding it so pleasant so far. I've enjoyed our brief chats at the corner shop but I'm really keen to get to know you better, especially since we do share some similar experiences, though they came from different walks of life. Absolutely. I've always loved hearing stories from those who've had, shall we say, alternative professional paths. As an artist and antique dealer, I've often been seen as a bit of an enigma by those in my line of work. I feel the same way about being a speech and language therapist. So many people have trouble understanding the day-to-day of the job, even though it's so rewarding. It's creative too, in its own way, when you think about it. Exactly! Creativity is such a thread that runs through both or professions, don't you think? I often find that it's about connecting symbols or ideas or sounds into something that makes sense to the people who interact with them. You must have such fascinating stories from your time as a dealer/gallery owner. I mean, you must've met all kinds of interesting people through the artwork you've dealt with, right? Oh, there are so many stories! Like the time I acquired a really unusual print that turned out to be quite valuable and all the drama surrounding that transaction. Or the families who've come to me with pieces that had been in their family for generations, and that moment when they see it and the history just comes flooding back to them. That really does sound like a true privilege, being able to help keep these stories, and the pieces themselves, alive. Speaking of stories, I've dealt with my fair share of language and speech challenges, which are also often linked to family histories and personal narratives. You've shared some of those with us at book club, if I'm not mistaken? I remember you talked about working with children whose speech had been affected by trauma or family dynamics.

Hey, I'm going to make pasta for dinner, can I ask you to pick up some fresh basil from the market? It's about a five minute walk. Of course, no problem. Are we still on for the usual squeeze of lemon or are you trying something new this time? A bit of both, actually. I'm thinking of marinating chicken in lemon-garlic, so a squeeze of fresh lemon would be perfect. Sounds delicious. I hope your experiments with chicken are working better this time... Remember how it turned out like a shoe sole last time? Oh, yes. That was not good. But I'm determined to try again, and today's marinade has been sitting in the fridge for a good few hours already. So, hopefully, that should work out better. Fingers crossed. Anyway, I should probably get moving. Anything else I should pick up while I'm there? That's all, thanks. Just the basil. Okay, got it. I'll be back in a few. Ah, Sarah! Fancy seeing you. You’re just in time, I was about to start on dinner. Help yourself to a glass and join us. Thanks, love! It’s great to be home. Smells amazing in here. What’s cooking? Pasta with lemon-garlic chicken and a bit of spaghetti squash. Alright, I'm about to add the chicken to the pan. How’s business been at the café? Busy, busy! We've had a lot of pre-Christmas orders for cakes and such. People seem to be falling for the idea of getting their Christmas baking done early this year. That makes sense. I noticed a lot of places doing early holiday deals too. Speaking of Christmas, have you started any decorations around here or in the café? I’ve brought out the lights and some of the Christmassy-patterned tablecloths over at the café. But for here, we can start with some of the decorations we bought when we were over in the States last year. I might get them out later. Did anyone want to start with something sweet before we dig into the main? I just picked up these amazing candy canes. They're not your usual peppermint but got these amazing flavour variants. That sounds perfect, actually. I just realized we could use some dessert for after dinner. What flavours do you have? I’ve got the usual peppermint, sure, also raspberry, orange, and a new one that’s like a cranberry and cinnamon mix.

Hey Mum, so what did you think of my first year's flat? I know it's not too far from the college but it was a bit cramped. It was really well thought out, I'm glad you managed it all so well on your own, but yes, a bit small for a man your size! Thanks, I suppose. I've been thinking of looking for a bit more space next year, maybe something just outside the city. That sounds like a good idea. You could get a small house in a town like St. Ives or Newmarket, they have a good commute to Cambridge. Plus, St. Ives has been getting more pubs and shops lately. That would be great. I read that property prices have started rising in the area though. True, but it's expected considering the growth of Cambridge as a city. It's important to be prepared financially, though. Yeah, that's something I'm trying to tackle this semester. I've started applying for part-time jobs at the library or something. Hopefully, that'll give me more financial security. Well done, planning ahead is the key. And how are you finding this year's course? Was the jump from undergrad to postgrad as substantial as I expected? It's been challenging. The first year was very vocational – learning loads of different techniques and approaches – but I think I'm finding my footing now. I've also been getting really involved with some research projects, which is taking up a lot of time. That sounds excellent. Research experience is invaluable. And have you started thinking about your thesis subject? I have, actually. I'm considering something around the future of publishing and how the rise of e-books has affected the industry, maybe from a local perspective. Ah, interesting. Your father was quite involved in the publishing industry wasn't he? There must be lots of insights you can draw from his experience. Yes, Dad's always been supportive and knowledgeable on that front. I'm sure his connections could help me get some good case studies. Remind me to send you that Cambridge University Press contact of mine. You know, networking is as important as the work you do. That would be great, thanks. Also, I've been meaning to ask you about Oxford. Our college has a good exchange program with their fine art department.

Ah, I'm so glad we could find a corner to chat. I'm just getting back into these alumni events after a gap. How about you? Do you enjoy coming back to Cambridge every so often? Yes, I really do. I love it now, but I have to say, when I first moved back to the UK from traveling, the familiarity was nice. Speaking of traveling, have you been anywhere interesting recently? Actually, I just got back from a trip to China. It was fascinating. The language was challenging, but it was really rewarding to learn a few phrases. You know, it's funny, people often underestimate how much history and culture you can learn from just the language itself. That’s a great point. I had the opportunity to give some lectures while on sabbatical in the Middle East. What struck me was the depth of history in those countries - you can feel it, even in the languages. Absolutely. It's the same when you learn a bit of Spanish or Arabic. You start to appreciate how different dialects and expressions carry their own stories within them. Really interesting. I'm curious, what was it like being able to give lectures in the Middle East? Was it a big change from teaching here in the UK? It was a substantial cultural shift, let's say. But the students were very enthusiastic. And it was remarkable how similar some of our subjects of study were, despite being from such different backgrounds. I could see that being really enriching. I've always wanted to explore the East more, but my work keeps me pretty tied up. But it proves the point about the interconnectedness of our studies, doesn't it? Whether we're excavating ancient villages or tracing the history of the English language, there's always something new to discover. Exactly! I've actually been experimenting with learning a bit of Chinese on my own. It's quite complex but intriguing. That’s great! I find language barriers can sometimes be the most interesting part of traveling. Like when I was in China, struggling to order food but then had this incredible conversation with someone who spoke just enough English to help. Stories like that truly stick with you. It does bring to mind my own experiences. I was on an excavation in the north of England and there were almost unintended cultural exchanges just in the way we observed our work and each other.

Right, so did you guys see that viral video last night? The one where the chef made the biggest pizza ever and then ate it all himself? Oh yeah! I thought that was quite funny but also a bit horrifying at the time. Still, now I’m considering making a smaller version for tomorrow. I don’t think making one for yourself is a bad idea. Cooking at home has been quite healthy for us lately, you know, especially since I've been working from home and need to budget more for my upcoming movie project. True. That actually reminds me, I need to rethink my orders from the suppliers next week. This recent trend of people staying home and ordering bread online has been really helpful but also challenging. How so, as a café owner? Well, pre-COVID we had a lot of walk-in customers and we could kind of predict what would sell. But now, being mostly delivery and takeaway, it’s harder to guess. Plus, there are a lot of things to juggle. You ever think about the amount of packaging for all these deliveries? Absolutely! As a baker, this is a huge problem for me too. I’ve tried to reduce packaging as much as I can, but logistics are tough. And while the demand for bread has been high in this uncertainty, I worry about the environmental impact. It’s a bit of a Catch-22, isn’t it? Staying in business vs being as sustainable as possible. Definitely. Speaking of which, have any of you noticed the conversations around class and occupation post-COVID? It’s been quite interesting. Oh, it’s been awful. I’ve seen so many posts on social media about people wanting to “just be normal” or “go back to the way things were” without realizing how privileged they are to feel that way. As someone from a small employer’s background, it feels like we’re facing another reality now. It's similar for me. Working and running my own bakery hasn’t stopped changing. You can’t help but think about the class system when you see who’s most impacted – it’s often those in lower supervisory and technical occupations like mine and those in service industries. And it doesn’t help that we see a lot of viral content that perpetuates this classism without even realizing. Like the “quarantine baking” trend, which for some was just a fun hobby, but for many of us, it’s been about survival.

I'm feeling overwhelmed with work and life lately. Between our lectures, the students, and trying to get articles and research published, it feels like there's just not enough hours in the day. I know what you mean. It's a vicious cycle, isn't it? The more we work, the more work we seem to have. But at least we're together and can share it. Which is a blessing, I keeps coming back to that. Right now, my main concern is this new funding application that has been hanging over me. I have to get it in by the end of the month, or our department is in big trouble. It just seems like so much pressure. Yeah, I remember when I had a project deadline and it was the same feeling. But remember, it's not just you. We're in this together, and I'm here to support you through it. And besides, even if we don’t get the funding, it's not the end of the world. We'll figure something out. That's just what I need to hear. Honestly, most of my stress comes from the fact that everything feels so precarious. The politics of the university, the budget cuts... it's really unsettling. Yeah, budgets and politics – never been my favorite topics, right? But it's not just the university, is it? I mean, look at the country as a whole. We have Brexit ongoing and they're still talking about tax reforms... doesn't feel very settled. Exactly. It feels like we're living in a constant state of change and uncertainty. But the thing is, no matter the external variables, together we’re a strong unit, aren't we? Absolutely. And we can deal with change. We're lecturers, and adaptability is part of the job description, right? I guess so. Although I wish there was a 'deal with endless bureaucracy' module at university. It does bring some benefits, though. Like the little extra income and health benefits. True. There's that. I should probably get started on that application. Hopefully, the beer has lifted my stress levels slightly. Drink up. You'll get it done. You're the most meticulous researcher I know. And I'll help any way I can when you need a second opinion. That means a lot, coming from you. Though we should keep an eye on our finances.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together like this. It feels like ages since we've done anything together. How are you all doing? I'm good! Just working a lot of hours at the publisher, but I love it though, the science world is really fascinating – do you have any preferred kind of science books? I've always been a history buff, but I've also got a soft spot for literature. Speaking of which, did you hear that new novel from that up-and-coming British author? I thought it was quite brilliant. No, I haven't. I've been a bit out of the loop these days. Retirement has been nice in some ways, but I do miss keeping up with new books. Do you read a lot in your line of work? Lots and lots. Sometimes it feels like too much actually, but it's the nature of being in publishing! I know what you mean. When I was teaching, I always made sure to read at least one new novel for every book club I organized. It was a lot of work, but so rewarding. Sure was. Nowadays, it seems like everyone’s busy doing... well, busyness. Yeah, the hustle culture can be a bit much sometimes, can't it? Definitely. Speaking of which, this meal is looking delicious. Who cooked today? I did. Figured we’d make something simple but homey. I was thinking of showing you all a couple of new recipes I’ve been trying out. You should! I’m always looking for new recipes to try. The best kinds of togetherness moments are just like this. I agree. You know, getting old has advantages too. Like being able to meet up whenever you want, because nobody's kids have to be picked up from school or sports! You aren't old, by the way. Well, I suppose so. Either way, it's nice to be able to make lunch on our own terms now. Besides, the older we get, the more we have to share, right? Whether it's recipes, books, or just life wisdom. I couldn’t agree more. Speaking of which, what do you two think of watching something after lunch? I’ve been wanting to rewatch some old films lately. I’m game. And while we’re at it, I’ve been meaning to show you all this ancestry research I’ve been doing.

Ah, I never thought I’d say this, but our ten-year-old Grace has really grown into these soft toys. You know, at first it was just her and the little dolls and stuffed animals, but then Sean hooked in here too with video games. I thought it was all going to be screens and phones for the rest of his life. Yeah, I kind of figured as much. Video games are cool and all, but they’re not as useful for learning things or socializing with others, you know? Besides, it’s really good for me to keeps changing what I’m interested in. Otherwise, I’d get really bored. That’s true, but it’s also important to have stuff that makes you happy and relaxed. I remember when I was a kid, playing with soft toys was among my favorite activities. It’s really nice when you mix both—games and making up stories with toys. [Looks up from the soft toys being used as a pretend car and makes a creative noise] Vroom, vroom! My big boy can drive now! [Chuckles] Well, looks like playing pretend never goes out of style. Now that I think of it, it’s maybe even more important for learning and social skills than we might give it credit. Exactly! With pretend play, you can learn about the world and people and stuff without even trying really hard. It’s kind of fun to create your own little stories and make stuff up. Plus, it’s good for my imagination, I think. Absolutely, Sean. And it’s not just about the benefits for you or Grace. It’s about spending quality time together, doing something doesn’t require screens or constant adult guidance. Just letting the kids [and big kids, wink] be creative. Right? I mean, look at this setup. [Points to the soft toys arranged as a little town or track] It’s a whole world here. We’re not just getting them to think or imagine; we’re encouraging play, which is so important for development and bonding. [Looks around at the setup with interest and nods] Yeah, I see that now. It does make sense. Plus, I can relate these play scenarios to what I see in my games sometimes, which is kind of cool. It does bring them a bit closer together, doesn’t it? [Looks at Speaker_4 playing and almost forgets about being the one caring for him most of the day].

Ah, good day everyone! Lovely to see you all's here. I hope today's road trip was alright, didn't get too tiring out there? Cheerio, well indeed! It wasn't too horrendous, had a few stops and enjoyed the views, though the traffic towards London was a right pain. Glad to hear! Speaking of pain, have you heard about the new art exhibition in the city? Apparently, they've got some stunning fractals there. Oh, really? That sounds interesting! I love art, especially something a bit out of the ordinary like fractals. Me too! Can we check it out later? Maybe before going out to have our picnic dinner? Lovely idea! Though first, we should probably sort out the car a bit before it breaks down on us. Have we checked that it's properly serviced? Yes, the children's parents service it regularly, so it should be okay. And considering we've got these galant offspring here, their parents also make sure the horses are in tip top shape before any major outings. For once, a smooth ride it should be. Ha! Oh, horses! Did I tell you about my boyfriend's new horse? He's been going on and on about it. Really? That's exciting! What's his name? It's called Thunderbolt, apparently he's been training for a competition. Speaking of things that go fast... does anyone else think the new speed cameras have gone a bit over the top? Oh, that's a conversation I'd rather not have myself! But it's a bit too topical for now, isn't it? Indeed. Let's keep it light. Turns the conversation to less serious side of things, shall we? Have a joke for us, anyone? What do you get if you cross Santa with a detective? I don't know, what? Santa Claus! You cheeky one!   Everyone laughs out loud, the conversation lightens up. Cheerful laughter! That's truly the best way to start the Christmas season, isn't it? Indeed, and considering the dinner plans, let's hope the cooking turns out as well as the joke. We could all do with a good festive laugh. Speaking of which, any idea what ANON's planning? Always a surprise with that one. You never know, but usually, it's her specialty roast chicken... and lots of mulled wine, of course. Ah, yeah, ANON's a master at whipping up a spread fit for a king, despite not working as a chef.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up tonight. It's been ages. How's work treating you, Alex? It's good, thanks! The marketing team at the agency just signed a new client this week, so we're all quite busy. I see, and you, Sarah how's your week been at the hospital? We've been hearing a lot about the shortages and how staff are feeling stretched even more than usual right now. Yeah, it's been tough, but everyone's really coming together. I have to say though, I just had a patient's family thank me for staying in early today. It just made my day. Yeah, it sounds like the pandemic's impact on the healthcare system is still pretty evident. I imagine most of us have a friend or family member in the NHS, so it's also personal for us. Right. And you know, it's funny. Just last week I had to refer to a couple of the staff on my team about patient care during a shortage. I'm always impressed by how they're managing it. I'm sure it's tough for all of the departments. But speaking of which, are we still on for that Italian meal we were discussing? Maybe we can all give ourselves a bit of a treat after this week? I'd love that! We could take it easy this weekend and just enjoy some good food, really good food. Ah, I'm a bit worried about this Scottish Independence business. What have you two fellows heard about it? Yeah, it's all over the news. They're having a referendum to see if they want to leave the United Kingdom. Just like Brexit then? But isn't there some kind of history behind this? Speaker_3 : Yes, mum. Scotland has been part of the United Kingdom for 300 years now, but for much of history before that, it was separate. Over the past few decades, there's been a growing movement for Scotland to become independent again. I had no idea. It's really been brought into the spotlight then, just like Brexit. How would you vote if you had a say, son? Well, I don't really understand all the ins and outs of it, but if Scotland does become independent, do they get to stay in the EU or not? That's a big question. The last I heard, if Scotland votes to leave the UK, they would need to apply to the EU as a new country. So, whether or not it would be accepted as a member is another whole debate. That complicates things, doesn't it? Suppose they do get to stay in the EU – what about the border between England, Scotland, and Wales? Would that become a hard border like with Ireland? I think that's one of the concerns, yes. It could affect trade and travel, as well as the unity of the isle. So, would Scottish independence impact our daily life in England much? On the surface, probably not immediately. But it could lead to constitutional changes, and depending on the terms of independence, things could shift over time. There's also the fact that England, Scotland, and Wales all share the pound. If Scotland becomes independent, will they use the pound still or have their own currency? That's another debate. Some say Scotland could continue using the pound, like some other countries do without being part of a formal agreement. But some are calling for a Scottish pound. I always take notes at school, but this is all new information to me. You know, most of the Scottish politicians are against independence. The ruling party in Scotland is the Scottish National Party , and even they are divided. I think it's going to be a close vote. It's almost funny thinking about how something that happened centuries ago keeps causing waves today.

I don't know's this stupid lad's got the cheek to blame his own sister for his mistake. Honestly, what's this world come to? Oh, it’s almost as if he doesn’t know any better! But have you heard his accent? Sounds just like the folk around here in Chester. Wait, you mean like the way he says 'wormit?', he says it so strong! Yep! That's a classic, isn't it? It's like the 'elision' with the 'w's, very similar to what we get up North, just like down in Yorkshire. Exactly, it’s the way we drop certain consonants or vowels to make words easier to pronounce. Like, up in Wakefield, we say 'gonna' instead of 'going to'. It’s quite noticeable if you’re used to it, but people from outside often can’t pick it up. I was in Forth so often this summer, and I started saying 'gonna' all the time. My friends from Derby thought I was mocking them! And while I was there, I got so used to hearing the 'flat a' so much - the way they say 'bath' more like 'bahth'. Oh, I know, it’s funny how you pick up accents when you’re really around them. I was in London once, and all I could hear was 'innit' everywhere! I’m the same when I'm down South; it seems like everyone around me is all 'innit this', 'innit that'. But when I’m back in Derby, it’s a bit too much. And when we're all together here, it's like we've got our own little accent party. From Yorkshire to Chester, to Derby - we’ve got a whole map on our tongues. Speaking of maps, have you noticed how Jeremy Kyle just loves to stereotype regions? As if anyone from 'down South' speaks like they're from a soap opera all the time. Exactly! It’s just so tiresome. But maybe that’s what gets people watching, you know, the drama and stuff. You know, it does show how different we all are but also how we’re not that different. We speak this way because that's what’s around us, our cultures, our history. Yeah, like how using 'elision' isn’t just about cutting out sounds, it’s about our roots and where we come from. And, it makes conversations more natural, in a way.

Ah, I'm losing my voice from screaming at the TV. We have to pick a winner for these Olympics, what's yours? Honestly, I'm not fussed. I've always been more into knitting than sports. I've spent the last week working on a blanket for our new nephew. What kind of names have you two thought up yet for the little one? Ah, names! Yes. I've been going back and forth between Jack and Harry. But, to be fair, it's really your niece that's keeps coming up with the most bizarre suggestions. This week it's been either 'Ball' or 'Socks', which I have to say is quite appropriate for someone dear to football lovers like us. Ball or Socks... that's hilarious. Well, from a language perspective, 'Ball' could work well. It's a pretty straightforward name and easy to pronounce across languages, if you ever plan on traveling with the little one. That's true, I hadn't thought of it from that angle. You're so analytical, even with baby names. I hope you don't start using that same approach with this game. Tottenham and Liverpool are giving it their all, but Tottenham is getting a bit too silly. Their corner kicks are all over the place. It's football, not ballet. It's fine if it gets a bit... lively. I did a bit of research on the old dialect of Scouse, it really is fascinating how much it's influenced the way people speak there. And Tottenham, they've got a broad range of fans doesn't they? Oh, that's true. Very proud and diverse fan base. I do love the banter though. Last match the fans were chanting about the opposition's "first touch". I just thought, isn't that a weird thing to boo someone over? Yes, it's quite peculiar. But it goes to show how much emotional investment people have. You know, it's interesting to think about how these games also play into national identities – and that often ties back to linguistic identity, for sure. Ah, yes, truly so. And speaking of national identity, we should probably give some of that to the English team too. This Euros has been a bit of a letdown so far. But maybe we'll turn it around.

Who knew I'd spend Easter Monday educating my friends' children about the intricacies of insectology and social hierarchy? The Bee Movie clearly struck a chord with everyone, didn't it? But isn't that just like, what's happening with climate change? Exactly! So, what about the other side of the coin? Do you feel like royalty or politics would make the world better or worse? I want to be a queen! Then I could make sure all the animals and trees are safe and everyone gets a fair share of food and things. But what about the people who disagree with what you want to do as queen? How would you make sure everyone is happy? That's a great point, Timmy. I mean, even if you're a kind and fair monarch, the system itself can still be problematic. In fact, that leads us to today's other interesting topic: the royals and their... "public" palatial residences. You mean like Buckingham Palace? I heard you have to pay to get in there now? Yes, and that’s pretty ironic considering we live in a system doesn’t practice open palaces as the movie plays with the idea that bees might want to sue for trespassing but then on the other hand here’s us paying to visit a royal palace. But weren’t there times when the royal family would invite everyone in for banquets and stuff? Seems like now it's more about lining their own pockets. While some might argue it's a way for the Royal Family to help fund the upkeep of these historic places… it does highlight a bit of hypocrisy if we think about what the film’s message was. Either way, it’s a bit ironic we’re discussing this on a day we explored the concept of a republic versus a monarchy through Hollywood's eyes and now we could perhaps muse about what this almost upsets in our own culture.

Ah, this is just what was needed after that trip to the tip. I swear, there was more rubbish in the yard than flowers in the garden at this time of year! Well, almost all of us will be in the same boat soon enough. As for advising, I’d say embrace the changes. Use the internet to stay connected, learn new things, maybe even start a blog about your life or gardening.

Hey, I was thinking we might want to grab some brunch this weekend. Got any recommendations for a decent spot nearby that isn’t too crowded? That sounds great! Hey, I just caught a new Pokémon in my game and I've been thinking of getting into Skyping to talk about it with my mates. Thought maybe one of you might even want to beat me down some Ramen. Ah, I'm going to tackle that cupboard first. We've got so many things stored in there that we never even look at anymore. Remember when we used to use this old 'gardening set' as kids? The weather today could use a bit more consistency, too. One minute it's sunny and the next, heavy rain showers. Yeah. It's been a bit of a challenge to decide whether to sit in the garden or not. I went out for a walk earlier and the rain caught me off guard.

Ah, I'm so glad we could take a walk today. The weather is perfect. It's these little moments together that I cherish. Absolutely. And I've missed our chats. It's been quite a while since we've had time to catch up, hasn't it? Now that we have this daily park routine with the baby, it feels like a win-win. It really does. I've also noticed... mosquitoes. Oh, totally, but to be honest, I've been using this lavender oil stuff, and it seems to deter them a bit. Though, let me tell you, even then, I find myself swatting at the air a little more often than I'd like. Good call. I'll definitely need to look into that. Perhaps we can make a fun trip out to get some... how about we plan a special spot? Maybe visit a park in the countryside on the weekend? Somewhere free of mosquitoes, that is! That's a brilliant idea! We could make it a family day out. And speaking of plans... have you thought anything about the upcoming music festival? The one that we love? You know, the one with the good music, but not the terrible traffic? Well, I have. But honestly, I keep thinking about the traffic horror stories from last year... Maybe we should skip it this time around? I really can't see any of us enjoying chaos like that with a little one in tow. Yeah, you're right. Maybe we can just enjoy it from home this year... or is the baby still too young for live music anyway? Except, we could do a family-friendly one... I can't imagine it being too crowded, given the short notice, but maybe we could take a chance? Oh, could be interesting. We could almost pop in if the mood strikes.

Hey everyone, did you know that many of the first Great Ormond Street Hospital Children's Hospital trust funds came from people who were fans and inspired by Peter Pan? Really? Barrie, who wrote Peter Pan, gave the rights of his play and novel to the hospital back in 1929. Speaking of themes, do you think the original Peter Pan story still has relevance today? It’s about never growing up, right? Absolutely! The idea of freedom and not growing up can be seen as a critique on adult society and adults wanting to control children.

Ah, I'm going to miss this little jaunt down to Taunton. Nothing like the quiet of the morning commute to put your mind at ease, though it's not exactly the most scenic drive. I know what you mean. Ah, I'm so glad we could take a break from all this manual labor. I'm nearly 70 and my joints are protesting already. Do you enjoy working with your hands? Not as much as I used to. Hey Mum, did you manage to sort out the last bits of our Malaga trip today? Ah, I'm just enjoying this lovely cup of tea, isn't it wonderful? Nothing beats a good old cuppa. Reminds me of the holidays when I was younger. Hey, I was going over some of the art history stuff we've been covering in today's class and I realized that even after all these years, I don't really understand how artists back then were able to manage working with limited technology and still produce such masterpieces. It's just so impressive considering everything we have at our disposal today and yet some of it still feels so...average. That's a great observation! I mean, think about it, Da Vinci was fracturing perspectives before we even knew what that meant. It's not even just technology, right? Their understanding of composition, light, and color was truly groundbreaking, and it's a shame we often skip over the technical skill side just because we have Photoshop or something. Absolutely, it's like we're sometimes privileged but also deprived in some ways. Easy access to tools can make us lazy, you know? And then on the other hand, imagine trying to explain Instagram filters to someone from the 16th century. It’s creative overload in both directions, I guess. Exactly, it's like the universe is playing a constant game of 'upgrade or die.' For me, looking at art from different eras is actually giving me some new ideas for my own projects. It pushes me to think more about basics—like the way light falls, the composition of the entire space, not just relying on Photoshopping the core out of a picture. That makes total sense. It's nice to see how focused they were on fundamentals, things we now take for granted in art or even graphic design. One thing that really struck me, though, is the humanity in these pieces. Like, even when the theme doesn't resonate with you 100% the feelings that come through... it's almost timeless. Right, and it's not just about creating something visually stunning—they were often commenting on society, politics, emotions... It's a completely different angle from today where sometimes it feels like art is either explicitly political or just trying to find its next viral hit. True, but changing times call for changing art. I guess we might view these historical pieces as anomalies or out of touch, but they had their own version of 'real' to capture. It’s something we’re trying to recreate with virtual reality experiences or interactive installations now. Maybe our future generations will look back at the early 21st century art and think about how much it represented this digital boom era in the same way we look at the Renaissance.

We want to assure they grasp the foundation before delving into the specifics of each of our topics. That makes sense, but we also have to consider the interactive aspects. We should engage the students right from the start, maybe with an icebreaker activity that relates to business communication across cultures. That’s a good idea. We could have them do a small group discussion based on a scenario. It would be more interactive and participatory than a standard lecture, right? Yes, and using case studies would be excellent. We can choose specific real-world examples that highlight both success and failure in different cultural contexts. Absolutely, case studies are a great way to illustrate and make the material more tangible. Plus, doesn’t real-world application make it more relevant and interesting for the students? Definitely. I also think if one of us can provide the foundation or general overview, the other two can delve into their specific area, and we wrap it up together with a Q&A session. That's a good structure. We should also make sure our consent form explains what each part of the seminar will entail. For example, if we use examples of businesses or actual video material, we need to let students know if they need to agree for that to be shown in the seminar. Right, we don't want anyone caught off guard or feeling like they're being asked for something without fully understanding the context. Good point.

I'm really struggling with teaching this year. It feels like no matter how hard I try, my students are not grasping the material as well as they used to. What's changed? Was there a particular module? I think it's partly the way the curriculum has been altered. It's more theory focused and less practical. It just doesn't seem to engage them like it used to. I know what you mean. I've noticed similar issues with my courses too. It makes me feel like I'm failing them, you know? As lecturers, our job is to help them learn, not to simply impart information. No, you're not failing them. These are systemic changes that might not be your fault. But what can you do about it, I mean, practically speaking? Honestly, it's hard to say. I've tried adjusting my teaching style, adding more interactive elements, but it's like the problem is deeper than that. Maybe I need to meet with the curriculum team to discuss it. You should definitely do that. It's worth bringing up. Also, in the meantime, have you considered incorporating more real-world examples or case studies? It might help them connect the theory to their own lives. That's a great idea. I hadn't thought of that. Thanks, maybe that's something to try. Of course! And remember, you're not alone in this. We're in this together. Except, we're on opposite ends of the world right now. True. We won't get to teach together for a while. Oh, by the way, are you excited about living in our new house? Yes! You saw the view from the roof, right? It's stunning. I can't wait to start decorating. Me too! I already have ideas for the walls and furniture. You could have saved some of those ideas for this house, you know. Ha! I came prepared. How is your move still going? Well, I'm almost done packing. The only thing left is deciding which hobbies I really need to bring here. I'm sure that sounds simple to you, but I can imagine it can get quite deep. Remember, if it doesn't fit in the house, it can come to visit! True! Maybe I'll just keep the ones that fit in a suitcase. Sounds like a plan. Are you looking forward to the smaller community lifestyle, too?

Ah, I'm so glad we could find time to catch up. It feels like ages since we last had a proper conversation without all the usual interruptions. Me too, sis! Life has been pretty hectic since I moved to London. Still trying to settle into this whole urban lifestyle after being in the countryside for so long. It's certainly a change. I moved about a year ago and even with a shorter commute, I'm still adjusting to the pace. I had to laugh though; coming from rural Sussex, I was surprised how many people get their groceries delivered in these areas. Hahaha, yes! I'm finding it interesting how London is ahead of the curve in terms of technological trends. Though, have you noticed how even here, there's still so much food wastage from big supermarkets? They send so many fresh fruits and veggies off to waste every day. It's disgusting, isn't it? When we were little, our grandparents barely let anything go to waste in their kitchen. They always said it was thanks to the war-time rationing. I hope as much recycling and reusing catches on here as quickly as it is in some parts of Europe. Absolutely. Regarding food waste specifically, I read that the new 'closed kitchen' initiatives they're trying out in Sheffield are interesting. It's about building local, circular food systems where businesses can connect directly with local growers to minimize waste and emissions. It'd be great to see that take off more widely. Really? I hadn't heard about that. Our grandparents, despite all their traditional ways, were always keen on community efforts. Maybe we should look into something like that where we live? I'm sure that kind of initiative would have brought our grandparents to their feet. Definitely. On that note, the TV series we started watching, weren't we both thinking of the arranged marital bits as a bit... quaint? If not slightly worrying? Quite. Reading and watching about it from a distance is one thing, but to consider it seriously for our own lives? Not happening for either of us, thankfully. Though, I suppose in some cultures, it’s still quite a thing, isn't it? It’s indeed still a reality for many, and not just in the obvious places. Again, it’s about those deeply ingrained traditions and community structures.

Hey, I'm going to make some pasta. You know, nothing fancy, but today's been a long one and I need something simple. You sound like you could use a break. Is it work related? Just a tough day with some new patients questions were tough to navigate and conversations were involved and tiring. That can be draining. As an assessment manager, I'm right there with you. Last week, we had to deal with a complicated case. The parents were really skeptical about our approach, and it required a lot of explaining and reassuring. Exactly! Explaining the psychological approach to people who don't fully understand it can be really challenging. Especially when they have their own ideas of what would work. Yeah, and it's not just making yourself clear, it's being sensitive to their concerns and worries too. Sometimes they see the big picture, but aren't looking at the individual details. It's like they have the framework, but the walls are missing. Absolutely. Sometimes it's hard to not get frustrated though or feel like you're being misunderstood? Sure, it happens. But it's part of what we do. We're not just psychologists; we're also mediators of sorts. Good thing is in the end, when you can help someone understand, the reward is worth it. Absolutely. But sometimes, to be honest, it feels like we're being asked to 'fix' things that in reality, aren’t for us to fix. Society, the system, all those complexities. I know what you mean. It's like being the front line and the lighthouse at the same time. You’re supposed to highlight the path, but if the sea is stormy, it doesn't mean the light isn't helping those that can see it. That's a good way to put it. It's a bit like cooking really; you can prepare the best dish in the world, but if the consumer doesn’t like the ingredients, that's their problem, not yours. I suppose so! But for me, I have a different frustration. The structure of our education system can feel quite rigid at times. It doesn't always fit with what students actually need. That must be challenging. Over the years of my work, I've seen repeatedly how education impacts health later in life. If we could only get better at adapting to individual needs from the start.

Ah, I'm losing my mojo, you know? We used to have so many things to do when we were young. Now, it feels like all the routes are closed off. You're right. There's a lot of time on your hands now, and it’s tough to fill it in a meaningful way. I find myself missing the energy and purpose I used to have. It's not just that. I think a big part of why we might feel this way is we're not as socially connected as we used to be. As we get older, it gets harder to make and maintain friendships. Exactly! Like when did social gatherings just stop? Now it's just this... this silence in our lives. And to think, there was a time when we gathered at the sea in the summer, gathered our families together - oh, the laughter, the joy... Ah, those were happy days, indeed. But I think a lot of it comes down to... how we view our situations. It's easy to slip into these negative thought patterns. But we've got to try and shift that around, haven't we? Absolutely. I've been on both ends - feeling down and then, actively making different choices to feel better. Volunteering has been a game-changer for me. It gives you a purpose and connects you with others. I used to think, why bother? But actually, it can make quite the difference. Like, what kind of volunteering, John? I've been helping out at a local wildlife trust. One time, I was there and we spotted these baby blue tits! So tiny and full of life. It's things like that which keep the heart young, you know? That sounds wonderful, John. I may have to look into that. Something like that could definitely give me a lift. I just wish, though, that I had a bit more money to spend. These bills, they seem to only get bigger. Same here, and it really makes me depressed thinking about it. We used to worry about bills on a weekly basis, but now… it's every day. I feel like we're just surviving, rather than living. It's a common issue, certainly. But speaking of budgets, we should maybe look into seeking advice or support. There are services available for people with money worries. And, if you're feeling depressed, talking to someone like a counselor could really help.

Hey, I just got this new hand cream and it's amazing. It's called Hand in the Wild by Dr. Botanic. Ah, that's the natural skincare brand, right? I've heard really good things. What do you think the ingredients are like? Oh, it's got loads of shea butter, cocoa butter, and some essential oils. The packaging looks great too, very earthy and minimalist, I love that about it. That sounds lovely! I've got sensitive skin and I need something gentle. Do you think it would work for me? I've noticed my nails and hands have been getting really dry lately. I think it would work really well. Sentitive skin just needs the right oils to balance it out. I read that shea butter is really good for that - it’s so nourishing. And cocoa butter’s always great too. Plus, if they’ve used essential oils that are known for being good for your skin, that’s an extra plus. That's good to know. I've been using this expensive brand's cream that I got at a beauty shop, but it's not really doing much this winter. Have you tried using different oils to massage your hands? Sometimes that can really help, rather than just slapping on some cream. I think the secret is really in massaging it in really well, so the skin can absorb it properly. That's a good point, perhaps I need to show my hands some love. I do a bit of a massage when I put cream on, but maybe I should focus on that part more. Exactly, and also try to use it at the right time. For example, immediately after washing your hands or before bed. That way, the oils can really penetrate during the night. Makes sense. Have you noticed the effect of drinking a lot of water on your skin? Some people say it really helps to hydrate from the inside out. Oh, definitely! While I was studying for my TEFL certificate, I had to teach a class on healthy lifestyles, and that was one of the key points - staying hydrated for skin health. If you're not drinking enough, it can really show in your skin, nails, hair... everything! Right! And I definitely need to be better at that. I know I hardly drink enough water during the day. Well, I started carrying around a refillable water bottle everywhere since lockdown started.

Alright mate, what've you got planned for the weekend? Not much, just some work stuff to catch up on. I've got a big interview for a masters next month. I'm a bit nervous, you know? No, mate! You'll be alright – you're questions are always spot on and you've handled harder situations before. That's reassuring to hear. I've also got to go check out that new museum exhibit.
