Have you heard about it? Yeah, it's really good, actually. They've got some amazing pieces from the local artists, plus a really interesting interactive display on the history of Liverpool. That sounds fitting then. Is it near to any good parking spots? I suppose I could walk from there. There's usually spots near the Lime Street area. If you're lucky, you might even find one near the museum itself. It's a bit tricky sometimes, but worth it once you're parked! Yeah, good point. I hate parking in Liverpool. Someone should make a better parking system. I’ve spent hours looking for spots in the past. Sure, but it's a small price to pay for all the lovely places to go and shop around this city. True. Have you had time to check out the new shops in the city center? They've opened up some great high street stores there. Not lately, but I'd love to take a look. Speaking of which, I've been thinking about doing some Christmas shopping soon. What about you? I'm usually the last minute person, but doesn't feel much like Christmas yet. Last year's the one that sticks out because of my work. There were a lot of families in hard times and it was tough seeing so many less fortunate side of things. Oh, I can relate to that. I noticed a lot of stress and uncertainty among students when schools started getting cancelled last year. It's one of the reasons I'm considering moving to a different part of the city. You ever thought about moving house? Yeah, it's a bit on the backburner right now. But for sure, I've thought about it. The area I live in is getting busy, and public transport is a bit of a gamble. Again, it's about those small prices. But if it means you'll be happy and less stressed... True.

Hey, I'm so glad we could catch up without the kids this evening. It's been ages since we've had an evening all to ourselves. Oh, absolutely! I've missed these talks. There's just something about sitting down without the little ones running around, isn't there? It feels like we can finally just talk. Definitely. I've been meaning to ask you, how are you finding life without a job right now? It must be a big change, especially after your very set routine with work. It's a whole different ball game. Honestly, it's been a bit of a struggle. I have to keep myself occupied all day, and it's not as easy as I thought. But then again, I get to spend this quality time with [child's name], and it's rewarding in its own way. That’s true. Step parenting can be challenging, but the moments with your little one make it all worth it, right? Absolutely. It's funny because sometimes it feels like the world is so focused on what mothers do, and I’m learning to find my own way within this role. It’s interesting and quite rewarding. I can imagine. I've been involved in step-parenting while teaching, and balancing both can be tough. But the most important thing is to let the child know you're there for them, and to create their own little space within your family, without overstepping perhaps. Exactly. I’m trying to navigate that as well. But it’s also shown me the importance of independence – not just for me, but also for [child's name] as they grow up. Independence is such a big theme right now. I've been thinking about it with my own teaching job. There's the push for independence in our children, but also in our own lives as women, as partners, and as individuals. Absolutely. I remember when I was teaching, I felt so strongly about instilling independence in my students. But now as a mother, and not working, I'm realizing how much of my own identity was tied to my job. It’s been a bit of a wake-up call, really. That’s so interesting. I’ve found myself going through something similar. I’ve always defined myself by my job, but now I’m exploring other interests and finding they bring so much joy.

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without any plans. It feels so refreshing to just chill and talk about whatever comes to mind. Totally. I needed a break from my thesis. There's something about unwinding at the pub and people-watching, though, isn’t there? Especially when we're just chilling with close friends or family. Absolutely. It feels like we're just catching up, right? Life gets busy and suddenly it's been ages since we last spoke properly. Yeah, and it seems like we're stuck in this weird loop, doesn't it? Even our conversations have started to feel like old habits, sticking to the familiar topics – TV shows, our friends, that new online shopping addiction ... or should I say, obsession? [Laughs] [Laughs] Oh, that’s definitely a fair call. I’ve found myself on Pinterest more often than I care to admit looking for birthday ideas or creative breakfast hacks. [Laughs] You and me both. I’ve recently become obsessed with finding the next great baking or DIY project. But have you seen that new cooking show on TV? It’s called "The Great Bake Off," right? I’m hooked. Reminds me of when I used to bake with my mum. It’s really making me want to get back into it, you know? No, I haven’t had a chance to watch it yet. But my mum always said baking was therapeutic. There’s something about following a recipe, getting messy, and ending up with something edible that’s strangely comforting. And with the "The Great British Bake Off" doesn’t come close to beating it in terms of "proper British culture," does it? Absolutely. I just watched an episode the other day. The mix of British humour and those incredible pastries just won me over. Though, I must admit, it’s a far cry from my usual PhD books. [Laughs] I totally get that. But it’s changing the topics up that really helps, doesn’t it? Plus, it’s nice to see people enjoying themselves and not thinking about their research for once. Exactly. Speaking of which, I finally managed to get tickets to a real football match. [Excited] Are you serious? Which team? Arsenal. I know, I know, I’m a Birmingham boy, but I’ve got a soft spot for them after my mates took me to a match back in uni.

Hey, I'm on eBay looking at some light fittings. I want to surprise you with new ceiling lights. There are some really nice ones from Italy. Oh, that's sweet of you! Is there anything in particular you've found? Yeah, I love these two. They're from a glassblowing house in Venice and they have such unique designs. The first one's quite minimalist and modern, and the second one's more geometric with metal accents. I like minimalist keeps coming up in our conversations. You know our house style. Hahaha, yes! True. But I also like the geometric lamp's whimsy. It's almost playful. Might just highlight the personality of our room. And the prices? Italy isn’t cheap, right? Good call. The minimalist one is £150 and the geometric one is £200. That's not bad considering they're unique. But before we decide, let's also look at what's around us. I was browsing on Rightmove and spotted a house that's up for sale about 20 minutes from here. It’s got three bedrooms, a pretty garden, and it's wider than the place we’re in. Really? That sounds interesting. Let me see the listing. Like I said, it’s about 20 minutes from here. And in our price range really if we keep an open mind about the area and the house itself. I like the look of it. It's a bit bigger than we have now but I kind of like the idea of a garden we could do something with. That's the thing. Right now, we’ve got nothing but a balcony. A garden could mean a lot for the little one and our lifestyle in general. Yes, definitely. And it's also nice to think about future possibilities. We could always make changes inside but having a backyard is a big plus. True. I’ll set up a time to view this for next Sunday. If it’s good, it might take our minds off getting new light fixtures for a while! You’ll always have a plan. Alright, let's schedule this. But just for fun, maybe we could also do a quick Saturday outing if the weather permits? Looking at the forecast, it's supposed to be sunny. You mean a weekend break? That could be nice for change of scenery. I like the plan.

Ah, lovely day today, isn’t it? Yeah, really is. Hope it stays like this for the rest of the week. Oh, definitely. I hate working in the rain, you know? Agreed! But I suppose it’s part of the job. Speaking of jobs, how’s yours going, Sarah? It's great, thanks. I love my job, of course, as much as I can, considering the circumstances. But it can be quite challenging at times. Are you still working at the clinic in Sevenoaks? Yes. It’s been quite busy lately, to be honest. But we manage. The team’s been pulling together. Though, let’s not talk about work for now. Right, let’s chat about something more light-hearted. What’s new with your family? Anything interesting happening? Oh, well, my sister just moved back home with her kids. Two little ones, so my mom’s been running around like crazy. And it seems like the whole house has become a playground. That sounds like a lot of fun though! I'm sure they’re giving your mom a run for her money. [laughs] Yeah, but in a good way. Kids are good for the soul. Speaking of which, I saw your post on Facebook about the new rescue dog you’ve taken in. Ah, yes! A little Terrier, named Betty. She’s a handful in the best way possible. She’s still adjusting, of course, but all in all, she’s been a joy. How’s Whiskers doing? Oh, great! Whiskers is doing much better now. He’s still grumpy, but less so. Maybe it’s the extra company. [laughs] I bet, Whiskers is like a grumpy old man whenever Betty is around. Yes, definitely. But it’s been nice to see them interacting more. Though, changing the litter box has become a bit more of an adventure. [laughs] Oh, I can imagine! Have you thought about adding a baby gate or something? Actually, yeah, that’s a great idea. [smiling] Maybe you can turn it into a dog obstacle course. [laughs] I’ll suggest that! So how about the job hunting for you two? How is that going? I've been applying to a few places but haven’t had much luck so far. It seems there’s lots of competition nowadays. Me too, I’ve been applying online mostly, but haven’t even heard back from most places.

Hey, I read this fascinating article yesterday on sleep science. Apparently, getting enough daylight today helps you sleep better tonight. You know, I was thinking we could plan a camping trip this weekend. What do you think? Oh really? That's interesting. I've always been intrigued by sleep – do you have the article with you? And about the camping trip, sounds like a great idea. When was the last time we went camping? Let me just check my phone. Ah, yeah, here it is. It was talking about how our bodies have a natural circadian rhythm, and if we get enough sunlight during the day, it actually helps trigger our body to produce more melatonin at night, which helps us sleep. That makes total sense. And I think a bit of digital detox while we’re at it wouldn’t hurt either. Exactly. And camping would be perfect. I’ve also realized that when I’m camping, even though I’m looking for a challenging route, somehow I always end up following the GPS. You and your love for maps. I remember once or twice, we nearly got lost because you wanted to take a specific route into town. Oh, the time we got turned around in Edinburgh! I thought the 'shortest route' would be a more adventurous way to get into the city core, but it turned out to be a bit too adventurous – we walked nearly twice the distance . Yeah, I kept saying 'let's just follow the GPS,' but you never listen. Well, doesn’t getting a bit lost sometimes lead to the best finds? True, but also, I don’t want to get lost during the camping trip. Got it! GPS on. Okay, okay. So camping, check. Just to make sure we’re on the same page, are we bringing any pilots with us to fly into the campsite? You mean like a friend who's a pilot? Or are you talking about some general 'flying into the campsite' concept? Either way, I think driving is our best bet. Because last week, I overheard a colleague talk about how her brother could have saved hours if they had gone by air, but in the end, navigating the campsite with a plane was a little too ambitious. Oh, I suppose you could try to land a small plane at the campsite but I think that would be too much.

Hey everyone, did you hear about that strict new rule our uni is imposing regarding our pets? I think it's super unfair. Omg, talked about that in the tea break! They say they're doing it because somebody's hamster kept running away and caused a bit of a drama in the library. Exactly! I had no idea hamsters could be such escape artists. But honestly, it feels a bit like overkill. Yeah, I agree. I mean, if it’s just about one person not properly looking after their pet, then maybe they should deal with that case specifically instead of making rules for all of us. Exactly, and I’ve been wanting to get a hamster for ages just cos they’re so cute. But now I’m reconsidering. It’s a shame though. What’s wrong with being a responsible pet owner? Like most of us want a little companion and we’re going to take good care of it. Yeah, and it’s not even like these rules are entirely clear. They’ve sent out this long email that’s really confusing and vague. We should probably draft a response or see if we can have a word with someone in management. I’m sure we’re not the only ones who feel this way. Good idea! I’ll try to gather some info on the exact policy wording and we can meet up later to work out a draft. Yeah, and maybe we can even pull together some examples of good hamster care to show they’re not always troublemakers. That’s a great idea, and who knows, maybe it’ll actually change things for the better. Not just for us but for future students too. Definitely. But for now, shall we just move on to something a bit more cheerful? Like, anyone want to share a good ginger joke? Oh, now that’s a move! Yes, please share! We really need a laugh. Alright, so why don’t ginger people sit on the beach? Don’t make me guess! Because they’d get beaten up by the sand! Har har. That was a bit of a low one 2, wasn’t it? But still, could have been worse. Yeah, and maybe someday I’ll find a great ginger joke I can use without feeling terrible about it. Totally. But thinking about it, do you guys remember when that viral ginger cat video blew up a few years back?

Right, so here's what we've got so far. We've got these two main factions; these are the people who control the continents. Remember, when you control a continent you get the extra bonus of receiving that many more units every turn. Yeah and I thought this was a bit dodgy at first, because some of these powers don't make a lot of sense historically, but it's quite fun, actually! But actually, I've always found Risk really helps me understand strategy. Like, when I was teaching, we used to play it at school to illustrate certain concepts. Exactly. So, we've just had a round of reinforcements where everyone gets new units based on their control of continents. And now, Aaron, your turn. You've got Northern America, Africa, and Europe - which we're still fighting over. Oh, Europe! That was a hilarious mispronunciation moment yesterday when my partner said something like 'Zhe Off Ron' . I'm surprised this game isn't more popular as an English learning tool, actually. You can learn so much about geography and fun mispronunciation while you play! Speaking of geography, let's also not forget the importance of the sea. Controlling Japan allows you to attack anywhere in the world, which is why everyone always wants it, no matter how small it is on the board. You know, I think I need to apply some of this strategy in my work. Last week I bid on a shipment from China, and it was a risk but paid off, literally. That's great. Seems like the commerce world and Risk have more in common than we think. The idea of weighing risks and taking confident moves. So, for my turn, I'm going to attack from Africa to South America. You've not fortified it well, Aaron. I'm sure in another universe, I'd be a defender, but for now, I'm just trying to keep up! Speaking of keeping up, did anyone else have those strong memories when they could play these games for hours and hardly notice the time? I used to do that with my kids when they were little. They'd be so into the game, they wouldn't want to stop even when it was past their bedtime. It's funny how they often see themselves in the game too - clashing over toy countries until the end of the world.

Hey, I'm losing my mojo for uni, you know? I'm just really unsure if I want to do this whole degree thing. Oh, don't start down that path, we need to focus on the brighter side. Still, I get the feeling, though. But think of all the things we haven't seen yet! We could be planning trips and stuff. Like going to a festival together! I want that, don't get me wrong. But still, it's this pressure... I keeps coming back. You get me though, Rachel. You'll always be my rock, even if I sound like I'm crumbling. Of course I get you. We've known each other since forever, and it's normal to question what we're doing here. But remember, we're in the same boat. And think how many people might be feeling the same right now. It's okay not to be okay with uni all the time, you know? Yeah, you're right. And you know, last week we were talking about Justin Bieber. Someone posted a picture of him playing at Glastonbury, he was like a cute baby compared to now. Oh god, I know. He was so adorable. And while he may seem so far from what we're doing, at the end of the day, he's probably feeling a lot of pressure too. Well, his pressure's probably worse because his music and career is his whole life, right? Absolutely! But sometimes, really successful people have similar doubts too. I read an article about Cardi B. and how she almost quit music because she thought she wasn't good enough. Oh, that's so interesting! It shows us that even celebrities have doubts, and if they can push through, so can we. Yeah, I just wish I had a clearer idea of what I want to do after. So what if you don't? What if you just take each step as it comes? You don't have to have it all planned out right now. True. I guess I just put too much pressure on myself. I want to make my family proud, but also do something I love. It's so hard to balance. Again, it's about those small steps. Look at it this way, you already made the choice to come to university, which is awesome. Just focus on passing your modules now.

Hey, so did you finish reading that part of the school's online notes for our project? I found it pretty confusing. Yeah, talked to my cousin the other day. He said he found it a bit overwhelming at first too. Still, now I think I get it a bit better. Oh right, yours stays in Wembley, right? Like how convenient that his mum's a teacher, makes life easier, doesn't it? Erm, yeah, it helps sometimes. But even with an academic household, there are still difficulties when discussing certain topics. What you mean? Like, we were having a chat about poverty and government intervention. His mum just says things like, "Plus, we have to look at the bigger picture of market forces and global supply chains," but how does that help the couple next door who can’t even afford food? Exactly! It’s like, we talk about things in school but when it comes to real life, people are just struggling. It’s not so far off from where I live in Slough, you know. For me, it’s like, on the news, they talk about how poverty is decreasing, but when you walk outside, it’s kind of hard to believe. Yeah, it’s all smoke and mirrors sometimes. It really makes you think about the kinds of life we're supposed to lead – like, consumerism for example, it’s always telling us we need more but is it really making us happier or more fulfilled? It’s all about what we’re 'supposed' to want. Just like how they say in that video we watched about scientific research – how we’re supposed to care about finding the next cure but then you look at the funding and it’s all about what will make money quick. Plus, the inequality of it all. I mean, look at our school, even though we’re all here trying to educate ourselves, there are still differences in what we can access at home. Yeah, I mean my friend’s little sister, her family, they’re really struggling. They don’t even have enough money for her to buy the same books we can just pop down and pick up at Waterstones on our lunch break. Speaking of books, have you read the latest Spider-Man? I heard it’s pretty good. Actually yeah, I did. I liked it! They came up with some interesting things for the character.

Ah, I'm so glad we could finally sit down and have a proper chat. I've been meaning to talk to you for ages about how the recording process is going. Everything alright with the music you've been working on? Yeah, it's going okay. It's just kind of frustrating when questions keep popping up outside of the actual piece itself. Like, last week I had this issue with feedback and my neighbour just happened to pop downstairs and give some unsolicited advice about moving my setup around. Oh dear! I can imagine. Neighbours always seem to think they're experts in everything, don't they? Exactly! But, on the plus side, he did mention a good physiotherapist just by the way. He's been dealing with bad joints himself after years of playing in a band. That's useful to know. I've been having a bit of trouble with my knees myself lately. Haven't decided yet if I need to start therapy or if it's just the usual age-related creaking. Oh, it's definitely worth checking out. Sometimes it's the little adjustments he makes that make a huge difference. I'm sure it is. Now talking of "little adjustments," how are you handling all the festivities? Any plans for new clothes in the new year? Ah, clothes. Well, to be honest, I've put on a bit of weight recently, so I feel like I need a whole new wardrobe. But, really, it's about finding something that makes me feel good about my body. I'm not sure diets are the answer - doesn't seem to work for me. Last diet I went on, I lost weight but my skin looked terrible, and I ended up bingeing because it was too restrictive. Understandable. I've tried so many of those "miracle diets" myself over the years, and they never seem to last. What really works is finding a healthy balance and loving and respecting your body, regardless of what changing scale says. Speaking of loving our bodies, did you try that new Indian place next to the shopping centre? No, I haven't. I've actually been trying to cook more at home to save money and also see if I can eat healthier that way. But, I do miss eating out sometimes. Ah, you should definitely try it someday. Their butter chicken is to die for, and it's not too expensive.

Right, so here's what we've got planned for our's film night. We've got three films lined up, and we'll take a vote later to decide which one to watch first. What are your thoughts? Are you in for some horror, drama, or comedy? That’s kind of exciting! I'm open to anything to be honest. But if I had to pick right now, I’d choose the drama. I feel like I haven’t watched one of those in ages, and I could really use something a bit more intellectually stimulating after that weird day at work. You wouldn’t believe how many hiccups there were with some new orders. Production was such a nightmare today! Oh dear, sounds like a perfect day for a drama then! And just like that, we’ve got our first film. The second one can be horror or comedy then—depending on the mood, perhaps. Exactly! Maybe a bit of a contest between horror and comedy for the second one. Let’s leave that decision for after the first film. We could even have a small prize for the winner. Someone has to bring something exotic next time we catch up, hehe. Brilliant idea! We should round it up into a little party. I can fetch some silly prizes from my event supplies—like the time we had a toga party for the office St Patties. Remember that? Oh, I do. That was hilarious. We're already arranging the movie, I'd say that's a good start for tonight. Speaking of which, in all seriousness, have you heard about the new conference centre in town? I saw something about it while I was surfing online today. Actually, I did the event planning for one event there last month. The space is really impressive, and if I’m honest, it’s going to put some of the other venues in Cambridge to shame. They’ve got some of the best audio-visual equipment I’ve ever seen, and the layout is so flexible. That sounds perfect then. From what I know, a lot of the business and academic conferences are moving to more updated places these days. I was involved in a production that had some issues with the venue last year. Just wasn’t equipped well enough. Exactly, which is why I’m so excited about this new venue.

Hey everyone, did you guys see that trailer for the new Marvel film? I'm really excited; it looks like it's going to be epic! Oh yeah, I've seen that! I love how Marvel is really stepping up their game now. Did anyone else catch the other one – the sci-fi film with the tiny robots? Yeah, that one looked really cool too! It's always brilliant to see new Sci-fi films actually dealing with interesting AI themes. Totally! Speaking of keeps changing the landscape. Think about Back to the Future... I mean, we're getting really close to 2015 now... I know, right? And did anyone watch that new British superhero film? No, actually. Was it good? I thought it was really well done. It had a great blend of action, humor, and social commentary. That’s often a great mix when it comes to good films. Off-topic a bit, anyone else catch that old film on Netflix about the Northern Irish peace process? Oh, I saw that one! Interesting how it portrayed all the different perspectives. Yeah, it was great for showcasing how complex and emotional the entire situation was. Speaking of complex and emotional, anyone here a fan of older films? Like, really old ones? Like, perhaps A Clockwork Orange, or Scarface? I've seen both, they’re quite different, but they both achieve something profound and unsettling through their storytelling. Agreed! A great film leaves you thinking about it long after the end credits roll. Definitely. That's one of the reasons I got into film in the first place – the potential for depth and variety. I mean, look at the range of things we're talking about here. Exactly! There's always something new to discover or revisit. You can learn so much from films, not just about the topics they cover, but also about the societies they come from. Totally, that's what makes films so brilliant. They're not just entertainment, but a way to understand and connect with different experiences and perspectives. And they almost always spark interesting conversations afterwards too. I love that we can all talk about stuff like this. It feels like film is one of those things that brings people together, regardless of where they're from or what they're studying. It’s really cool that we all come from different parts of the UK and can still bond over something like films.

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. Paris was amazing but exhausting. Tell me more! I've been thinking about the tourists and the crowds since we last spoke. What was it like for you? Oh, it was fantastic and chaos in equal measure. We were so lucky with the weather and there was so much to see, but the crowds at the Eiffel and Louvre... it was like a fractal of chaos! And how was the food? Are you still on a French culinary high? Oh absolutely! Even lazy brunches with a decent baguette and cheese makes me day. The picnic in the park was just perfect. So what happened when you climbed the Eiffel Tower? [chuckles] Well, we were all standing in line, and suddenly a gust of wind swept through and nearly took someone’s hat. It was very dramatic. [laughs] I bet it was. You know, between the thrill-seekers and the wind, it sounds like a potential injury risk. Yeah, it was funny and a little unsettling. But we’re all fine, thankfully. That’s the main thing. Any other close calls? Well, we nearly missed our Eurostar because of the Metro strike. But my housemate planned an alternative route using buses and taxis. It was a bit of an adventure but worked out in the end. [smiling] That’s quite the story. How about your holiday pal, weren’t you supposed to meet up with friends from uni? Ah, yes! We did manage to meet the first day. But one of them sprained his ankle trying a new dance move... of all things. So it was fun but a bit low-key. Oh dear, poor thing. I hope it wasn’t too painful. It was, but he’s taking it in good spirits. [empathetically] That can be tough. I know all about it when it comes to sports injuries with my patients. Exactly. [thoughtfully] You know, this almost makes me wish we could just chill here at home. Sometimes, I feel the same. But then I think about the food. [Laughs] [chuckles] Well, for now, let’s use that Paris inspiration to make some French clafoutis. Oh, excellent idea! I remember you bought some cherry jar last time we shopped. Yes, perfect timing. So let’s plan a Paris-inspired dinner. Brillant! Mmm, that sounds lovely. Who’s bringing what?

Hey there, Sarah! How was your weekend? Hey, John! It was quite alright, thanks for asking. Spent most of it catching up with old uni friends, and we did some shopping. How about you? Any plans for the weekend? Same old, same old. Wanted to finally catch up on some grading and get ahead on my research. But I suppose that part didn't really happen. Any big decisions or announcements regarding work? Like, are there any changes to the schedule coming up for us or anything like that? Not really, everything seems to be fine here in retail, though I have been considering asking for a bit more time off soon. Been thinking about having a little break before the summer starts. You know, like go to Chichester or somewhere else. Want to join? Oh, that sounds lovely! I'd love to. What's it like working retail? As much as I love language and all things linguistic, sometimes I wonder what it would be like in a completely different job. Retail can be intense at times, especially on pay day and when those big sales come or whenever something new comes in that everyone wants. But it's interesting and quite rewarding seeing people leave happy, you know? Plus, the people I work with are great too. And while the work isn't about linguistics in the way my job is, I do sometimes think about how we can improve communication at work. Ah, I'd love to hear more about that. I've been reading up on the British National Corpus and how it really helps with dialects and understanding language usage. It’s all about empathy and clarity in communication, isn't it? Absolutely, it's fascinating how much the way we speak can influence the way we think and act. I do sometimes find myself using more formal language at the office or less so depending on who I'm talking to, a bit like the blurred boundaries between registers we talk about in linguistics. Yeah, and even things like who we are referring to in a sentence and how you structure that can speak a lot about the relationship and power dynamics. I was watching Judge Judy the other day and it was a case about a couple’s decision to start a business together. Funny how a simple sentence can reveal so much about their relationship, isn't it?

Hey, I'm going to show you how to cook rice. It's pretty easy. You don't need to do much to it but you've got to make sure you don't overcook it. Hi there, isn't cooking rice just so boring? You just stick it in boiling water and leave it, right? Not really, mum. It's a bit more than that. If it's overcooked, it gets really sticky and mushy. Which is fine if that's how you like it, but usually you want it fluffy. Fluffy? Like in a pudding? Kind of, but rice pudding's actually very different. It's made to be soft and creamy. Cooked rice on the other hand, should be separate grains. So you're saying if I want to cook rice for the curry we're going to have for dinner, I should do it separately from the curry, right? Exactly. You cook the rice first, then you can put both together later. That way, the rice doesn't soak up too much of the curry sauce and it stays nice and fluffy. Alright, but can't I just put the rice and curry together and boil it? You can, but the rice might get too overcooked and the curry can make it stick together too much, especially if it's got a lot in it like potatoes or peppers. Plus, we’re making curry with some really good stuff from that new Indian place we saw last week, and I want that to shine. So it's better to cook them separately. You're really particular, aren’t you? More experienced cooks are, I guess. But seriously, the right texture makes a big difference in how it tastes. And we've got this new curry mix we picked up yesterday, it's got all these yummy spices and a bit of a kick from the jalapenos. It would be a shame to overcook the rice and lose the punch of the curry. I see what you mean. But what about mixing salt or anything else into the rice? That's definitely something. You could add a pinch of salt when you're boiling the water for the rice. Some people swear by that. But you’ve got to be careful not to add too much, or the rice could end up tasting funny and you can always add more during the meal if it needs it.

I hope you all's had a good day today. I've just been thinking about what we're going to do after Sixthform, so I was wondering if you lot have any plans. Want to work, study more, or is it just travel? Actually, I've been thinking a lot about Uni, but I'm still not fully sure what I want to study. I've been looking at Sociology, Anthropology... I just don't know if it'll lead to a job that I'd want to get into, or something stable. Some jobs can come out of those, like working in social work or something similar. Plus, it’s just a good skill set to have. Yeah, absolutely - and even if you don’t go into a career directly related to what you studied, it’s the analytical and critical thinking skills that are really valuable. But, let’s not pretend - the job market right now is tough, especially for graduates. I know. That’s a bit of this whole thing. It feels like everything's moving so fast and if I make the "wrong" decision now, it could impact everything. And to make it worse, we can't even do much about our current financial situation. Being long-term unemployed, it feels like we're stuck in this loop, no escape. It's really frustrating. I wish I could help you with that, but I don’t have a magic solution. Though, you might want to look into some of the part-time jobs that can combine with studies. And let the Uni career services have a look at your CV together, they could give some advice. And even if we don’t know what we’re doing next, being around each other always helps. At least we know we’re dealing with the same uncertainty together. Thanks – it means a lot for us to be supportive for each other like this. It’s something real, isn't it? It's all we’ve got most days – each other. Speaking of real things, we should plan a BBQ when the weather gets better. A good break from all this uncertainty, maybe? That’s a brilliant idea! We can plan something fun that doesn't cost much but still feels like a celebration. Sounds perfect – like we need to remind ourselves life isn’t just about what's next, but also about enjoying now.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up tonight. It's been ages. How have you been, Ian? Yeah, thanks for inviting me over, Sarah. Life's been pretty quiet here. I've spent time tending to the garden and walking around the village. That’s so lovely! I often find myself stuck in an office all day, organizing conferences and events. It's nice to have a change of scenery, but sometimes... I just wish there was more time in the day. I get that. Sometimes I think about my time before retirement, when work actually kept you active. I have to keep finding ways to keep busy, but I don’t have the same energy I used to. Speaking of keeping busy, how’s your exercise routine been going? I've started making time each week to go to the gym and it's made a huge difference! Exercise... well, I try. Between the garden and the local park, it’s a bit of a workout. But I wish I could jog or cycle like I used to. Perhaps I'll start walking further. For me, it's more about finding joy in daily activities rather than vigorous exercise. That's a good approach! I also try to find time for friends like tonight. It’s important to keep up our friendships, right? What about you, Sarah? How do you manage to keep up your relationships with everyone in your line of work? Oh, it's tough sometimes, really. Communication is key, but even that can be a challenge. And with the pressure of deadlines... I often feel like I’m connected but somehow disconnected at the same time. I think that speaks to our different lives, doesn't it? I miss the structured career. But I suppose every age and stage brings its own challenges. For sure! Listen, maybe we could catch up more regularly? There's usually some event or other in Cambridge. Would you be interested in coming along? That would be lovely, Sarah. I'd enjoy that. Great! I’ll start making a mental note and send you details when I have them. That would be great. And maybe one day you can show me around the gardens. I could use the company and learn a bit more about what you do. I’d love that, Ian! I’ll definitely take you on a garden tour.

Right, I think it's time we cleared up the table. Dad, can you spare a few minutes to help us? It's not a big load, but every hand makes light work. Yeah, sure! I'm happy to help. Sorry, Mum, for not stepping in sooner. No need to apologize, darling. We all have our own part to play in keeping our home nice. Actually, why don't we make this fun? We could even turn it into a bit of a task. You know, like we used to do soccer drills in the garden – quick pickups and passing the plates. It's a bit similar. Dad, you're thinking about the absurd ways to turn chores into exercises, aren't you? Yeah, you guys are so weird. But it could work... Okay, let's grab a few plates and glasses. Someone starts and we all follow, like a relay race. Who's up for a quick turn this evening? Oh, I can't resist. Let's do it! This is actually kind of fun. It’s different. Well, wasn't that a piece of cake? See, even chores can be made fun. True dat, Mum. So, lads, I was thinking, it's not just about the physical work. As you grow up and take on more responsibilities, you all will have tasks and challenges that you might not want to do but need to get through. Whether it's studying for exams, practising a sport, or even shaving — which, by the way, will become a very real thing for you next! Shaving! You mean like facial hair? You aren't seriously expecting me to do that next year? Yeah, for sure. I've seen some of my mates, they're so much older than us, but zero beard. Alright, alright, let me not be the bearer of premature news... but seriously, young men, the point I'm making is that things are going to change, and you'll encounter tasks that are challenging but necessary. This little clearing-up game was our version of that. You're right, Dad. And while that might sound a bit serious, it’s practical advice for life. Remember, no matter how big a task feels, breaking it down like we just did can make it less overwhelming. That makes sense. So like, preparing for exams or big tests is like cleaning the table, right?

Right, I'm going to stop by the tip first, I've got some old furniture to drop off. Decided that after all, it's just cluttering up the house and someone else might find a use for it. That's a good idea, especially after all those recent flooded basements questions. It kind of makes you think about what stays and what goes, eh? Absolutely. And now I've got this space, I can look at getting some new stuff. Actually, ANON mentioned this place up in High Lane that's really good with second-hand stuff if you know what you're looking for, and they also had some good offers last time I heard. I used to love going around in our local tip, just like you said, you never know what you might find. And sometimes places like that need the stuff more than we do. Speaking of tips, ANON's mate, ANON - remember the one who was having a tough time with her family? - managed to wash all her mum's clothes last weekend while they were at the hospital. Someone should be giving her a medal or something. For? For washing someone else's clothes and they didn't even ask her to do that? I mean, I'm all for helping others but that sounds rather extreme. Yeah, but according to ANON, her friend said, "Well, it needed doing, and nobody else was around to do it." It's nice in a way, but I wouldn't want anyone to think it was expected of her all the time. Young people always have a generous heart, but we also need to highlight when it's okay to say no or suggest that chores should be shared. It's that kind of treating others as though they're lesser that makes me groan sometimes. That's true. Saying no or setting boundaries can be really hard for some, especially younger people who often are so eager to please others. Speaking of setting boundaries, have you heard about the new building going up down by the old library? It'll probably be a great resource for the community but I can already imagine the mess next year – more traffic, more noise, and probably more washing of public boundaries. Aye, so much for peace and quiet! Can't see how people wouldn't get frustrated with the construction.

Hey Mum, how are you doing? How was your day? It was good thanks, busy at school. We're starting the exam period soon, so that's the main focus. How about you? How was work? It was okay, just dealing with a fair amount of redundancy questions again. Can't believe so many people are getting laid off right now. Yes, that's so unfortunate. I'm right there with you at school. Just trying to deal with budget cuts and all. But that's how it is I guess, nothing much we can do about it. No, you're right. But it's frustrating when all the effort we put into our projects gets scrapped in an instant. It just makes you question why you're doing it all in the first place sometimes. Tell me about it. I had to cut a project short that I was really looking forward to with the children. But at the end of the day, it's about how we respond, right? So, what are your weekend plans? You free for anything? I was thinking of going to the gym on Saturday. Just need a bit of stress relief. You and Dad might find it strange but it really helps me clear my head. I can understand that. I need to start doing more of that as well. I used to enjoy the gym, can't believe I've let it slide. Maybe we can go together sometime? That'd be great, Mum! We could even do a small workout at home if you prefer. It's not just about the gym, it's about staying active. Yeah, definitely something we could do. So, is the house extension still on? I heard it's been a bit of a nightmare. It is. Seems like the builders keep finding new things that weren't included in the original plan, so it's been delaying our timeline. But we're hoping to get it done by the end of the next month. Grandad and Nan are coming to stay over a couple of weekends so we want it sorted for them. Ah, I was so looking forward to some family time. Let's hope it gets fixed up soon then. And speaking of families, how was Granny last time you spoke to her? She's doing okay, thanks for asking. Still sticking to her healthy eating habits.

Hey Mum, so what are we going to do first thing in the morning during our summer break? Oh, let me think about it for a second. Why don't we start off with swimming? I need to work out and it’s nice and refreshing now that the days are getting longer. No way! Mick stays up until 8! Now, now. Mick won’t mind if he sleeps in a bit early on keeps coming right on schedule, will he not? Yeah, okay. But what time will we start our activities? I was thinking we could get in early with swimming, just like I said. Maybe around 9? Can we even bring Lego to the pool? Hmm, I suppose that could work if... Hold on, swimming with Lego sounds quite a challenge. Maybe we'll stick to the pool toys for now and save the Lego for afterwards. Yeah, okay. That sounds fun. What do we do after swimming then? How about a bit of practice time for your guitar? And can't forget the chores. We could split them up – one day, maybe you can help me with laundry, another, we can tidy up the living room together. An, I can help you with jobs 'round the house. I like doing jobs. I know that. After all the work, we can have a bit of down time if you like. Maybe watch the next episode of Stick with Mick together, or do some drawing. Or we can try learning something new. What do you think about me teaching you and Mick some basic Japanese phrases? We could practice and maybe you could pick it up a bit for the holidays. That sounds cool, though a bit challenging. What’s the plan? I was thinking just 15 minutes each evening so we don’t tire ourselves out. And maybe we can include a bit of it in the chores, like me calling out a job in Japanese and you and Mick responding. An! An. I’ll say an! That could actually be fun. Sure, let’s give it a go. Just to be safe, let’s make sure no one gets too tired. We can always mix it up if need be. Maybe one day we swim, another day is Japanese and guitar, and then we have a relaxed afternoon together. That sounds like a plan. Thanks for taking the time to plan this out.

"You've got to understand though, no one is truly what they seem." "Yeah, that's like some TV show I watched, right? 'Everyone has a secret.' People can be so complicated though, huh? It's questions like this that make me prefer writing fiction sometimes. You make up people's secrets!" “Exactly! But actually, I've been thinking a lot about writing a script. Which is kind of funny because I've always been a reader. You?” “You know, I actually taught a workshop on scriptwriting to a few of my students last year. I used this really good film as an example. It just shows how a bit of preparation can help shape the narrative. And sometimes less is more, you know?” “Ah, absolutely. That’s what I find interesting about reading screenplays – its brevity compared to books. But sometimes, I miss the detail in a book. Do you ever find similar issues in teaching? Your students often expecting literary depth in writing assignments?” “Yeah, it's a struggle, especially with this new youth. They view symbols and metaphors through these pop culture lenses. Like the dentist episode of [TV Show], no one can understand 'interstices' without the entire cultural context. “I used to have this dentist who was super laid back, but then he’d drop something cynical like 'Just remember, this is one profession where we're all about drilling for oil', and it would crack me up every time. What's been the weirdest patient comment you've had during a check-up?” “Honestly, it was a kid who jumped on the procedure table and just started singing 'You're gonna lose that girl' from The Sound of Music. At first, I was taken aback, but it actually relaxed everyone around. “You know, that's one of my favorite Julie Andrews films. Entertainment can be so universal. Speaking of universal experiences though, I'm making some changes in my life… Like, I've been on furlough for a while now, and I've been trying to find new projects. Have you ever taken a break from teaching and done something totally different?” “Oh totally, took a gap year right after uni. Lent my mum's car and just drove around Europe. Did meetups, music gigs, and bicycled across some countries using Citibikes. The best way to learn local accents! “ “That's seriously cool. Did you enjoy staying in hostels or trying new food?

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without the children this morning. It's so chaotic these days isn't it? Agreed! It's always nice to have some quiet time. Still getting used to the new routine after the baby came? It's definitely a transition but everyone seems to be settling in quite well. Good, I'm glad to hear that. Speaking of new, did you finally crack how to make those fluffy Easter keepsakes for the school? Oh, we had an absolute nightmare with the glue. I have to say, I've never had such a gluey mess in my life! Haha, gluey mess - that's quite the technical term from a teacher! Anyway, we managed to get it all sorted out eventually, and it turned into a fun little team effort with the children. They were excited to see their own creations taking shape. That's great to hear. I'm sure they turned out lovely. So, have you given any more thought about where this year's Easter holiday might be? Not really, to be honest. We were thinking maybe we could visit your mum again. The children loved the last time and she always has so much to do with them. That sounds lovely! Your mum always has a way of keeping them entertained doesn't she? She does, really. She's also been fantastic about the new baby. That's wonderful. I think she might appreciate it too, it's not always easy for grandparents when there are new arrivals. Yes, I was thinking that too. We could make it into a proper family outing. Perfect idea. I can even suggest we do it over Easter. It'll be nice to all be together. That would be amazing! But first, changing the subject slightly, how are things going on your end? Just the usual really. I've been meaning to get back to trying out some new recipes. Have you ever tried making Easter cakes? Not seriously, no. Are they as tricky as I imagine? Oh, they can be if you're aiming for anything intricate or fancy. But there are some really simple ones you can do with the children too. That sounds fun actually. I might give it a go if there's time before Easter. You should. We could even make it a family activity. That would be great.

Ah, I'm so glad we could finally meet up, Susan. It feels like ages since we last saw each other. How are the Manchester kids settling in? They're all well, thanks for asking. They're quite enjoying the new school so far and making new friends, but I miss them terribly. Especially when this kind of warmer weather isn't possible back in Manchester. I completely understand. It must be tough leaving your roots behind, right? Definitely. But it’s for work — my husband keeps changing jobs due to his career progression and opportunities. You know how it is, right? Yes, very much so. I’m going through something very similar. My husband is also looking into new opportunities down in Oxford, but I prefer the vibe of the north. Yeah, each of us has to decide what works best for our family, I suppose. Speaking of changes, I recently started a new project in my language school. We're introducing a Spanish program for younger kids. It’s been quite hectic, but I love the challenge. For me, it's been a return to the basics. My school is looking to modernize its curriculum, so I’ve been involved in that. I love the idea of bringing in new ideas in education; it really keeps the job exciting. It does. And teaching languages, especially at this stage, is so rewarding. The kids pick it up so quickly. I find that in my experience as well. But have you had any issues with getting the resources or accreditation for the new program? Yes, getting the necessary accreditation has been a bit of a hurdle. The process seems more complicated than it needs to be, but we're just about there now. That sounds familiar. Our school has a few older, less tech-savvy teachers who aren’t keen on the changes. It can be quite challenging to move everyone forward together. Absolutely! But we should speak to younger teachers more. They usually are more on board with changes. Plus, technology can be such a great aid. I’ve been using online platforms like Duolingo with my older students, and it’s been a huge hit! I’ve heard of Duolingo. We’ve been using something similar for grammar reviews. The kids seem more engaged when it’s interactive. Exactly! As for advising younger teachers, I always suggest starting with small changes and gradually introducing more tools.

Right, so everyone's seen the homemade matzah's I brought over? I made them myself this morning, just to add a bit of home flair to the dinner. Oh wow, they're actually really good! I mean, matzah's can be quite dry but these are nice and crispy. Thanks! I had a little help from my flatmate who’s a part-time baker. Cooking's become a big hobby of mine since I've been at uni, and Passover's a great excuse to practice making traditional foods. Speaking of traditional foods, I was thinking, has anyone ever tried making Seder plate foods from scratch at home? I mean, I’ve been wanting to try my hand at preparing the bitter herbs or charoset but I never really know where to begin. Oh, I did that last year. It’s actually quite simple once you know the basic recipes. The bitter herbs are usually just horseradish and parsley. Charoset, you can make it with apples, nuts, honey, and wine. It’s all about the right proportions. Yeah, and the fun part is how different it tastes depending on where you are from. Italian Jews make different charoset with dates and figs, for example. I once tried it at a Passover in Italy; it was quite interesting. That’s fascinating! Have you guys ever been to Italy? I've always wanted to visit but my budget's a bit limited as a grad student. I went to Italy a few years ago, and it was fantastic. But you know, you don’t need to travel far to learn about different Jewish traditions. Last week I was working on an article about the Jewish community in Paris, and I learned all about their unique customs and kosher food scene. Oh, speaking of food, I saw a recipe online for a certain little bird that's apparently a delicacy. It’s called an ortolan? It's from France, I believe and it’s supposed to be quite a challenge to make. Yeah, I heard about that. I mean, it’s not something for the faint of heart. The preparation is quite gruesome, but apparently, it’s so rare and unique that it’s a coveted experience for some foodies. Urgh, perhaps not for Passover dinner, then. But you know, the real challenge I’m facing is figuring out how to make my matzah balls.

Thank you all for coming over. I'm thrilled to finally have our book club back. It's been quite some time. How are we all doing? I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I've just finished re-reading A Little Life, and I have to say, it left me questions again this time around. So, I'm excited to discuss it and hear everyone's take on it. I loved it too, but I have to admit, I couldn't help but pick up secondary materials to understand some of the character development better. Have any of you done the same? Yes, actually. I spoke with Sarah last week, and she seemed just as confused by certain choices as we did. Perfect, let's share our insights. Right, but before we dive in, shall we start with how everyone's week has been? It's wonderful to catch up. Well, work's been busy. I mean, we're always busy in finance, but it's been particularly hectic. And on the personal side, my knitting's been thriving. I love the flow it gives my mind while watching TV. Knitting's a great stress release. Oh, have any of you been watching any fun TV shows lately? I've been binging on The Crown. It’s so well done. I've been watching Small Axe. It's quite powerful. The way it handles race relations in Britain is...thought-provoking. I agree, it's really well done. It makes you think about how much we assume about our own history. Yes, definitely thought-provoking. It also reminded me how little I knew about the Windrush generation, and I went on to read one of the suggested books. That’s interesting. How did you find the book, if you don’t mind me asking? It was enlightening. But personally, I find it hard to fully absorb and reflect when reading from a device. I much prefer physical books. Paper feels more tangible, and I can highlight and interact with my reading better. I completely agree for pleasure reading. However, for work or when I'm on the go, eBooks are essential for convenience. Speaking of convenience, does anyone have suggestions for a new series or movie based on this book or related themes? Maybe something harder-hitting or more dramatic to follow A Little Life? Not off the top of my head, but I did hear a lot of buzz about Normal People when it first came out.

Ah, I'm so glad we could find this place, Pikko Mikko Pub. It’s a gem of a pub in Joensuu. I've been meaning to try out my new Nokia for a bit, but I need a bit of your expertise to set it up just right. Sure thing, let me see it. Oh, isn’t it lovely? But, wait a moment, you've got a Nokia? I thought they stopped making phone models... right? Actually, they still do for Finland. It’s weird how they have kept their brand here. Anyway, I'm looking forward to setting it up, but I've not had anything new to play with in a while. Well, starting fresh is always exciting. Especially with the new line up. Do you have any preferences, like the Symbian or now the more modern OS we've? To be honest, I'm a bit confused with the choices. Symbian was standard before, and now it seems they’ve moved to newer systems. But I’ve heard good things about the newer models. How about you, have you had a chance to look at any or even try one? I have actually. I tried out the new Nokia 8. The camera quality is impressive, and the battery life is quite decent. But the system it runs on is quite different if you're coming from Symbian. Do you want it to be Android or do you prefer something else? Hmmm, I’m not sure. I’ve had mixed experiences with Android phones. I've been thinking about maybe sticking to something more traditional for now, but the camera on this 8 model looks fantastic. How seamless is the transition if I were to choose it? There’s definitely a learning curve, especially if you're new to Android. But Nokia’s version has been quite user-friendly. They've made sure the transition isn’t too rough. And, if you're used to a certain type of phone layout, the Nokia models tend to retain some traditional features. That's comforting. I guess it's time I step into changing times. Can you walk me through the basic setup? Where do we start? Sure. First, we need to switch it on. Then, just follow the on-screen instructions. It will prompt you to connect to Wi-Fi or use data to download any updates. You might have to set up a Google account if you want to use the Google services.

Hey Mum, did you know that red pandas are actually from Asia? But I'd really love to have one as a pet. Ooo, they're so cute! But unrealistic as pets, I'm afraid. How about we get a dog for now? Yaaa! Can we have a dog? Or a Malamooche, as Aunt Sarah said? A Malamooche? Now that's a new word. Did Aunt Sarah explain what that is? Yes, it's just an old word for any kind of dog. It's kind of like saying 'pooch' or 'hound' – just another word for dog. Right, makes sense. So, we can't really get a red panda but maybe a dog would work well. And what about your birthday party arrangements? Have you thought about it? Actually, yes. I think I'd like it to be at my house. And we could have board games and gymnastics as the main activities. And maybe we can ask Aunt Sarah to bring a few Japanese films – she loves them. That sounds like a great plan! Board games and gymnastics for the kids. And Japanese films for older kids or the adults. And about the cake? Any idea? Do we need a cake? Maybe we can have cupcakes or something. And we could have a nice fruit salad as well. Fruit salad! Yeah, and can we get an iPad too? I want to play some games! Alright, alright. Okay, it seems like we're making progress. Let me just jot down the ideas here. You can use mine if you need. Thanks, love. So, to summarize:   Birthday party at home   Board games and gymnastics   Fruit salad and cupcakes   Maybe a cake if we really need it   Japanese films for older kids/adults   Ipad games for the kids And what about presents? Should I send out invitations? Invitations are a must! And for presents, let's say no gifts and instead ask the guests to bring a small donation to your favourite animal shelter. Oh, that's a great idea! They can help some cute animals instead. Exactly. Now, let's talk about the schedule. When do you want your birthday party to be? How about the 20th of next month? That gives us enough time to prepare and it's not too close to the start of the school holidays. Perfect. We'll make sure everything is ready then. Can we play games before we do the gymnastics?

Right, so everyone's seen the photos from my first year's flatmate Grace's Christmases in Australia. They're just wild and clearly the highlight of her year, wouldn't you say, all of you? Yeah, it’s almost like it’s the opposite of Christmas here! But speaking of differences, have you noticed how different cultures perceive the holiday? I mean, Christmas in the Philippines is a very big deal, but it's not centred around family and drinking like it often is here. Oh, I've got a keepsake from my first year at university when my flatmate's family invited me to their Thanksgiving. It was such an eye-opener for me at the time, having never been to one. The food, the festivities, just like Christmas but without the gifts. And the places we've all called home - oh, the differences are just incredible. I lived in Bognor Regis for most of my life and you'd think it's as British as it gets, but then you have Barrow-in-Furness, similar in size but so entirely different in culture. Exactly! So, where were you at Christmas? I’m really curious about all the different traditions. I’ve spent some Christmases in Manila and it’s the biggest celebration of the year. Kids in Manila think Santa Claus is the Philippines' version of the Three Kings bringing gifts. So, instead of waiting for Christmas morning for gifts, kids wake up for weeks but certainly for a few weeks before Christmas, really for the 'Trece Pascuas' celebration. That's quite different from my childhood Christmases in Bath where the focus was indeed the day itself. As a student, finding the right kind of wine to drink with dinner or just having a quiet night in with less stress was the goal. [laughs] The right kind of wine? We’re just kids getting into drinks for the first time. But personally, my first few Christmases in uni were all about forgetting exams and just having a good time. You really notice accents and dialects then, don’t you? Oh for sure. Our friend here from Bognor uses words I’ve never heard before. But I mean, speaking of accents, if anyone uses "standard southern accent" as a descriptor, I’ll have to remind them even Londoners sound different almost street by street. And I swear, every Londoner thinks they're the only ones using "innit" properly!

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up tonight. It's been ages. How have you all been? Stressed to the max, to be honest. Got all of Edward's administrative stuff to deal with, and it’s neverending. But, the show’s on tonight, so at least I have some kind of escape. Oh, totally understand. I've been struggling with my writing lately too. I've been working on a new detective series, and I just can't get past this one plot point. But even with all that, it's always nice to catch up. You'll tell me all about your Thanksgiving, though? I've been wondering about the usual festivities. Oh, it was lovely. Sentimental, just like every other year, but there's something lovely about it. We had my mother over, and the children making the usual chaos. And food! So much food. Though, I have to say, I've been thinking of changing things up a bit. What do you both think about trying Indian food? I saw an intriguing recipe for tandoori chicken the other day on my Kindle. Sounds good to me! For me, it's usually a roast or something similar, but a bit of spice might be good. Where did you find the recipe though, while on your Kindle? I've been meaning to look at that myself. Ah, it was in a cookbook I picked up. It's one of those nice, easy-to-navigate ones. You can see all the ingredients and the steps in advance, which really helps. I also enjoy reading the comments, people usually have tips and modifications. I like that idea. I've found that it's helped me keep the progress on my kindle much better organized since I started using it. And, if I may be so bold, could we arrange something soon? More specifically, together, maybe a TV series marathon. That sounds fun! What kind of series? Perhaps something detective related? We could each pick one and then rotate through each other's choices. Oh, we might as well plan a whole week. Each of us gets a night for our series. I say we do it over a meal, each bringing a dish related to the series. Could be fun, if anyone is up for it. I'm in. Just need to finish this month's work and then I'm all yours.

Ah, I'm losing patience. I don't think I've ever felt so helpless. These new pensions policies, they're all about squeezing the little people like us, innit? I know, dear! It seems like every time we turn, the system’s stacked against us – always on the back foot, just trying to keep our heads above water. That's a great way to put it, Alan – and right you are. But don't forget, there are still options. Perhaps it's time we review how we could get a better grasp on our finances. You know, cut out some of those non-essentials. [sighs] It's not just the money. It's the feeling like we don't count. Like we're just waiting for the retirement party from life itself. I understand that feeling, John. But look at you, Alan. You're still sharp as a tack, full of knowledge and experience. There must be ways you can put that to use. And you’re always good with carpentry, right? Could you sell some of your work or even teach classes? That’s a great idea, Irene! Alan, why not start with what you know and enjoy most? You'll find that when you're doing something you love, the money will follow, at least enough to make things easier. And you can always look at ways to monetize through technology. Perhaps take your craft to online platforms or even teach local community classes. I never thought in those terms, really. But you're right, Al. I always loved building and fixing things and working with my hands. I could likely make a bit extra that way. Exactly! Just last weekend, I helped my granddaughter with her homework and I realized how much the kids today value real skills and knowledge, practical stuff that we weren’t encouraged to learn as much about when we were younger. You could also consider informal skills exchange or even volunteering at local schools or community centers. Volunteering! Now there's a thought. You'd be surprised how much good you can do and how it feels to be contributing again. Plus, it often leads to new networks and opportunities. All this talk...blimey, it's given me a bit of hope! You know, Al and Irene, I think I’ve been dwelling too much on what I lost and not enough on what I still can do.

Hey everyone, did you hear about the strict party etiquette's upcoming workshop Grace organized today? I think it's super important for all of us to be mindful of the little things, don't you?      Oh, absolutely. It’s just the kind of thing we need to get right, given how much of our work involves interacting with clients and colleagues from various backgrounds.      Yeah, and I've heard it'll include some very helpful tips on table manners, service etiquette and how to handle criticisms — even if it is about our work, right?      That's right, and I'm particularly interested in anything they might say about communicating effectively with people from different regions, like our northerners versus Londoners. Might just highlight the differences between our own dialects as well.      It’s interesting how even the smallest things can impact how you’re perceived. I’ve worked with clients from so many different language backgrounds and cultural norms, and sometimes it’s the little things that can make the difference whether it’s a good or bad first impression.      Exactly! And speaking of making a good impression, how was your weekend? I noticed it was pretty chilly outside, plenty of opportunities to see different insects running for shelter, I imagine.      You know, actually, I had a little adventure at my flat. Found a moth trying really hard to get inside the bright light. First, I was about to let it in to save it from perhaps dying outside, but then I wondered if it wasn’t better in its natural environment really. Thoughts?      That's a tough one, isn't it? On the one hand, it's kind and caring to want to help it out. On the other, we could be disrupting its natural behaviour and maybe causing more harm than good.      More harm than good? Surely a warm light isn't natural, right? I'd probably shoo it gently away from the door or window and hope it finds some other way to get through the night.      I actually wrote a piece about that years ago on making ethical choices in wildlife conservation and education. The general consensus is that unless it's clearly injured or you're sure it’s an endangered species, it's often best to guide it back outside gently or to a safe place outdoors rather than disrupt its natural processes.      Did one of you know there's almost going to be a 'save the insect' movement at the university next semester?

Hey, I'm so over PE today! The first lesson's always the worst when you still can't quite shake off that weekend feeling and you know you've got to run laps even though the sun is beaming down and you're already dehydrated. Oh, completely! But did you see that new sports field they've got outside now? It looks really nice. But even with the nicer facilities, PE can still suck sometimes, you know? Like when you ruin a race or drop a ball in a crucial game. Oh, I know what you mean. That actually reminds me - Ellie from my class actually tripped today during soccer. Like, proper tripped and face-planted into the mud. She's okay, don't worry, but it was hilarious and embarrassing at the same time. Ah, poor Ellie! Yeah, those things always happen to someone else and it's funny until you're the one falling over. True, true... Anyway, have you started preparing for those GCSE exams already? They're coming up next year, right? Yeah, they are. We've already started on some of the topics, but it still feels like ages away. I'm pretty sure we’re going to get told every day 'you should be studying harder for your exams'. It’s like, we totally know, really we do! But at the moment, it’s hard to focus because we've still got current lessons to take care of as well, you know? Yeah, definitely. I get that stress already from just talking about it. But you know what’s harder? Choosing what subjects to take for next year. My friends and I have been debating which are the easiest to pass or the most useful to have for college, and it's just a headache. Exactly! I’ve been trying to talk to my parents and teachers about it, but it doesn’t seem like anyone really knows yet. It’s like we’re all guessing. Guessing is probably better than knowing sometimes though. I heard that some teachers recommend taking certain subjects just to keep your options open after GCSEs, even if you're not interested. But that just adds to the confusion. That’s true, but it does give some of us an edge if we have extra qualifications and all that. Yeah, plus it makes the hours of revision feel a little more worth it.

Thank you so much for inviting us out for dinner, mum. We have enjoyed your cooking so much these past few months. It’s always such a treat when you can use this old chicken recipe of yours. Speaker_3 : You're welcome, and I’m glad you like it. You know, I found this recipe back when I was involved in one of my first sales jobs. It’s been part of my family tradition ever since. Now, speaking of work, how was your week at the sales desk? Anything interesting happen? Speaker_3 : Well, it was pretty standard, sweetheart, but I had one funny incident – one of the customers seemed particularly interested in organic products, despite questioning their price. Organic is expensive but sometimes the benefits make it worth it, right? I feel the same way about making time for well-planned meals. Exactly, which is why I love your dinners! They are so homey and yet very well thought out. Speaking of which, shall we plan ahead for another get-together soon? Maybe we should all help with the next dinner? Now that’s a great idea! I’d be happy to help plan or cook something. Speaker_3 : You’re kind to offer, but I’ve enjoyed cooking for you all. It’s my way of showing I care. However, I am always up for some extra hands. Maybe then we could make it a regular event? Sort of like a 'Throwback Thursday' in our own way, but with food from your childhood. That sounds lovely and gives us a chance to catch up regularly doesn’t it? Plus, it’s a great way for us to exchange different culinary experiences and bond over them. Speaker_3 : That really warms my heart. More family time together would be a joy. I grew up in a big family so having everyone regularly around is something I cherish. Yes, regular meals together are really important and it’s been missing lately with everyone's changing schedules. Definitely. I think we should all schedule a time that works for most of us in the next couple of weeks and make it happen. We can take turns so it’s fair and we all get a chance to share some of our own favorite dishes. Speaker_3 : Excellent. That sounds almost as good as this dinner. We can also think about if there are any other activities we could do together regularly.

Ah, good morning! How was your week? Oh, you know. It's been busy. The council was causing delays again with the routes, so I had to beat my van around town a bit more than normal. That's a real pain, isn't it? I heard rumors there were going to be roadworks near the new development. Yes, that's right. I saw the signs posted up right outside the school. Made my route a bit longer than usual. Anyway, how was your week? It was quite productive. We managed to lock in a large sale with a new client. I have to say, it's been a challenge but I'm really proud of the team. That's great to hear! I read online about the company. They're expanding quite rapidly. Yeah, they're a great company to work with. It was a bit of a struggle, though. One of the directors was quite set in their ways, so we had to come up with quite a few concessions to win them over. So, business has been good then? Very good. Now, how is your family? I understand the kids are back at school now? Yes, they've just started back. The youngest is going through a tough spell, really struggling with maths at school. She got a detention this week because she wasn't completing her homework as she should. Oh no, isn't that just typical? I remember when my kids were around that age, I had to almost help with the homework myself! But it's part of growing up, showing them that it's important to keep the structure even if they're not enjoying it. I know, it can be quite frustrating. But she's just getting into her teenage years, so I'm trying to balance support with letting her learn from her mistakes. Oh absolutely, that's the way to go. And what about the elder one? Still into science club? Yes, he's really passionate about it. He's talking about becoming a scientist when he's older. He's already doing experiments at home, just like when his grandfather used to guide him. Reminds me of my own father actually. That's so great! It's good to have kids interested in something they love. Even if it's not the most job-secure field, I mean. I was reading an article about how certain sciences still struggle for funding.

Hey, so how's uni treatin' ya?? We've not caught up in ages. Fine, thanks! Just struggling through the exams at the moment, but I've got a week off after this next one, so hoping to have some fun then! You've been keeping busy, what have you been up to lately? Yeah, been pretty busy at the bar, but it's good work. I've actually started considering if I want to do a masters in business to get me ahead. Oh that's a plan. You've worked at the bar for ages, haven't you? What made you decide to stay with that instead of doing more studies? Honestly, I just love interacting with people and drinking beer makes everything better, lol. But also, when I did my undergrad, we had an invitation to this seminar on hospitality and it kind of sparked this interest in managing my own place one day. That's cool, a lot of people underestimate just how much running a bar or pub requires. You deal with all sorts of people, right? Definitely. I've met this wide range of characters, from locals who come in every week to different tourists when the football's on. It's quite fascinating, the conversations you have. I can imagine! As a student, I don't often get the chance to connect with people outside my university bubble like that. But speaking of different walks of life, how's it dealing with the silly accents? You're from Hull, right? I never fully understand the dialect, but it always sounds friendly. Haha, yeah, us Hullensians have a unique way of speaking the Queen's English, apparently. It's not that different but some words, like "owt" for "anything", can catch people out. I grew up with it so I don't even notice it most of the time. Ah, I see! I’ve had friends who were confused by it, but it's always nice to hear it when I visit my relatives in Leeds or Birmingham. Accents are really personal, aren't they? Exactly! I remember moving to Salford for uni and everyone just assumed I was working class because of the accent. It can be a bit stereotypical at times, but it's part of who I am and I embrace it. How about you? Your Midlands accent is quite subtle in the wider British accent spectrum, isn't it?

Hey everyone, did you manage to sort out any last-minute plans for your holidays? Yeah, I managed a quick weekend away to York with my family before the semester started. They've got a beautiful Christmas market this year, isn't it? That’s right – I heard it’s fantastic! I've had the luck of staying in the UK for my holidays this year, so I'll probably stick around and see where the occasion takes me. I’m going to set up my laptop up in a cozy café somewhere and get some work done – mixed with a bit of holiday reading, of course. Sounds good, just need to make sure you have time to indulge in all that festive food. You'll know you're not working if you're in the middle of a mince pie. Speaker_2 [chuckles]: Indeed! And while you’re working, you can watch the various Scrooge re-runs... [laughs] That’s the spirit! But honestly, I couldn’t resist a little bit of old Ireland for the holidays next year though. For me, a trip to Rome would be quite the experience this year – all about the different pasta types and the Eternal City’s ancient history. I might even have to write about it for the library’s newsletter at some point. [giggles] Please do – we could all use some travel inspiration while working through the holiday season. Speaking of holiday food, isn't it bizarre how all regions have their own take on traditional dishes? Oh definitely – in my part of Ireland, doesn’t everyone have that debate over the proper way to make colcannon?! And in London, we argue about who serves the best mince pies or Christmas puddings. More food for thought! You know, it’s a funny thing – our job is all about information and now we’re all swapping holiday information instead.
