While we wait for that to cook, let's talk about places we've been to—anyone been to the Venetian canals? Actually, yes. It was a highlight for me on my visit to Veneto. The history, the art, the canal boats… even if it's touristy, it's still magical. So, have you guys ever walked along the canals in Birmingham? You know, back home? Birmingham has canals?! Of course. The Birmingham Canal Navigations. We grew up around it. It's not the same as Venice, but it has its charm. I'd love to walk along those, especially if it's as beautiful as in Venice or as quaint as in Amsterdam. Melbourne also has a lot of canals. We have a regatta in the Docklands every year—it's quite a sight. The boats are all decorated, and it's a big party. That sounds amazing. Seems like the British, Aussies, and Italians just love their canals. Speaking of our waterways, anyone remember when they tried to reclassify some of London's river names? That was quite a fuss. Yes! You mean they wanted to call the River Thames something like “Thames River” for tourists? Yeah. The Brits can be quite protective of those names. Canals or rivers, it seems like waterways have a special place in our cultures. Just like in the bible—water is life, right? Actually, yes. But also, in Jewish tradition, you can baptize in just about any natural body of water. I know that because I worked in this really cool kosher restaurant over the summer. Really? That's fascinating. I’d love to learn more about that. How strict are those rules? They’re pretty strict, but it depends on the tradition. Some communities are more strict about the water source or the process, but what you might not know is that some Jewish sects apply the rules differently when it comes to non-meat food.

Right, so did you hear about James' latest hook-up? Yeah. It sounds like it didn't go well. He's being pretty cagey about it though. What are you on about, again? Aye, yeah, wasn't Tinderinal? Now he questions his existence. Lol, seriously though, he said the guy was "intellectual" but ghosted him after the first date. Erm, Ghosting is a thing. But even worse is coming across someone on a dating app and then seeing them in person and realising, oops. Like at our uni, I ran into someone from Tinder in class. Yeah, that's a real highlight. "Hey, you're not as interesting in real life." Oh god, we need an app that has mandatory virtual dates before real ones. At least then we'd get a feel for each other's... intelligence? Haha, might save a lot of awkwardness! Or maybe we just need fewer expectations from uni meetups. I’m just sick of the whole toxic dating culture around this place. One side it's all about showing off, and the other side is "I'm so chill, I ghost all the time." True. It’s like at our uni, we’re all trying really hard to fit in while trying to connect somehow, yet everyone's scared to put themselves out there. Honestly though, I think it’s comforting to have a group in uni that’s really supportive. Yeah, shout out to our little "chosen family" here. We're all keeping each other's spirits up with awful jokes and real advice. You say that now, but if one of us started dating the guy we all secretly side eye, there'd be an intervention. True. I mean, our housemates would definitely intervene. "No, darling, that's not going to happen and it's for your own good." Speaking of housemates, did you all hear about Sarah's flat mate? Apparently she’s trying to make sure we all have a joint movie night because we're all so antisocial. That's actually a great idea! It would be funny to have a night without screens right? Just sitting around, sharing stories, and probably complaining about our uni work. I love that idea, but I have my doubts. It usually ends up with one of us watching something “deep and meaningful” which will suddenly make us all "overthinkers" and nothing gets done.

Ah, I was just reading about how strict they've become with benefits. I never thought we'd reach a point where people would have to jump through so many hoops just to get a roof over their heads. You two remember when this all started? Oh, absolutely! It's like they've created an entire system designed to discourage people from claiming what they're entitled to. I mean, we've spent most of our lives working and paying taxes, and now it feels like we're being punished for falling on hard times. You're right, Tom. I've seen it happen to so many people I once cared for, those kids I used to look after – they're grown up now with families of their own, and they're going through the same struggles. It's down to the system, not the people. Exactly! I saw a report on the news last night about how even the smallest misstep can lead to a sanction. It's all about creating a culture of fear, isn't it? Make the public think that freeloaders are the problem rather than the fact that the system itself is far from perfect. And don't even get me started on the application process. You have to be some kind of bureaucratic genius just to navigate it correctly. I've tried helping others fill out the forms but it's so complicated. If the government wanted people to navigate this successfully, they wouldn't design it like a maze designed by an enemy. Ah, but have you thought about how TV portrays this, John? Shows like Benefits Street can only contribute to the negative perception. It never shows the real reasons people are on benefits, only that 'lazy scroungers' are the problem. True, and the politicians are too happy to use such portrayals to further their own agendas. We've got to counter this narrative somehow. But how? As much as I hate to say it, it feels like it starts with our own community getting together and speaking out. Not just about benefits but about all the issues confronting us and our children’s future. Because at the end of the day, it's our lives we're talking about. Definitely. I've had so many discussions with the local community, and there's definitely willingness to speak out. But we need to be united on this.

Ah, I'm so glad we could finally sit down and have this meal together. I've been looking forward to it all day. Thanks, love. It's the small things like this that make life worth living. How was your day? Just another busy one, as usual. I'm not sure I've had time to process everything I've got going on. But that's part of the fun, I suppose. Now, don't start complaining. You know how it is with work. There's always something that can be done. You just need to learn to prioritize, and then, okay, sometimes there's just too much to do in one day. Oh, that’s like you to try and simplify everything. You’re always saying that, but when I try to tell you about a project, well, you know how it is. You’ve heard it all before. Well, it's your project. But, seriously, when you decide you want to start raising funds for that community center, it's amazing the number of requests and meetings I have to attend. Oh, that side of it. I'm sure it is. I’m busy enough with just the paperwork and proposals for this, while the kids need their sports fees paid in and school’s trips are always costing more than the school budget can handle. It's nice to see you take an interest in those, though. The kids growing up can be overwhelming sometimes, can't it? Definitely. And with the working hours I need to put in, doesn’t leave much time for anything else. I keep wondering how we’re supposed to balance everything. Honestly, I just remind myself that the days will get done one way or another. And as for balancing, well, maybe we need to start planning better. We could spend more time together without necessarily worrying about the chores. That’s easier said than done. But, okay, that does sound nice. Maybe we can plan a small weekend away next month? Just somewhere local, but time together without worrying about work or chores. That truly sounds lovely. I’ve always enjoyed going to see the light shows in Birmingham or taking a walk in Cannock Chase. Yes, and perhaps we could just enjoy the moment without having to worry about everything we need to accomplish. Do you remember that time we went to Stratford for the theatre?

Ah, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. I've been meaning to reach out for ages. How are you really doing out here? I'm alright, thanks for asking. It's been quite challenging at times. A bit of culture shock and, of course, the weather isn't helping. But I've had some really interesting students and colleagues, and I'm enjoying teaching. Yes, I can imagine. Teaching can actually be quite fulfilling. I used to teach English too before things slowed down. But even with keepsakes, it's a whole different ball game when you're not in the industry, isn't it? Even with my TEFL training. Absolutely, it's a very dynamic field. You have to keep up to date with methodologies, materials... I read a good blog post from Cambridge a while back - oh, and did I mention I studied there? Really? Well, you're living out my dreams! Cambridge was my home too, for a while. Really? That's quite a claim. It's not every day you meet someone who understands the cobbled streets and the feel of a pint at the Eagle. Not to mention the silly quads and river punting. I used to live near the river so the sound of the university was always soothing. Do you still go back often? Only when visiting for work or family, to be honest. Living abroad makes you feel quite disconnected sometimes. It wasn't always in my plans, really - to be away for so long. I totally get that. I've been feeling quite disconnected myself, being out of the job market and the country that raised me. But it's good that you're pursuing your passion, if teaching is it. It is true, I try to make the best of it, and the work ethic of the younger generation is impressive. Speaking of chasing passions, I’ve had thoughts of going back to studying, perhaps in therapy or some related field. That’s interesting. I've been considering therapy myself. It's hard to find a good fit that you trust but I've heard people say it’s like finding a missing puzzle piece. Have you started anything formal yet? Not yet, just thinking about it. I wish it didn't have to be about 'problems' to benefit from it. Just to have someone objective to talk to about life.

Hey, I'm so glad we could catch up without an agenda. It feels so British to be sitting here with cups of tea, doesn't it? Definitely! I've missed these casual catch-ups. How's work been treating you? You must be churning out content like crazy in your field. You'd think so, but the truth is, my job is pretty varied. I'm working on a couple of websites at the moment, trying to get creative and set them apart. But even with keeps changing, I still get to see the direct impact of my work, which I love. That's great! I can't imagine doing anything else than coding or questioning the status quo. Though, let me tell you, even doing research sometimes feels like you're just churning out papers and reports. Ah, being a student and juggling everything else can't be easy either. Have you made any big decisions for your future? Not really. I'm still juggling various options. But this semester, I've started getting into climate science, which I hope will guide my path more clearly. That sounds quite challenging yet interesting. Have you thought about different career paths in that field? Yeah, everything from working in government to private research sectors. But the field is so broad, right? It's like the more you learn, the more you realize how little you know. Totally relatable. I've been trying really hard to keep up with trends and shifts in my industry too. And with the "new normal" of remote work, doesn't it feel like everyone is now a potential customer or client? Absolutely! It's been a bit surreal adjusting to seeing everything through the lens of online. But I suppose that's where your skills come in, right? You're the one keeping content fresh and engaging for a web-first world. True enough. It's quite a balancing act though. While you're slogging through a dissertation, I'm trying not to get too caught up in short-term metrics and algorithms of online engagement. I can relate to that. Sometimes I feel like just because something is measurable, it's considered valuable. It can be easy to lose sight of the bigger picture. Exactly. We could go on about this all night, couldn't we? But let's maybe talk about something less heavy.

Oh, I'm so sorry, I didn't mean to wake you. It's just that I thought we would want to discuss our plans for the day before everyone gets up and things get too hectic. Morning! Hmm, ouch, questions before coffee, haha. What do we have planned today? Well, I'm suggesting we all practice our circus skills! Remember Sam mentioned he wanted to try some balancing during the day and Emily mentioned she wanted to try juggling. Circus skills? Can we start after breakfast? I’m not sure I’m ready for that in my pajamas yet. Of course, of course. After a decent breakfast - and maybe a nice hot shower. Hmm, I might even try some Australian phrases after that! You know, how to say "g'day" and "barbie". That would be fun. So, plans are set then. Circus skills and Australian phrases it is. Exactly. And we should definitely fit in some eating time in between. After all, the circus performers at the Neon Moon event last week recommended really focusing on a good diet to maintain energy levels for physical activities. Neon Moon event, you say? Did you see anything in particular that caught your eye, Mum? Yes! There were these fantastic aerial performances and… oh, the fire dancers! It reminded me how mesmerizing it is to see people push their limits in creative ways. We should look up some beginner tutorials online or grab some inspiration from what was showcased there. Fire dancers? Wow, that sounds thrilling yet risky. Is this part of the circus skills plan for us today? Well, today we'll start with simpler things. Like balancing or juggling, as I mentioned earlier. But who knows, maybe in the future we could set up a homemade fire-safe structure to try some twirling batons or something similar. For now, though, let's aim for the safer options, and still be very careful. I've always wanted to try those! We’ll make sure to start with basics and use safe practice surfaces. Now, shall we get moving and enjoy that breakfast? Brilliant idea, I could do with some breakfast. Me too! And then, maybe after breakfast, can we make some sandwiches or something for a picnic? If we have enough time and the weather’s good, we could practice at the park. That’s a great idea! If it doesn’t rain, that sounds lovely.

Ah, I'm losing patience. I don't think our politicians ever have enough time today to address these pressing social issues. It feels like everything they do is just a band-aid rather than proper solutions. I know what you mean. Especially now, the immigration debate seems to overshadow every other topic. But it’s so complex; and often, the loudest voices are those of the media and the extremes. It makes real discussion and useful policy-making almost impossible. Yeah, and social media doesn’t help either. So much is opinion rather than facts. It seems like many politicians are just playing to these platforms, rather than really engaging with the issues. Exactly, that’s why I sometimes wish for more of a journalist-led approach to news. They're the ones who can actually delve into details, investigate, and present a balanced view, rather than chasing clicks and sensationalism. Perhaps that’s where education comes in. If everyone understood how policy-making worked, the media, and even politicians themselves, would be held to account more effectively. I’ve never really understood much about it myself. I just know this is a topic that always seems to come up at home. Politics often is family dinner conversation for us, I think because it's part of my job. But it's fascinating seeing how different people approach the same issues, often based on where they're from or what they do. Family history always seems to play a role too. Doesn’t yours in Wales have a really strong tradition of community and education-focused politics? I mean, you've got the "Radicals of Merthyr" doesn’t come from nowhere. Oh, that’s so true! It’s this strong sense of social justice, which has been passed down through generations. We talk about those who were involved in early trade unions and workers' rights, and of course, the Chartist movement. It's amazing to think about how much that history shapes our values today. Really? That’s great! I’ve always struggled to connect historical events with our current situation. History does repeat itself often in ways that teach us valuable lessons. For example, look at the current push for devolution throughout the UK. It’s not unlike the calls for greater Welsh autonomy that were growing decades ago. Or even the immigration debate has almost identical tones to the tensions over Irish and Scottish migration in the past.

Hey everyone, gather round for a story time! I've been thinking about these character profiles we've been creating. How about we mix and match some traits from our Helen Moss-inspired characters and create something entirely new? Maybe we could even set the story here in Comberton and tie it into this year’s Linton Book Festival questions. Like the story where Maud the magpie solves a ghost mystery at King's College right here? And maybe her sidekick, Sam, is from Norwich? And we even get to solve backwards spells alongside a puzzle trail at the Book Festival? Oh, that sounds amazing! But since we set it here, maybe we could include our very own kitchen as part of the mystery? Like, Sam discovers a clue in the pasta cupboard or something! That’s brilliant! Yes, let's definitely weave the setting and Book Festival into it. So, what kind of clues would we want in the story? And should we pair our characters with trusted local animals or magical beings? I think a trusty companion animal could be really cool! Maybe a hedgehog for Maud or a fox for Sam? And maybe the hedgehog could have ears that can hear ghosts or the fox could make transformations happen? Well, then how about we make a list of the most important clues and character traits right now, so we can build a cohesive story? For example, maybe Maud has a key from the festival that opens a hidden part of the college? Okay, where should we start? Let's make a quick mind map here in the kitchen. We'll have the Book Festival theme, a few clues, and character traits right in the centre. We can branch out from there. There! That’s our story map. Now let’s add clues like a lost festival badge, a mysterious book in the college library, and a hidden room in some old cottage around here. And maybe a special chant to make the transformations happen for the fox? Again, brilliant suggestions. Alright, let's write them in. Now, for character traits... We could say Maud is clever and brave, but also has a bit of a mischievous streak. And Sam could be more cautious, thinking things through, but with a hidden talent for magic? And while they’re solving the mystery, maybe they meet a local expert at the festival?

Who knew I'd spend my Monday evening debating the ethics of meat. Grace, you're nearly a vegan, aren't you? Yet, I've been reading about this new 'shmeat' thing that's been developed. What do you think about that? Hmm, shmeat questions are always interesting. I don’t think I could be a full vegan, but I've cut down my meat consumption a lot. I'm intrigued by shmeat, though I'd need to know more before I'd try it. For one, is it really better for the environment than regular farming? And what about animal cruelty, is it eliminated entirely in its production? [laughs] I’m here for the debate. Sentient meat just sounds like a line from a sci-fi novel. But genuinely, if it can taste similar to meat - which we all know well - and doesn’t have the environmental or ethical impact of traditional farming, why not? [chopping vegetables] While we're on the topic of ethics, do you take vitamin tablets? I saw a study that suggests for most people, they're a waste or even detrimental. Unless you have a deficiency. I used to take them but stopped about a year ago when I realised I was just peeing them out. I try to get all my vitamins from the food I eat. But if I'm totally honest, sometimes [giggles] it can be quite hard to keep track, especially if you have a busy lifestyle. I still take them occasionally, depends on my diet and mood. But you're right, we should focus on getting them from real food and only supplement where needed. I mean, doesn’t real food taste better anyway? [nods] Very true. And that kind of aligns with what you're saying about meat. If we could get all our protein needs from plant sources that were mass-produced with minimal environmental impact, ethically harvested... [interrupts] But Harvesting? Plant or animal, there's always an impact, right? While I agree with changing the way we produce food, especially to reduce animal cruelty, I also don’t think we can ignore that there’s impact with any form of mass farming or harvesting. Absolutely. It’s about making better choices, for sure. Maybe for some of us that means becoming vegetarian or vegan and for others, supporting sustainable agriculture and farming practices. I've had these debates with people and sometimes I wonder, isn’t there a certain level of hypocrisy in turning up our noses at cows being bred for meat but then driving cars that pollute the air?

Right, I'm going to make sure to switch on the washing machine during dinner so it's all ready for when we're done eating and chatting. I don't know about you guys but the thought of a clean load waiting for us to hang out really does make me feel like we can relax properly after a long day – do you find that too? Oh absolutely! But have you tried the new eco mode on our washing machine? It's supposed to be pretty good, actually. Now, speaking of cleaning, did you hear that Sarah and Jon are moving out of their current flat due to a whole bunch of damp and mold? Yes, I did! They're actually deciding whether to just rent a new place or have a big clear-out of all their stuff to reduce down to the essentials, as they’re planning to move in less than a month. That does sound quite stressful. Sarah's always seemed to enjoy having a bit more stuff around though. Yeah, it’s quite the challenge when it comes to throwing things away. I couldn’t believe the amount of stuff my mum had stored away in her attic! It was like a whole new era of this house opened up and it reminded me of when we found Grandma’s old letters in the attic during our last family get-together. Ooh, that must have been so interesting to read! Letters can tell you such a lot about someone’s life. It’s like a direct line into the past. A bit like those old videos we found from New Year’s in 2010. Did you guys see the one where I was trying on everyone’s party hats and ended up wearing like five at once? Oh my goodness, yes! And then you danced on the table and... . We should pull those out again for New Year’s this year. Definitely. Speaking of which, have you decided yet what to do this year? It’s going to be quite subdued globally and all, but we should make a plan for something fun. Well, I was thinking of suggesting a family quiz night. We can make sure to include questions about TV shows and food just to make it relatable and fun. And maybe we can all make a dish we’ve tried recently that we really enjoyed.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all come together tonight. It feels like ages. How has your week been, Alex and Ben? : It's been great. We’ve got quite a bit to talk about. : Yeah, just so many things popping up in class. That sounds like a lot. I’ve been pretty busy myself, actually. We've got this incredible event coming up at work. It’s a bit out of character, given what we normally do, but it’s going to be fun to see the outcome. Out of character, how? Well, we’re planning a two-minute silence to mark an important anniversary. Everyone’s reactions are going to be interesting. What anniversary? And why a silence? It’s for a historical event—something tragic that happened years ago. It’s an unusual way to mark it, but we want to show respect. It will involve a lot of contemplation and discussion. That does sound different. I’m more used to events that are more... celebratory. But I can see how this would be meaningful. Yeah, it will. It’s about learning from the past and hopefully avoiding similar things in the future. It’s become quite a bit of work, though. We’re also arranging a nice lunch afterward, so it’s not all somber. I see. What about for your birthday? I'm pretty sure Mum said you were overdue for a proper celebration. Well, I guess the two-minute silence might satisfy the 'silent celebration' part of my birthday! No, the truth is, we tend to celebrate more quietly together as a family these days, less of the big parties. If you think about it, quiet can be quite nice. Allows us to truly appreciate the company and what’s being said. Indeed. It’s often in the quiet moments that I reflect on how things are really going. Speaking of quiet, when I was in London, I went to this exhibit on butterflies. They had some of these tiny forks that they called 'butterfly forks'. They were so... delicate and pretty. Butterfly forks?! That sounds like a fancy name for a regular dinner fork. I can imagine though. I went to the Natural History Museum in London last year. They have this massive specimen room with... I think I saw some butterfly specimens there. But butterfly forks, that sounds like a marketing gimick.

Alright everyone, let's talk about our holidays first. We've got some options today. The sun is shinning and I think we should try out a beach trip this year. We can escape all of this exam marking somehow. A beach trip, yay! Can we go to Cornwall? That's so much fun! Yeah! But last summer was too windy and cold. And, can we go to Adventure Island this time too? Adventure Island? That depends. It can be quite pricey and given our tight budget at the moment due to all my training sessions, I'm not sure. But it's fun, dear! I can have fun just watching you two play. And we can go to the beach first. You're right, little one. Cornwall has some wonderful beaches. And perhaps we can squeeze in a visit to V&A's William Morris exhibition, I heard it's going to be here in London soon. Cool! But let's make sure it doesn't clash with exam week. We also have to make sure that everyone is comfortable with the food. Mom's got a new food intolerance this year, remember? Yes, I remember. I’ve been diligently checking labels on everything we bring while shopping. But Cornwall has some great family-friendly restaurants that are quite accommodating to dietary needs. And can we have fish and chips at the beach? I'd say that's a no, little one. It'd be a waste of a good meal if it ends up being too cold for sitting and enjoying it. And we also need to keep in mind that Mum might not be able to eat all the usual beach food. Then maybe we could end the day with fish and chips in town or something? That could work. More importantly, do any of you remember what was wrong with the food last year so we can avoid a repeat? Oh, last year we were allergic to something in the picnic and it got uncomfortable pretty fast. Right, so no sharing food this year. Let's also check with all the restaurants beforehand to avoid any mishaps. And can we go for a second day trip? Like to the Eden Project maybe? The Eden Project is a great idea and it’s very accessible. It’s something almost all of us can enjoy regardless of the weather. I’ll look into making those arrangements once we finalise the dates.

Hey, I'm losing my mind with all this coursework. We have these mock exams coming up and I barely have time to breathe let alone complete everything. Oh, for sure! I'm in the same boat. I was up until almost 3 last night trying to get this drama essay completed. Mrs. Jenkins is kind of scary about this subject and I feel like my future depends on this essay. I wish I could sleep as well as you, man. Last night, I was up until 1 am and I still got very little done. I'm just worried I'll fail and have to repeat this year. Naw, you won't fail. What's more, I heard Mrs. Jenkins is actually pretty chill about this. She just says it to make us take it seriously. My brother was in her class last year and he said she's actually very supportive as long as you show you're trying. That makes me feel a bit better. But man, speaking of creative classes, Mr. Brown's been a little... off this quarter. I barely get useful feedback and it's so frustrating. I know, right? Like, last Tuesday, he just spent the whole lesson rambling about how he wishes he was young again and the school system has ruined fun in learning. I mean, sure, we need some fun in learning but he's our teacher, not a motivational speaker. Haha, exactly! Anyway, did you hear about the upcoming party next weekend? A few friends are throwing it at Adam's place. It could be a good way to unwind from all this stress. Haven't you heard? It's going to be awesome! They're planning a movie marathon and a barbecue in the garden. The only issue is, I've got to check with Mum if I can go. She's really strict about these things because of my allergies. But I just tried to explain that Adam's parents are really considerate about food allergies and they'll make sure it's safe. Yeah, maybe you can ask Adam to help you make the case. You know how his parents are always super organised. Plus, party food is usually pretty basic and easy to avoid if you need to. Right. Also, have you seen the latest Hunger Games movie? My sister was saying it's a must-watch.

Alright, so I've decided I need a new bike. I have been doing a bit of research online but it's all getting a bit confusing. Do you know much about this? Maybe you could give me some advice. Of course, I'd be happy to help! But let's start questions. What kind of riding are you thinking of doing? Street, mountain, commuting...? Hmm, I guess commuting and maybe some casual riding on weekends. Not really into mountain biking or anything too hardcore. That's a good start. So, you'll need something comfortable, reliable, and probably a hybrid bike. They're great for general riding. Hybrid? What does that mean exactly? So, hybrid bikes are basically a mix of road bikes and mountain bikes. They're designed to handle well on paved roads but still have some of the features you need for mild off-road or rougher city riding. They tend to be comfortable and user-friendly, which is great if you're not doing intensive bike training. That sounds like exactly what I need! Okay, so what should I look out for when shopping for one? A few things. First, the frame material. If you’re on a budget, you can’t go wrong with aluminium. It’s light, strong, and reasonably priced. If you’re willing to spend a bit more, carbon or high-quality steel can offer better performance and durability. Then, you want to look at the gears. How many speeds do you think you’ll need? I don’t really know. I guess more is better? Not necessarily. If you’re just riding on the flat and not climbing much, you might not need 20 or 27 speeds. Six or seven should be more than enough. On the other side of that, if you plan to ride hilly areas, having more gears will be really useful. You just want to make sure the gear ratios are right for the kind of riding you do. That makes sense. I guess changing the gears and learning how to use them would also be something I’d need to think about. Absolutely. But most of the time, it’s pretty simple once you get used to it. And finally, components like brakes and suspension are important to consider. Hydraulic disc brakes are great because they work well in wet weather and almost all of them are just as powerful as mechanical ones.

Hey everyone, did you know that Chinese takeout was actually introduced to the UK back in the early 20th century? It was such a hit when it first came out that it helped shape British food habits. Is that right? I never knew that. That's interesting. Speaking of which, what questions are we going to ask today? Well, I'm still getting used to the menu, to be honest. I'm pretty sure I can order rice, noodles, and vegetables, but I'm not sure about the sauces and meats. You'll need to know some basic ingredients. For example, Szechuan dishes are quite spicy because they often include Sichuan peppercorns. And then there's hoisin sauce, it's sweet and makes everything taste like roast pork even if it isn't. Ah yes, that's what I was thinking. I've heard you can't go wrong with a Szechuan dish, as long as you can handle the heat. Exactly! But what about something like black bean sauce? I'm not sure what that's like or even if it's vegetarian. Black bean sauce is actually very common and usually vegetarian. It's a fermented bean paste, but it doesn't have meat typically. You'll find it in dishes like okonomiyaki or its popular mixture with tofu. Okonomiyaki? That sounds interesting. But isn't that more of a Japanese dish? Good catch! You're right, it is more typically Japanese, but the sauce component is a part of fusion food and some Chinese places also use it. Okay, it seems like there's a lot to learn. Do you have any recommendations on what we should start with? We're just planning a casual dinner at home. For beginner orders, I'd suggest General Tso's Chicken or Kung Pao Chicken since they're popular and relatively straightforward. Both are sweet and salty but are quite different in terms of spiciness and ingredients. You know what? We could try both. Like a sort of comparison dinner. Or does anyone have a different pick? I like that idea. Actually, what about something truly authentic? Maybe dishes from the regions closer to England? For authenticity and proximity, you could go with Cantonese-style dishes. They're often less spicy and more universally familiar. Sweet and Sour Pork, for example, or perhaps a humble noodle soup? I can't think of a better plan.

Ah, I had a fascinating day yesterday at work, Alan's seminar on regional dialects today really got me thinking about my own accent. Ah, that must have been really interesting. You know I still can't quite shake off that occasional Scouse now and then! Ha! It's just so ingrained. Speaking of accents though, have you heard the latest on the NHS? It's a bit dire from what I'm hearing. Oh yes, very dire. The lack of funding is really coming to a head, isn't it? Exactly. I had to deal with a student who wrote an essay on the subject today. It's really disheartening. It's not just about the funding though, the issue of staffing is huge too - and we're seeing it everywhere. Even on your own street, I heard you have problems with the neighbour's kids at times, right? Yes, there have been issues with that. But you know, it's often a symptom of deeper social issues - like their housing situation or lack of youth services. For me, it's often about trying to connect with them, showing interest, even if it's just the smallest thing. That's true. I've found in my job as a nurse practitioner, that sometimes the smallest bit of human connection can make a big difference. And yet, it's so under prioritised in policy, isn't it? Absolutely. It seems as though all the focus is on quick fixes rather than genuine community building. And yet, that's where a lot of problems likely originate and can be resolved. There was an article I read recently about Finland, their whole approach to healthcare and education is so different. Ah, yes! They’re a fascinating example, aren’t they? Their focus on comprehensive public services and societal well-being really does seem to lead to better outcomes for everyone. From what I know, they actually view the health and well-being of citizens holistically. Not just through the lens of illness, but also mental health support for kids, education, housing. Exactly. It's a different concept of how public services should work altogether. And it seems to lead to such high satisfaction rates and health outcomes. Yeah, and just in terms of care for the elderly or vulnerable people, it's exemplary. Do you think that could ever work here though? It’s not so much whether it would work or not – it's about the political will to make such large-scale changes.

Ah, good day, John. I hope you've been keeping well. I brought some biscuits from the bakery down the road. Hopefully they don't taste too much like chicken feed, but I thought you might be tired of eating out of cans. Ah, Alan, you're always kind. I don’t mind a bit of chicken feed, as long as it's part of a proper meal that makes you feel welcome. Now, why don't you come on in, sit down, and tell me what's up in the wide world outside my little corner. You look like you've got something on your mind, and I'm all ears. Indeed, John. I’ve been following the news about welfare cuts. It just seems like there is an endless cycle of ensuring people barely scrape by, but without real solutions to get people back on their feet. Well, you're right about that. I've met so many fine people around here who want to work but barely get the chance. And these police actions on the streets... it's like they don't understand their own community any more. Absolutely. I mean, it's not just about being able to work; it's about being treated with dignity and respect too. And while the news covers so many issues, the media often misses the daily struggles and stories of everyday folk like you and me. You know, I've lived through so many different times and governments, but somehow, things never seem to really change, do they? Except maybe for the immigrants that come in now. They seem to work hard and do well for themselves... and yet the locals are often left to struggle. That’s a complex issue, John. Immigration... the way it’s talked about in the media and in politics can be quite nasty, can’t it? It’s as if forgetting our own country's history of migration and contribution. But at the end of the day, it's about equal opportunities, and we should strive to make sure everyone has access to work, education, and health care. Equality – I wish there was more of that in this city. I often think about my family when I hear about these issues. All of them worked hard for every penny they ever had. It's not right that so many young people today see no path ahead.

Right, I'm starving. I'm so glad we decided to have lunch here today. The sun is lovely and it's always a treat to come to the Printing House. Absolutely. It's one of my favorite places. I've just got the new book from the presses – do you want to see it? It's got some fascinating new research on regional dialects. Oh, that sounds interesting! I've always found language variation so intriguing. Do you think it's something we could use in our work here? I think it could be quite valuable. There's always a market for accurate, localized educational material. It's not always easy to find, though. I agree. As someone who works in ELT research, I know firsthand how much our learners appreciate language content tailored to their specific context. I suppose that's true from a publishing point of view too. Localization makes a product more relatable and, as a result, more appealing to readers. Exactly! And these days, it's not just about regional accents – it's also about regional vocabularies, grammar, and even cultural references. We really need to keep our ears to the ground. I find the differences between the North and South quite fascinating, while the East and West can be so distinct too. Absolutely! And the level of variation within each region can be huge. It's amazing how specific to certain towns or cities dialect features can be, especially in England. For example, if you're from Sunderland, the use of "I might never do that" to mean "I'll definitely do it" might come across as odd to someone from London. Oh, yeah! People from outside the North would probably find it confusing. I've dealt with a few instances of that in my role as a corpus administrator. It's funny, but sometimes it feels like it's a completely different language. It really can be like that. And it's not just limited to the UK – think about the variations within the US, or even within New York City alone! That's so true. I've had to deal with these sorts of challenges often when publishing books on language. The key is finding the right balance between being true to the local dialect and making it understandable to a broader audience. That's the tricky bit. However, it's also an opportunity.

Ah, good morning! How was your week? Same old. You know how it is, balancing research and teaching. But I've been finding it pretty interesting lately. Got some new insights on how students pick up languages differently depending on their age or cultural background. Really? That's fascinating. I kind of feel like the whole process stays pretty constant once you hit a certain age, but I suppose that's a bit naive of me. Oh, I'd agree to an extent. However, my research suggests that context keeps changing as students get older. For instance, early language learners often pick up faster, possibly because they're not lazy like us about using vocabulary apps! Fair point. Though, let me tell you, even trying to get adults to keep up with the nuances of modern slang is a whole different battle. What's been keeping you up recently apart from research? Oh, just your usual stuff - looking for topics on culture and education for an upcoming international conference. It's fascinating how similar our approaches are across countries, but also how different the resources and expectations are. Absolutely. Now that I'm looking more into it for my own study, it's astounding how many different ways there are to teach. You know, I found this great article about using TV shows and the internet to aid English acquisition. Did you come across anything interesting in that line? Well, actually, my colleague was discussing the impact of video materials in language teaching the other day. There's an increasing trend towards using authentic media as teaching materials. One thing that really caught my attention was a study on how learners from different cultural backgrounds respond differently to the same material. For example, humour and cultural references are things we take for granted, but they can be quite culturally specific and sometimes off the mark if not done right. Seems like true enough, especially in this day and age with so much global media consumption. I noticed a lot of my adult students really enjoy learning through familiar TV or movie characters who speak English. It's really engaging and helps to break down cultural barriers a bit too. Definitely. It’s all about making the material relatable. I’ve had some students from non-English speaking cultures who picked up idiomatic expressions or certain expressions of politeness much quicker by watching how native speakers interact on shows like “Friends” or “The Crown”.

Ah, good day everyone! Lovely to see you all's here. I hope today's no too busy for us. I've got a few things to discuss, talked about our little house project and perhaps some arrangements for upcoming family gatherings. Aye now, let's get down to it then! Can questions be asked if things don't make sense? I'm not one for puzzlement when words get too curly! Irma, as long as I can keep up, I'm set for questions. But remember, keeps it simple, dears. We've had our share of complications before! Alright, let's try keep it simple today then, despite our individual complexities. Firstly, I've been considering the garden project. As you know, I've always liked the idea of having a well-planted backyard. What do you all think? Should we go with the raised beds or keep it more... traditional? Granny, that sounds like fun! But couldn't we also make it so it's easier for you and Granddad or even for me to help with? Maybe something more accessible? Oh, I see where you're coming from, lad. An accessible garden for all ages. Good thinking. But let’s make sure we can get to things easily, not just for us but for anyone who comes over. I agree with Aunty. Accessibility is key. And maybe we could also add some really good blooming plants? For the bees, and all that. And maybe even some herbs? Brilliant! I like that idea. Herbs, herbs would be perfect. We could use them in cooking, and if we're planning more family gatherings, we can have them available for fresh use in the kitchen. Plus, the bees are a great idea. If we're going for herbs, can we maybe have a section for mint? I love mint in everything! Mint, eh? Can't go wrong with mint. Let's not forget about lavender. It’s calming, good for soothing tea, and smells divine. Perfect, we've got a plan! Again, keeping it simple yet effective. And accessible... and of course, just for fun and use. I was wondering, can we maybe add a small bench or two? Somewhere to sit and enjoy the garden, especially if it's looking all lovely? Aye, that's a good one too! Maybe under the apple tree? Or maybe one that can be moved around, if anyone needs a bit of shade or a different view?

Ah, I'm so glad we could take this walk together. It's been ages. Look at these beautiful gardens, aren't they wonderful? Absolutely! I particularly love all the various tea plants. We should probably visit one of the tea plantations up north soon. Definitely on our list! Speaking of lists, isn't it lovely how everything rolls into order when you're out here? You seem to have the most breathtaking calm right now. Oh, yes. I guess it's this combination of fresh air and green scenery. Makes me feel most at home, even though it's a bit different from England. Right, it's just the lushness of it. Even the stone paths have their own character, you know? So different from the UK. Ah, yes - the old world meets the new. Though sometimes I find myself yearning for the familiarity of a London walk. You know, with all the sounds and the hustle and bustle. But this spot? It's similar in charm. And it's funny because it reminds me of the garden behind my grandmother's house. For me, it's the gardens in and around Norwich. My grandmother used to take me to Norwich City's football ground. You wouldn't know it now but the 'City' part has so many beautiful parks around. I've always wanted to visit Norwich. The East Anglia region looks so wonderful in photos, but I imagine even more picturesque in person, especially during spring. Spring is lovely there, yes. Alright, I'm glad you said that 'visiting places' because I've been wanting us to start putting together a photography project from our travels. That's a great idea. We've both been meaning to do more with our photos. Seems like the right kind of together-time, a bit like the project we did on digitalization in education last year? Exactly! It was such a dive deep into something we really cared about. I love that aspect of collaborating on projects. You know, working together on something we both value. True. I think what really gets me is the way our perspectives complement each other. You always bring out the historical side so eloquently, and I zero in on the current utility of whatever we are looking at. That's almost too accurate. But you know, the real job I love doing is presenting those complementary views to students.

Oh my god, Cassie, did you see Hannah last night's Instagram? She looked absolutely wild; like she was having the time of her life! Oh yeah, unreal! I mean, I love a good night out as much as the next person, but wasn’t she a bit...much? I'm not sure I could keep up with that energy for an entire evening. Haha, absolutely. I'm pretty sure if I went as hard as she did, I'd still be sleeping for the next week! Right?! And then there's @Kyb, seeing his video from the bar. It was hilarious, but at the same time, what's with that pub crawl idea of his? Oh, was he the one planning that? Well, from what I saw earlier - oh we need to talk about this menu! What even is this? It's like they’ve turned into a food truck or something... It's ridiculous! Next time we’re going to bring in our own food, for sure. And their "healthy option" is just a smaller version of a fry-up... Yeah, healthier in size only, I reckon. The rest of the menu though? More adventurous than the entire Stampede festival combined! Well, at least it gives us something to talk about later, right? A university canteen, you'd think they'd pull it together, but... Alright, alright, focus on the positives. Our night was pretty fun, right? Despite us getting a bit carried away at the pub and the lads catching us doing the 'Achy Breaky Heart' on the dance floor... Oh God, that’s a story for the ages. The look on our faces as we realized we weren’t even close to the right tempo... I sworn we should’ve just stopped changing the music and danced to our own beat. True – I mean, some people would pay to see that. Anyway, and then there was that moment when we decided to do a run home... Ah, that was funny! We took off and were halfway down the road before realizing we almost left our phones and all our friends behind... Yeah, plus, the joys of running in heels. Totally worth it though – we finished with a roaring applause from our mates for completing the "Torture Run". True Story. We were also talking about DIY exercise classes – like, a workout that really throws you through a loop.

Ah, I'm so glad we could all meet up like this. It feels like ages since we've done anything together. Yeah, it's great! I have some updates on transcribing. Want to hear? Wait, let’s catch up on family news first. What's the situation with Mary’s visit? Oh, that's right! Grandmother Mary's coming next week. I've actually been quite busy with that. Really? What have you been doing? Well, I've been tidying up, making sure the guest room is ready. But also, I've had to set up her old laptop so she can watch Fifa with her grandson. Ah, Fifa. I heard big news about that - they changed the game's mechanics again. Really? My editor did mention something about that. Yes, it’s quite the debate. Some people love it, but others are very unhappy. It’s like every year, isn't it? Now that you mention it, have you seen the new team lineup for this season? Actually, I was just transcribing an interview about that. Quite interesting. They changed a lot of things. Interesting, but frustrating at times. It feels like they keep changing without considering the players or the community as much as they should. True, but sometimes changes can be for the better. For instance, in my industry, they used to do some planning without considering environmental impact. Now, they're much more mindful. It’s about the progress that change can bring. That makes sense, but if change is poorly managed, the impact can be negative. I just wish, sometimes, that they would ask the people who regularly play. The ones who actually know what works or what doesn't. Exactly! They should take a cue from the oil industry in that aspect. You can't just change everything without considering who it impacts – and that includes both the community and the people playing. True, but accountability is key. If changes aren’t for the better, people should be held responsible. You could say that about more than just games and industries, couldn't you? Oh definitely. In my previous role, if certain changes didn’t work out, we’d regroup, discuss, and then adjust. In transcription, I’ve realized that often, what’s said can be different from what’s meant. Ensuring accuracy and clarity is a bit like that, isn’t it? Yes, and I think that applies to a lot of life, not just Fifa or work.

Right, I'm going to bin strike to bed first, I've got a big day ahead; I've got to set up this BlackBerry phone for Granny. It's her first smartphone, and I've never done this before, so I really need to get it right now, before tomorrow, when she's visiting. Oh, don’t stress too much, Uncle Tom. I remember getting my first phone and it was a bit overwhelming at first, but it’s all quite straightforward once you start. If you need help, I'm here. I remember when phones were just phones, and you knew exactly what you had. I’ve always struggled with all these gadgets, but I trust you, you're a London lad, tech must run in your veins. Oh, big deal, Tom - "London lad" and all. Give it your best shot though. It's great that Granny is branching out into smartphones. Thanks both. It's actually just the setup bit I'm nervous about. Once it's on and set up, I think she'll be fine. But yeah, the whole voice recognition software is a bit daunting. Anyone have any experience with that? Actually, I recently set it up for my dad, and it wasn't so bad. You just make sure the settings are all to her voice, and it should learn quickly. But honestly, technology can be frustrating at times, can’t it? Speaking of frustrating, did you hear about the bin strike? Can you believe they stopped collecting from the 15th? What are we going to do with all this trash? Just great, isn't it? The flat is already messy, and now we're all piling up more stuff. But the council said they're working on it, hopefully it’s sorted by the time Granny gets here. Good point. Speaking of visitors, did we remember to mention to Granny that next door's really insomniac and has the TV on all night? You never know if she’s going to be sensitive to noise… Ah, I hadn’t thought of that. Yeah, and if we're talking about noise, did you manage to find those glasses of mine? I seem to have misplaced them again. Hang on, those you lost downstairs? I think I saw them somewhere in the living room... Oh, thank goodness. I was starting to doubt whether they’d ever turn up again.

Oh, did you see the Premier League today? Manchester United lost to West Ham, what a surprise! I don't know who to root for anymore, all of them are playing badly. Just another day in football – unpredictable as ever. I kind of liked West Ham’s win though. But speaking of surprises, have you been feeling okay out here in Poland? I know you’ve been dealing with the SAD, hope it hasn’t been too bad. Yeah, still adjusting to the lack of daylight. But we’ve been getting along. I’ve been trying to keep busy with some part-time TEFL jobs here and there. It’s been interesting, just a bit trying. You know, preparation for exams can be stressful, even when it’s just language. Totally understand. I remember when I did my PGCE, it was endless prep and marking. But your students must appreciate your English expertise, right? Some of them do, sure. But sometimes I worry a bit too much – that I'm not doing enough, that maybe they won’t be ready for their exams. You’re too hard on yourself. You’ve been doing this for years. Remember that time at the farm up north? That was really nice, working outdoors. It’s a break from technology and teaching – though I love both, I need my breaks sometimes too. Yeah, those were good times. It’s all about balance. But it’s funny you mention farming. Just the other day I was talking to a friend back home and we were talking about how much easier it would be if we could escape to the countryside and work on a farm together. As much as I love the idea of the countryside, I’m not sure I’d want to trade in city coffee for animal chores! But hey, next summer vacation, maybe we can plan something? Definitely, we should plan a trip. Wait, so I just got a message from a friend back home – apparently a niece got accepted into the university she applied for. That’s great news! How old is the niece? She’s 18, just finished school. Very proud of her. It makes me think about all the current students I have, preparing them for their exams and for their future. We have that shared sense of responsibility for our students, don’t we? It’s a big part of our work.

Right, so I'm just so glad to have you lot over. It's been ages since we've all been together. How are things going at work for everyone? Can't complain. You know I love my work, but it can get pretty routine sometimes, though. You three with all your jobs, questions are always coming up and conversations are always interesting. I totally understand. As a production controller, I'm right in the middle of a big project at the moment. It's challenging but rewarding when things run smoothly. That's great. You'll tell me all about it, okay? Definitely. I've been questioning if I should try to move into something like that, even though I suppose it’s quite different from labouring but maybe I need a challenge or change. Well, you never know what you're capable of until you try. Absolutely, and we’re always here to bounce ideas around. That’d be nice, speaking of which, these are amazing! For a labourer this is fancy cooking and it certainly tastes it. Thanks! I kind of assumed we’d cook this evening. Good thing my mum taught me how to make proper Yorkshire pudding. She did? That must have been amazing learning from her. I learned my way around the kitchen, but it's always tricky making new dishes. One thing cooking has taught me, and all of you probably know this too, is patience. I mean, doesn’t cooking feel like slow and meticulous work sometimes? Very true! It's kind of meditative, isn’t it? Now, about dating – has anyone got any exciting news? I just tried this new dating app and it’s so hit or miss. Oh, I’m still trying to navigate the ins and outs of it all. But I did meet someone recently who shared my interest in football, which was a nice change of pace from the usual boring questions. Sounds like we’re all in similar boat. I keep trying different profiles, but zero success lately. We’ll show you the ropes and have you sorted soon. Though, speaking of which, I saw this amazing trench coat in London and I’ve been dying to get my hands on it. It looks so slick. That sounds awesome! I’m just about to invest in some new clothes for work. Dressing for success makes a difference, right?

Hey mate, great to see you again! How was your day? It was alright. Just got back from the library after a deep dive into some linguistic studies. You know how it is. Indeed. Speaking of language, did you catch the piece about the Chinese questions students asked during their visit today? Actually, yes. I was one of the researchers who moderated the session where Chinese students and guests questioned the way language is taught here. And how was that? It was quite enlightening, I think. They had some really sharp observations about how we approach English grammar compared to how they teach Mandarin. It's fascinating to see the different perspectives. Totally. Did you get any feedback about the lesson on the uses of 'will' and 'will have'? Yeah, they were particularly interested in how we use the future tense in English compared to Chinese. They pointed out some overlaps and some areas where English grammar is more nuanced. That's a good point. I sometimes find English grammar really challenging to explain, especially to non-native speakers. Absolutely, it’s a complex system, even if we're native speakers. But I think that's what makes teaching English so rewarding – the need to clarify the nuances of the language. True. Have you seen those Chinese guest speakers carrying around their mobiles? They are always posting to WeChat or something. Almost non-stop, isn't it? It’s really changed the dynamics of life around the world, I think. Even in China, they are always connected. I was talking to a friend from Beijing and the way they use WeChat is almost like our use of WhatsApp, but combined with mobile payment and online shopping. Exactly. It’s just part of their daily life now. I noticed a lot of our Chinese students prefer to use WeChat for communicating with each other as well. And what about teaching TEFL in China? Any plans to go there and teach? I've given it some thought. The experience would be incredible, not only professionally but also personally. I’ve taught in various settings so far, but China would be a whole new world. You know, I met a colleague who taught TEFL in China and he shared this fascinating story about being invited to a Chinese birthday where the whole family and friends gathered, and then they came back with the birthday boy for the second celebration.

Hey, I'm on my way home from work, can I pick you up or should we meet somewhere? Sure, sounds good to me. You wouldn’t happen to have some garlic naan with you? There's a really nice new place around the corner from the office, but I kind of want something familiar right now. Oh, I knew you liked naan. I've got some left over from that takeaway from last night, right here. Now, shall I pick you up? Our place or somewhere else? Are you still at work? If you could pick me up it would be divine, actually. I’ve been stuck in meetings all day and just need to unwind. Yeah, just finishing up something here. You know, as much as I love planning, some of these projects can feel like never-ending tasks. What's been keeping you all tied up in meetings? It's a new client—building management systems. It’s creative work but also highly detailed. I barely had time for lunch today. Oh, that sounds tiring. And I heard you’re also preparing for that guest lecture at the university next month. Is that right? Yes, that’ll be busy but I’m looking forward to it too. I love the research and the teaching. It’s good to feel like I can share my knowledge to benefit others, you know? Absolutely, I know how much you value that. A bit like how I feel about this corpus project. It’s all about making really complex concepts accessible to others. That must be fulfilling and challenging in equal measure. I can imagine how much detail and organization is required. How’s your team doing with the update? They're all doing really well. Some people have the knack for getting into the weeds, which is useful, but I also make sure they remember to come up for air sometimes. It's all about balance. Wise words. I bet you could write a bestseller on work-life balance if you wanted to. Speaking of which, is there anywhere in particular you thought of for dinner tonight? I'm open for suggestions. Funny you should say that. I was thinking maybe that new Indian place you mentioned or perhaps we could try that new Italian place that just opened downtown. Or perhaps you could cook something at home. I haven’t had your cooking in ages.

Right, so I'm over at Annie's tonight for dinner. It's been quite a while since we all last got together. Annie, how've you been keeping? Ah, you know, muddling through. Had a bit of a tough time with seasonal allergies, so I haven't been at my best. But I'm improving, slowly. Yeah, I’ve been pretty stressed with work actually. We've got a pretty big production deal going on and it requires a lot of coordination keeps me busy. But it’s a challenge in a good way. That sounds tough. I’m lucky to not be in such a dynamic role but I can imagine how demanding that must be. Indeed. Speaking of challenges, did anyone else see the news about Lewisham Hospital? There's an invitation to comment on the future of local healthcare provision? Yes, I did. Actually, Ron highlighted it to me when we last met up. Did you grab it? It'd be good to share thoughts on that together next time we catch up. I haven’t seen it. Maybe we should touch base when you’re less busy and go through the details. I think that’s a good idea. Annie, how’s everything over here? You’re looking well; you must be managing the household and your part-time writing very well? ANON: Oh, thank you, Sarah, really well. Just trying to keep the house in order and focus on my novel and some short stories. It’s been quite a balancing act but enjoyable. Speaking of balancing, how’s Helen been doing in her studies? We haven't caught up much since last term started. She’s doing great. She’s actually started volunteering at a local library. She’s enjoying it quite a bit. That’s fantastic to hear! Voluntary work is excellent for gaining experience especially if she’s considering a career in education or something similar. ANON: She's also been helping me out with some of the conference events I’m organizing, which has been a huge help. That’s such an awesome opportunity for her. Again, excellent experience. Yeah, definitely. It’s good to see her getting involved with those kinds of things, even if it’s just helping out with things like setting up rooms. ANON: I just hope she doesn’t get too drawn into the events industry.

Hey, I'm so glad we could catch up without any distractions. Work has been super hectic lately. Did you hear about Sarah from the marketing team? Yeah, I did. You two are still good friends, right? Yeah, we were quite close when we worked on that branding project together. But honestly, she and her partner just got a pretty messy break-up. I'm a bit worried about her. She seemed pretty shaken up at the team meeting this morning. Oh no, that's tough. Breakups can be traumatic. You should probably reach out to her and check in, see if she needs someone to talk to. Remember when we were just starting out and I used to be her confidante about all the dating drama? Maybe she'd still be open to that. That's a great idea. And yeah, I should. She doesn't seem like she's handling it too well. It's also funny because Alex from our office is basically obsessed with dating apps. He's been on a dating streak that's pretty impressive. You'd think it'd make him happy but between what he shares and what I overhear, he's really struggling with commitment. That's interesting, but also kind of sad. I've seen with some of my clients that often this flurry of 'easy' connections just makes the uncertainty worse. Exactly, and apparently he's got a bit of an ego about it too, posting all the dates he's going on as if it's some kind of achievement. It's bizarre. It can be really misguided. I see this with a lot of young people nowadays. They confuse prowess on dating apps with emotional maturity or happiness. It's like they're treating relationships like tasks or status symbols rather than meaningful human connections. That really rings true. I just hope Sarah finds some peace and a bit of stability soon. And maybe Alex will eventually hit a wall with his dating spree and realize what's truly important. Same here. There's also another topic brewing at work - the team dynamics with the new manager. It's been a bit tense since she took over. I'm trying to navigate that professionally but people seem to be confused and a bit nervous about what direction she'll take the project. Oh yeah, I've heard whispers about that.

I recently read an interesting article about the legend of Robin Hood and how it reflects upon the theme of good versus evil. What do you both think about the idea that sometimes good actions can be seen as 'evil' behavior if the rules and norms are broken, even if the intention behind them is good? Ooh, that sounds really complicated! Like, if someone steals money from a rich man to give to poor people, is that good or bad? I think it depends. If it's just for one person to be rich, then maybe it's bad. But if the poor people really need it and it makes things fairer, then maybe it’s good even if it was 'evil' to do it. That's a wonderful way to frame it! It shows that good and evil aren't always as clear-cut as black and white. It's the context, intentions, and consequences that determine whether we see something as good or evil, isn't it? But how can it be both? Like, if it's stealing, that's supposed to be always bad. Right? Exactly! That’s the interesting part. Rules and laws are made based on the context and the time. Sometimes, the rules don’t fit the situation, or the people who make the rules are themselves being selfish or unfair. Then, someone brave and kind, like Robin Hood, might decide to break those rules to do what they believe is 'good'. That's why legends like Robin Hood are so interesting - they challenge our ideas about what good and evil mean. But let’s not forget about other legends and folk tales where good doesn’t always win. What about the stories where the good hero doesn’t triumph? Ah, yes! That's very true. Think about the ballads like 'Sir Patrick Spens' or 'Thomas the Rhymer'. They often have bittersweet endings or tragic heroes. These stories often capture a sense of tragedy and unfairness - so much so that 'evil' doesn't always get punished and 'good' doesn’t always win. It might be about accepting the circumstances, no matter how bleak, and finding strength or honor in doing what is right despite the outcome. So, those stories aren't saying that evil is good, but that sometimes doing good doesn't mean everything turns out alright? Exactly! It also says that the value of good actions is sometimes in the act itself, not just in the outcome.

Hey everyone, did you hear about Annie's school filming trip? They have to make a short movie and are all super excited. Yes, I talked to her about it last night. Ah, I'm so glad we could find a spot here. It's been ages. How's your PhD coming along? I remember you were buried in research deep into this Trump chaos the last time we spoke. Hi there! And it’s so much more than just jobs—it’s the whole community, the social structure that's been disrupted.

Ah, I'm so glad we could take a break from everything. Took your parents up on their kind offer and decided to come and visit. Thought it'd be nice to just... talk, you know? You've been working on some fascinating stuff at your place. Any updates? Yeah, absolutely. Both students and projects have been keeping me on my toes. But it’s been rewarding. I recently had a student who was creating an art project about endangered species and the role of media representation in raising awareness. The idea that a certain type of representation can both raise awareness and perpetuate harm...it's really complex. Exactly! It’s so often assumed changing the representation will solve the problem, but we also need to address the underlying societal issues that lead to that representation in the first place. Absolutely. I always take my students back to Blue Peter badges for a laugh...remember them? It's a funny anecdote, but it still sticks.

Ah, I'm losing my touch with modern technology, can someone explain how these 'self-checkout' machines work? You just walk up, scan your items, and then pay? No more proper human interaction. Ah, I'm so glad we could find some time to chat about your latest project today. I've heard you were working on analyzing academic literacy in university lectures, right? That sounds fascinating. What led you to focus on that area? Yeah, it's something that's been on my mind for a while. You see, when I worked in recruitment before moving into academia, I noticed that companies often look at how articulate and well-written employees are, and this can of course influence hiring decisions. I started wondering how influential academic literacy is for us as lecturers, how it impacts students' performance and future opportunities. Oh, that makes perfect sense! Even back in my own student days at St. Andrews, I remember some of our tutors emphasizing how important writing was, not just for English or history, but across all subjects. And in my role as a teacher now, I've definitely seen students struggle with written assignments purely because of a lack of understanding of academic language, tone, and structure. Exactly! So in my project, I've been looking at whether our current courses are doing enough to support students' development of academic literacy. I've been reading some interesting research that suggests academic literacy is actually a more complex set of skills than we might assume — it's not just about grammar or vocabulary, but also about argumentation, summarization, and so on. I see. That certainly resonates with my experiences. One of the key challenges we face is how to integrate these skills into the curriculum without overwhelming students, especially those who might not see themselves as strong writers or who lack practice in academic writing contexts. I'm finding that it's not necessarily that our courses don't cover it, but perhaps it's not being contextualized properly. Many of our students might not see the relevance or need to develop these skills, thinking they're just 'common sense' or something that only literature or commerce courses worry about. But research shows that students who are more aware of academic literacy tend to perform better across all subjects, not just explicitly 'literacy-focused' ones. Absolutely! And I think part of the challenge also lies in assessment — are we making clear to students how academic literacy is being evaluated, and more importantly, how it will benefit them after graduation. For example, in my own subject area, I've started including more explicit 'writing for purpose' tasks that are career-focused, to make the relevance clearer for students.
